0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of the incarnation, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things — belief and life. Not mere assent to facts, but faith in a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The eighth and final sign is the resurrection itself, which the prologue has been anticipating from its first verse.

The seven "I AM" statements are the theological spine of the Gospel. Each one appropriates the divine name revealed at the burning bush (Exod 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM") and fills it with the content of Jesus' saving work: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. These are not metaphors about a human teacher but divine self-disclosures of the Son of God. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him — they know exactly what he is claiming.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 14–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is the most sacred text in Scripture. John's Gospel ends not with a commission but with a question: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John's Gospel opens not with a manger or a genealogy but with eternity. 'In the beginning was the Word' — the echo of Genesis 1:1 is deliberate and staggering: the one who spoke creation into existence is himself uncreated, personally distinct from God yet fully God. The Prologue is the theological key to the entire Gospel: every miracle, every discourse, every confrontation is the story of the eternal Word living among his own creation. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him — but to all who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God. The incarnation is both the most glorious and the most rejected event in human history.

The poem does not stay in eternity. Twice it is interrupted by a man with a name and a date — There was a man sent from God, whose name was John (vv. 6-8, 15) — and the interruption is deliberate: this Gospel will not let the eternal Word float free of history. The Baptist is not the light. He is the witness, and the entire worth of his work depends on the difference being kept.

Between those interruptions the Prologue tracks how the light was received, and it goes downhill before it turns. The light shines in the darkness and the darkness has not overcome it (v. 5) — a present-tense verb for the shining, and a settled past tense for the failure to put it out. The true light was coming into the world and falls on everyone (v. 9). He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him (v. 10). Only then the turn: those who received him were given the right to become children of God, born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (v. 13) — three doors shut before the one is opened.

And it ends higher than it began. From his fullness we have all received grace upon grace (v. 16), one grace succeeding another rather than a fixed allowance running down. Then the landing the whole passage has been climbing toward: no one has ever seen God, and the only Son, who is at the Father's side, has made him known (v. 18). The verb behind that phrase is the one our word exegesis comes from, and in the Greek it has no object at all. He did not bring the explanation. He is it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word (Logos) is not an abstract philosophical principle but the personal Son of God through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. John's Christology is the highest in the New Testament: Jesus is fully God, co-eternal with the Father, the agent of creation, the source of life. The incarnation does not diminish his deity — 'the Word became flesh' while remaining the Word. Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ; the law came through Moses. The contrast is not abolition but fulfillment: the law pointed to the one in whom grace and truth are personally embodied.

Verse 2 is a safeguard rather than a repetition. Having said the Word was God, John at once restores the distinction — He was in the beginning with God — so that the identification cannot swallow the persons. The Prologue's architecture is carried by its verbs: the Word simply was, while everything created came to be, and in verse 14 that second verb is used of the Word himself. He never became God; he became flesh.

The new birth of verse 13 is stated in three negatives before its single positive: not by descent, not by natural desire, not by the decision of any human head of a house — and therefore not by anything a person can inherit, produce or decide. Sonship is conferred, not achieved. The right of verse 12 is exousia, a granted legal standing, and the word used of believers throughout this Gospel is children, never Son, which is reserved for Jesus alone — a distinction that protects the uniqueness of Christ and enlarges rather than reduces the gift.

Grace and truth in verses 14 and 17 is the covenant pair God proclaimed over Moses at Sinai (Exod. 34:6), which is why verse 17 must not be read as setting Moses against Christ — a reading Jesus himself forbids at 5:46. Moses was shown the glory from behind and told to write it down; the Prologue claims that the same grace and truth have now arrived in person. And verse 18 closes the door natural religion keeps trying: God has never been seen as he is, and the only one who has never left his side has come out and told us — the telling being a life rather than a lecture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Calvin writes that the Prologue is the key that opens the entire Gospel: whoever grasps who Jesus is before reading a single miracle will interpret everything correctly. Sproul observes that 'the Word was God' (not 'a god') is one of the clearest affirmations of Christ's full deity in all of Scripture. Keller notes that the Logos concept would have resonated with both Jewish (the creative Word of God) and Greek (the rational principle of the universe) audiences — John is announcing that the one both traditions were groping toward has arrived in person.

Calvin's emphasis on the darkness has not overcome it is the one a reader in a dark season needs: the light has never yet been extinguished, however far it has been reduced — and the church's own history is the evidence, since it has been down to a very few candles more than once and has never gone out. The verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated; it says the dark did not put the light out, and the shining verb is in the present tense while the failure to overcome is in the past.

The pastoral force of the three denials in verse 13 is usually missed. Because nothing whatever in the new birth was contributed by the one being born, there is nothing in it he can later fail to keep up — which is the answer to the Christian who cannot locate a moment of conversion and has concluded it never happened. No one remembers being born; the evidence of a birth is not a memory but a pulse. John gives the tests himself in his first letter, where believing the Son is the present-tense proof of a birth already completed in the past (1 Jn. 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the beginning was the Word' — not 'came to be' but 'was.' Before the beginning existed, the Word already existed. There was never a moment when the Word was not. 'With God' — the preposition suggests face-to-face personal relationship, distinction of persons within the Godhead. 'The Word was God' — not a god, not divine in a lesser sense, but fully and essentially God. The Trinity is not yet named but is already present: two persons in eternal communion, both fully God.

That phrase 'not a god' is worth more than an assertion, because a reader may well have had it disputed on his own doorstep. The Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation renders the last clause 'the Word was a god,' and the argument offered is that the Greek here has no definite article before 'God' in that final phrase, though it does in the phrase before it. The observation about the article is perfectly correct. The conclusion drawn from it is not.

In Greek, a noun standing before the verb in this construction regularly drops the article and tells you what something is by nature — not which individual it is. John is doing something very precise, and English cannot quite carry it. He needs to say two things at once and not let either swallow the other: the Word is not the same person as the Father (so, 'the Word was with God'), and the Word is nonetheless everything the Father is (so, 'the Word was God'). Had he added the article to that last clause he would have collapsed the two persons into one and denied the distinction he had just made. Had he meant 'a god' he would have written a sentence no Jew could utter, since a second and lesser deity is precisely what Israel's whole faith existed to deny.

And the very next verse closes the door. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. Whatever exists that is not God was made through the Word — so the Word cannot be among the things that were made. There is no room left for a created, junior deity. He stands on the Creator's side of the line, which is the only line the Bible ultimately draws.

Step back from the argument for a moment and ask the plainer question. Why the Word? Of all the titles available to him — Son, Lord, Christ, King — why open a Gospel with a noun that sounds like a piece of grammar?

Because a word is the thing that comes out of a person and tells you what is inside him. You can watch a man for a year and learn very little. He says one sentence and you know something about him you could never have worked out by looking. God is not visible. But God has an eternal Word — not a sound he makes, but a Person he is — and that Person has now walked into a room and spoken to people who could hear him.

The title also lands in two directions at once, and John knows it. A Jewish reader hears Genesis: And God said, Let there be light — a world that exists because God spoke. He hears the prophets, where the word of the LORD came to a man and rearranged his life, and Isaiah's promise that God's word does not come back to him empty but does the thing it was sent to do (Isa. 55:11). A Greek reader hears logos, the reason and order holding the universe together, the thing his philosophers had been reaching for and never quite touched. John takes the noun both of them were straining after and does something neither expected with it. He does not say the Word is a principle. He says the Word had a face, and we ate with him.

Now read the Prologue watching one thing only, and the whole passage opens up: watch the verbs. In these two verses the Word simply was — four times, in a tense that describes a state running back with no starting point in view. From verse 3 onward the verb for everything else changes. All things came to be. There came to be a man sent from God, whose name was John (v. 6). Everything that is not God is spoken of with the verb of beginning. And then in verse 14 that second verb is finally used of the Word himself — the Word became flesh. He never became God. He became man. That single switch of verbs is the architecture of the entire passage, and it carries more weight than any adjective could.

Which leaves the question of why verse 2 exists at all, since it appears to add nothing. It is not padding; it is a guard, and it is set exactly where a reader is most likely to fall. The Word was God, standing on its own, could be heard as saying the Word simply is the Father under a second name — and John has just spent a clause denying that. So he goes back and says it once more with the distinction restored: He was in the beginning with God. The face-to-face is repeated after the identification, so that neither one can swallow the other.

What the church would later spend three centuries learning how to say — one God, and the Son is not the Father — is already here in the second sentence, before a single event has been narrated.

It is worth being clear about what the alternative to this sentence actually is. It is not a neutral universe; it is a silent one. If the beginning was matter, then before there was anyone to love there was nothing being loved, and the deepest thing about reality is force — impersonal, uninterested, and very old. Everything warm arrives late and by accident, and will go out. John says the deepest thing about reality is a conversation. Before there was light, before there was time to measure, before there was air to carry a voice, there was a Father and a Son, and they were not sitting in silence.

Here is a test you can run on yourself. Ask what you picture God doing before he made anything. Most of us, pressed, imagine something like waiting — a solitary figure with nothing to occupy him until the world turned up. If that is honestly the God you pray to, then you are praying to someone who needed you, and you will never quite shake the suspicion that you have turned out to be a disappointing return on his loneliness.

The God of this verse was not lonely. He did not make you because he was short of company. He made you out of a fullness that was already complete without you — which means his interest in you is not the strained interest of a man with nothing else to do. It is the interest of a Father who had a Son to love before there was a universe, and who has decided to bring you into it.

Genesis begins at the beginning. John begins before it. Whatever else you do not yet know about God, you may know this much and steady yourself on it: he was never silent. Before anything existed that could hear him, he was speaking — and what he was saying was a Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The comprehensive scope of creation: 'all things' — nothing that exists came into being apart from the Word. This eliminates any eternal matter independent of God; the Word is not one creative force among many but the sole agent through whom the Father creates. 'In him was life' — not derived life but original, self-existent life. This is the life of God himself, not merely biological existence. This life is the light of men — the source of all rational, moral, and spiritual illumination that humanity possesses.

Notice that John says it twice, once forward and once backward: All things were made through him, and then without him was not any thing made that was made. The second clause is not a flourish. It is a fence. State only the positive and someone will go looking for an exception — some corner of reality, some raw material lying about, some dark thing that got in by another route. John closes the gap before anyone can reach for it. There is no back door into existence.

Which means something bracing about the world you woke up in. He made the wood the cross was cut from, and the ore in the ground that became the nails, and the hands that would drive them, and the breath in the lungs of the men swinging the hammers. Nothing was ever used against him that he had not first supplied. That is not a poetic flourish; it is simply what all things means once you follow it into the story this Gospel is about to tell.

(One honest note for anyone comparing translations: the oldest manuscripts carry no punctuation, and some early readers ran the sentence on — without him was not anything made. That which has been made was life in him. Your Bible may carry a footnote to that effect. The difference is real but small: on either reading the Word is the Creator, and on either reading the life is in him. It is a question of where the full stop goes, not of what is being claimed.)

In him was life. The noun is zoe, and it is one of this Gospel's favourite words — you will meet it three dozen times before the end. It does not mean the state of not being dead. Everything alive has life the way a room has light at four in the afternoon: on loan, from elsewhere, and shortly to be withdrawn. John is saying that in the Word life is not on loan. He does not have it. He is it. Every other living thing in the universe is running on something it was handed.

Try the test the apostle Paul once put as a question: what do you have that you did not receive (1 Cor. 4:7)? Not your possessions — your heartbeat, your next breath, the fact that your body has again this morning chosen to work. There is not one item on the list that you arranged. That is either terrifying or it is the most restful fact available to a human being, and which of the two it turns out to be depends entirely on what the giver is like. John has twenty-one chapters to show you.

Say this carefully to the reader who has been sitting with a diagnosis, or watching someone thin out in a bed. The Christian hope at that point is not that life is generally stronger than death — it plainly is not, and pretending otherwise is cruelty dressed up as comfort. It is that there is one place in the universe where life was never borrowed and therefore cannot be called back in, and that this Gospel exists to tell you he has come within reach. He does not offer to extend the loan. He offers himself.

Then the strange bridge: and the life was the light of men. How does life become light? In this Gospel light is never merely information. It is what lets you see where you are and know what you are looking at — and, less comfortably, it is what shows up whatever else is in the room. That is why the very next sentence is about darkness, and why by chapter 8 he will say it outright: I am the light of the world. The thing to hold on to is that the light is not a body of teaching he brought with him. It is the overflow of the life he is. Nobody is illuminated by studying him from across the room. People are illuminated by being near him.

Everything that lives is borrowing. He is where it is borrowed from.

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The darkness has not overcome it' — the Greek word can mean both 'overcome' and 'comprehend.' Both meanings apply: the darkness of fallen humanity has neither extinguished the light nor understood it. But the light shines on, undefeated and uncontained. John the Baptist enters the narrative as a man sent from God — not the light itself but a witness to it. The distinction is crucial: even the greatest human prophet is only a witness, not the source.

It is worth slowing down over that verb, because the ambiguity is not a translator's problem to be tidied away. The Greek is katelaben, and it means to seize, to lay hold of, to take something and have it. It is used of an enemy overtaking a man on the road, and it is used of a mind finally getting hold of an idea. So the King James read it as comprehended and most modern versions read it as overcame, and both are honest translations of the same word.

John almost certainly wants both, and you can prove it from his own book. The darkness in this Gospel does try to put the light out — that is what Good Friday is — and it fails. And the darkness in this Gospel repeatedly fails to understand what it is looking at: a teacher of Israel who cannot follow a sentence about birth (3:10), men told plainly why they cannot hear (8:43), Pharisees asking whether he means them (9:40). Both meanings come true in the narrative. Do not choose between them; the sentence was built to carry the two.

Then look at the tense, because it is the pastoral heart of the verse and it is easy to walk past. Every other verb in the opening lines is in the past — was, came to be, was made. This one is present. The light shines. Not shone; not will shine. It is the only present-tense verb in the whole passage, and John slips it in at the exact point where the darkness enters. Whatever else has finished happening, this has not finished happening. It is going on while you read.

And the second verb is the opposite: a single, settled, finished aorist. The darkness has not overcome it — one decisive non-event. Put the two together and you have the Christian's actual position described with unusual accuracy. The dark is real and present-tense, and so is the light; but only one of them has already had its verdict handed down.

Now the guard, because a sentence this confident sits one step from a cruelty. This verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated. It does not say the light is bright, or warm, or winning by any margin you can see from where you are standing. It says the dark did not put it out.

If you are reading this in a season where God seems to have gone quiet and the light appears to be one candle in a very large room, you are not failing to believe the verse. You are living inside its first clause. The verse does not ask you to feel that the dark is losing. It asks you to notice that the light is still lit, and that this has now been true for a very long time and through much worse than yours.

A test: think of the darkest stretch you have come through. Ask, not whether it felt survivable at the time, but whether the light went out. Almost everyone who has walked with God for any length of time discovers that the honest answer is no — that it thinned, that it was hard to see, and that it was there. That is not a small thing to have found out. It is the verse, confirmed in the only laboratory available to you.

And then, with no warning at all, verse 6. We have been before the beginning; we are now in a wilderness with a man who has a name. John does not ease the transition, and the abruptness is the point. The verb changes, exactly as it does for everything created — there came to be a man. He has a start date. The Word does not.

Notice what has just been claimed by putting these two sentences side by side. The eternal thing has an address. It can be dated, and there are people who can be named in connection with it, and if you had been in the Jordan valley in the late twenties you could have gone and looked. Christianity's strangest claim is not that God is eternal; most religions will grant something like that. It is that the eternal turned up in a particular decade, in a specific stretch of river, and that a man with a job and a diet and a family was sent from God to point at him. Four hundred years of prophetic silence end in that one line, and the first thing God says after four centuries is: look over there.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's entire ministry is defined by what he is not: not the light, not the Christ, not Elijah (he will deny this in v. 21), not the Prophet. He is the witness. The function of witness is to point away from oneself toward the one testified to. The purpose of his witness — 'that all might believe through him' — establishes from the outset that faith is the response the Gospel calls for. All the signs, discourses, and encounters in John's Gospel are designed to produce belief.

The word for witness is martyria, and it is one of the load-bearing beams of this Gospel — it and its relatives turn up nearly fifty times. John is writing something shaped like a trial. There is a claim being made, and a case being assembled, and witnesses called one after another: the Baptist here, then the works Jesus does, then the Father himself, then the Scriptures (5:31-37). The reader is not being addressed as an audience. He is being addressed as a jury, and a verdict is expected.

It is also the word from which we get martyr, and the drift of that word from testimony to death is not an accident of language. It happened because of what testimony repeatedly cost. The man in this verse will lose his head for it before the Gospel is halfway through.

Then a preposition worth staring at: that all might believe through him. Through him. God could have arranged for people to believe by direct broadcast, without an intermediary, and he did not. He appointed a man with a strange diet and a rough manner, standing in a river, and routed faith through him. That is God's ordinary method and it has not changed. Almost certainly you can name the person it came through for you — and almost certainly they were not impressive, and almost certainly they knew it.

Verse 8 then does something blunt that is easy to skim: He was not the light. Why would that need saying? Nobody reading a Gospel is at risk of confusing a desert preacher with the Son of God — except that people were. There were still disciples of John the Baptist decades later and hundreds of miles away; Paul ran into a dozen of them at Ephesus who had received John's baptism and had never so much as heard there was a Holy Spirit (Acts 19:1-7). This flat denial is not a rhetorical flourish. It is a correction being issued to a live movement, by an author who knew it was still going on.

Which is the practical weight of the verse for anyone who serves. John's whole identity here is stated in negatives — not the light, and in a moment not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet. That looks at first like a diminishment. It is the opposite. A witness is not a lesser version of the thing he testifies to; he is a different kind of thing altogether, and the value of his work depends entirely on his not being confused with it. A signpost that people admire and stop at has failed. A signpost that they walk straight past, on their way to where it pointed, has done the whole of its job.

Here is the test, and it is a hard one. Think of someone you have taught, or discipled, or raised. Now imagine them going on to know Christ better than you do, in a church you have no connection with, and rarely thinking of you again. Does that land as joy or as loss? The honest answer is a fairly exact reading of whether you are being a witness to the light or quietly setting up as a small light of your own. John will give his own answer to that test in chapter 3, and it is one of the loveliest sentences in the Bible: He must increase, but I must decrease.

He is not the light. He never once sounds disappointed about it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'The true light' — genuine and original, as opposed to derivative or shadowy. Every human experience of light, beauty, reason, and goodness is a dim reflection of the one who is the source. 'Gives light to everyone' — the general illumination of common grace through which all humans have some knowledge of God and morality. 'The world did not know him' — the great tragic irony: the Creator enters his own creation and is unrecognized by it. Not ignorance but willful non-recognition.

Two things in this verse need handling honestly rather than smoothly, because it is a sentence people fight over.

The first is a matter of grammar, and your Bible may differ from the one in the next pew. The phrase coming into the world can attach to the light — the true light was coming into the world — or it can attach to everyone, which is how the older versions read it: the light that lights every man that comes into the world. The Greek allows both, and the difference is not doctrinally serious. But it is the kind of thing that makes a reader think one of his Bibles is wrong, and it is better to know that this is a question of which word a phrase leans on, not a dispute about what is true.

The second is heavier. Gives light to everyone has been made to carry a great deal — that all people are already savingly enlightened, that every religion is a road up the same mountain, that no one really needs to be told anything. The verb is photizei, and it means to shed light on something as much as it means to switch a light on inside someone. And John himself settles the question in the very next breath, which is why the two verses sit in one entry: the light shone on the world, and the world did not know him. Whatever universal illumination means here, John states plainly, one line later, that it did not by itself produce recognition. The sun rising over a city is not the same thing as the city waking up.

What the verse does secure is real and worth having. There is no human being who is simply outside the reach of this light. Every flicker of conscience, every ache after beauty, every stubborn refusal to believe that cruelty is merely a preference — all of it is light, and it is his, and it is falling on people who have never heard his name. Paul says the same thing in Romans 1 and draws the same conclusion: it is enough light to leave a man without an excuse, and not enough to save him. Which is precisely why somebody has to go and tell him.

Then verse 10, where John says world three times in a single sentence and each time it turns the knife. He was in the world. The world was made through him. The world did not know him. There is no villain named, no plot described; the tragedy is done entirely with a repeated noun.

Isaiah had already found the image for it, and it is more humiliating than anything John could have invented: The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know (Isa. 1:3). An animal in a stall recognises the man who feeds it. A dog knows its owner's step on the path before the door opens. What John is reporting is a failure of recognition beneath the level of an animal's — the creation standing in the presence of the one who specified every atom in it and registering nothing at all.

And notice that this is said before any of the hostility begins. There is no persecution yet, no trial, no cross. The first thing said about the world's response to God arriving in it is not that it fought him. It is that it did not notice.

Now the question a thoughtful reader will actually be carrying, so let us not pretend it is not there: would I have known him? Almost certainly not. That is the plain sense of the verse, and it is meant to land. The people best equipped to recognise him — the ones with the Scriptures, the calendar, the prophecies, the daily sacrifices — are precisely the ones this Gospel will show missing him. If recognising God depended on being religious, well-taught or sincere, the record of the first century is against you.

Which is exactly why the next few verses do not go where you expect. Having established that nobody recognised him, John does not turn round and urge the reader to look harder. He says something else entirely, and it arrives in verse 13: those who did receive him were born of God. Recognition was never going to come from the side of the ones who could not see. It had to be given.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'His own' — Israel, the covenant people prepared through centuries of scripture, prophecy, and promise to receive their Messiah. They did not receive him. But 'all who did receive him' — not a subset of Israel but anyone, Jew or Gentile — receive the right to become children of God. This is adoption: by nature we are not God's children; by grace through faith in Christ we are made so. The receiving and the believing are the same act described from two angles.

The Greek here is sharper than any English version can quite manage, because John changes the gender of a word halfway through the sentence and the whole tragedy is in the change.

He came to his own — that phrase is neuter and plural. His own things. His own property, his own place, his own home. Then his own people did not receive him — and now the word is masculine. His own folk. The household. So the sentence runs: he came home, and the family would not let him in. The verb is the one used for welcoming somebody in off the road and giving them the spare room. He was not turned away at a border by strangers. He was left standing at his own door by people who knew the address because it was theirs too.

And they were not badly prepared. This is the point that stings. They had the Scriptures, the promises, the temple, the calendar, centuries of longing and a national hope built entirely around his arrival. Nobody on earth was better set up to recognise him. The failure did not happen for want of information.

Say a word here to the reader for whom this is not history. Some who follow Christ pay for it at home — a father who stopped speaking, a family who treat the faith as an embarrassment to be managed, a wife who did not sign up for this. If that is you, notice that this verse puts you in company you did not expect. He knows what it is to be the odd one in his own house, and he knows it from further in than you do, because his own people were not merely unsympathetic; they eventually killed him. Whatever it has cost you at home, you are not walking a road he sent you down and never took himself.

Then But, and the sentence turns. Three words in this half-verse deserve to be slowed over.

First, the right. The word is exousia, and it does not mean power or ability. It means authorisation — the standing to do something lawfully, the right recognised by whoever gets to recognise such things. It is a legal word, not a moral one. God does not merely make it possible for people to be his children; he confers the standing, and the standing holds because of who conferred it. That is worth having on a day when you do not feel like anybody's child. Your standing was not issued by your feelings and is not withdrawn by them.

Second, children. John writes tekna, and he is being deliberate, because across this entire Gospel he never once calls a believer huios — son. That noun he reserves, without exception, for Jesus. It looks at first like a demotion and it is exactly the opposite: it is the safeguard that lets the gift be as large as it is. Jesus is Son in a way nobody else will ever be, by eternal right. We are children in a way we never were before, by gift. Both are kept whole, and neither is diluted to make room for the other.

Third, become. Not discover, not realise, not remember. The verse does not say people found out they had been God's children all along. Something happened to them that had not previously happened. There is a real doctrine of the universal fatherhood of God — he made everyone and he sustains everyone and his kindness falls on everyone — but this is not it, and John will not blur them. By creation everyone is his. By this, some are his in a way that requires a birth.

Which is where a careful reader will feel the pressure and ought to. If the right is given to those who receive and believe, has the believing not just become the qualifying act — the one contribution that is finally mine? Verse 13 exists to shut that door, and John shuts it before anyone can get a foot in it. Read on before you decide.

A test, for anyone unsure whether this has happened to them. Ask what word rises first when you think of God — and be honest, because the polite answer is not the true one. Judge. Employer. Landlord, keeping an eye on the state of the property. Distant relative. Or Father. Not whether you can defend the word Father theologically, but which one your stomach reaches for at four in the morning when something has gone wrong. That reflex is telling you something about what you actually believe you have been given, and this verse is what it needs to be corrected by.

And say the plain thing to whoever needs it: if your own father was absent, or frightening, or simply never much interested, you are not disqualified from this verse — you are its natural audience. The word Father is not being defined for you by the man who taught you to flinch at it. It is being defined by the Son who is going to spend twenty chapters showing you what his own Father is like.

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new birth is entirely God's work — not inherited (blood), not chosen by human desire (flesh), not produced by human decision (will of man), but of God. Then the most staggering sentence in the Bible: the Word became flesh. The eternal, uncreated, all-powerful Son of God took on human nature — not pretending, not appearing, but genuinely becoming what he was not while remaining what he was. 'Dwelt among us' — the Greek word is 'tabernacled,' evoking the wilderness tabernacle where God's glory dwelt. He is the new tabernacle, the new meeting place of God and humanity.

Take the two verses one at a time, because between them they carry the weight of the whole Prologue, and each has a reader who needs it for a different reason.

Three denials before the affirmation. John does not simply say the new birth is God's work. He says it three times in the negative first, and each denial closes a specific door that people have actually tried to get in by.

Not of blood — and the Greek is plural, bloods, which sounds odd until you know that in the thought of the time a child was reckoned to come from the mingled blood of both parents. So the first door shut is descent. Not because of who your people were. This is aimed first at anyone leaning on Abraham — an argument Jesus will have to have out at length in chapter 8 — but it lands just as squarely on a Christian family. A godly mother is one of the great mercies of God and it is not a birth certificate. Grace does not travel down a bloodline. Every generation is converted from scratch or not at all.

Nor of the will of the flesh — the second door is natural desire, the whole biological machinery of wanting and conceiving and producing. Nothing in the ordinary equipment of being human generates this.

Nor of the will of man — and here the word is not the general one for a human being but the specific one for a male, a husband, a father. That is deliberate, and in that society it was pointed. The head of the house decided whether a newborn was acknowledged and taken into the family at all; a word from him settled it. John says: not that either. No head of any house can decide you into God's family. Not your father, not a priest, not a minister, not a church membership roll — and, though it is the hardest one for us to hear, not you. The decisive vote is not yours to cast.

Three closed doors and then one open one: but of God. It is the same fence-building John did back in verse 3, where he said all things were made through the Word and then said it again backwards so nobody could hunt for an exception. He is not being repetitive. He is sealing the room.

Now the harder half — the reader who cannot find the moment. There are Christians who read a verse like this and go cold, because the language of being born again makes them go looking for a date, and there is no date. No aisle, no night, no thunderclap. They have believed as far back as they can remember, or the thing crept up on them over years, and they cannot point to the hour. And they conclude, quietly and for a long time, that whatever happened to other people has probably not happened to them.

Read the verse again and notice that it says nothing whatever about your being able to locate it. It tells you who did it. That is the entire content. It is a statement about the agent, not about your memory of the event.

Which is exactly what you would expect, on the analogy John has chosen. Nobody remembers being born. Not one person alive has a recollection of the most decisive physical event of their existence, and nobody treats that as grounds for doubting it happened. You do not establish your birth by memory. You establish it by breathing.

So the evidence is present-tense, and John gives it — not here, but in his first letter, where he wrote for exactly this reader. We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers (1 Jn. 3:14). Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God (1 Jn. 5:1).

Stand on that second sentence for a moment, because the tense in it is the whole answer: the believing is present and the birth is already completed. He does not say believe and you will be born. He says that if you are believing, you have been born — the birth is behind the faith as its cause, not in front of it as its reward. If you are believing today, the event you cannot remember has already happened, whether or not anybody was watching at the time.

Then run the honest test, which is not a memory test at all. Do you find yourself wanting things you did not use to want? Is there sin you once enjoyed that has gone quietly sour on you? Do you pray when nobody would know if you did not? Have you had every reason to walk away from Christ and found that you could not? None of those is a feeling. All of them are a pulse.

And keep the guard on the other side, because this must not be turned into a blanket. The answer to a person with no evidence of any kind is not that they were probably born long ago and simply forgot. It is that this verse tells them where to go and who can do it. If nothing in that list is true of you, the news is not that you should look harder for a memory. It is that God gives births, and that people ask him for them.

And the Word became flesh. Here the verb finally arrives. Through the whole opening the Word simply was, while everything created came to be; and now, for the first time, the verb of beginning is used of him. He never became God. He became this.

Look at which noun John picks. He does not write that the Word became a man, though that is true. He does not write that he took a body. He writes sarx — flesh — which is the crudest, weakest, most mortal word available to him. It is the word for meat. It is the word for what a man is when you consider that he gets tired, gets hungry, gets thirsty, bleeds when cut, and dies.

John, who has spent thirteen verses climbing to the highest claim in the New Testament, sets the two words side by side without a cushion between them: the Word, and flesh. Every heresy about the person of Christ in the next four hundred years is an attempt to soften that collision, and John's own letters show him already fighting it: any spirit that will not confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh is not from God (1 Jn. 4:2).

Make it concrete, because it is meant to be. It means he had to be taught to walk and fell over doing it. It means teeth coming through, and splinters in a carpenter's hands, and sweat, and the particular kind of tiredness where you fall asleep in a boat in a storm. It means that at some point somebody changed God's nappies. If that sentence is uncomfortable, it is doing its work; the whole point is that God did not send a message, or a projection, or an appearance. He arrived in a body that could be hurt.

And dwelt among us — eskenosen, he pitched his tent. This is not a decorative verb. John reaches back to Exodus and expects you to come with him.

Stage it. Israel is in the wilderness with no land, no city, no temple and no address. They build a tent to God's specification, and when it is finished the glory of the LORD comes down and fills it so completely that Moses cannot go in (Exod. 40:34-35). That is where God chose to live: not in a palace, not on a mountain-top out of reach, but in a portable structure of goat hair and dyed skins in the middle of the camp — pitched where they pitched, struck when they struck, moved when they moved. From the outside it was the least impressive dwelling imaginable. Inside it was unbearable with glory.

John is telling you that this happened again, and that this time the tent was a body. The plain, unremarkable exterior that nobody in Nazareth found worth a second look. The glory inside. God once more choosing to camp in the middle of his people rather than to summon them somewhere.

And it is a tent, not a house — which is honest about what the incarnation was. He did not settle. Thirty-odd years is a short pitch. But do not draw the wrong conclusion from the temporariness: the tent came down, and the Gospel ends with him saying he is going to prepare a place, and the Bible ends with the same word coming back one last time — the dwelling place of God is with man, and he will dwell with them (Rev. 21:3). The tent was temporary. The camping among us was not.

We have seen his glory. The verb means to gaze at with your own eyes, to look at something and keep looking. This is an eyewitness sentence, written by an old man who is claiming he was in the room.

But which glory did they see? Here John does something you would not predict. In this Gospel the hour when Jesus says he is glorified is not the mountain of transfiguration, which John never even narrates. It is the cross (12:23; 17:1). The glory these men saw was chiefly a man dying badly in public. Hold on to that when you next find yourself looking for God's glory in whatever is going well; John looked hardest at it in the one place nobody would think to.

Full of grace and truth — and this is the phrase that unlocks the two verses that follow, so do not read past it as a pleasant pair of nouns.

Go back to Sinai. Moses asks the one enormous thing: Please show me your glory. He is told that no man can see God's face and live, and he is put in a cleft of the rock and covered with a hand while God passes by. And what God proclaims as he passes is his own name: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod. 34:6). The last two words in the Hebrew are chesed and emeth — covenant love and covenant faithfulness, mercy and reliability, the two things you most need to be true about anyone you are going to stake your life on.

John writes: we have seen his glory, full of grace and truth. He is quoting Sinai at you. What Moses asked to see, and was given a fraction of, from behind, through a crack in a rock — they watched it eat fish on a beach. That is the claim. And it is why the next verses will not set Moses against Christ but will run straight through him: the glory Moses was shown a piece of is the glory that walked into Galilee whole.

Here is the test, and it is worth answering slowly. When you picture God — not the doctrine, the picture that actually shows up when you pray — what is he like? Most of us are carrying something assembled out of guesswork, temperament, and whatever our own father was like. John's answer to all of it is that you are no longer permitted to guess. God has been seen. He has a face and it has been described by men who were standing near it.

Moses asked to see the glory and was hidden in a rock. John says: we saw it, we heard it, and we ate with it.

Consider what had to be true for that sentence to be written. The Word — who was in the beginning, through whom every atom that exists was spoken into place, who had never in all eternity been anything less than God — became flesh. Not visited it. Not wore it like a coat and took it off again. Became it. He took a body that could be tired, and hungry, and frightened, and killed; and he pitched it in the middle of a camp of people who would not know him; and he did all of it without ceasing for one instant to be what he had always been.

Glory came down into a tent again. This time the tent had a face.

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John the Baptist's testimony inserts itself into the Prologue: the one who comes after me in time existed before me in eternity. The ranking is ontological, not merely chronological. 'From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace' — the image is of the sea overflowing to fill every vessel that approaches it. The Greek suggests wave upon wave of grace, grace replacing grace, an inexhaustible supply flowing from the one who is himself full of grace and truth.

Two things about the way this verse arrives. First, John cannot leave the Baptist out even here — twice now the great poem about the eternal Word has been interrupted by a man with a name and a location. That is not clumsy editing. It is this Gospel refusing, from the first page, to let the Word float free of history. Every time the language lifts off, a witness is put back in the room.

Second, the tense. The verb is in a form that means the cry has been raised and is still standing — he cried out, and the sound of it has not stopped. John the Baptist has been dead for sixty years by the time this Gospel is written, and the testimony is still ringing in it.

Then the riddle itself, which packs three different time-words into one sentence: He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me. Later in arrival. Ahead in rank. Earlier in existence. The middle claim is explained by the third, and the third is the one no one else in Israel could have made.

And here is the detail that gives it its edge, which you only get by reading Luke alongside. John the Baptist was born about six months before Jesus (Lk. 1:26, 36). They were cousins. He was the older man. So what is actually being said here, out loud, in public, is a man pointing at a younger relative he has known about his whole life and saying: he existed before I did. Not he outranks me — anyone can say that of a superior. He was there first. There is no polite way to hear that sentence. It is either the claim of the Prologue or it is madness, and the man saying it has staked his reputation, his following and eventually his head on it.

For from his fullness we have all received. The word is pleroma — the whole contents, everything that is in him, nothing held back in reserve. And the word that governs it all is all. Not the apostles, not the mature, not those who have been at it for thirty years. The oldest saint you know and the person converted last Tuesday are drawing from the same supply, and neither of them is drawing on a smaller tap.

Grace upon grace — and the little preposition underneath it is worth having, because the English can be read as merely quantitative, as if the point were simply that there is a lot. The Greek word normally means instead of, one thing taking the place of another. So the picture is not a heap. It is a succession: grace giving way to grace, each one replaced by the next, the way waves arrive — no wave is the last one, and no wave is the same wave.

Say that to the Christian who has begun to suspect he is running out. Most of us, somewhere in the middle years, quietly start doing arithmetic: I have confessed this same sin so many times now, I have had my share, whatever I was given at the beginning must be getting thin by this point. That is the arithmetic of a fixed quantity, and it is the wrong arithmetic entirely. The grace you are living on this morning is not the grace of your conversion, stretched and rationed and going grey at the edges. It is a new one. The old one did its work and was replaced, and this is what has been happening every day since, whether or not you noticed a single one of them.

Keep the guard on it, because grace that keeps arriving can be misheard as grace that does not mind. It is not indulgence; a wave is not a shrug. What is being described is a supply that outlasts your failures, not one that is indifferent to them. The man who reads this and concludes he may now sin comfortably has not understood the sentence — he has understood the size of the supply and missed entirely whose fullness it is coming out of.

A test you can run this week: at the end of a day you would call a bad one — short-tempered, prayerless, the same old thing — ask whether your instinct is to stay away from God until you have improved, or to come and draw again. The first instinct assumes a fixed allowance you have overdrawn. The second is the only one this verse leaves standing.

Nobody is on their last grace. There is another one behind it, and behind that one a fullness that has not been touched.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast with Moses is not abolition but fulfillment and surpassing. The law was given — it came from outside, as commandment. Grace and truth came — they arrived in person, embodied. 'No one has ever seen God' — not even Moses, who saw God's back (Exod. 33:23). But the only God who is at the Father's side — reclining at table in intimate fellowship, as John will often picture it — he has made him known. Jesus is the living exegesis of the Father: everything God is, the Son makes visible in human flesh.

Two things in this verse will stop a reader comparing Bibles. The first is that where this version has 'the only God,' an older one has 'the only begotten Son.' That is a genuine difference in the manuscripts, and it is not a small one, since the first reading calls Jesus God outright. The earliest copies we have support 'the only God'; the majority of later ones read 'Son.' Either way the sentence teaches the same thing — the reading with 'Son' still says he is at the Father's side and has made him known, and the whole prologue has already said he is God in verse 1 — but it is worth knowing why your Bible differs from your grandmother's here, and worth noticing that the older manuscript evidence points, if anything, to the higher reading.

The second is the word 'begotten' itself, which has confused generations of readers into thinking it means Jesus had a beginning. It does not. The Greek word means one of a kind, the only one of its sort — Isaac is called by the same word in Hebrews 11:17, though Abraham had another son. It speaks of uniqueness of relationship, not of origin in time. This is exactly why the Nicene Creed insists on the strange-sounding phrase 'begotten, not made': whatever the Son's eternal relation to the Father is, it is not the relation of a creature to its Creator. He was not produced. He is, and always was, the Father's own.

Now to the sentence itself, and to a mistake that has done real damage: reading this verse as though Moses were the villain of it.

Watch the two verbs, because they are not the same verb and John chose them carefully. The law was given — a passive, and Moses is named as the channel it came through. Grace and truth came — and the Greek is the Prologue's own verb of arrival, the same one used four verses earlier when the Word became flesh. The law was handed over. Grace and truth walked in. That is the contrast: not a bad thing replaced by a good one, but a description delivered and then the thing itself turning up in person.

And there is a decisive reason not to set the two men against each other, which is that Jesus in this very Gospel forbids it: If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (5:46). You cannot use John 1:17 to demote Moses without running straight into John 5:46. Moses is not the opposition. He is the first witness for the prosecution's opponent.

The clinching point is the one already planted in verse 14, and this is where it pays. Grace and truth is not a fresh pair of Christian nouns. It is what God called himself on Sinai when Moses asked to see his glory and was hidden in the rock: abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod. 34:6). Those two words are the ones John has been holding since verse 14.

So the sentence is not saying Moses got the rules and we got the kindness. Moses was shown the grace and the truth — from behind, through a crack, in a proclamation he was told to write down — and John's claim is that the same grace and the same truth have now come up the road on two feet. Moses had the account. We have the person the account was about.

(A small thing worth noticing in passing: this is one of only two places in the whole Gospel where John writes the full name Jesus Christ. He has spent seventeen verses on the Word, the light, the life, the only Son — and then, at the moment the eternal meets the historical, he puts down a man's name and his title, as if to say: this one, the one you have heard of.)

No one has ever seen God. A reader who knows his Old Testament will object immediately, and he should. Moses and the elders went up the mountain and saw the God of Israel and ate and drank in front of him (Exod. 24:9-11). Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up (Isa. 6:1). Jacob said he had seen God face to face and lived. So what does John mean?

He means that nobody has ever seen God as he is in himself, unmediated and unveiled — and that every genuine sighting in the Scriptures was accommodated, screened down to what a creature could survive. But he means something more startling than that, and he says it himself later in the book. Of Isaiah's vision in the temple, John writes that Isaiah saw his glory and spoke of him — meaning Christ (12:41). That is the answer built into this Gospel. The Old Testament sightings of God were not exceptions to this verse. They were early appearances of the one this verse is about.

Then a phrase the older translations render more literally than the modern ones: he is in the bosom of the Father, tucked into his side. Keep that image, because John is going to use it once more and only once. At the last supper, one of the disciples is lying at Jesus' side — and it is the identical phrase, the same word, the same posture (13:23). The position the Son eternally occupies with the Father is the position John found himself given with the Son. He is not choosing his words loosely. He is telling you that he knows, from the inside and from one evening at a table, what kind of nearness the sentence describes.

And the last verb. He has made him known renders one Greek word, exegesato — from which we get exegesis. It means to lead out, to draw out into the open, to narrate something in full; it was used of guides taking you through a place and of priests unfolding an oracle nobody else could read. What is striking is that in the Greek the verb has no object at all. The sentence ends: he has explained. Full stop. Not explained a doctrine, or a subject, or an aspect of God. He has done the explaining, and he is what the explaining consists of.

So take the whole verse as the Prologue's landing, because that is what it is. It opens with a locked door — no one has ever seen God — and it does not leave the door locked. It says the one person in existence who has never been anywhere but the Father's side has come out and told us, and the telling was a life.

Here is the test. Every one of us is carrying a picture of God assembled out of odds and ends: what our father was like, what we were told as children, our own temperament, the last sermon that frightened us. Take one thing on that picture that you are fairly sure of — that he is disappointed in you, say, or reluctant, or watchful, or hard to get hold of. Now ask where you would find that in Jesus Christ. Not whether you can defend it from a text somewhere; whether you can find it in him. If it is not in him, it is not in God, because he is the exegesis and there is no other copy.

Nobody has seen God. And a man who had been leaning on his chest wrote that sentence down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John the Baptist's testimony before the Jerusalem delegation is a masterclass in self-emptying: he denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet, and identifies himself only as 'the voice of one crying in the wilderness.' His entire identity is absorbed by the task of pointing to the one coming after him. The next day he sees Jesus and delivers his greatest sermon in a single sentence: 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' Two of his disciples follow Jesus; Andrew finds Simon; Philip finds Nathanael. Each encounter is unique, each testimony is personal, and Jesus's response to Nathanael — 'you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' — identifies him as the new Bethel, the true meeting place between heaven and earth.

The section opens as an official inquiry. Priests and Levites are sent down from Jerusalem — and behind them, we are told in a bracket, the Pharisees (vv. 19, 24), the most serious and most admired religious men in the country. Their question is jurisdictional, and it is a fair one once you know why baptizing was provocative: immersion was how a Gentile convert entered the covenant people, and John is applying it to Jews. He is treating the sons of Abraham as though they needed to come in from outside. Only the Christ, Elijah or the Prophet could reorder Israel like that, and he has just denied being any of the three.

His answer refuses his own credentials and changes the subject: among you stands one you do not know (v. 26) — present tense, in this crowd, while you are asking. He is not worthy to untie that man's sandal (v. 27), a duty rabbinic tradition held to be too degrading to ask even of a disciple — and in chapter 13 the one whose sandal he could not touch will kneel and wash his disciples' feet. All of it happens at Bethany across the Jordan (v. 28), on the far bank, in the crossing country where Israel first entered the land.

John's certainty is not intuition. Twice he says I myself did not know him (vv. 31, 33) — startling, since Luke tells us they were cousins — and he explains why he was sure: God had told him in advance what sign to watch for, and he watched, and he saw the Spirit descend and remain (v. 32). That verb, meno, is making its first appearance in a Gospel that will use it forty times and build the whole of chapter 15 on it; and the first thing it describes is not our abiding in Christ but the Spirit's abiding on him. It surfaces again immediately as a domestic detail, when the first disciples ask where he is staying and then stay with him (vv. 38-39).

The gathering that follows runs on a single repeated verb — found, found, found — and the direction reverses once: Jesus finds Philip and gives the first command of the Gospel, Follow me (v. 43), which is also the last thing he says to Peter on its final page. Simon is renamed Rock before he has done a single thing to deserve it (v. 42), by an author who knows his reader will reach the courtyard in chapter 18. Nathanael's objection to Nazareth is small-town rudeness from the next village along, and Philip answers it with no argument at all — Come and see, the same three words Jesus had used the day before. Jesus commends him for having no deceit in him (v. 47), the word used of Jacob at Genesis 27:35 — a son of Jacob with none of Jacob in him — and then tells him he has seen him under the fig tree (v. 48), before Philip ever called him.

John is also counting days. The next day falls three times (vv. 29, 35, 43) and chapter 2 opens on the third day — laying out something very close to a week, which is hard to read as accidental in a book that began In the beginning. It ends at a wedding, with wine, and a glory manifested.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gathering of the first disciples in John 1 is a theology of testimony: John testifies to Jesus; Andrew testifies to Simon; Philip testifies to Nathanael. The gospel spreads through personal witness. Each person who encounters Jesus becomes a testimony to others. The titles accumulate — Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man — each one true, each one partial, each one pointing toward the one who exceeds all titles. Faith begins with testimony, but it must end with personal encounter: 'Come and see.'

Two guards belong to this section. The first concerns the phrase the Jews, which appears here for the first time and some seventy times in the Gospel: in John it functions as shorthand for the Jerusalem religious authorities, not for a people. The author is a Jew, every disciple is a Jew, and Jesus says in this same book that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). What is recorded is an argument inside a family about the family's own hope, and reading it as one people's verdict on another inverts it — a misreading Christians have made at terrible cost.

The second concerns the Lamb. Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (v. 29) should not be assigned lazily to one background. John's own frame is Passover: he alone dates the condemnation to the hour the lambs were killed (19:14) and applies the Passover regulation about unbroken bones to the body on the cross (19:36). But the words spoken here — takes away the sin — are Isaiah's, since of all the candidate lambs only the servant of Isaiah 53 bears sin. Genesis 22 supplies the unanswered question (where is the lamb?), and the daily sacrifice explains why there had to be a last one. The verb is a present participle and the noun is singular: not a list of offences but the whole condition, taken up in order to be carried away.

The gathering of the disciples also settles the relation between this Gospel and the others. The call by the Sea of Galilee in Matthew and Mark is not an alternative version of this meeting but a later and decisive summons; here men are introduced to Jesus and begin to believe, and later they leave the nets for good. Faith by stages is the normal pattern, not a defective one — which is also the burden of vv. 50-51, where a man who has believed for minutes is told he will see greater things, and the greater things turn out to include a cross.
verseByVerse.examples:
Keller notes that 'Behold, the Lamb of God' is the most comprehensive atonement statement in the New Testament: the lamb of Passover (Exod. 12), the lamb of the daily sacrifice (Lev. 1), the suffering servant who is led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa. 53:7), and the apocalyptic Lamb who alone is worthy (Rev. 5) — all in one person. Stott observes that Andrew's first act after meeting Jesus is to find his brother: the natural overflow of genuine encounter with Christ is the desire for others to share it.

The pastoral centre of this section is that nobody in it recruits by argument. Andrew fetches his own brother — the hardest possible person, and the one least impressed by him — with a seven-word sentence containing no case at all. Philip's testimony is theologically magnificent and factually wrong twice over (Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph), and John lets both errors stand on the page because Nathanael came anyway. Nobody is waiting for a witness to be finished before he is useful.

Two cautions worth carrying out of it. Andrew won his brother the same day, and that is the exception rather than the pattern; Jesus' own brothers did not believe during his lifetime (7:5). Anyone who has prayed for a relative for decades is not being rebuked by this chapter. And I saw you under the fig tree should be handled on both sides: it is the comfort of the believer whose faithfulness nobody is counting, and it is exposure for the reader who would rather his private life stayed private — with the point being that the one who has complete access to it is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he mentions the tree and says nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delegation from Jerusalem is official: priests and Levites represent institutional Judaism come to audit the Baptizer's authority. John's answer is a double confession — he did not deny but confessed — that stresses the voluntary, uncoerced nature of his self-identification. He is not the Christ. The negative precedes the positive in John's testimony, just as the law prepares the way for grace. Reformed theology has always insisted that the herald's glory is entirely derivative: John shines only by reflected light from the one who is the Light itself.

This is the first appearance of a phrase that will turn up some seventy times before the book is finished, and because it has been put to appalling use it is worth stopping over here, at its first occurrence, rather than letting it accumulate unexamined. The Jews, in this Gospel, is almost always a shorthand for the religious authorities in Jerusalem — the men with institutional standing, who send delegations and convene meetings and eventually take a case to Pilate. It is not a term for a people.

The plain facts settle it. John who wrote this book was a Jew. Every disciple in it is a Jew. Its central figure is a Jew who keeps the feasts, is called Rabbi throughout, and says in this same Gospel that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). The delegation in this verse is Jewish and so is the man they are interrogating and so is everyone else standing in the river.

What is being described is an argument inside a family about the family's own hope, which is the sharpest kind of argument there is — and the moment it is read as one people's verdict on another it has been turned inside out. Christians have done that, at scale, with results that do not bear describing. Read the phrase as the Gospel uses it: the authorities in Jerusalem, and not your neighbour.

Now the scene, because it is more official than it sounds. Priests and Levites are temple staff, sent down from Jerusalem — roughly twenty miles and a considerable descent — to establish by what authority an unlicensed man is conducting a religious rite in the open country. This is not curiosity. It is an inquiry, and inquiries are opened when something has grown large enough to be a problem.

Their question is the one the whole chapter is about: Who are you? It is the right question, asked of the wrong man, by people who will shortly be standing within a few feet of the answer without recognising him.

And notice what John does with the opportunity, because it was a real opportunity. He had crowds. Luke says people were questioning in their hearts whether he might be the Christ (Lk. 3:15). The country was ready, the delegation had come to him, and a career was available. He puts it down in the first sentence he speaks in this Gospel.

The doubled verb catches how emphatically he does it: He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed. The word is the one used elsewhere in the New Testament for confessing Christ. It is the vocabulary of standing up and saying a thing publicly when saying it costs you. Here the confession is a subtraction. I am not the Christ.

Here is a test worth running, because this temptation almost never arrives as an ambition. It arrives as an offer. Somebody credits you with more than is true — more wisdom than you have, more spirituality, more authority in their life than any human being should hold — and the correction would be awkward and would cost you something. Do you make it? Most of us let a small overestimate stand because pulling it down would be embarrassing. John pulled his down in front of a government delegation, at the height of his influence, when the misunderstanding running in his favour was the largest religious question in the country.

The first words out of the last prophet's mouth are about who he is not. It clears the ground for the only sentence he actually came to say.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The questioners work through Malachi's Elijah and the Mosaic Prophet of Deuteronomy 18 — the two expected forerunners of the messianic age. John denies both titles. He is not a figure in his own right but a voice. Yet Jesus will later say John is Elijah who was to come (Matt. 11:14) — in function, not in person. John's denial is not contradiction but humility: he will not allow the crowds to construct a messianic identity around him that would compete with the one coming after.

Read the three answers in sequence and watch them shrink. I am not the Christ — a full sentence. I am not — two words. No — one. He is diminishing on the page as he speaks, and by the time they get a positive answer out of him in the next verse he will not claim to be a person at all, only a sound.

There is something else in the Greek that a reader of this Gospel should be told, because it will pay dividends for twenty chapters. What John says here is ego ouk eimi — I am not. That is the exact formula, with a negative in it, that Jesus will use again and again without one: ego eimi, I am. I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. I am the good shepherd. Before the door of Jesus' great self-declarations is opened, the last and greatest of the prophets stands in it and empties the phrase of himself three times over. One man says I am not, so that the other can say I am.

As for the two titles, both were live expectations with addresses in the text. Malachi ends the Old Testament by promising that God will send Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5) — the very last thing said before four centuries of silence, and therefore the thing everyone was still waiting for when the silence broke. And Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like himself, to whom Israel must listen (Deut. 18:15-18). The delegation is working through the list.

His denial and Jesus' later statement that John is Elijah who is to come (Matt. 11:14) are not in conflict, and the resolution is worth having plainly: Jesus is describing a role, John is refusing a reputation. The angel had told his father that he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Lk. 1:17), which is exactly what Jesus later says he did. What John will not accept is the popular version — the returned prophet as a figure in his own right, with his own following, around whom a movement could be built. He is not going to let anyone put him in the frame.

There is a real freedom in that, and it is available to more people than notice it. A great deal of Christian exhaustion comes from quietly accepting jobs that were never ours: being the one who holds a family together, the one with the answers, the one whose faith everyone else is leaning on. Those roles are flattering while they last and they will break you, because they belong to somebody else. John is not being modest here. He is being accurate, and accuracy is lighter to carry.

Try it as a question: what are people counting on you for that only Christ can actually supply? Not what you have failed to do — what you have been allowed to be, and should not be. Saying no to it will look like a loss of standing. It is the removal of a weight you were never built to take.

He gives them three answers and every one of them is a subtraction. It is the shortest self-description in the Gospels, and the man who gave it is the one Jesus called the greatest born of women.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pressed for a positive identification, John reaches for Isaiah 40:3 — the great comfort passage of the exile's end. He is a voice, nothing more. Not even a messenger with a name, just a sound that announces the coming of one greater. Calvin observes that John's self-effacement is the model for every minister of the gospel: the preacher is the voice; Christ is the Word. Every sermon that exalts the preacher rather than the Lord has confused the voice for the speaker.

Notice the pressure in their question, because it is very human: We need to give an answer to those who sent us. They have to file a report. Somebody in Jerusalem is expecting a finding, and this man keeps saying what he is not. Give us something to write down.

What he gives them is barely anything at all. I am a voice. Not a prophet, not a teacher, not even the voice of a man — a sound. And a voice is the one thing in the world that stops existing the moment it has done its work. It is not a monument or an office. You cannot preserve it. It exists only while it is being used, and then the words it carried go on without it.

Stage the verse he reaches for, because it is not a random proof text. Isaiah 40 is the great turn in that book — the end of the judgment chapters and the beginning of comfort, addressed to a people in exile who have concluded that God has lost interest. Comfort, comfort my people, it opens. And then a voice in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.

The picture behind it is a road gang. When a king was coming, riders went ahead of the royal party and the road was made ready — hollows filled, rocks cleared, the surface levelled, because a monarch does not pick his way over broken ground.
