That is the job John claims. He is not the king and he is not the escort. He is the man out in front with the news that someone is coming and the road is in no condition for it.

Two things follow from his choosing that passage. The first is that the one being announced is, in Isaiah, the LORD — God himself coming to his people. John applies it to a man who will walk up to him next morning. He has just made the Prologue's claim without using any of the Prologue's language. The second is that this comfort was spoken to exiles: people who had been waiting so long they had stopped expecting anything. That is who the announcement is for. Not the people who are ready, but the people who have given up on the road being used.

And the road-making is the part we would rather not translate. Preparing the way is not decoration; it is demolition and haulage. What has to come down is whatever a king would have to step over — which, in the sermons John actually preached, turned out to be quite specific: what you do with your coat and your food, how you handle money that passes through your hands, whether you use your position to squeeze people (Lk. 3:10-14). He did not tell them to feel differently. He gave them roadworks.

Here is a test for anyone in Christian work of any kind, paid or not. Ask what would remain of your ministry if your name were removed from it. If the honest answer is not much — if the thing only functions because people are attached to you — then you have built something other than a voice. A voice is content to be forgotten the moment it is understood, and it does not consider this a tragedy, because being forgotten was always the plan.

They came for a name to put in a report. He gave them a job description and a piece of Isaiah, and no name at all.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This parenthetical note is theologically significant: the delegation is Pharisaic. The Pharisees are the guardians of legal observance, and their concern about John's baptizing without recognized authority will surface again throughout the gospel. Institutional religion is interrogating the prophet. The pattern recurs throughout John: Jerusalem, with its temple and its lawyers, cannot recognize the one it has been waiting for because it has domesticated the waiting into a system.

A single verse in brackets, easy to read straight over, and it changes who is in the room. The first delegation was priests and Levites — temple staff, the professional clergy. This note tells us who was behind the sending, and it is a different constituency altogether.

It is worth knowing who the Pharisees actually were, because Christians have made the word into an insult and in doing so have lost the whole point of them. They were not the temple establishment; that was the priestly families, who were wealthy, political, and in many cases not especially devout. The Pharisees were a lay movement — a few thousand men, mostly ordinary tradesmen and teachers, who had made it their life's work to take the law of God with complete seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. They tithed their herbs. They knew the Scriptures by heart. They believed in the resurrection, in angels, in the coming Messiah, and in a God who cared what you did on a Tuesday. Ordinary people admired them enormously, and were right to.

Hold that steadily, because the tragedy of this Gospel depends on it. These were not obvious villains. They were the serious ones — the people you would have picked out of any crowd as most likely to recognise God at work. If sincerity had been enough, or knowledge of the Bible, or moral effort, or a genuine longing for the Messiah to come, they would have been first at the river and first at the cross. They had all four. It was not enough.

Which is exactly why the word has no business functioning as a name for other people. When a Christian says Pharisee he almost always means someone stricter than himself, and the usage is nearly the opposite of the truth. The Pharisee problem is not strictness. It is the state of a man who is so certain he is on God's side that there is no longer anything God could do that would surprise him — and therefore nothing God could do that he would be able to recognise. That condition is available at every point on the scale of strictness, and it is most available to those who have been right about something for a long time.

So here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in proportion to how much you know. What would it take to convince you that God was doing something you had not authorised — something outside your tradition, through people whose theology you would want to correct, in a form you find unimpressive or embarrassing? If no answer comes, that is worth sitting with. It does not mean you are wrong about the things you are right about. It means the mechanism by which you could ever be corrected has been quietly disconnected, and the men in this verse are what that looks like at scale.

They travelled twenty miles to investigate. They asked reasonable, careful questions. They went home with a report. And the one they had been waiting for their entire lives was standing in the crowd the whole time.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question is jurisdictional: by what authority does an unauthorized nobody wash people in the Jordan? John's answer reframes the entire exchange. The real question is not about John's credentials but about the one standing unrecognized in their midst. The great tragedy of official religion is that it can be so focused on procedural legitimacy that it misses the presence of the Living God. The one they are interrogating John about is already among them — and they do not know him.

The question only makes sense if you know why baptizing was the provocative part, and most readers do not, because we associate baptism with churches and christenings. To them it meant something else entirely, and it was offensive.

Ritual washing was ordinary in Judaism — there were stone pools for it all over Jerusalem, and a devout man might immerse himself many times in a month. But there was one washing that marked a person's entry into the covenant people from outside, and it was administered to Gentile converts. A pagan who wanted to become a Jew was circumcised, brought an offering, and was immersed: washed clean of the paganism he was coming out of.

Now put John in the Jordan. He is baptizing Jews. Sons of Abraham, circumcised on the eighth day, keepers of the law, are wading into a river to be washed like incoming pagans. That is the outrage, and the delegation's question is entirely reasonable given it: by what authority do you treat the covenant people as though they were outsiders needing to come in? Only three figures could conceivably reorder Israel like that — the Christ, Elijah, the Prophet — and he has just told them he is none of the three.

It is also, incidentally, the sharpest sermon anyone had preached in four hundred years, and he preached it without saying a word. Descent will not do it. Your ancestry will not do it. You need what a pagan needs, and you need it in public, in cold water, where the neighbours can see.

His answer does not defend his credentials at all. He changes the subject to the only subject: among you stands one you do not know.

Every word of that is worth weighing. Among you — not coming, not somewhere else, not in Jerusalem where you have just come from. In this crowd. Stands — the verb is present and settled; he is not passing through, he is here, and he has been here while you were asking your questions. One you do not know — and these are the best-informed religious men in the country, standing within yards of him.

That last clause is the one to be careful with, because it can be turned into a weapon against people who do not need it. It is not an instrument for making a settled Christian doubt whether he really knows the Lord. The people it is aimed at were confident of their standing and had come to audit somebody else's. If you are worried by the sentence, it is a fair sign it is not describing you — the men it describes were not worried at all.

But it does leave a question that anyone can afford to ask honestly, and long church attendance is no protection from it. There is a way of being near Christ for years — the services, the vocabulary, the diary, the opinions — which is nearness of the kind these men had to the Jordan: physically present at the event, and not in it. The test is not how much you know about him. It is whether there is anything in your week that only makes sense if he is real. If everything you do would survive his non-existence unchanged, that is worth knowing now rather than later.

They had come out to establish who John was. He tells them, in effect, that they have the wrong man under investigation, and that the right one is close enough to touch.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John borrows the language of a slave's duty — untying the master's sandal — and declares himself unworthy even of that service. The Baptist's self-abasement before Christ is total and deliberate. Bethany across the Jordan places this testimony in concrete geography: the wilderness threshold, the Jordan crossing, the liminal space where Israel once entered the land. Now a new and greater crossing is being announced. The geography of redemption is always particular.

There was a rabbinic saying about this, and it gives the sentence its edge. A disciple was expected to serve his teacher in almost every way a slave would — fetching, carrying, dressing him, waiting on him. But there was one duty considered too degrading to ask of a student, and it was the one to do with the feet: untying and carrying the sandals. That was slave work, and a disciple was not to be asked for it.

So read what John is saying. He does not say he is unworthy to be the man's disciple. He says he is unworthy to do the one job that even a slave's list contained and a disciple's list did not. He has reached for the lowest available rung and then said he cannot reach it.

Hold that, and then remember what happens twelve chapters from now. In an upper room, the one whose sandal strap John was not fit to loosen takes off his outer garment, ties a towel round his waist, kneels on the floor, and washes the feet of men who are at that moment arguing about which of them is the greatest. The task too low for the herald is the task the King performs. That is not a pleasant irony; it is the shape of the whole Gospel, and this verse is where the measurement is taken that makes chapter 13 unbearable.

Then the geography, which John gives in the flat manner of a man who was there and remembers where he was standing: Bethany across the Jordan. Not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived — a different place, on the far bank, out in the open country. It was obscure enough that early copyists were unsure of the name, and some manuscripts read Bethabara instead, which is why your Bible may carry a footnote here.

What matters is which bank. Everything so far has happened on the wrong side of the river — the side Israel was on before they went in. This is the crossing country: where the nation came out of forty years of wilderness and entered the land, where Elijah struck the water and went up in a whirlwind and left his cloak behind (2 Kgs. 2:8-13). John is standing at Israel's front door, on the outside, telling the covenant people they need to come in again.

And notice that the man himself is not the story of the location. This is the only spot in the chapter where the narrator pauses to say where all of this took place, and he says it after the sandal sentence, as if the address is a footnote to the self-abasement rather than the other way round.

A test that comes out of this rather than being imposed on it: think of the lowest job in your church — the one nobody puts on a rota because everyone assumes somebody else does it. Stacking the chairs. The bins after the meal. The lift home for the person who talks too long. Ask yourself, without answering out loud, whether you would be glad to be known as the person who does that and nothing else. John measured his own worth against exactly that scale and came up short, and Jesus called him the greatest man ever born.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold the Lamb of God" is the interpretive lens for the entire fourth gospel. The Passover lamb, the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, the daily temple sacrifice — all converge in this cry. Jesus does not merely model redemption or teach about it; he takes away sin, actively bearing and removing it. The ranking paradox — after me yet before me — announces the eternal pre-existence of the one who entered history later than John. Incarnation does not diminish deity; it expresses it.

Everything depends on which lamb he means, and the honest answer is that the question can be settled — not by choosing the most convenient option, but by letting this Gospel tell you which one its author had in mind.

There were, in fact, four lambs available to a Jewish imagination, and they are not interchangeable.

The lamb of Genesis 22. Isaac walks up a mountain carrying the wood for his own sacrifice and asks the only question in the Old Testament that this verse could be an answer to: Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering? His father says: God will provide for himself the lamb. And then God does not — not that day. A ram is caught in a thicket and a boy walks back down the hill, and the sentence about the lamb is left standing, unpaid, for two thousand years. When a man by a river points at another man and says Behold, the lamb, a very old question is being answered.

The daily lamb. A lamb every morning and a lamb every evening, in the temple, without a break, for centuries (Exod. 29:38-42). Constant, regular, and never finished — which was its own testimony, because a sacrifice you have to repeat tomorrow has not dealt with anything permanently.

The Passover lamb. A year-old male without blemish, killed at twilight, its blood on the doorposts, and the destroyer passing over that house (Exod. 12). Note carefully: the Passover lamb was not a sin offering. It did not take away anybody's sin. It marked a house as belonging to God and turned aside the judgment falling everywhere else.

The lamb of Isaiah 53. Like a lamb that is led to the slaughter... he opened not his mouth. And this is the only one of the four in which a lamb bears sin: the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all... he bore the sin of many.

Now let John decide it. Two things in his own account are decisive, and neither is in any other Gospel. First, he alone dates the crucifixion so that Jesus is condemned on the day of Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour (19:14) — the hour the lambs were being killed in the temple. Second, when the soldiers come to break the legs of the crucified and find Jesus already dead, John alone tells you which Scripture was fulfilled: Not one of his bones will be broken (19:36). That is not a general prophecy. It is the Passover regulation, from Exodus 12:46, about how the lamb is to be handled.

So John's frame is Passover. But the words spoken over him here — who takes away the sin of the world — are not Passover language at all. They are Isaiah's. Which means the Baptist has done something no one before him had done: he has put the Passover lamb and the sin-bearing servant into one person and pointed at him.

Take the two together and you have the whole doctrine. Isaiah tells you how it works — the iniquity is laid on him and he carries it. Passover tells you what it does for you — judgment is real, it is passing through, and it does not come into the house marked with blood. Genesis supplies the question, and the daily lamb explains why there had to be a last one.

Two details in the sentence itself. The verb takes away means both to lift something up onto yourself and to carry it off — and both are needed, because he does not remove sin from a distance. He takes it up in order to take it away. And it is in the present tense, a participle: not took away once, long ago, but taking away, described as what he is.

Then the noun: the sin of the world, singular. Not sins — not a ledger of separate offences to be worked through item by item. The thing itself. Sin as the condition, the whole weight of it, treated as one object that can be picked up.

Which is where the pastoral question arrives, and it is almost always the same one. People rarely doubt that Christ takes away sin in general. They doubt whether he takes away the particular thing they have never told anyone — the one that feels less like a sin than like a category. Look at the grammar again. If he had said sins, you would be entitled to wonder whether yours was on the list. He said the sin of the world, which is the total, and a total does not have exceptions in it. Whatever yours is, it was included by the only method that could have included it: everything was.

Guard the last phrase against being made to say more than it does. Of the world is not settling the old argument about the extent of the atonement, in either direction. What it is denying is that this is a national arrangement. The men listening had come from Jerusalem; their categories were Israel and everyone else. John says the word that breaks the fence, and the rest of this Gospel will keep breaking it — a Samaritan woman, a Roman officer's household, some Greeks who ask to see him.

And the first word is an imperative: Behold. Look. It is the only thing the greatest prophet since Malachi ever asks anybody to do. He does not say understand it, or feel it, or resolve to do better about it. He says look at him — which is, as it happens, the one instruction a man carrying something too heavy is still capable of obeying.

One more lamb belongs on the list, and it is the one the writer of this Gospel saw for himself. In the vision on Patmos, John looks for the Lion of the tribe of Judah who has conquered, and turns to see a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain — and the whole of heaven falls down in front of it (Rev. 5:5-6). The Baptist points at a lamb walking toward him on a riverbank. Sixty years later the same author is looking at the same lamb on the throne of the universe, still bearing the marks. Whatever else the title means, it is not a stage he passed through. It is what he is called in glory.

Stand back from the argument and watch what is coming down the riverbank. The one who put the ram in the thicket is walking toward the altar himself. The one who had accepted every offering Israel ever made — every bull, every goat, every pair of pigeons, every morning and every evening for fifteen hundred years — is coming to be the last one. All that blood was rehearsal. Every knife lifted in that country was pointing forward, and the thing it pointed at has just come round the bend of the Jordan on his own two feet, unbound, in no hurry, of his own accord.

He did not have to be caught. He walked toward the man who would name him.

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's honest confession — he did not know Jesus by supernatural insight but required the Father's appointed sign — establishes the gospel's epistemological principle: God reveals himself on his own terms and by his own appointed means. John's ministry of water baptism was not self-initiated; it was divinely commissioned for the specific purpose of creating the occasion for revelation. Every ministry is instrumental. The goal is always the unveiling of Christ, not the establishing of the minister.

I myself did not know him. That sentence needs a fact from another Gospel to land properly, and it is a startling one: they were relatives. Mary and Elizabeth were kinswomen; Gabriel told Mary so in the same breath as the announcement (Lk. 1:36). These two men were cousins, born six months apart, and their mothers had spent three months of a pregnancy together.

So I did not know him cannot mean he had never met him. It means something far more useful to us: knowing Jesus as a relative, as a neighbour, as a face you have seen at family gatherings all your life, is not the same thing as knowing who he is. The Baptist had every natural advantage — the shared blood, the family stories, a mother who could have told him precisely what happened when she was pregnant — and he says flatly that none of it told him. He had to be shown.

That is worth a great deal to two sorts of reader. To the one raised in a Christian home, who has heard it all since infancy and sometimes wonders whether familiarity has spoiled it: the greatest prophet in Israel's history was in exactly that position and needed God to reveal it anyway, and God did. Proximity is not the qualification, and it is not the disqualification either.

And to the reader who has begun to distrust his own certainty — whose faith feels as though it rests on a mood that comes and goes: notice where John's certainty came from. Not from inside him. In the next verse we will find that God had told him in advance exactly what sign to watch for, and he watched for it, and he saw it. His confidence rested on something that happened outside himself, on a particular day, in front of witnesses. That is where yours rests too. The events this book reports did not happen inside anybody's feelings, and they do not stop having happened on the mornings when you cannot feel anything at all.

Then the purpose clause, which reframes the whole ministry: for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel. The baptizing was never the point. The crowds were never the point. The entire operation — the wilderness, the camel hair, the preaching, the queues in the river — existed to create an occasion at which one person could be identified. It was scaffolding. And scaffolding is judged by the building, not by how impressive it looked while it was up.

Here is the test, and it applies to anything you are pouring yourself into. Ask what your work is scaffolding for. Not what it achieves, not whether it is going well — what it is for, and whether that thing is a person. A ministry, a marriage, a job done Christianly, the raising of children: each of them can be measured by whether it ends in someone seeing Christ more clearly, or whether it has quietly become the building rather than the scaffolding.

He baptized thousands so that one man could be pointed at. He seems to have thought that was a good return.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit's remaining on Jesus distinguishes him from every other anointed figure in Israel's history: prophets, priests, and kings received the Spirit for a season and a task; Jesus bears the Spirit permanently and without measure (3:34). The dove — evoking the Spirit hovering over creation (Gen. 1:2) and the dove that returned with the olive branch (Gen. 8:12) — signals new creation and covenant peace. The one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit can do so because the Spirit rests upon him without diminishment.

Stay with that word remained, because John has just used, for the first time in his Gospel, one of the two or three most important words in it.

The verb is meno. It turns up around forty times before the book closes, and it is the word behind the whole of chapter 15: Abide in me, and I in you... apart from me you can do nothing. Everything this Gospel will eventually say about the Christian life runs through that verb. And its first appearance is not about us at all. It is about the Spirit settling on the Son and not lifting off again.

That order matters more than it looks. The abiding does not begin with your effort to hold on to Christ. It begins with the Spirit resting on Christ permanently, and everything downstream is a share in that. He is told to abide in the Father's love; we are told to abide in his. What is being asked of us in chapter 15 was first true here, in a river, before anyone had been asked anything.

Watch for the same verb three verses from now, incidentally, when the first two disciples open their mouths. They ask him where he is staying, and they go and stay with him. It is the same word, used of an afternoon in a rented room. John will make an enormous doctrine out of it later; he starts it as a domestic detail about where a man is sleeping.

And notice how completely this scene depends on a spoken instruction. He who sent me to baptize with water said to me... John did not work it out, and he did not sense it. He was told in advance precisely what to watch for, and then he stood in the water and watched for it, possibly for months, looking at every face that came down the bank. God gave him a sign specific enough to be falsifiable and then honoured it.

What lands here is the whole Trinity in a sentence and a half, without a word of the later vocabulary: the Father who sends and speaks, the Spirit who descends and settles, the Son on whom he settles. Nobody in the scene is arguing for the doctrine. It is simply what happened at the Jordan, and the definitions came three centuries later to protect the report.

Then the promise that this remaining makes possible: this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. Set the two baptisms side by side and the difference is plain. Water is applied from outside; it goes on you, and it comes off. The Spirit is not applied. He is given, and he stays — because the one doing the giving is the one on whom he has already been seen to stay.

Say a careful word here, because this phrase has been used to make Christians anxious about whether they have had a second experience they may have missed. The New Testament's own position is blunt about it: Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Rom. 8:9). There is no category of Christian who is still waiting for the Spirit. If you belong to Christ, the thing John is announcing here has already happened to you, whatever it felt like at the time and whether or not there was anything to feel.

Which allows a better test than the anxious one. Do not ask whether you have had an experience. Ask whether anything in you objects when you sin — not guilt about being found out, but a genuine unease that was not there before. Ask whether the word Father ever comes out of you without being manufactured. Ask why you are still reading a page like this at all. Those are not feelings. They are the residue of someone who has moved in.

The dove came down and did not leave. That is the whole announcement, and everything the Christian life is made of comes out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's final testimony in this section is the gospel's central confession: the Son of God. Some manuscripts read "the Chosen One of God," which is also a rich messianic title. Either way, John's function is complete — he has seen, he has borne witness, and now he recedes. The eyewitness language (I have seen, I have borne witness) is juridical: John is a legal witness whose testimony carries weight because it is grounded in direct perception. The fourth gospel is deeply concerned with the reliability of testimony about Jesus.

Both verbs are in a tense that means a completed action whose result is still standing: I have seen, and it is still true that I have seen; I have borne witness, and the testimony is still on the record. He is not describing a moment of enthusiasm. He is entering a statement that cannot now be withdrawn — and, in a Gospel shaped like a trial, that is exactly what a deposition is.

The manuscript question here deserves a little more than a mention, because the alternative reading is not merely another rich title — it fits the scene with unusual precision. Some early copies read the Chosen One of God. If that is what John wrote, he is quoting Isaiah: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him (Isa. 42:1). Which is, word for word, what has just happened in front of him — a servant, a choosing, and the Spirit put upon him and staying. And it would tie this sentence back to the Lamb of five verses ago, since the servant of Isaiah 42 is the same figure who by Isaiah 53 is led to the slaughter.

Either reading is true and neither is at risk. Son of God is what the whole Prologue has already established and what the book will end by asking you to believe (20:31). Chosen One would anchor the Baptist's testimony in the Servant Songs. It is worth knowing that the difference exists, and worth noticing that it does not cost you anything.

It is also worth knowing what the title would have meant to the men standing there, because it did not mean to them what it means in the creed. In Israel's Scriptures son of God could be said of the king — You are my Son; today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7) — and so the crowd would have heard a claim about the Messiah, the anointed king. John, writing sixty years later for readers who have now read his first chapter, means all of that and the thing verse 18 said as well. The title grows as the Gospel goes on. It does not change its mind.

And this is the last we hear from John the Baptist in this section. He appears again briefly in chapter 3, to say the sentence that sums him up — He must increase, but I must decrease — and then he is arrested and killed offstage, and this Gospel does not even narrate it. He gets no death scene. He came, he pointed, he went.

There is a particular comfort in that for anyone whose service to God has been unglamorous and looks likely to stay that way. The greatest man ever born of women, on the Lord's own assessment, has a public career of a few months, spends it telling people to look at somebody else, is imprisoned on a private grudge, and is executed to settle a dinner-party promise. From the inside it can have looked very like a wasted life. He had seen, and he had borne witness, and it turns out that is the whole job description — and that two thousand years later the seeing and the witnessing are still standing in the perfect tense.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third consecutive day in this chapter, John repeats his testimony — now to his own disciples. The repetition is deliberate: faithful witness is not one announcement but a sustained, consistent pointing. John looks at Jesus walking by and simply says what he has already said. There is something deeply Reformed in this: the preacher's task is not novelty but fidelity, not new revelation but faithful repetition of the one gospel. Look — there he is. The Lamb of God.

Something easy to miss is happening here, and it costs him everything he has left.

He is not preaching to a crowd this time. He is standing with two of his disciples — his own men, the ones who had attached themselves to him, who fasted when he fasted and prayed the prayers he taught them (Lk. 11:1). And he looks at a man walking past and says the sentence he knows perfectly well will take them away from him.

He says it in four words. He does not preface it, or soften it, or ask them to stay in touch. He does not even repeat the whole of what he said the day before — the sin of the world, the ranking, the pre-existence. He simply says Behold, the Lamb of God, and lets it do what it is going to do. The next verse is the two of them walking off after somebody else.

The verb for how he looks at Jesus is worth having: it means to fix your eyes on something, to gaze rather than glance. He is not gesturing vaguely down the road. He stops and stares, and that is what the two of them notice first — not the words, but where the man is looking.

And this is now the third day running that he has said the same thing (vv. 29, 36). Not a new insight, not a fresh angle, not something worked up for a different audience. The same sentence, again. There is a whole doctrine of preaching in that. The pressure on anyone who has to speak regularly is the pressure to say something they have not said before, and the pressure is almost entirely vanity. The man Jesus called the greatest prophet had one line and used it until it took his followers away.

The cost is the part to sit with. He is not resigning at the end of a full career; he is at the height of his influence, and he is dismantling it deliberately, one pair of disciples at a time. When people came to him later complaining that everyone was going over to Jesus, he gave them the image of a best man at a wedding: the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and listens for the bridegroom's voice and rejoices greatly at it, and whose joy is now complete (3:29). Not resigned. Not managing a disappointment. The happiest man at the party is the one who is not the groom and never thought he was.

Here is the test, and it is the harder half of what most of us mean by humility. It is not difficult to say that Christ is greater than you. It is difficult to be glad when someone you have taught, prayed for, and carried transfers their affection and their attention to him and stops needing you — and does it in front of you. John did not merely permit that. He caused it, on purpose, three days in a row.

Two of them heard it. One was Andrew. The other, unnamed, is almost certainly the man writing this down sixty years later, still remembering exactly where he was standing and what the old prophet said.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The power of faithful testimony: two disciples hear John and immediately follow Jesus. John loses his followers by pointing them to Christ, and this is his joy and his purpose. Effective ministry always produces this result — the congregation moves from the preacher toward the Savior. Keller notes that the best preaching makes people fall in love with Jesus, not with the preacher. John's disciples do not ask permission; they simply turn and go. The word of witness, when the Spirit attends it, produces immediate response.

One sentence, and it contains the first use in this Gospel of the verb that will describe the Christian life from here to the last page: they followed him.

At this moment it means nothing more spiritual than walking behind a man on a road. That is worth noticing, because the word never quite loses that meaning. It does not mean they admired him, or agreed with him, or had settled anything. It means they got up and went the same way he was going, and were now some distance behind him with no idea what to say.

Stage what this actually looked like, because the next verse tells you. Two men are trailing a stranger down a road in silence. They have not introduced themselves. They have no question prepared. They are close enough to be noticed and far enough back to pretend they are not following, and the situation is becoming awkward — and it is Jesus who has to turn round and rescue it by speaking first.

That is how following him usually starts, and it is worth saying plainly to anyone whose beginnings were unimpressive. There is a kind of testimony that makes conversion sound like a decision taken in a clear moment with full understanding. This is what the first one in this Gospel looked like: a sentence overheard, two men walking off after somebody without a plan, and an embarrassed silence that had to be broken from the other end.

And the thing they had to go on was very small. Four words from a man they trusted, pointing at a man they did not know. No miracle had happened. Nothing had been explained. Everything in the next twenty chapters — the water into wine, the raising of Lazarus, the upper room, the empty tomb — is downstream of two men taking one sentence seriously enough to move their feet.

Which is the other half of the verse, and it is the half that costs. John loses them here. This is what his ministry produces: not a following, but a transfer. He said the same sentence three days running until it emptied his own circle.

The test that comes out of this one is simple and awkward. Think of the last time somebody said something true to you about Christ — in a sermon, in a conversation, on a page. Did anything move? Not did you agree with it; agreeing is free. These two men heard a sentence they had heard before, and the difference this time was that their feet were involved.

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' They said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and see.' They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'What are you seeking?' — Jesus's first words in John's Gospel are a diagnostic question that cuts to the heart of every human life. What is the deep desire behind the following? The disciples' response — 'where are you staying?' — is indirect but honest: they want to be where he is. 'Come and see' — the most important invitation in the Gospel. Not 'here is an argument' but 'come and experience.' The tenth hour (4pm) — they stayed the rest of the day. One afternoon with Jesus changes everything.

Stop at the fact itself before touching the content. These are the first words out of the mouth of Jesus in this Gospel — the first thing the Word says once he has begun to speak — and they are not a statement. They are a question, and it is a question about what you want.

He does not ask what they believe. He does not ask what they have done, or whether they are sorry, or what they understand. He asks what they are looking for. The whole of the encounter is opened by an enquiry into desire.

And John has built his book around that verb. It is the same word — zeteo — that Jesus uses in the garden when the soldiers arrive with torches and he steps out to meet them: Whom are you seeking? (18:4, 7). It is the same word he uses on resurrection morning, when a woman is crying at a tomb she thinks has been robbed and a man she takes for the gardener says, Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking? (20:15). The first question in the book and the last question in the book are the same question. Nobody in this Gospel gets to Jesus without being asked it.

Which makes it, unavoidably, a question aimed past the disciples at whoever is reading. And it is worth answering honestly rather than piously, because the pious answer is nearly always a lie. Most people come to Christ seeking something other than Christ: relief from a fear, a way out of a mess, certainty, respectability, a marriage saved, the return of a peace they remember having.

Look at what he does with that. He asks the question — and then he does not screen anybody out on the strength of the answer. He does not say wrong reason, come back when your motives are pure. The question is not a filter. It is the beginning of an education, and this Gospel is largely the record of people arriving with a small want and being given something they had not known to ask for.

Notice, too, that they duck it. Asked what they are seeking, they answer with a question about an address: where are you staying? That is exactly what people do when a question goes too deep too fast — they change it into something practical. He lets them. He does not force the deeper conversation; he answers the question they were able to ask.

But the word they reach for is the very one from six verses ago. Where are you staying — abiding, the word that was used of the Spirit settling on him and not lifting off. And the verse ends with they stayed with him that day: the same verb again. They asked where he abides, and the answer turned out to be that they could abide there too. The doctrine of chapter 15 is already running under this conversation, and nobody in it knows.

Come and see. Not an argument, not a summary, not a leaflet — an address and an afternoon. It is worth guarding this against a use it often gets: it is not a recommendation to stop thinking. This is the Gospel that says it was written so that you might believe, on the basis of evidence deliberately selected and recorded (20:30-31). Come and see is not the opposite of examining the case. It is an invitation to examine it from close up rather than from the road.

Then the detail that gives the whole scene away: it was about the tenth hour. Around four in the afternoon. Why on earth is that in the Bible?

Because the man writing it was one of the two, and he is somewhere in his nineties, and he still knows what time of day it was. He does not remember what was said in that room — he never tells us, and you can feel the reader wanting him to. He remembers the hour. That is exactly how memory works around the afternoon your life divided in half: the content goes and the frame stays, the light in the room, where you were sitting, what time it was when you looked up.

They came with a question about accommodation. They stayed until dark, and sixty years later one of them was still writing about it.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first act of discipleship in John's gospel is evangelism: Andrew finds his brother. We have found — the plural is striking, as if discovery demands sharing. The Messiah: Andrew translates the Hebrew title for John's Greek readers, and in doing so announces the fulfillment of Israel's entire waiting. One afternoon with Jesus, and Andrew knows. This is the nature of encounter with Christ — it is self-authenticating, it produces certainty, and it immediately generates the desire to bring others. The chain of witness has begun.

A reader who knows the other Gospels will stop here, because this does not look like the story he was told. In Matthew and Mark, Jesus walks by the Sea of Galilee, sees Andrew and Simon casting their nets, says "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men," and they leave everything on the spot (Matt. 4:18-22; Mark 1:16-20). No Baptist, no Jordan, no fetching of a brother. Here, by contrast, Andrew meets Jesus at the Jordan through John's testimony, spends an afternoon with him, and goes to find Simon — and it all happens months before the boats and the nets. Which account is right?

Both, and they are not describing the same moment. What John records is a first meeting; what the others record is a later, decisive summons. Read them in order and a natural sequence appears rather than a contradiction: here at the Jordan these men are introduced to Jesus and begin to believe; then they go back to their fishing in Galilee, having met him but not yet left all for him; and then, one morning by the lake, the call comes to drop the nets and follow for good. This is how most people actually come to Christ — not in a single lightning-stroke but by stages, an introduction that ripens into a following.

John tells you where it started; Matthew and Mark tell you where it became everything. The renaming fits the same pattern: Jesus marks Simon as Cephas at the first meeting (v. 42), a promise spoken over him long before the man grows into it.

Now look at Andrew, because this Gospel mentions him by name three times and he is doing the same thing on every one of them.

Here he brings his brother. In chapter 6, with five thousand people to feed and the disciples calculating what it would cost, it is Andrew who says there is a boy here with five barley loaves and two fish — and then adds, honestly, but what are they for so many? (6:8-9). In chapter 12, when some Greeks come asking to see Jesus and Philip does not know what to do with the request, he takes it to Andrew, and Andrew takes them in (12:20-22). Three appearances, and every single time he is bringing somebody to Jesus: his brother, a boy with a packed lunch, and a group of foreigners nobody was sure were allowed.

He never preaches a sermon in the New Testament. There is not one recorded saying of his that is not either an introduction or a question. And the man he brought in this verse becomes the one who preaches at Pentecost and has two letters in the Bible.

That is worth sitting with if your own gift feels like nothing much. Andrew is a connector, and connectors do not leave a record. Nothing he did would have looked like anything from across the room. But the whole of Peter's life — the confession at Caesarea Philippi, the walk on the water, the three denials, the restoration on the beach, the sermon that added three thousand in a morning — enters the story because his brother could not keep quiet for an afternoon.

Notice which brother it is, too: his own brother. The nearest possible person, and therefore the hardest. Nobody is less impressed by your spiritual development than the person who watched you grow up. Andrew has known Simon all his life, has presumably been out-talked by him at every meal they have ever eaten, and goes and tells him anyway.

And here the guard is owed, because this verse gets used to prod people who do not need prodding. Andrew found his brother the same day, and it worked. That is not the pattern; it is the exception, and the New Testament knows it. Jesus' own brothers did not believe in him during his lifetime (7:5) — the man in whose house they grew up could not persuade them, and they came in later, after the resurrection, at God's speed and not his. If you have been praying for a brother, a son, a husband for twenty years and nothing has moved, this verse is not a reproach. It is a reminder that Andrew's job was to fetch him, not to convert him, and that the fetching is the only part any of us has ever been responsible for.

We have found the Messiah — and there is an irony in the pronoun he does not notice. They found nothing. They were standing on a riverbank because a prophet was sent to tell them where to look, and Jesus turned round and spoke first, and by the next chapter it will be Jesus doing the finding (v. 43). Every person in this chapter who says they have found him was found.

Here is the test. Name the person you would least like to raise this with — not a stranger, someone close, precisely because they know you too well for it to be comfortable. Now notice that Andrew's opening line was seven words long, contained no argument, and made no case. It was a piece of news and an invitation to come and look. That is the whole of what was asked of him.

He is remembered as Simon Peter's brother. Simon Peter is remembered at all because of him.

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' first act toward Simon is to rename him. He does not ask Simon's credentials or confirm his readiness; he looks at him with penetrating knowledge — "you are Simon the son of John" — and then announces what Simon will become. Cephas/Peter means rock. The name is prophetic, not descriptive: Simon at this moment is anything but rock-like. But Jesus names people according to what he intends to make them, not according to what they currently are. Election precedes transformation; the new name precedes the new nature.

The verb for how Jesus looks at him is the same one used six verses ago of the Baptist looking at Jesus — a fixed, deliberate gaze rather than a glance. Simon is being examined. And what comes out of the examination is not a verdict but a name.

Watch the tenses, because the whole entry is in them. You are Simon the son of John — present tense, and it is the accurate description: here is who you are, and here is whose family you come from, and I know both without being told. You shall be called Cephas — future. Between the two tenses there is a gap, and the gap is the rest of Simon's life.

The name is Aramaic. Kepha means a rock or a crag, and John stops to translate it for readers who do not have the language — which is itself a small piece of evidence that this happened, since a nickname that has to be explained to your audience is not a nickname anybody invented for literary effect. It stuck so hard that Paul, writing to Greek-speaking churches twenty-five years later, still calls him Cephas by reflex (1 Cor. 1:12; Gal. 2:9).

Now the thing that ought to stop a reader. At this moment Simon has done nothing whatever. He has not confessed anything, left anything, promised anything, or been tested in any way. He has been standing in front of Jesus for a matter of seconds, brought there by his younger brother, and he has not yet said a word that anyone thought worth recording. The name is handed to him before there is a single piece of evidence for it.

And the evidence, when it comes in, runs the other way. This man will take Jesus aside and tell him he has got the plan wrong. He will swear he is ready to die and then, a few hours later, in this same Gospel, stand at a charcoal fire in a courtyard and say three times that he does not know him — the last of the three with the man himself within sight. If you were naming him from his record you would not call him Rock. You would call him something with more give in it.

John knows all of that as he writes this verse. He was there for the courtyard. He is deliberately putting the name on the page in chapter 1, for a reader who will reach chapter 18 and remember it.

So here is the thing this verse is actually teaching, and it is one of the great comforts of the Christian life: the names God gives people are not descriptions of their performance. They are declarations of intent. Gideon is addressed as mighty man of valour while he is hiding in a winepress threshing wheat in secret because he is frightened of raiders (Judg. 6:11-12). Abram is renamed father of a multitude while he is childless and old. In every case the name arrives first and the man walks toward it, usually badly, and usually for years.

Which is exactly where most Christians live, and it is worth naming plainly. You have been told you are a child of God, a saint, a new creation, and the daily evidence is a man or woman who lost their temper before breakfast. The gap is not proof that the name is false. The gap is the normal condition of everyone God has ever renamed, and Simon is in this Gospel partly to prove it.

Guard it on the other side, though, because a promise is not a permission. The name did not make Peter's failure unreal or unpainful — he went out and wept bitterly, and this Gospel takes him back to a charcoal fire in chapter 21 and asks him three times whether he loves him, once for each denial. The name did not spare him the reckoning. It meant the reckoning was a restoration rather than a dismissal.

Try the test. Ask what name you would give yourself this morning, honestly, from the evidence. Now ask which one God has actually used of you in writing, and notice that he issued it knowing every single thing you have since done with it — including the part you have never told anyone. He was not misinformed when he named you. He looked at you the way he looked at Simon, and then he said what he intended to make.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Follow me" — Jesus' call to Philip is direct and unmediated, in contrast to Andrew and Peter who came through witness. The divine initiative is sovereign and varied: sometimes God works through testimony, sometimes through direct address. Philip's hometown — Bethsaida, the same village as Andrew and Peter — reminds readers that the first disciples are ordinary Galileans, not Jerusalem elites. The kingdom comes to the margins. The gospel of grace always begins where human pride is least established.

Before the content, the calendar — because John has been counting, and this is where the count becomes visible.

He has marked off successive days since the delegation arrived: the next day (v. 29), the next day again (v. 35), and now the next day once more. And then, at the start of chapter 2, on the third day there was a wedding at Cana. Add them up and John has laid out something very close to a week, which is difficult to read as an accident in a book that opened with the words In the beginning.

The exact arithmetic is debated, and it is honest to say so; commentators reach six days or seven depending on how the last interval is counted. But the shape is unmistakable, and so is where it lands. A week that begins with a man announcing that the light has come into the world ends at a wedding, with water turned into wine, and the sentence this, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory (2:11). Genesis 1 is a week that ends with a man and a woman brought together and God looking at what he has made. John's week ends the same way. He is not illustrating the creation account. He is claiming that the same person is doing the same kind of thing again.

Now the call itself, and the change of direction in it. Everyone so far has been finding somebody: John points, Andrew finds Simon, and in a moment Philip will find Nathanael. Here, for the first time, the verb turns round. He found Philip. Nobody fetched him. Nobody had prayed for him as far as we are told. Jesus went to Galilee and found him.

And what he says to him is the first command out of his mouth in this Gospel: Follow me. Two words, no explanation, no terms offered, no indication of where. It is also — and this is worth carrying to the end of the book — the last thing he says to Peter on the last page, twice over, on a beach after breakfast: You follow me (21:19, 22). The first command and the final command are the same command. Everything in between is what it looks like to obey it.

Then the geography, which is doing more than colour. Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Its name means something like house of fishing, which tells you what the place was for. And it is one of the three towns Jesus later names in a lament: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago (Matt. 11:21).

Hold those two facts together, because they will not resolve into anything comfortable. Three of the twelve apostles came out of Bethsaida. And Bethsaida, as a town, is the object of one of the severest sentences Jesus ever spoke. The place that supplied the most did not itself believe.

That is a real comfort and a real warning in the same sentence, depending on where you are standing. If you have come out of a family or a church or a town where the gospel was heard for years and did nothing, you are not carrying its verdict; three men walked out of Bethsaida and followed him. And if you have grown up inside a great deal of exposure to Christ and have never actually moved, this verse says that the exposure is not the same thing as the following, and that being near where God is working is a more dangerous position than being far from it, not a safer one.

Two words, to a man who had not asked. It is still, by a distance, the most life-altering sentence anyone has ever had addressed to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip echoes Andrew: the first impulse of those who find Jesus is to find others. And Philip frames his testimony in the richest possible terms: Jesus is the one Moses and the prophets wrote about. The entire Old Testament is a forward-pointing testimony to Christ. Philip understands immediately that following Jesus is not abandoning Israel's scriptures but fulfilling them. Every rabbi, prophet, and psalm pointed here. This is the Christian reading of the Hebrew Bible: not replacement but completion.

Philip has been a disciple for perhaps an hour, and the first thing he does with it is go and find somebody. He was found by Jesus in one verse and is finding a friend in the next. Nobody has taught him to do this, and nobody has told him he is allowed to.

His summary of Jesus is magnificent and it is also, in two respects, wrong — and it is worth being precise about both, because the combination is one of the most encouraging things in the chapter.

The magnificent part first. Him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote. That is not vague piety; it is a claim with contents, and it is worth refusing to leave it fuzzy. Moses had written of a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear (Deut. 18:15), of a seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head (Gen. 3:15), of a ruler from Judah to whom the obedience of the peoples belongs (Gen. 49:10), of a star coming out of Jacob (Num. 24:17).

The prophets had written of a virgin's son called God with us (Isa. 7:14), a child on David's throne called Mighty God and Everlasting Father (Isa. 9:6-7), a servant pierced for our transgressions (Isa. 53), a ruler from Bethlehem whose origin is from of old (Mic. 5:2), a king coming humble and mounted on a donkey (Zech. 9:9).

Jesus himself will later put it as a standing accusation: You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me (5:39). And on the Emmaus road he does exactly what Philip has just done, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Lk. 24:27).

Now the part he gets wrong. Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. He was not from Nazareth in the sense that mattered prophetically; he was born in Bethlehem, which is the very thing Micah had specified and which the crowd will throw at each other in chapter 7 as a reason he cannot be the Christ. And he was not the son of Joseph, as the whole New Testament and this Gospel's own first chapter insist.

John does not correct him. The mistakes stand on the page, and Nathanael comes anyway, and by the end of the conversation he is confessing more than Philip knew how to say.

Sit with that if you have ever kept quiet because you were afraid of getting it wrong. The first missionary sentence in this Gospel contains a geographical error and a theological one, and God used it to bring in an apostle. Philip's grasp of Christ was partial, second-hand, an hour old, and expressed inaccurately. What he had was true enough to be worth passing on, and the passing on is what he was asked for. Accuracy grows. Nobody is waiting for you to be finished.

There is a shape here that will not stop repeating. John points at Jesus and Andrew goes. Andrew fetches Simon. Jesus finds Philip. Philip finds Nathanael. Not one link in that chain is a sermon, and not one of them is a stranger. Every single one is somebody telling somebody they already knew.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael's skepticism is geographic prejudice — Nazareth was an obscure village without messianic pedigree. Philip's answer is the perfect apologetic: Come and see. Not argument but invitation; not proof but encounter. Jesus' greeting to Nathanael is both discernment and honor: a true Israelite, without deceit, like Jacob made new (Jacob the deceiver becomes Israel the God-wrestler). Jesus sees in Nathanael what Nathanael cannot see in himself — the grace of integrity.

The remark is funnier and smaller than it sounds, and knowing why makes it land better.

Nazareth was a hamlet — the archaeology suggests a few hundred people at most, up a hill off the main road. It is not mentioned once in the Old Testament. It is not mentioned by Josephus, who lists dozens of Galilean towns and knew the region as a commander. It is not in the Talmud. There is no prophecy attached to it, no history, nothing. And Nathanael, we learn at the very end of this Gospel, was from Cana (21:2) — the next village along. This is not lofty prejudice from a man in Jerusalem. This is one small place being rude about another small place a few miles away, which is a thing small places have always done.

Which makes the objection more useful than a grand one would be, because it is the ordinary form of the thing. Most people do not reject Christ after weighing the evidence. They decline to look, on the grounds that nothing worth having has ever come from that quarter — that sort of church, that kind of person, those people, that book. It is not an argument. It is a reason not to have to make one.

Philip's answer is the best answer anybody gives in this chapter, and it is three words with no content: Come and see. They are the same three words Jesus used the previous afternoon (v. 39), now travelling — the invitation is being passed along the chain exactly as it was received.

He does not argue about Nazareth. He could have; he could have pointed out that the Messiah was to be born in Bethlehem and started a debate about origins, and he would have lost, because he had his facts slightly wrong. Instead he refuses the terms and offers the man a look.

Guard that against the use it usually gets, though, because come and see is regularly quoted as if it meant stop thinking. It means nothing of the kind. This is the Gospel that says at its close that these things were written down, from a much larger body of evidence, precisely so that you might believe (20:30-31) — the whole book is a case being made. The invitation is not to suspend your judgement. It is to bring it closer, because there are some things about which no amount of discussion at a distance is worth one look from nearby.

Then Jesus' greeting, and there is a wordplay in it that a Jewish ear would catch instantly. Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit. The word for deceit is dolos — and it is the word used in the Greek Old Testament at Genesis 27:35, when Isaac, shaking, tells Esau what has happened to his blessing: Your brother came with deceit and has taken away your blessing.

So: here is a true son of Israel — a man descended from Jacob — with none of Jacob in him. Jacob was the supplanter, the man who got everything he ever wanted by deception and spent twenty years running from the consequences. Jesus looks at Nathanael and says: not this one. And having opened with Jacob, he will close the conversation five verses later with the night Jacob slept on a stone.

Notice what it does not mean. It does not mean Nathanael is sinless, and it does not mean he is nice. The last thing out of his mouth before this was an insult about Jesus' home town — and it is precisely for that, in a sense, that he is commended. Here is a man who says what he actually thinks. There is no gap between what is in him and what comes out of him. He was rude, and he was honest, and Jesus prefers that to smoothness by a wide margin.

Which is worth saying to the Christian who has always felt himself to be the awkward one — too blunt, too doubtful, the person who asks the question everyone else is too polite to ask, and who has quietly concluded that the smooth people are the spiritual ones. This chapter has a smooth man in it somewhere no doubt, and it is not him that Jesus stops to praise. It is the sceptic from the next village who said the wrong thing out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' omniscience breaks through the ordinary: he knew Nathanael before their meeting, saw him in a private moment under the fig tree — a traditional site of Jewish study and prayer. The question "How do you know me?" is Nathanael's proto-confession; he already suspects something extraordinary. Jesus' answer demonstrates divine foreknowledge that is not cold surveillance but intimate attention. He was watching. He knows. This knowing is the foundation of all pastoral comfort: the Good Shepherd knows his sheep by name.

Take the two halves of the answer separately, because they do different work.

Before Philip called you — that is the order, and it is stated deliberately. Before the human contact, before the invitation, before Nathanael had the first idea that anything was happening: he was already the subject of attention. Everything Philip did was second. There is a whole doctrine in the preposition, and nobody in the scene uses a single technical word for it.

When you were under the fig tree, I saw you. And here it is worth being disciplined, because this is a verse people fill in.

We are not told what he was doing. Preachers have supplied it for centuries — that he was studying the Scriptures, since rabbinic tradition speaks of studying under a fig tree; or that he was praying; or, most attractively, that he was reading Genesis 28 about Jacob at Bethel, which would explain the answer Jesus gives three verses later. Any of those may be right. The text says none of them, and the honest thing is to say so rather than to invent a scene and preach it as though it were reported.

What we can say is what the effect proves. Whatever happened under that tree was private enough that being told I saw you turned a sceptic into a confessor inside a minute. A man who had been mocking Nazareth thirty seconds earlier now says Rabbi, you are the Son of God. Something was said or thought or wept under that tree that no other human being knew about, and it had just been referred to by a stranger.

The fig tree itself carries one more echo worth having. In the prophets it is the picture of settled peace — they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid (Mic. 4:4). A man under a fig tree is a man in the one place he feels unobserved.

Which is where the verse needs handling on both sides, because it is a sentence that comforts one reader and undoes another, and both of them are in the room.

To the one who feels unseen — the years of praying in a room nobody knows about, the caring for someone that nobody is counting, the faithfulness that has produced no visible result and no acknowledgement — this is the verse. He saw you. Not deduced you, not was informed about you: saw. And notice he does not say what he saw, then or now. He simply lets you know that the private place was never as private as it felt.

To the one who has something under his own fig tree that he would very much rather were not seen — and most of us do — the same sentence lands as exposure, and it is no use pretending otherwise. He saw that too. But look at what he does with what he saw. He does not use it. He does not name it. He mentions the tree and stops, and the whole weight of the encounter is not accusation but welcome. The one person who has complete access to your private life is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he has never yet used the information to shame anybody. He uses it to prove he knows who he is talking to.

A test, then, and it is a fair one: how do you feel about being fully known? Not by God in the abstract — by this man, in detail, on the specific matters. If the answer is dread, the problem is not that he sees. It is that you have not yet believed what verse 29 says about him.

He had been watching Nathanael before Nathanael had heard his name. That is either the most frightening sentence in the chapter or the most comforting one, and which it is depends entirely on the face of the one who was watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael's confession — Son of God, King of Israel — is the fullest so far in the gospel, and it comes from the skeptic. One word of supernatural knowledge produces a comprehensive christological confession. Jesus receives the titles without correction but points forward: you have only begun. The disciples' entire journey will be a movement from initial confession toward deeper understanding. Nathanael believed because of a sign; he will come to believe because of resurrection. Faith grows. It does not remain where it first stands.

Both titles are larger than Nathanael can possibly know, and the second one has a future he would not have wanted to hear about.

King of Israel is not a devotional phrase. It is a political claim, and in an occupied country it is the kind of claim that gets people killed. Follow it through this Gospel and watch where it goes. A crowd will shout it at him with palm branches on the road into Jerusalem (12:13). And then Pilate will have it written out in three languages and nailed to a board above his head, and the chief priests will object to the wording, and Pilate will refuse to change it (19:19-22). The title Nathanael gives him in a field in Galilee is the title that ends up on his execution notice. He is right, and he has no idea what he is saying, and the man he says it to knows exactly what it will cost.

Then Jesus' reply, which can be read two ways and is probably gentler than it looks on the page. Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? It could be a mild reproach — that faith resting on one impressive moment is a thin foundation. But nothing in what follows sounds like a rebuke. He does not tell Nathanael his faith is inadequate. He tells him it is small compared with what is coming, which is a different thing entirely and much kinder.

That distinction matters, because Jesus in this Gospel is notably unfussy about where faith starts. He will tell a court official that people will not believe unless they see signs and wonders — and then heal his son anyway (4:48-50). He will invite Thomas to put his finger in the wounds. He never once turns away a small faith for being small. What he does, repeatedly, is refuse to let it stay that size.

You will see greater things than these. Not different things — greater. The direction is set: whatever brought you in is the smallest thing that will ever happen to you.

Say the honest word to the reader for whom this is uncomfortable, because there is one. Some Christians have a moment they have been living off for thirty years — a conversion, an answered prayer, a week at a conference when God seemed close — and everything since has been a slow decline from it, and the moment has quietly become a museum rather than a beginning. This verse says the moment was never meant to be the peak. It was the fig tree. It was the thing that got you to look up.

And the honest word on the other side, which the verse also requires: the greater things promised here were not more private words of knowledge. They were a cross and an empty tomb. What Nathanael actually went on to see, on any account, included the worst week of his life. Greater does not mean more pleasant. It means more of who this person is — and there are parts of who he is that can only be seen from somewhere painful.

Here is the test. What is the most recent thing you learned about Christ — not remembered, learned? If the answer is some years old, that is not a reason for guilt. It is a reason to take this sentence as addressed to you: he told a man who had believed for about four minutes that the good part had not started yet.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus alludes to Jacob's ladder (Gen. 28:12) — the vision at Bethel where heaven and earth were joined by a stairway of angels. Now Jesus declares himself the ladder. He is the point of contact between the divine and human realms, the one through whom heaven's resources flow to earth and earth's worship ascends to heaven. The Son of Man — Jesus' preferred self-designation — carries both Danielic glory (Dan. 7:13) and the vulnerable humanity of Ezekiel's prophetic address. He is the God-man who is himself the place where God and humanity meet.

Two things before the ladder, both easy to walk past.

The first is Truly, truly. This is the first of twenty-five double amens in this Gospel, and the doubling occurs nowhere else in ancient literature — no rabbi, no prophet, no other writer talks like this. And the singular is strange enough on its own. Amen is what you say to somebody else's statement: it means yes, that is reliable, let it stand. It is the congregation's word, said after the prayer. Jesus puts it in front of his own sentences, twice, before he has said anything. He is endorsing his own words with the word designed for endorsing somebody else's, which is either a piece of extraordinary presumption or a claim about who is speaking. He never argues for his authority in this Gospel. He simply talks as though it is not in question.

The second is a pronoun. Everything to this point has been addressed to Nathanael personally — I saw you, do you believe. Here the you goes plural. He turns from the one man to the whole group, and by extension to everybody reading. The fig tree was for Nathanael. This is for all of us.

Now stage Genesis 28, because the power of the allusion is entirely in the circumstances, and they are not respectable ones.

Jacob is running. He has just cheated his brother out of the blessing by dressing in his clothes and lying to his blind father's face, and Esau has announced his intention to kill him, and he is escaping north with nothing. Night catches him in open country. He has no tent and no bed; he takes a stone and puts it under his head and sleeps in the middle of nowhere, alone, guilty, and about as far from a holy place as a man can be. And that is where heaven opens over him — a stairway with the traffic of God going up and down it, and God himself standing above it promising to be with him and bring him back.

He wakes up frightened and says the sentence that names the place: Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.

Read that against verse 26 of this chapter, where the Baptist tells the delegation from Jerusalem: among you stands one you do not know. It is the same discovery, two thousand years apart, in almost the same words. God turns out to have been present in the place where nobody thought to look for him.

There is even a translator's crux in Genesis that Jesus may be settling here. The Hebrew says the angels were ascending and descending on it — or on him; the word is ambiguous, and the ancient rabbis knew it was and discussed both. Jesus says: on the Son of Man. Whether or not he is deliberately resolving the ambiguity, he is doing something no one expected with the picture. Jacob thought he had found a place. Jesus says the point of contact is a person.

And notice the order, which is odd in Genesis and odd here: ascending first, then descending. Angels are presumed to live in heaven; you would expect them to come down before they go up. They start at the bottom. Wherever the ladder's foot is, that is where the traffic begins — and Jesus has just said where the foot is standing.

Which is the whole point, and it is the reason this verse is the right end to the chapter. Jacob stumbled on the gate of heaven by accident, in the dark, and marked it with a stone and poured oil on it and called it Bethel, house of God, so that he could find it again. Every religion since has been trying to do the same thing: locate the place, secure the access, mark it so it can be returned to. A temple. A shrine. A practice. A state of mind you were in once and have been trying to get back to.

Jesus tells a man who has been a believer for about five minutes that the ladder has legs. The meeting-point between heaven and earth is not a site you have to find and not a condition you have to achieve. It is a person who walks about, and who found Philip, and who saw Nathanael under a tree before anyone called him.

The chapter opened in eternity with the Word who was with God. It closes with a promise of heaven standing open over a man from Galilee — and between the two, a week has gone by, several people have been fetched by their friends, and God has begun the whole thing again.

And the ladder is a person. Not a place, not a rite, not a mountain, not a season of unusual devotion — a man with a name, who gets tired and sleeps in boats, and up and down whom the whole traffic of heaven runs without pausing. Jacob found the gate of God by accident in the dark and was terrified of it. This one goes looking for men under fig trees, calls them by name before they have been introduced, and invites them to come and see.

Heaven is open. It is open over him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The first sign in John's Gospel is deliberately chosen: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding in Cana of Galilee. The setting is festive, domestic, and thoroughly human. The need is real but not urgent — running out of wine is an embarrassment, not a tragedy. Yet Jesus's response reveals the character of his kingdom: he provides not just enough but an abundance of the finest wine. The six stone jars used for Jewish purification rites hold the old covenant's cleansing water; they are filled to the brim and transformed. The sign points beyond itself: the old purification is giving way to the new wine of the kingdom, the joy of the messianic age replacing the straining observance of the law.

The chapter opens on the third day (v. 1), completing the count of days John has been keeping since 1:19 — something very close to a week, in a book that began In the beginning, ending at a wedding rather than in a garden. Cana was Nathanael's own village (21:2), so the man who had asked whether anything good could come out of Nazareth is present when Nazareth's carpenter makes the wine. Jesus and his disciples are guests (v. 2), the invited additions to somebody else's celebration.

Two verses carry the human weight of the scene.
