Mary's instruction to the servants — Do whatever he tells you (v. 5) — is the last thing Scripture records her saying, and it repeats the shape of Pharaoh's word in the famine: Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do (Gen. 41:55). And the servants' obedience is blind: told to draw and carry (v. 8), they hand the master of the feast a cup of what they had just drawn from a washing jar, with no evidence anything had changed. The proof came after the obedience, never before it.

John then plants the detail everything else hangs on. The steward did not know where it came from — though the servants who had drawn the water knew (v. 9). That contrast is the chapter's quiet argument about who is given understanding, and where from is a question this Gospel will keep asking, right up to Pilate's Where are you from? (19:9). The section closes at Capernaum (v. 12), where he goes with his mother, his disciples, and his brothers — men who at this stage did not believe in him (7:5), and who came in later.
verseByVerse.theology:
John calls the miracles of Jesus 'signs' (semeia) — they are not mere wonders but pointers to a deeper reality. The water-into-wine sign points to who Jesus is (the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom) and what his mission accomplishes (the transformation of the old into the new, abundance replacing scarcity, joy replacing labor). 'His hour had not yet come' — the hour of the cross, the hour of glorification, which will be the ultimate sign to which all others point. The disciples see the sign, believe, and their faith is the intended fruit of every sign in this Gospel.

The material of the sign is the point of the sign. The six jars were there for the Jewish rites of purification — the physical apparatus of a whole system for dealing with uncleanness — and Jesus does not replace the vessels but fills them. The water of ceremonial cleansing becomes the wine of a wedding feast: not the destruction of the old order but its transformation into joy. The quantity settles the tone. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and eighty gallons, at a village wedding already several days old, is not a measured response to a stated need; the disproportion is itself the message.

Semeion is established here as this Gospel's word for a miracle, and the choice is deliberate: John never uses the Synoptics' dynamis (mighty work). A sign is a signpost, valueless if you stop at it, and the crowds of chapter 6 will do exactly that. Seven signs are selected, and 20:30-31 states the purpose. He manifested his glory pays the claim of 1:14 — and the first instalment of that glory is a wedding present given anonymously in an unknown village. And his disciples believed in him, though they had already believed (1:41, 45, 49): faith in this Gospel grows and is tested rather than being settled once.
verseByVerse.examples:
Sproul notes that the abundance of the provision — six jars of twenty to thirty gallons each — is a sign of the inexhaustible generosity of the kingdom. Calvin observes that Jesus honors the institution of marriage by performing his first miracle at a wedding. Keller points out that 'the best wine last' is the pattern of the gospel: the world offers its best first and then disappoints, but Christ gives his best at the end — the resurrection, the new creation, the eternal feast.

The pastoral register of the first sign is lower than readers expect and deliberately so. Nobody is ill and nobody is dying; a family has run out of drink and will be humiliated for years in a culture where hospitality was an obligation with teeth. The first miracle of the incarnate Son was performed because somebody was going to be embarrassed — which sets the threshold for what may be brought to him far below where most praying puts it. Mary's three words state the trouble and propose nothing: They have no wine.

You have kept the good wine until now is the gospel's shape against the world's. Everything else front-loads — the advertisement better than the product, youth spent early, the decline negotiated afterwards. But the promise must be guarded: it is not an assurance that circumstances improve, and it should not be handed to a suffering Christian as though it were. Plenty of lives get harder. What is promised is a better end, not an easier road — which is precisely why it speaks to the reader who has concluded his best years are behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third day resonates throughout John's gospel: it is the day of resurrection, the day when God acts decisively. A wedding in Cana — a marginal village in Galilee — is the setting for the first sign. The incarnate Son of God attends a village wedding as a guest, not as a monarch receiving tribute. This is grace: God present in the ordinary celebrations of ordinary people. Mary is simply "the mother of Jesus" throughout John, never named — she matters as the one who brings Jesus' attention to human need.

Before anything else, finish the sum John has been quietly doing since the delegation arrived from Jerusalem.

He has marked the days off one at a time — the next day, the next day again, the next day (1:29, 35, 43) — and now he writes on the third day. Add them and you have something very close to a week. Commentators reach six days or seven depending on how the last interval is counted, and it is honest to say the arithmetic is not certain. What is not in doubt is that a book which opened with the words In the beginning has just laid out a week and arrived at the end of it.

And look at where the week lands. Genesis runs six days of making and ends with a man and a woman brought together, and God looking at what he has made and calling it very good. John's week ends at a wedding, with more wine than anyone could drink, and the sentence this, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory (v. 11). He is not decorating the creation account. He is saying that the same person has started again, and that this time the week ends not with a garden but with a party.

Then the village. Cana is small enough that we would not know it existed but for this Gospel — and it is worth remembering who came from there. At the very end of the book John mentions, almost in passing, that Nathanael was of Cana in Galilee (21:2). Which means the man who had asked, a few days earlier, whether anything good could come out of Nazareth is now standing at a wedding in his own village watching Nazareth's carpenter make the best wine anyone there had ever tasted. Jesus told him he would see greater things. It did not take long.

Understand what a wedding was. Not an afternoon — a week. The whole village came, and stayed, and the groom's family was responsible for feeding and supplying all of them for seven days. Hospitality in that culture was not a courtesy but an obligation with teeth, and the celebration was often the largest thing a family ever did.

Notice the order of the guest list, too, because it is not what you would expect. The mother of Jesus was there — she is named first, and simply present, as family or close friend of the household are present. Jesus also was invited, and his disciples with him. He is the add-on. It is worth admitting the obvious possibility, though the text does not press it: a party of half a dozen extra men arriving unannounced at a village wedding may be part of the reason a household ran out of drink.

And she is never given her name in this Gospel. John, who names Nathanael and Nicodemus and Lazarus and Malchus the servant whose ear was cut off, calls her only the mother of Jesus. She appears exactly twice in the whole book: here, at the first sign, and at the cross, where she is standing when the hour finally arrives (19:25-27). Both times he addresses her the same way — Woman. This scene and that one are the two ends of a single thread, and the word he uses to her here is the word he will use to her from the cross.

Which leaves the plainest fact of the chapter, and it is the one most likely to be walked past. The eternal Word who was with God before there was light spent one of his first recorded days as an incarnate man at a village party, and stayed long enough to notice the drink running out.

Say that to anyone who has quietly come to believe that holiness and enjoyment are in tension — that the serious Christian is the one who does not much like anything. There is a kind of piety that would have been more comfortable if the first sign had been performed in a synagogue. It was performed at a wedding, for a family who would have been embarrassed, and it produced roughly a hundred and twenty gallons more than the occasion strictly required. Whatever God is like, he is not what that piety assumes.

Here is the test. Picture Jesus arriving at the last celebration you were at — a wedding reception, a birthday, a table of people laughing too loudly. If the honest image is of the room going quiet, the question worth asking is where that picture came from, because it did not come from this chapter. He was invited to this one. He went. And he was the reason it did not end early.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crisis is social, not mortal — running out of wine at a wedding brought public shame in an honor culture. Mary's report is simply factual: they have no wine. She does not tell Jesus what to do; she tells him what is wrong and trusts him to respond. This is the pattern of intercession: bringing need to Jesus without prescribing the solution. He who is sovereign over all things knows better than the one praying how and when and whether to act. Mary's faith is in his character, not his compliance.

To feel the verse you have to feel the size of the failure, and by our standards it looks like nothing at all.

Nobody is ill. Nobody is in danger. A family has run out of drink at a party. In a culture built on honour and shame, however, that is not a minor domestic hitch. The obligation to provide was serious, the whole village was present, and the shortfall would be discussed for years — the wedding where the wine ran out, the family who could not manage it. Some have suggested the groom's household could even face a legal claim from the bride's family for failing their obligation; that may be pressing the evidence, but the direction is right. This was a humiliation with a long tail.

So it belongs to a category most of our troubles belong to and most of our praying does not. It is not a tragedy. It is an embarrassment. It is the sort of thing that will be noticed, and remembered, and told about you — the shortfall, the thing you could not provide, the moment everyone saw you had reached the end of what you had.

Which is exactly the register the first sign is performed in, and that is not an accident. Jesus could have opened his ministry by raising a dead child. He opens it by rescuing a family's reputation at a party. Whatever else that tells us, it tells us the threshold is far lower than we assume.

Now look at what she actually says, because it is three words long and there is nothing in it.

They have no wine. No request. No suggestion. No argument for why he should act, no reminder of who she is, no proposed method. She does not say could you do something or you must help them or surely you could. She states the situation and stops.

That is not a technique, and it should not be turned into one — there is nothing wrong with asking God for specific things, and the Psalms are full of people telling him exactly what they want. But there is something worth learning in the restraint. A great deal of praying is really the presentation of a plan for approval, and the anxiety in it comes from the fact that we have already decided what the answer has to look like and are now negotiating for it. She lays the problem down where he can see it and leaves the method with him — which turns out to be wise, since what he does is not remotely what anyone would have asked for.

And notice the direction she faces. There is no evidence she had ever seen him do anything of this kind; John says plainly in verse 11 that this was the first of his signs. She has thirty years of knowing him and no track record of miracles at all. What she has is a settled conviction about what he is like, and she takes a problem to him on the strength of it.

Here is the test, and it is more searching than it sounds. Name something currently going wrong in your life that you have decided is too small to pray about. Most people can produce one inside a few seconds — the awkward conversation, the thing at work, the shortfall nobody knows about yet. Now notice that you did not classify it as small. You classified it as unworthy, which is a judgement about God rather than about the problem, and it is precisely the judgement this chapter exists to overturn.

The first miracle of the incarnate Son of God was performed because somebody was going to be embarrassed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Woman' — not a term of disrespect in the first century, but a formal address that creates a gentle distance: Jesus is distinguishing his filial relationship from his messianic one. 'My hour has not yet come' — the hour of the cross, when the wine of his blood will be poured out, is the hour toward which everything in John's Gospel moves. Yet Mary's response is the model of faith: she does not argue or explain; she simply tells the servants to obey. She trusts without understanding the timing.

But the clause between the two — "what does this have to do with me?" — is the one readers actually stumble over, and it should not be passed by. In English it can sound like a brush-off, and coupled with "my hour has not yet come" it seems to be a refusal — after which, puzzlingly, Jesus goes ahead and does exactly what the situation required. Did his mother change his mind? Did he decline and then relent?

Two things dissolve the difficulty. First, the phrase is a Hebrew idiom (literally "what to me and to you"), and its force depends entirely on tone: it can be a rebuke, as when demons cry it at Jesus, or it can be the gentle "this is not for you to arrange" of one who is about to act on his own footing. Paired with the courteous "Woman," the softer sense is plainly meant.

Second, "my hour" everywhere in this Gospel means one thing — the hour of the cross and the glory that follows it (7:30; 8:20; 12:23; 17:1). So "my hour has not yet come" is not "I will not act now"; it is "the hour of my full unveiling is still ahead." That is exactly why the sign is done so quietly that only the servants know how the wine came to be: this is a veiled foretaste, not the public hour itself.

This one scene has been made to carry a great deal of weight in debates about the mother of Jesus, and it will not carry the load either way. It is no snub of Mary — he honours her faith and grants the need. But neither does it show her directing him: he acts on his own authority and in his own timing, and her last recorded words in all of Scripture point not to herself but away from herself, to him — "Do whatever he tells you." That is the truest thing Mary ever said, and it is the right word over every life: not do what I tell you, but whatever he tells you.

Two things to add, and the first closes a circle that only becomes visible at the end of the book.

He calls her Woman here, at the first sign, and says his hour has not yet come. She appears only once more in this Gospel. It is at the cross, when the hour has arrived, and she is standing near enough to be spoken to — and what he says is Woman, behold your son (19:26). The same address, at the two ends of his ministry: once when the hour was still ahead, and once when it had come. He does not stop being her son; he arranges her care with almost his last breath. But from the moment of this verse he relates to her as the one whose hour is coming, and she has to learn to know him that way, which is the hardest thing any mother in history has been asked to do.

And then her sentence, which is the last thing Scripture records her saying. Do whatever he tells you.

It has a precedent, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. There is a famine in Egypt, and the people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh says: Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do (Gen. 41:55). The same shape exactly — a shortage nobody can fix, a crowd turning to the wrong authority, and the answer being to go to the one man who has what is needed and do what he says without asking how. Mary is standing in Pharaoh's position and giving Pharaoh's advice, and it is the only sensible advice anyone in this chapter gives.

Notice what it costs the servants to take it. In a moment they will be told to fill six enormous jars with water when the problem is a shortage of wine, and to carry a cup of it to the man in charge of the catering. There is no explanation offered at any point. They are simply asked to do a series of things that make no sense in the direction of the need, and the wine appears somewhere between the drawing and the serving — which is to say, after they had committed themselves and before they had any evidence.

That is worth holding on to when obedience feels pointless. A great deal of what Christ asks is like carrying water to a wine steward: it does not look connected to the thing you are actually worried about, and you will not know whether it worked until after you have done it. She does not tell them to understand him. She tells them to do what he says.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six jars — one short of the number of completion — holding up to 180 gallons of water for Jewish ritual washing. Jesus does not create new vessels; he transforms existing ones. The water of Jewish purification becomes the wine of messianic joy. Reformation, not abolition: the old order is not destroyed but fulfilled and surpassed. The servants fill them to the brim — lavish obedience that leaves no room for addition. God's grace, when it comes, always exceeds what was expected or requested.

Everything in this sign turns on what the water was for, and John tells us in the same breath as the measurement: the jars were there for the Jewish rites of purification.

Picture them. Stone, not pottery — deliberately, because stone was held not to contract ritual uncleanness the way earthenware did, so a stone jar could always be relied on. Large, waist-high, standing where guests would come in. And their entire function was to hold water for washing: hands before eating, vessels, the removal of whatever defilement a person might have picked up in the course of an ordinary week.

That is the raw material of the miracle. Not a well, not a spring, not a wine jar standing empty. The water of religious cleansing — the physical apparatus of a whole system for dealing with the problem of not being clean enough to come near God — is what he asks them to fill, and it is what comes out as the best wine anyone at that wedding had drunk.

The sign is not that Jesus can produce a drink. The sign is that the machinery of purification has become the wine of a wedding feast. What people had been using to try to get clean has turned, in his hands, into the thing you serve at a celebration. And nothing was thrown away to do it: he does not smash the jars and conjure new vessels. He fills the old ones. The washing-water is not condemned; it is fulfilled and turned into joy.

Then the quantity, and it is worth doing the arithmetic because the number is not decorative. Six jars at twenty to thirty gallons each is somewhere between a hundred and twenty and a hundred and eighty gallons. Call it seven hundred litres, or something close to a thousand bottles. For a village wedding. For a party that was already several days old and where the guests, by the steward's own admission a few verses later, had drunk freely.

Nobody needed that. The need was for enough wine to get through the evening without disgrace, and what arrives is a quantity the family could not have consumed if the wedding had run a month — and it is theirs to keep. That is the thing about the sign that a careful reader should not tidy away. It is not proportionate. It is not a measured response to a stated need. It is absurd, and the absurdity is the message: this is what the kingdom is like, and it does not deal in exactly enough.

And the servants filled them up to the brim — which is a small phrase doing real work. They could have half-filled them; it would have been less effort and no less obedient in the letter. The detail is recorded because it is the human contribution to the miracle and it is the only contribution available: they could not make wine, they could only fill jars, and they filled them until the water was level with the rim and there was no room left for anything else.

Here is the test. Think of the last thing you knew you were being asked to do and did adequately — the visit made but kept short, the apology offered with a qualification attached, the giving that was calculated to be defensible. None of that is disobedience. It is simply not to the brim. Nobody at the wedding would have criticised a servant for filling a jar three-quarters full, and nobody would have got a hundred and eighty gallons of wine either.

Six jars of water for getting clean, filled to the top by men who did not know why. It came out as the best thing anybody there had ever tasted.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servants take the water-become-wine to the master of the feast without any explanation. They act in simple obedience to Jesus' word, trusting the result without seeing the transformation. The moment of miracle is private; the servants know what the guests do not. This is the pattern of grace: the work of transformation happens invisibly, through ordinary means (water, stone jars, servants), and the result surpasses all natural expectation. The servants model what every Christian is called to be — obedient carriers of what Christ has made new.

This is the moment of the sign, and John refuses to describe it. There is no gesture, no word of command over the jars, no shimmer on the surface of the water. He said fill them; they filled them. He said draw some out and take it to the man in charge; they did. Somewhere in that sentence the water became wine and the text does not say where.

That is deliberate, and it is characteristic of this Gospel. John is far more interested in what a sign means than in how it looked. But it also leaves the servants in a position worth standing in for a moment, because it is the position faith usually occupies.

Consider what they were being asked to do. The wine has run out. The steward is the man whose job it is to know what is being served and to stop anything unsuitable reaching the guests. And they are to walk up to him, in front of the party, and hand him a cup of what they personally drew out of a washing jar twenty seconds ago. If nothing has happened, they are not merely mistaken; they are two men presenting the master of ceremonies with a cup of hand-washing water at a wedding.

They had no evidence. They had watched the water go in. Nobody had told them anything had changed. The only thing standing between them and public humiliation was a sentence from a guest, and a woman's instruction to do whatever he said.

And note the order, because it will not reverse. They do not taste it first. The proof comes after the obedience, not before it, and there is no version of this story in which the servants get to verify the wine in the kitchen and then decide whether to carry it out. That is not a defect in the arrangement. It is what trust is, and every other arrangement is something else wearing trust's clothes.

Then the detail that makes the whole scene: the servants knew. John tells us so in the next verse, in a bracket, almost as an aside — though the servants who had drawn the water knew. The steward tastes it and cannot account for it. The bridegroom gets the credit and has no idea what for. The guests drink it and never learn anything happened at all. The only people in that building who understand what has just taken place are the ones who were carrying the jars.

That is not a random touch, and it is not a lesson about social class. It is a statement about how this knowledge is distributed. It went to the people who did what he said. Not to the man with the office, not to the one being honoured, not to the room full of people enjoying the result — to the servants, who obeyed a strange instruction without an explanation and therefore found out.

Try the test. Think of something you understand about God now that you did not understand five years ago. Then ask how you came to understand it. It is very unlikely that you read your way to it. In almost every case the answer will be that you did something — kept going, forgave someone, stayed, gave, told the truth when it cost — and the understanding arrived on the far side of the doing. There are things about Christ that cannot be learned from a seat. They are only ever found out by people carrying something.

He never touched the water. He told some servants to move it, and they did, and that was the miracle.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master of the feast, unknowing, pronounces the theological verdict: the best wine comes last. This is the pattern of the kingdom: the world gives its best first and the rest disappoints, but Jesus saves the best for when it is most needed. The servants know the secret; the master does not — knowledge of Christ's power is given to those who obey, not to those who merely observe. 'Kept the good wine until now' — the messianic age, with all its abundance and joy, has arrived.

A question is often asked at this point, and it should be answered rather than sidestepped: was it real wine? It was. The steward's remark settles it — he says that a host serves the good wine first and the poor wine after the guests have drunk freely, which is a comment about what alcohol does to a palate and makes no sense of grape juice. Jesus made something between a hundred and a hundred and fifty gallons of it, and he made it very good, for a village wedding whose family would have been shamed by running dry.

That is worth facing squarely, and it is worth not over-reading. Scripture is entirely capable of holding two things at once: wine is a gift that gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 104:15) and is the standing biblical picture of the joy of the age to come, and drunkenness is a sin the same Scripture condemns without softening (Eph. 5:18), as is putting a stumbling block in a weaker brother's path (Rom. 14:21). Nothing here licenses excess, and nothing here shames the Christian who abstains, whether from conviction or from hard experience. What the sign does say is that the God who came among us was not a killjoy. His first miracle was not a rebuke or a healing but a wedding present, and an extravagant one.

Two more things in the scene, and the first is a question this Gospel will keep asking.

The steward did not know where it came from — and the word for that is pothen, where from. It is going to follow Jesus through the whole book. The crowd in Jerusalem will say they know where this man is from and that settles it (7:27). A blind man will tell the authorities that the remarkable thing is precisely that they do not know where he is from (9:29-30). And at the very end, Pilate, out of his depth in his own judgment hall, will ask him straight out — Where are you from? — and get no answer at all (19:9). The first person in this Gospel to taste what Jesus has done and be unable to account for it is a wine steward at a party, and he will not be the last.

The second is an irony John surely enjoyed. The steward, having no idea where the wine came from, calls over the man he assumes is responsible and congratulates him. The bridegroom. He is being praised for the one thing at his own wedding he had nothing whatever to do with.

And within a chapter John the Baptist will use that exact word about Jesus — the one who has the bride is the bridegroom (3:29). The real bridegroom is standing in that room. The compliment is being paid to the wrong man, by a man who does not know what he is saying, which is a thing that keeps happening in this Gospel and will happen most famously when a high priest explains that it is better for one man to die for the people (11:49-52).

Then the steward's sentence, which is better theology than he knew: you have kept the good wine until now.

That is the shape of everything God does, and it runs against the shape of everything else. The world front-loads. The advertisement is better than the product, the first year of the job is the best year, the holiday is at its finest in the brochure, and youth is spent early. Almost every pleasure available to a human being is arranged so that the best of it comes first and what follows is a slow negotiation with the decline. God works the other way round. Israel got the shadow first and the substance later. The disciples got three years of walking about Galilee and then Pentecost. And the whole of Scripture ends not with a garden restored but with a city, and a wedding, and a supper.

Say it carefully, though, because it is easy to turn into a promise that was never made. The best wine last is not an assurance that your circumstances will improve, and it must not be handed to someone as though it were. Plenty of Christian lives get harder rather than easier; health goes, work narrows, the people you love are buried one at a time, and there is no verse anywhere that guarantees the second half will be more comfortable than the first. What is promised is not a better stretch of road. It is a better end, and an end that is not the end.

Which is why this matters most to the reader who has begun to suspect that his best days are behind him — that whatever he was going to be, he has now been; that the years when he felt most alive, most useful, most in love with God are in the past and are not coming back. That instinct is entirely reasonable, and on any account but this one it is correct. This verse says that for anyone in Christ the arrangement has been reversed, and that the steward's compliment is a statement about the management of the whole universe: he has kept the good wine until now, and now has not happened yet.

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Manifested his glory' — this is John's theological summary of every sign. The miracle is not primarily about wine; it is about the disclosure of who Jesus is. The disciples believe — the intended response to every sign in this Gospel. Belief is not merely intellectual assent; it is personal trust in the one who has revealed himself. The movement to Capernaum, his base of Galilean ministry, follows naturally. The ministry has begun.

This is the verse where John hands you the vocabulary for the rest of his book, so it is worth stopping properly at one word.

He calls it a sign — semeion. That is a deliberate choice, and you can prove it by what he never says. Matthew, Mark and Luke commonly describe the miracles as dynameis, acts of power, mighty works. John does not use that word for them at all. He uses the word for a signpost.

The difference is the whole of his method. A mighty work invites you to be impressed by the one who did it. A signpost is not for admiring. It has no interest in itself; its entire value lies in pointing away from where it stands to somewhere you have not got to yet, and a traveller who stops at a signpost and praises the carpentry has missed the point so completely that it would have been better if he had never seen it. That is precisely what will go wrong with the crowds in chapter 6, who eat the loaves and want to make him king and are told they came looking for him not because they saw signs but because they had their fill of the bread.

John selects seven of them for this book — the wine here, the official's son at Capernaum (4:46-54), the man at the pool who had been ill thirty-eight years (5), the feeding of the five thousand and the walk on the water (6), the man born blind (9), and Lazarus called out of a tomb (11). The counting is debated at the edges, but the pattern is not, and he tells you at the close exactly what he was doing: Jesus did many other signs... but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (20:30-31). Seven signs, and then the eighth thing, which is not called a sign at all because it is what all of them were pointing at.

Note also that he calls this the first — and the Greek word is the one he opened the Gospel with. In the beginning was the Word. This was the beginning of his signs. The book is quietly starting again.

And then the phrase that pays a debt from the Prologue. He manifested his glory. Fourteen verses into chapter 1 John had written we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father — a claim with nothing behind it yet. Here is the first instalment, and it is worth noticing what it consisted of. No voice from heaven, no light, no throne. A wedding present, given to people who never found out who had given it, in a village nobody had heard of. That is what the glory of God looked like the first time these men saw it, and John wants that lodged in the reader before the harder disclosures start.

Let that stand a moment without being turned into a lesson. The glory of God — the thing that filled the tent until Moses could not go in, the thing that drove the priests out of Solomon's temple so that they could not stand to minister, the thing Isaiah saw for one second and cried out that he was undone — was in a back room in Cana, quietly seeing to it that a young couple were not humiliated on their wedding day. Nothing shook. Nobody fell down. The steward went on doing his job and the bridegroom accepted a compliment he had not earned, and the glory of the eternal God went round that room in clay cups.

And his disciples believed in him. Which ought to stop you, because they already had. Andrew had said we have found the Messiah; Nathanael had said you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel. What are they doing believing again?

Because faith is not a switch that is thrown once and then stays where it was put. It is nearer to a thing that grows, and gets tested, and grows again — and this Gospel will show it doing both. The same men will be terrified in a boat, will be scattered on the night he is arrested, and one of them will announce that he will not believe the resurrection without putting his hand into the wound. If your faith today is recognisably larger or smaller than it was five years ago, that is not evidence of instability. It is evidence of the ordinary condition of everyone in this chapter.

Then verse 12, which reads like a travel note and contains something a great many readers need.

He goes down to Capernaum with his mother and his brothers and his disciples. That is the first mention of his brothers in this Gospel, and John will tell us plainly what their position was: For not even his brothers believed in him (7:5). So the group walking that road together includes men who lived in the same house as the Son of God for the best part of thirty years, watched him at close quarters, are travelling with him now — and did not believe.

Sit with that if you have been praying a long time for someone in your own family. Familiarity did not convert them. Proximity did not convert them. A flawless life lived in front of them for three decades did not convert them, and neither did this wedding. And yet the man who was almost certainly the eldest of them, James, is later found leading the church in Jerusalem, called a pillar by Paul, and writing a letter that is in your Bible (Acts 15:13; Gal. 1:19; 2:9). Somewhere between chapter 7 of this Gospel and chapter 15 of Acts, the brothers came in.

What changed them was not more exposure. It was the resurrection, and Paul happens to record that the risen Christ appeared to James personally (1 Cor. 15:7). Whatever passed between those two, it did in an afternoon what thirty years under the same roof had not.

And the last clause is nothing at all: they stayed there for a few days. After the first sign, after the glory, after the disciples' faith took a step forward — a few quiet days in a fishing town with nothing recorded. That is worth having in mind the next time an ordinary fortnight follows a Sunday when God seemed close. It is the pattern. Most of the Christian life is Capernaum for a few days.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John places the temple cleansing at the beginning of Jesus's ministry, where the Synoptics place it at the end. Both are historically accurate — Jesus likely cleansed the temple twice, or John is making a deliberate theological statement by frontloading the event: from the start of his ministry, Jesus is in conflict with the temple establishment and its corrupted worship. 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' — the disciples will understand this only after the resurrection. Jesus himself is the new temple, the true meeting place of God and humanity, the one through whom all access to the Father now comes.

The detail that gives the scene its edge is where the market stood. The temple's outermost and largest court was the Court of the Gentiles — the only place on earth where a non-Jew could come and pray, fenced off from the inner courts by a barrier warning foreigners that they passed it on pain of death. That is the court the livestock pens and currency tables had filled. The trade itself had a rationale (the temple tax required Tyrian coinage; sacrificial animals had to be certified unblemished), which is the uncomfortable part: nothing here began as wickedness. A set of individually defensible conveniences had between them made it impossible for an outsider to pray, and nobody had decided it.

The action is graded, and the grading matters. The animals are driven out, the tables overturned, the coins poured out — but the pigeon-sellers are only told to take their birds away (v. 16), pigeons being the offering of the poor (Lev. 5:7) and released birds not returning. Nobody is reported injured, and the authorities respond not with a charge of assault but with a demand for credentials (v. 18): they dispute his standing, never the abuse itself.

The disciples remember Psalm 69:9 (v. 17) — and John gives it in the future tense where the psalm has the past: zeal for your house will consume me. What they are watching is not merely zeal but the beginning of what will kill him. Destroy this temple (v. 19) is an imperative, a dare to do what they will in fact do; at the trial the witnesses will move one pronoun and report it as I will destroy this temple (Mk. 14:58). The forty-six years of verse 20 dates the scene to about AD 27-28, and the building they were boasting of would be finished for roughly seven years before Rome pulled it down.

The section ends with a crowd who believed because of signs, and with Jesus refusing to entrust himself to them (vv. 23-24) — the same verb both times, they believed into him and he did not believe into them. He needed no one to testify about man, for he knew what was in man (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is an act of prophetic authority: Jesus acts as the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Mal. 3:1), purifying the house of prayer from the commercial transactions that have turned worship into a market. The zeal that consumes him is zeal for the Father's house — the passion of the Son for the honor of the Father. 'My Father's house' — his first recorded words in Luke (2:49) and his claim here: the temple belongs to his Father, and he has authority over it because he is the Son.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge. In 1:14 the Word pitched his tent; here the tabernacle has become the temple, and John states that the temple is a body (v. 21); and the Bible ends with a city in which John saw no temple at all, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22). My Father's house (v. 16) is the claim that licenses the whip — the same phrase Luke records from him at twelve years old in the same building (Lk. 2:49).

Verse 22 supplies this Gospel's account of how understanding arrives. The disciples heard the saying at the time and grasped nothing of it for three years; the resurrection made the old sentence legible and the memory surfaced with its meaning attached — which is the promise of 14:26 in operation. They believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken, two objects of one verb, with no distinction drawn between them.

Verses 23-25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader. What is described is faith produced by spectacle and not yet tested — the crowd of chapter 6 who turn back at the first hard saying (6:66). John uses of them the identical phrase he used of the saved in 1:12, believed in his name: the difference is not in the vocabulary but in what the faith does when the wine runs out. Anxiety about whether one's faith is real is not a symptom of this condition; the people described here were entirely untroubled. And Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing — the next thing he does is give Nicodemus the fullest account of the new birth in the Bible.
verseByVerse.examples:
Calvin notes that the buying and selling were not wicked in themselves but had invaded the sacred space set apart for prayer, turning the house of God into a place of commerce. The sign of the temple's destruction and raising in three days is the central sign of the entire Gospel: the cross and resurrection are the ultimate manifestation of Jesus's glory, the event to which all other signs point.

The anger of this scene needs handling in both directions. It is not incompatible with meekness: anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged, and Mark's account has Jesus arrive in the evening, look round at everything, and act the following morning (Mk. 11:11-15) — he slept on it. But the passage is not a warrant for aggression on God's behalf. Two things separate it from that: all of it is aimed at the dishonouring of God and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself, since under personal injury he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23); and it is the Son acting in his own house with the owner's authority.

The searching application is not the easy one about churches selling things. It is the Court of the Gentiles question: whether anything in the ordinary operation of a congregation — its assumptions, its vocabulary, the things everyone knows and nobody explains — makes it hard for an outsider to get near God. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space.

And the chapter's last word runs straight into the next scene: the printers' chapter break hides a joint. Verse 25 ends he knew what was in man (anthropos), and John's next sentence begins Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus — the general statement and its illustration set against each other like a caption and a photograph.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John places the temple cleansing early in Jesus' ministry — a deliberate theological statement. The Synoptics place it in Passion Week; John places it at the outset, framing Jesus' entire ministry as confrontation with corrupt religion. The temple courts have become a marketplace: animals for sacrifice sold at premium prices, currency exchanged at exploitative rates. What was designed as a house of prayer for all nations has become an economy of exclusion. Religion divorced from God's character always becomes commerce.

But the placement itself is the most-discussed difficulty in this Gospel, and it deserves more than a passing note, because saying John 'placed' it here can sound to a careful reader like saying John moved it. Matthew, Mark and Luke all put a temple cleansing in the last week of Jesus's life, days before the crucifixion. John puts one at the very beginning, with two and a half years of ministry still to run. So what happened?

There are two serious answers and a Christian may hold either. The first is the simplest: it happened twice. That is not the strained solution it sounds. The abuse was structural and profitable and would have resumed within a month of any one-off protest, and the details in the accounts differ in ways that fit two occasions rather than one — here Jesus makes a whip of cords and speaks of 'my Father's house,' while in the Synoptics he quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah about a house of prayer and a den of robbers. The authorities' question differs too. A man who did this once and was not stopped would be very likely to do it again, and a movement that began and ended with the same act of protest is entirely coherent.

The second answer is that John, who is writing last and openly arranges his material by theme rather than by calendar, has set this episode at the front as the doorway into everything that follows. That is not a claim that he invented anything or shifted a date to deceive; ancient writers were free to order true events for meaning, and John tells us plainly that he is selecting (20:30-31). On this reading the cleansing stands here for the same reason the prologue does — to say at the outset who this is and what he has come to do.

Either way the point of the scene is untouched, and it is worth holding on to when the chronology debate has run its course. The Lord has come to his temple, exactly as Malachi said he would (Mal. 3:1), and the first thing he does there is turn over the furniture.

Two things worth adding: what the trade actually was, and where in the building it was happening. The second is the one that turns a scene of general disapproval into something specific.

Start with the trade, because it is important to see that it had a rationale and was not obviously a racket. Every adult male Jew owed an annual half-shekel temple tax, and it had to be paid in a particular currency — Tyrian coinage, which was accepted because of the reliability of its silver content, and which most pilgrims arriving from around the empire did not have. So money had to be changed, and changing money involves a commission.

Likewise, an animal brought for sacrifice had to be without blemish and had to be certified as such, and a lamb carried a hundred miles has a poor chance of passing inspection. It was far more practical to buy one on site, pre-approved. Nothing in that system is corrupt on the face of it. It is convenience, and it grew up because people needed it.

Which is the first thing to say about it. The problem was not that somebody had smuggled something wicked into the temple. It was that a set of entirely reasonable arrangements, each defensible on its own terms, had between them turned worship into a transaction — and had done so gradually, with nobody deciding it. That is nearly always how it happens. Institutions do not usually rot by scandal. They rot by convenience.

Now the location, and this is the part most readers have never been told. The temple had concentric courts, and access narrowed as you went in: the innermost for priests, then Israelite men, then women. The outermost and by far the largest was the Court of the Gentiles — and it was the only place in the entire building where a non-Jew was permitted to come and pray. Beyond it stood a barrier with notices in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner who passed would have himself to blame for his death. One of those stones has been dug up and can be read today.

The market was in that court. The only square yard of earth on the planet where a Gentile could come near the God of Israel had been given over to livestock pens, currency tables, and the noise and smell of a cattle market on a festival week. The provision for the nations had been repurposed as retail space for the insiders.

That is why, in the other Gospels, the sentence Jesus shouts is from Isaiah and includes the clause we usually leave off: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations (Isa. 56:7; Mk. 11:17). The offence is not merely commerce in a holy place. It is that the arrangements of the religious had made it impossible for the outsider to pray.

Then let the verb do its work. He found those who were selling. He is not told about it; he arrives and looks. This is the Lord coming suddenly to his temple, as Malachi promised, and the first thing recorded is an inspection.

Which supplies a test that is more searching than the usual application of this passage. The usual application is about churches selling things, and it is not wrong, but it is easy and it is about somebody else. The harder question is the Court of the Gentiles one: is there anything about the way your church actually operates — its assumptions, its vocabulary, its arrangements, the things everyone knows and nobody explains — that would make it hard for an outsider to get near God? Not hard to enjoy. Hard to get near. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whip of cords, the overturned tables, the scattered coins — Jesus' action is deliberate, physical, and prophetic. This is not a moment of uncontrolled anger but of holy zeal acting out judgment. My Father's house: the possessive claim is simultaneously a christological statement (he is the Son) and a prophetic indictment (they have profaned what belongs to God). Calvin notes that Jesus cleanses the temple precisely so that genuine worship can take place. Reformation always begins with the clearing out of what has defiled the holy.

This is the passage people either enjoy too much or are quietly embarrassed by, and both reactions are worth taking seriously, because a great deal has been done in the world with the sentence Jesus made a whip.

Begin with what the text actually says, since the Greek is more restrained than the paintings. He made a whip of cords — improvised, from the rushes or ropes lying about a place full of tethered livestock; not an implement he brought. And the phrase rendered he drove them all out is followed immediately by with the sheep and oxen, which many read as specifying who the all were. It is grammatically possible to read it as including the traders, and honest to say the point cannot be settled from the words alone.

What is beyond dispute is that no one in the scene is struck. There is no injury reported, no blood, no arrest, and the authorities who arrive a moment later do not accuse him of assault — they ask him for his credentials. Whatever happened, it was not a brawl.

Look instead at how the action is graded, because the grading is the giveaway. The animals are driven out. The coins are poured out and the tables turned over. And the pigeon-sellers are told: take these things away. He does not tip over their cages — and the reason is almost certainly that pigeons were the offering of the poor, the sacrifice prescribed for those who could not afford a lamb (Lev. 5:7), and released birds do not come back. Even in the middle of it, the one thing he will not do is destroy what belongs to people who have nothing.

Now the pastoral question, which is real and which is usually handled badly in both directions. Is this consistent with the man who was meek and lowly in heart?

It is, and the way to see it is to ask what anger actually is. Anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged. A man who can watch his own child be harmed and feel nothing is not gentle; he is absent. The reason this scene sits so oddly with us is that we have quietly redefined gentleness as the absence of strong feeling, when in Scripture it is strength that has been brought under command.

Everything here is under command. He does not do it on impulse — Mark's account has him arriving in the evening, looking round at everything, and going out to Bethany for the night, and doing it the following morning (Mk. 11:11-15). He slept on it. Whatever this was, it was not a loss of temper; it was a decision made and executed the next day.

And then the guard, which is owed, because this passage has been used to justify a great deal that has nothing to do with it. It is not a warrant for Christians to be aggressive on God's behalf. It is not cover for the man whose temper is a standing problem in his household and who has learned to call it righteous anger.

Two things separate this from that, and they are not subtle. First, every scrap of it is aimed at the abuse of God's honour and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself — when the injuries were personal he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23). Second, this is the Son acting in his own house with the authority of the owner, which is precisely the authority the next verse is challenged about. If your anger is regularly about your own treatment, this passage is not about you.

Then the phrase that gives the whole act its footing: my Father's house. Not the house of God, not our Father's house — my. It is the same word Luke records him using at twelve years old, in this same building, to the parents who had been searching for him for three days: Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house? (Lk. 2:49). His first recorded sentence and this one make the same claim, roughly twenty years apart and in the same courtyard.

That is what licenses the whip. He is not a reformer with strong views about temple administration. He is the Son, standing in his own family's house, dealing with what has been done to it — and the word he uses for what it has become, a house of trade, is a word for a market hall. Somebody had turned his Father's home into a shop.

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Psalm 69:9 is applied to Jesus: the zeal of the Son for the Father's honor burns as it burned in the psalmist. The disciples' memory of scripture is the interpretive key to understanding Jesus's action. The Jewish leaders' response is not theological reflection but a demand for credentials: what sign? They want authorization, proof of authority. But the sign Jesus will give them is not one they can evaluate on their terms — it is the sign of the resurrection, which requires faith to receive.

There is something in the quotation that is easy to walk past and is almost certainly the point of it. John has changed the tense.

Psalm 69 says zeal for your house has consumed me — past, done, a thing that has already happened to the psalmist. What the disciples remember, and what John writes down, is zeal for your house will consume me. Future. And the verb underneath consume is not a mild one; it means to eat up, to devour entirely.

So the sentence they find themselves remembering as they watch him overturn the tables is not look how zealous he is. It is a prediction. This will eat him. What we have just seen him do is the thing that is going to get him killed — and in the plainest terms it was: the temple authorities are the ones who will finally move against him, and the charge that surfaces at his trial comes straight out of this same episode. The disciples watch a man clear a courtyard, and the verse that rises in their minds is about where it ends.

(Psalm 69 will not leave this Gospel alone. It is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, the long complaint of a righteous man hated without cause, and John will reach for it again at the cross when they lift up the sour wine (19:28-29). The zeal and the vinegar come out of the same psalm.)

And notice the verb attached to the disciples: they remembered. That word is going to matter in this chapter, because it happens twice and the two are not the same. Here they remember at the time — the Scripture surfaces while the coins are still rolling. In verse 22 they will remember something else, and it will take them three years and a resurrection to do it. Both are recorded, which is a mercy, because most of us have had both.

Now the practical question, since zeal is a word that makes tired Christians feel worse. What is being described here is not a temperament. Some people are naturally intense and some are not, and the intense ones are not thereby more godly; a great deal of what passes for zeal in religious life is simply a strong personality with a subject. What the disciples saw was not energy. It was a man who could not be indifferent to his Father's honour because he loved his Father, and the zeal was the shape the love took when the honour was being damaged.

Which means the question to ask is not am I zealous enough — a question no one has ever answered helpfully — but what does it take to move me. Everybody has something. Find the last thing that genuinely stirred you, that you could not simply let pass, and you have located what you love. The disciples watched their Master and concluded, from the evidence, that what he loved was his Father's house.

Then the demand in verse 18, and there is an irony in it that only grows as the book goes on. What sign do you show us? — asked in a Gospel built entirely out of signs, seven of them, by men who will be shown every one and believe none.

But look carefully at what they are and are not disputing. Nobody says the market should stay. Nobody defends the money tables or argues that the Court of the Gentiles was the right place for livestock. The abuse is conceded without a word. What is challenged is his standing to do anything about it: not you are wrong but who authorised you. That is the characteristic move of an institution under criticism, and it has not changed in two thousand years. The safest way to avoid a charge is to query the credentials of whoever brought it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' riddling word will follow him to the cross (Matt. 26:61) and become evidence at his trial. The authorities hear an architectural claim and respond with architectural logic: forty-six years of Herodian construction cannot be undone and redone in seventy-two hours. They are not wrong about their temple; they are catastrophically wrong about his. The pattern of misunderstanding in John is not stupidity but spiritual blindness: the natural mind cannot perceive the things of the Spirit without new birth.

Note first what kind of sentence this is, because it is stranger than the translations can show. Destroy this temple is an imperative — grammatically a command. He is not saying if you destroy it. He is saying: go on, then. Do it.

It is a challenge thrown at men who have just asked for his credentials, and it has the form of a dare that both parties know is not really a dare. They will not lay a finger on Herod's stonework. They will, in about three years, do precisely what he has invited them to do to the temple he actually meant.

And here is where it goes, which is worth following, because it is one of the clearest cases in the Gospels of how testimony gets bent. At his trial, witnesses are produced who say: We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands (Mk. 14:58). And as he hangs there, the people passing by shake their heads and jeer: Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days (Mk. 15:29).

Compare the pronouns. He said you destroy. They reported I will destroy. One word was moved, and the sentence changed from a prophecy about what they would do to him into a threat about what he would do to them. Nothing was invented. Something was shifted, and that was enough to hang a capital charge on.

The reply he gets is a piece of pure literalism, and it is the first appearance of a pattern that runs through this whole Gospel. They hear a claim about masonry and answer with a building schedule. In the next chapter a teacher of Israel will hear born again and ask whether a grown man can climb back into his mother (3:4). A woman at a well will hear living water and point out that he has no bucket (4:11). A crowd will hear bread from heaven and ask for a permanent supply (6:34). Every time, the misunderstanding takes the same form: the words are taken at the flattest possible level, and the flat reading is always the one that keeps the hearer from having to deal with him.

Their figure is worth pausing over, because it is the hardest date in the Gospels. Herod began rebuilding the temple in about 20 or 19 BC; forty-six years brings us to somewhere around AD 27 or 28. This one exasperated remark by a hostile official is one of the main pegs on which the chronology of Jesus's ministry hangs.

And there is a bitterness in it they could not have known. The building was not finished when they said this, and it would not be finished for another thirty-five years — the work went on until roughly AD 63. Then, in AD 70, the Romans burned it and pulled it down so completely that the stones came apart. They were boasting to the Son of God about a construction project that would be complete for about seven years.

They were not wrong about their temple; forty-six years of it could not be redone in three days, and nothing could. They were wrong about which temple was standing in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's editorial explanation is the interpretive key: the temple is his body. Jesus is himself the locus of God's presence, the place where heaven and earth meet, the dwelling of the divine glory. When the resurrection came, the disciples' memory connected back to this word and produced faith — not just in the resurrection but in the Scripture that foretold it. Resurrection does not only vindicate Jesus; it illuminates everything he said and everything the Old Testament promised. The resurrection is the hermeneutical event that makes all Scripture legible.

Follow the thread John is pulling, because it runs the length of the Bible and this verse is the knot in the middle of it.

In chapter 1 he wrote that the Word pitched his tent among us — the tabernacle, the tent in the wilderness where the glory came down. Here the tabernacle has become the temple: the fixed house, the place you travelled to, the address where God could be met. And John says the address is a body. Not a building that contains the presence, but a person who is it.

It ends where you would expect once you have seen the direction. At the very close of the Bible, John is shown the city that is the end of everything, and he records the one thing about it that startled him: And I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22). There is no building at the end. There was never going to be.

Now the sentence about the disciples, which is the pastoral heart of the passage. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this.

Read that carefully and notice what it concedes. They did not understand it at the time. They were standing right there. They heard the words with their own ears, they had every advantage of proximity, they were the inner circle — and it meant nothing to them for the best part of three years. Whatever they thought was happening in that courtyard, it was not what was happening.

Then it landed. Not through study, not through someone explaining it, but because an event occurred that made the old sentence suddenly legible, and the memory came up out of nowhere with its meaning attached. That is what he had promised would happen: the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you (14:26). This verse is that promise working, recorded by a man who was on the receiving end of it.

Which is the thing to take away for anyone in the middle of something they cannot read. There is a great deal of pressure on Christians to understand what God is doing while he is doing it — to have an account of the illness, the redundancy, the years that went nowhere, the prayer that was not answered. That pressure does not come from this book. The men closest to Jesus, watching the most important events in human history at a distance of a few feet, understood almost none of it until afterwards, and were not disqualified for it. What was asked of them was not comprehension. It was staying near enough to remember.

And notice the two objects of their believing, set side by side as though it were the most natural thing in the world: they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken. One verb, two things believed, and no distinction drawn between them. A sentence he said in a courtyard is placed alongside the Hebrew Scriptures as the same kind of object. Nobody in the verse argues for that. John simply writes it down, and it is one of the highest claims in the chapter.

Here is the test, and it is one you can only run backwards. Think of a stretch of your life you did not understand while you were in it, and ask whether you understand any of it now. Most people who have walked with God for twenty years can name at least one thing that made no sense at the time and is now the very thing they would not give back. That is not a technique for the present difficulty; it will not tell you what this one is for. But it is evidence about how the Lord works, gathered from your own life, and it is worth having in hand while you wait for the rest.

The last word on the temple belongs to the building. For a thousand years God had consented to be met in a house of stone — the smoke, the blood, the courts, the curtain, the one room no one could enter but once a year and never without blood. All of it was scaffolding around an absence. Then a man stood in the middle of it and said the meeting place was himself; and three years later they took him outside the wall and killed him; and the curtain in that house tore from the top to the bottom with no hand on it.

The house was never the point. The Son was the point, and the house had been saying so, in stone, for a thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sign-faith — believing because of miracles — is a real but fragile beginning. Jesus receives these believers but does not entrust himself to them. The Greek word for "entrust" is the same as "believe": they believed in him, but he did not believe in them. This is not cynicism but omniscience: Jesus knows the difference between intellectual assent to evidence and the saving faith that perseveres through suffering and offense. Not all who follow the miracle-worker will follow the crucified one. Keller notes that many want Jesus' blessings without Jesus himself.

The wordplay is worth setting out in full, because English cannot carry it and it is the whole verse. Many believed in his name — episteusan. But Jesus did not entrust himself to them — ouk episteuen. It is the same verb both times. They believed into him; he did not believe into them. John has put the two clauses side by side deliberately, and the effect in Greek is like a door swinging shut on its own hinge.

This is a frightening sentence, and it should be handled slowly, because it is the passage above all others that unsettles people who are already unsettled. If it is possible to believe in his name and be held at arm's length, how does anyone know which side of that line they are on?

Take first what is actually being described. These are people whose faith has been produced entirely by spectacle. They saw signs, and they were impressed, and impressed is what they are. Nothing has yet been asked of them; nothing has yet cost them anything; the whole thing has been going well and they have been carried along with it. John is not saying their belief is fake. He is saying it is untested, and that Jesus, who can see the whole of a person, knows exactly what it is worth and is not going to build on it.

He also shows us what happens to it. In chapter 6 the same crowd is fed on a hillside and follows him across a lake, and then he says something they find intolerable, and John records the outcome in one of the saddest verses in the book: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (6:66). That is this crowd, three chapters later, meeting the first thing they did not like.

Now the guard, and it needs saying plainly because the wrong reader is always the one who takes this to heart. If you are troubled by these verses — if you have read them and gone cold and started auditing your own conversion — notice that the people being described here were not troubled at all. They were delighted. Nobody in that Passover crowd was lying awake wondering whether their faith would hold, because nothing had yet happened to make them wonder. Anxiety about the reality of your faith is not a symptom of the condition described here. It is nearly always a symptom of caring whether it is real, which is the one thing this crowd conspicuously did not do.

And notice that John uses exactly the same phrase of these people that he used in the Prologue of the saved: believed in his name (1:12). He does not have a separate vocabulary for false faith. The words are identical, and the difference does not lie in the words. It lies in what the faith turns out to do when the wine runs out — which means the question is not, and never was, whether your believing began with the right feeling. Nothing in Scripture asks you to establish that. What it asks is whether you are still holding on.

There is a further comfort hidden in the grammar. He did not entrust himself to them — but he did not send them away either. He goes on speaking, and the very next thing that happens in this Gospel is that one member of the Jerusalem religious establishment comes to him at night with a compliment about signs, and gets the longest and tenderest explanation of the new birth anywhere in the Bible. Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing. It is a refusal to be naive, and it is the opposite of a dismissal.

Try the test, and it is not about your feelings. Think of the last thing following Christ actually cost you — not an inconvenience, a cost: money you will not get back, a friendship that cooled, a truth told when a lie would have been easier, a resentment you had every right to and let go anyway. If nothing comes to mind at all, that is worth knowing, and it is knowable now rather than later. If something does, then whatever you feel about your faith, it has already been out in weather, and this crowd never was.

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' knowledge of the human heart is comprehensive and unsolicited — he needs no information about people because he already knows. This divine omniscience is both terrifying and comforting: terrifying because nothing is hidden from him, comforting because his love is not naive. He knows the worst about every person and loves anyway. The one who "knew what was in man" chose to give himself for that very man. The cross is not an act of ignorance; it is an act of full-knowledge love, offered in the face of complete understanding of human sin.

Two things finish the chapter, and the second one is a joint that the printers of our Bibles have accidentally hidden.

First, the word that keeps appearing where you would least expect it. This is a Gospel obsessed with witness: John the Baptist is called to bear witness, the works bear witness, the Father bears witness, the Scriptures bear witness, and by chapter 5 Jesus will lay out a whole case with the witnesses named one after another. Testimony is the connective tissue of the book. And here, in the middle of it, John records the one subject on which he needed no one to bear witness. Everything about himself he was content to have testified to by others. About human beings he required no evidence, because he already had it all.

Second, and this is the thing to carry into the next page: the chapter division is in the wrong place.

Verse 25 ends with the word man — anthropos — for he himself knew what was in man. And the next sentence John wrote, before anyone had invented chapter numbers, begins: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. Same word, back to back. He knew what was in man — and here comes one.

Nicodemus is not a new subject. He is the illustration of the sentence that has just been made, and John has arranged it so that the general statement and the particular case sit against each other like a caption and a photograph. You are about to be shown, in one man, exactly what it is that Jesus sees when he looks inside somebody: a good, learned, genuinely searching member of the ruling council who has understood nothing, and who is going to be told that what he needs is not more instruction but to be born.

Which is also, incidentally, why the two halves of this chapter belong together. Verse 23 has a crowd believing because of signs. Nicodemus opens his mouth in a moment and says no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him — the crowd's exact position, in the mouth of the best-qualified man in Jerusalem. He is the sign-faith of verse 23 with a doctorate.

Then the double edge, and it will not resolve into one feeling. That Christ knows what is in a man is either the worst news or the best, and most of us hold both at once on different days.

It is the worst because there is no version of your life in which you get to present the edited copy. Not the account you give your friends, not the one you give yourself at three in the morning — the actual contents. He has read it. The one thing every human being spends real energy on, in one way or another, is managing what other people are allowed to see, and with him the whole apparatus is simply irrelevant.

And it is the best for exactly the same reason, on one condition — that you know what he did after reading it. This is not a verse about surveillance. It is the last line before the cross begins to be visible in this Gospel, and the man who knew what was in man went to Jerusalem anyway, into the hands of people whose contents he had read in full, and died for them. If he had loved us on the strength of a favourable report, the love would be worth nothing, because the report would have been wrong. There was no report. He looked.

Here is the test, and it is a short one. Is there anything you are hoping God has not noticed? Name it, silently, now. Then notice that the naming told him nothing, and that the chapter that follows this sentence is the one containing the words God so loved the world.

He knew what was in man. He knew what was in Judas on the night he dipped the bread and handed it to him. He knew what was in Peter when he looked at him and called him a rock. He knew what was in the men who would drive the nails, and in the crowd that would ask for Barabbas, and in every soul that has ever come to him carrying a rehearsed version of itself. He read the whole of it. He did not look away, and he did not revise the plan.

He went to the cross having already seen the worst thing about every person he was dying for.

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Nicodemus comes by night — a detail that is both literal and symbolic. He is a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, a teacher of Israel; he comes with flattery and openness, and Jesus cuts through all of it with the most radical statement in the Gospels: 'Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.' The new birth is not religious improvement or moral reformation; it is a sovereign act of the Spirit, as unpredictable and uncontrollable as the wind. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, cannot comprehend it — his very inability illustrates the need for it. The conversation ascends to the highest theological altitude in the Gospel: John 3:16, the summary of the entire Bible.

The chapter break hides a joint. Chapter 2 ends with the word man — he knew what was in man — and John's next sentence is Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. Same word, back to back: the general statement, and then its illustration. And the specimen chosen is the best in Jerusalem. A Pharisee, a member of the Sanhedrin, and shortly to be addressed as the teacher of Israel. If conviction, learning, discipline or religious office could get a man in, this one is already inside.

His bewilderment is the engine of the dialogue. Told he must be born anothen — a word meaning both again and from above — he hears the first sense and asks whether a grown man can re-enter the womb (v. 4). Jesus lets the misunderstanding stand, because a second natural birth would change nothing: that which is born of the flesh is flesh (v. 6).
