What is needed is birth of a different order — of water and the Spirit (v. 5), the promise of Ezekiel 36:25-27, where every verb belongs to God and there is not one instruction in the passage.

Verse 8 is a pun English cannot carry: pneuma is one word meaning both wind and Spirit, so Jesus is not saying the Spirit is like the wind but speaking of both at once. And the you of verse 7 is plural — through Nicodemus he is addressing the whole religious establishment. Nicodemus should have recognised the shape of it from his own Scriptures (v. 10): Ezekiel's new heart, Jeremiah's covenant written inward (Jer. 31:33), Moses' promise that God would circumcise the heart itself (Deut. 30:6).

Then the ascent. Only one person is qualified to speak of heavenly things, because only one came down (v. 13); if the earthly things are refused, the heavenly have no chance (vv. 11-12). The Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted the serpent (v. 14) — a word meaning both raised on a pole and exalted, and John will later stop the narrative to say it referred to the manner of his death (12:33). The section closes with the verdict already in place before Christ arrives — condemned already (v. 18) — and with judgement redefined as disclosure rather than sentence: the light came, and people loved the darkness (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills. No human being can produce it, control it, or predict it; the Spirit sovereignly regenerates those whom God has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man — as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness — is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God's motive is love for the world; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. The light has come, and the verdict of each person is revealed by whether they come to the light or flee from it.

The kingdom of God — the dominant phrase of the other three Gospels — occurs in John only here, at verses 3 and 5, and never again. And the verb shifts between them: without this birth a man cannot see the kingdom (v. 3) and cannot enter it (v. 5). The problem is not that he is outside a door he can see; he cannot perceive the country. This is why argument alone never works, and why Nicodemus is the proof of it.

Verse 6 states the impossibility as a principle of kind, not of quantity: like produces like, and nothing in creation generates something of a higher order than itself. Flesh here is not the body — this Gospel has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world — but human nature working with its own resources, including the best of them. So the failure of religious effort is not a failure of sincerity or degree. Effort was never the mechanism.

Verse 16 requires two corrections that make it larger rather than smaller. So loved renders houtos, an adverb of manner rather than degree: in this way God loved — he gave. The size of the love is not asserted but demonstrated. And the world in this Gospel is not a neutral term for the planet's population but humanity organised against God (1:10; 7:7; 15:18-19). The object of the love was the thing set against him. Verse 17's not to condemn is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgement exists — verse 18 says the opposite in the same breath. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anyone; that the drowning is real is why it was launched.
verseByVerse.examples:
Calvin writes that 'born again' (or 'born from above') is the most comprehensive description of salvation in the New Testament: it captures the totality of the transformation (rebirth, not reform), its source (from above, from God), and its necessity (without it, the kingdom cannot be seen). Sproul notes that Nicodemus's night visit is the first of several encounters in John where the darkness represents the condition of the human soul before the light breaks in. Keller observes that John 3:16 is not a formula to be memorized but a universe to be explored: every word contains inexhaustible depth.

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation, and the arc is the answer to anyone who thinks the night visit was a failure. He appears twice more, each time further into the open: in chapter 7 he speaks up in the council for due process and is shouted down (7:50-51); and after the crucifixion, when the twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he comes to a Roman execution in daylight with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39) — the quantity used at the burial of a king, carried through the streets by a member of the Sanhedrin. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon.

The bronze serpent repays being staged rather than cited. Israel complains; snakes come; people are dying through the camp. God's remedy is not to remove the snakes but to have Moses cast an image of the very thing killing them and raise it on a pole — an image, commanded by the God who forbade images, of the instrument of death — and the only requirement laid on a dying man is that he look. It is deliberately the one thing someone face down in the sand can still do. (Israel kept the bronze snake, and seven centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it and smashed it, calling it Nehushtan, the bronze thing — 2 Kgs. 18:4. Even the instrument of mercy becomes an idol if the look lands on it rather than through it.)

Verse 10 is the verse for the reader who knows his Bible and feels nothing. Nicodemus knows the texts and can almost certainly recite them; what he has never done is apply the promise of a new heart to himself, because he has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary. Note the tone of the rebuke, though: Jesus asks a question, does not end the conversation, and goes on to give this one bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than anyone else receives in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus has every credential the world honors: Pharisee, ruler, teacher of Israel. He comes by night — whether from fear of colleagues or in the darkness of spiritual incomprehension, John's night is never merely chronological. His opening is courteous and theologically generous: he acknowledges Jesus as a God-sent teacher authenticated by signs. But this generous assessment, while more than his colleagues offer, is still catastrophically insufficient. A teacher come from God is not the same as the eternal Son of God. Nicodemus has not yet seen what he needs to see.

Do not let the chapter number fool you into thinking a new subject has started. The sentence immediately before this one ended with the word man — he knew what was in man — and this one begins Now there was a man of the Pharisees. Same word, back to back, with nothing between them in the original. John has just told us that Jesus can read the contents of a human being, and now he opens one up in front of us to show what the reading looks like.

And he has chosen the best specimen in Jerusalem. Not a tax collector, not a prostitute, not a man with an obvious hole in his life. A Pharisee — one of the serious ones, the movement that took the law of God with total seriousness in the details of an ordinary week. A ruler of the Jews, which means a member of the Sanhedrin, the seventy-one men who governed the religious life of the nation. And in a few verses Jesus will call him the teacher of Israel, with the definite article, as though he held a recognised position rather than merely a good reputation.

If a man could be got into the kingdom of God by conviction, learning, discipline, moral seriousness or religious office, this man is already inside. That is why John put him here. The point of Nicodemus is not that he is a hypocrite. The point is that he is the best we have.

Then by night, and John never uses that word carelessly. It may be simple prudence: a member of the council calling on an unlicensed Galilean preacher whose first recorded act in Jerusalem was to overturn the temple furniture would not want to be seen doing it in daylight. It may be that night was the customary time for study and he wanted an unhurried conversation. But this is the Gospel that has already said the light shines in the darkness, and that will say in a few more verses that men love the darkness — and it is the Gospel that records, at the blackest moment of the story, the three words and it was night (13:30). The man comes out of the dark toward the light. Where he goes from there is the whole of his story.

Because he is not finished. This is the first of three appearances, and each one is further out into the open. Here he comes at night with a compliment. In chapter 7, when the authorities are moving against Jesus and the room is against him, Nicodemus speaks up — not bravely, but he speaks: Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing? (7:50-51). He is shouted down.

And then, after everything, when the twelve have scattered and the movement is finished and there is nothing left to gain and everything to lose, Nicodemus walks up to a Roman execution in broad daylight and helps take the body down, bringing with him about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39). That is not a devotional gesture. That is the quantity used at the burial of a king, carried through the streets by a member of the Sanhedrin in front of anyone who cared to look.

The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon. Whatever happened in the conversation that follows did not finish that evening, and it did not fail.

Now hear what he actually says, because it is generous and it is not enough. Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him. Every clause of that is true. It is also, precisely, the position of the crowd John has just described in 2:23 — people who believed because they saw signs, and to whom Jesus did not entrust himself. Nicodemus is that crowd with a doctorate.

And notice the pronoun. We know. He is speaking for others; there are colleagues who think this and have not come. He arrives representing a committee, and he will leave having been told something that no committee can act on.

A teacher come from God is a large thing to say and an infinitely small thing to say. It leaves Nicodemus in the position of a student, which is a position he understands and can occupy with dignity. What he is about to be told is that he does not need a better teacher. He needs to be born.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not answer the compliment; he answers the need. Nicodemus has not asked a question, but Jesus hears the one beneath the pleasantries: how do I enter the kingdom? The answer is total: new birth. Not reformation, not education, not religious advancement — birth from above. This is the Reformation's great rediscovery: grace is not the improvement of nature but its replacement, not the assistance of the will but its regeneration. You must be born again is not a demand that Nicodemus comply but a declaration of what God alone can do.

There is a deliberate ambiguity in the word Jesus chooses, and it is the hinge of the whole conversation. The Greek word (anothen) carries two meanings at once: it can mean "again," a second time, and it can mean "from above." Jesus intends the second — a birth that comes down from God — but the word will let Nicodemus hear the first, and hear it he does.

That is not stupidity on his part; it is the natural reach of a mind that has no category for what is being said. He takes "born again" to mean "born a second time" and asks the only question that makes sense on those terms: can a grown man crawl back into his mother's womb? The misunderstanding is built into the very word, and Jesus lets it stand, because the crude literal question exposes exactly the point.

A second natural birth would change nothing; flesh would still produce flesh (v. 6). What Nicodemus needs is not a repeat of the first birth but a birth of a different order altogether — one whose source is not below but above, not the womb but the Spirit. English cannot hold both senses in one word, which is why your Bible must choose "again" or "from above" in the margin. Jesus meant both, and needed both: it is a new birth, and it comes from heaven.

Two further things about this sentence, and the first is a small statistic that carries weight.

The kingdom of God is the phrase Jesus uses more than any other in Matthew, Mark and Luke — it is the headline of his preaching, the subject of most of the parables, the thing the whole Galilean ministry is about. In the Gospel of John it appears exactly twice, here and in verse 5, and then never again in twenty-one chapters. The great theme of the other three Gospels surfaces once, in a night-time conversation with one man, and is used to tell him that he cannot get in.

And notice the verb, because it changes when Jesus repeats himself. Here it is see the kingdom. In verse 5 it is enter it. Without this birth a man does not merely fail to get in; he cannot make out what he is failing to get into. The kingdom is not a locked room he is standing outside of, rattling the handle. It is a country he cannot perceive. That is why the argument never works from the outside — you cannot persuade someone toward a thing they are constitutionally unable to see, which is exactly what Nicodemus is about to demonstrate.

Which brings the practical weight of it. Nicodemus has spent his life on a project of improvement, and by any measure available it has succeeded. He is not being told that the project was fraudulent, or that he did it badly, or that he needs to try harder at it. He is being told it was the wrong category of thing altogether. You cannot educate your way into a family. You cannot be promoted into a bloodline. A man may study a language for forty years and speak it beautifully and still not be French.

Here is the test. Ask what would have to change for God to be more pleased with you than he is today. If the honest answer is a list — pray more, lose the temper less, be more generous, sort out the thing nobody knows about — then the answer is being given in the wrong currency, and this verse is aimed at exactly that instinct. Every item on that list may be worth doing. Not one of them is a birth.

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus's question is not absurd; it is the honest bewilderment of natural reason confronting supernatural necessity. He takes Jesus seriously enough to push back. Born of water and the Spirit — the most debated phrase in this passage — likely evokes Ezekiel 36:25-27 where God promises to sprinkle clean water (purification) and put his Spirit within his people. The new birth is the fulfillment of the new covenant promise: God himself will do what Israel could not do, cleansing and transforming from within.

Since it really is the most debated phrase here, the other readings deserve naming. Some take the water to mean Christian baptism, and read the verse as teaching that baptism is the instrument of the new birth — the historic position of Rome and, in a different form, of Lutheran teaching. Some take it to mean natural birth, the water of the womb, so that Jesus is saying a man must be born once physically and once spiritually. Others take it as John's baptism of repentance: you must come by the road John has been preaching, and then receive the Spirit.

The Ezekiel reading remains the strongest, and the reason is Jesus's own rebuke two verses later. He expects Nicodemus, as the teacher of Israel, to have known this already — which points to something Nicodemus could have read in his Bible, not to a Christian sacrament that did not yet exist. Ezekiel 36 puts the water and the Spirit together in exactly this order, in exactly this promise, and Nicodemus should have recognised it on the spot.

On baptism, the fair thing to say is that this verse cannot be made to carry the weight of baptismal regeneration on its own, and that the wider witness of the Gospel runs the other way: John says repeatedly that it is believing that gives life (1:12; 3:15; 20:31), and the dying criminal at Luke 23:43 receives Paradise unbaptised. Baptism is the sign of this birth and a precious one. It is not the machinery of it. What Jesus presses on Nicodemus is not a rite he has missed but a work of God he cannot perform on himself.

One thing worth adding, since the Ezekiel passage is named above and deserves to be seen rather than cited.

Israel is in exile. The temple is rubble, the land is lost, the name of God has been dragged through the mud of the nations by the very people who carried it — and into that, God says this: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses… And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you (Ezek. 36:25-27).

Count the verbs and notice who is doing all of them. I will sprinkle. I will give. I will remove. I will put. There is not one instruction in the passage. God is not telling a defeated people what to do about their condition; he is telling them what he intends to do about it, unilaterally, while they are in no position to contribute anything at all.

That is the passage sitting under this verse, and it is why Jesus can be surprised that a teacher of Israel does not recognise the shape of what is being said. The water and the Spirit were promised together, in that order, seven hundred years earlier, to people who had proved beyond argument that they could not fix themselves. Nicodemus is being told that the promise has arrived, and that he is one of the people it was made about.

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The principle is ontological: flesh produces flesh; Spirit produces spirit. Natural birth, however extraordinary the parents, cannot produce spiritual life. This is total depravity stated with compressed precision — not that the flesh is worthless in every sense, but that it is categorically incapable of generating the life of God. The new birth is not the improvement of the old nature but the creation of a new one. Sproul notes that we do not cooperate in our own birth; the initiative, the power, and the completion belong entirely to the Spirit who blows where he wills.

The principle is one everybody already accepts everywhere else. Like produces like. An apple tree does not, under any circumstances or with any amount of encouragement, produce a pear. Water does not rise above its source. Nothing in creation has ever generated something of a higher order than itself, and there is no reason to expect human nature to be the exception.

So the sentence is not an insult aimed at the body. Flesh here does not mean the physical as opposed to the spiritual — this is the Gospel that has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world. It means human nature working with its own resources: everything a person is by birth, including the best of it. The intelligence. The moral seriousness. The religious instinct. The genuine longing after God that had a member of the Sanhedrin walking through Jerusalem after dark to find one.

All of that is real, and none of it is spirit, and no quantity of it turns into spirit. Which is why the conversation has to go where it goes. If the flesh could produce even a little of the life of God, then the correct advice to Nicodemus would be to produce more of it — and every religion on earth gives exactly that advice, in one dialect or another.

There is a hard comfort in this for anyone who has spent years trying and getting nowhere. The reason the effort did not work is not that it was insufficient. It is that effort was never the mechanism. A man standing in a field willing an apple tree to bear pears is not failing through lack of sincerity.

And there is a warning on the other side, for the reader raised inside all this. Nothing transmits. Not the family, not the church, not the years of sitting under good teaching, not the vocabulary you can use fluently. Flesh gives birth to flesh in a manse as reliably as anywhere else.

Try the test, and it is a quiet one. Think of the last genuinely good thing you did that nobody knew about and that cost you something. Now ask where it came from — whether you talked yourself into it, or whether you found, somewhere in the middle of it, that you wanted to. Wanting to is not something the flesh generates on its own behalf. It is the sort of thing that has to be put there.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'You must be born again' — the 'you' in Greek is plural: not just Nicodemus but the Pharisees, the rulers, the whole of religious Israel. The wind analogy is precise: the Spirit's work is real and perceptible (you hear the sound) but not traceable or controllable by human observation (you do not know where it comes from or goes). The new birth is sovereign, mysterious, and undeniable in its effects. No one can predict who will be born again, or when, or trace the exact path of the Spirit's movement in a human soul.

English cannot carry what Jesus does here, and it is worth knowing what is being lost, because it is not an illustration — it is a pun, and the pun is the argument.

Pneuma is one word meaning both wind and Spirit. There are not two words being compared; there is one word being used twice. The same is true in Hebrew, where ruach is the wind over the waters in Genesis 1 and the breath in a man's nostrils and the Spirit of God, all at once. So the sentence in Greek runs something like: the Spirit blows where it wishes… so it is with everyone born of the Spirit. Jesus is not saying the Spirit is like the wind. He is saying a thing about wind and a thing about the Spirit in the same breath, and letting Nicodemus feel the join.

And there is a second word doing the same work: you hear its sound is phone, which is the ordinary word for a voice. The wind has a voice. So does the Spirit, and by the end of this Gospel the sheep will be the ones who know it (10:4-5).

Now the analogy itself, and it is more exact than it first appears. Wind is not vague. It is one of the most powerful forces on the planet; it takes roofs off and puts ships on rocks. What it is not is manageable. Nobody has ever arranged for it, or scheduled it, or made it come. You cannot see it at any point — only what it is doing to everything else. And it goes where it decides.

That is the answer to the question Nicodemus has been circling. He wants to know how. He is a teacher, and teachers deal in method; a method can be taught, examined, transmitted and improved. Jesus gives him weather. Not because the new birth is vague — nothing in this chapter is vague — but because it is not the kind of thing that has a technique attached.

Which needs saying carefully, because it can be misheard in two directions. It does not mean nobody can know whether they have been born again; John wrote a whole letter to settle that question. And it does not mean there is nothing to do. Wind is unmanageable and sailors are not therefore idle: they cannot make it blow, and they can put up a sail, and it makes all the difference whether they have. Reading, praying, sitting under the word, keeping company with God's people — none of these produces the wind. All of them are sails.

Notice also that the you in verse 7 has gone plural, as the note above says. He is no longer talking only to the man in the room. Through Nicodemus he is addressing the whole religious establishment — and past them, everyone who has ever assumed that being properly brought up, properly taught and properly serious would be enough.

Here is the test. Think of a Christian whose life plainly has something in it that yours does not — a settledness, a kindness that costs them, a hunger for God you have caught yourself envying. Now ask whether you could account for it. Where it came from, when it started, how they got it. Almost always the honest answer is no; there is simply an effect in the room and no visible cause.

That is what this verse says it looks like from the outside. You hear the sound. You cannot trace the wind.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can these things be?" Nicodemus asked. Jesus answered him, "Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus's second "How?" is deeper than his first: not mocking incredulity but genuine confusion. Jesus' response is gentle but pointed — the teacher of Israel should recognize the contours of the new covenant promised in Ezekiel and Jeremiah. The failure is not intellectual but spiritual: the Scriptures he has spent his life studying were pointing to exactly this, and he has not seen it. Expert knowledge of the Bible does not guarantee encounter with its subject. Knowing the text and knowing the God of the text are not automatically the same thing.

The article is the sting. Jesus does not say are you a teacher of Israel — he says the teacher, as though Nicodemus held a recognised standing rather than merely a good reputation. This is the man other teachers consulted.

And the rebuke is precise about what he should have known. Not the Christian gospel — that had not been preached yet, and Jesus does not blame him for failing to anticipate it. He should have known the shape of it from his own Scriptures, and the promises are not obscure ones.

Ezekiel was told God would sprinkle clean water and put a new spirit within his people. Jeremiah was told of a covenant written not on tablets but on hearts, so that no one would need to say know the LORD because they all would (Jer. 31:33-34). Moses himself, at the very end of his life, told a nation he knew would fail that the LORD your God will circumcise your heart — the outward sign made inward, done by God, on the organ that actually decides things (Deut. 30:6).

All three say the same thing: Israel's problem is not information and the solution will not be effort. God will have to operate. A man who had spent forty years in those texts had every piece of the puzzle on the table in front of him.

So the failure is not a gap in his reading. He knows the verses. He can almost certainly recite them. What he has never done is apply them to himself — because the promise of a new heart is only good news to a man who has concluded that his own heart is the problem, and Nicodemus has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary.

This is the verse for the reader who knows his Bible and feels nothing. It is a real condition and it deserves to be named rather than scolded. A person can hold correct positions on every disputed doctrine, follow an argument through Romans, spot a bad sermon inside two minutes, and have the whole apparatus running on nothing. The knowledge is not the problem — Jesus does not tell Nicodemus to read less. But the same equipment that lets a man handle Scripture well can also let him handle it at arm's length, permanently, as a subject rather than as a summons.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable in proportion to how much of the Bible a person knows. When was the last time a passage went through the defences — not taught something new, but got past the part of the mind that assesses and landed on the part that hopes or fears? If that has not happened for a long time, the answer is not more study. Nicodemus proves that. The answer is the thing he is being told about, and it is not something he can arrange.

Note the tone, though, before this turns into an attack on learning. Jesus asks a question. He does not dismiss him, does not end the conversation, and goes on talking to him for another eleven verses — giving this one bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than he gave anyone else in the Gospels. The rebuke is real and it is not a rejection. It is what it looks like when the light shines on somebody it intends to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The "we" is striking — Jesus speaks as the representative of a divine communion, bearing witness to what God knows from within. The testimony is rejected not for lack of evidence but for lack of spiritual receptivity. The argument moves from the less to the greater: if you cannot receive the earthly analogy (wind, birth), how will you receive the heavenly reality it points to? Revelation always exceeds comprehension; faith always outruns sight. Nicodemus is being called to trust a witness whose knowledge of heavenly things surpasses all earthly verification.

The plural is genuinely odd — we speak of what we know — and it is worth naming the possibilities rather than gliding over it. It may be the Son speaking with the Father and the Spirit, out of the communion the Prologue described. It may be Jesus placing himself alongside John the Baptist and the other witnesses whose testimony has already been given and refused. It may simply be the plural of one who speaks for heaven rather than for himself. What is certain is the contrast, because the second half of the sentence is plural too: you do not receive our testimony — and that you takes in the whole body Nicodemus came representing.

Then the argument from the lesser to the greater, and it is worth being clear about what the two categories are. Earthly things does not mean trivial things. It means the things that happen down here — a birth, a wind over a field, water and Spirit at work in a man in Jerusalem. Those are the things Jesus has been talking about for eight verses. Heavenly things are what is about to come: a descent from heaven, a lifting up, a Son given, the love of God for the world. If the visible end of it cannot be received, the far end has no chance.

Which is a principle with a wide application, and it cuts against a common instinct. People frequently want to begin with the heavenly things. The questions that get asked first are almost always the furthest out — predestination and free will, what happens to those who never heard, the timetable of the last days, why there is suffering. They are real questions and this commentary does not sneer at them. But notice the order Jesus insists on. He will not take a man to the mysteries of heaven who has not yet dealt with the mystery standing in the room, which is that he needs to be born and cannot arrange it.

And notice what is not being said. He does not say Nicodemus cannot understand; he says he does not receive. The obstacle is not intellectual horsepower — this is the best-equipped mind in the country. Testimony is not the sort of thing you solve. It is the sort of thing you either take from the witness or refuse, and refusing it is not a failure of comprehension but a decision about a person.

Here is the test. Think of the doctrine you find hardest — the one you circle back to, the objection that has never quite been answered to your satisfaction. Now ask honestly whether the plain things have been settled: whether the reality of your own need, and the sufficiency of Christ for it, are matters you have dealt with, or matters that remain conveniently open while the harder question absorbs the attention. Sometimes an unresolved difficulty at the far end is exactly what it appears to be. Sometimes it is a very well-appointed waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grounds his heavenly authority in his heavenly origin: he can speak of heavenly things because he has come from heaven. No mystic, no prophet, no ascent-tradition figure has this — the Son of Man alone has descended. Then the pivot: the serpent of bronze lifted on a pole in the wilderness (Num. 21:8-9) becomes a type of crucifixion. Those who looked to the lifted serpent lived; those who look to the lifted Son of Man will have eternal life. The cross is not an accident; the must signals divine necessity — it must be so because God's redemptive plan from the beginning required it.

Lifted up is the third time in three chapters that this Gospel has used a word with two meanings and intended both. The darkness did not overcome — or understand — the light (1:5). A man must be born again — or from above (3:3). And now hypsoo, which means to raise something physically off the ground, and also means to exalt, to promote, to lift to honour.

By now this is plainly a method rather than a coincidence, and John does not leave it to be guessed at. He uses the word twice more (8:28; 12:32) and then, the second time, stops the narrative to explain it in his own voice: He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die (12:33). So the double meaning is fixed. The lifting up of the Son of Man is a crucifixion, and it is a coronation, and there is no version of this Gospel in which those are two separate events. The throne is the cross. The exaltation is the execution. He is never more visibly the King than when he is nailed six feet in the air with a placard over his head announcing it.

Now go back to the desert, because the picture Jesus reaches for is one of the strangest things in the Old Testament and repays being looked at properly.

Israel is in the wilderness, nearly at the end of forty years, and they complain — about the food, about the route, about God and Moses in the same sentence: there is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food (Num. 21:5). Then the snakes come, and people begin to die, all through the camp, in numbers. And when they cry out, God's answer is not what anyone would design. He does not remove the snakes. He tells Moses to make one — to cast a serpent in bronze and put it up on a pole where the whole camp can see it — and the instruction is that anyone who has been bitten and looks at it will live.

Consider how much is wrong with that remedy on the face of it. It is an image, made at the direct command of the God who had thundered from Sinai that they were to make no graven image. It is an image of the very thing that was killing them, raised in the middle of the camp like a standard. And it does not require the dying man to do anything at all — not to repent visibly, not to bring an offering, not to travel anywhere. A man face down in the sand with poison already in him has one thing left that he can still do, and it is to turn his head.

The bronze snake had an afterlife, too, and it is worth knowing. Israel kept it. Seven hundred years later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it, and gave it a contemptuous nickname — Nehushtan, roughly the bronze thing — and broke it in pieces (2 Kgs. 18:4). Even the instrument of God's mercy will be turned into an idol if it is kept long enough. The look was never meant to land on the bronze.

Then the word that governs the whole sentence: so must the Son of Man be lifted up. Not may, not will choose to. Must. It is the language of necessity, and John uses it about the cross repeatedly. Given what God had determined to do about sin, and given what sin is, there was no other route. The cross is not a tragedy that overtook a good plan; it is the plan, and it was the plan before there was a wilderness or a serpent or a nation to be bitten.

Which leaves the reader who feels his sin is the thing killing him — and that reader is not being melodramatic; it is what the passage says is happening. The instruction to him is not to fight the snake. It is not to explain how he came to be bitten, or to demonstrate improvement first, or to feel the appropriate degree of horror. It is to look. That is the whole of it, and it was deliberately made the one thing a dying man can still manage.

Look at what the sign in the desert was really saying, and then at what it was pointing to. God's remedy for a dying camp was to lift up an image of the very thing that was killing them, and to ask nothing but a look. Fifteen hundred years later the Son of Man was lifted on a Roman post outside a city wall — and what hung there was sin. Not his own; he had none. Every ounce of it, gathered onto one body, in daylight, where the whole camp could see.

He became the thing that was killing us, so that looking at him would be the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scope of the promise is universal in offer and particular in application: whoever — any who will — believes. Eternal life is not merely life extended in duration but life of a new quality, the very life of God shared with those who trust in the lifted Son of Man. Sproul emphasizes that this eternal life begins now, not at death — the one who believes already possesses what death cannot take. Nicodemus came seeking the kingdom; Jesus offers something more — not merely entry into the kingdom but the life of the King himself.

This is the first appearance in the Gospel of the phrase that will end up being its whole purpose — eternal life — and it arrives attached to a snake on a pole, which is not where anyone would have put it.

Two words are worth having. Aionios does mean unending, and the endlessness is not to be quietly dropped in favour of something more sophisticated. But the noun matters more than the adjective: zoe, the word from 1:4, the life that was in the Word from the beginning and was never on loan from anywhere. Eternal life is not primarily a very long time. It is a kind of life — his kind — shared out.

Which is why Jesus can define it later in a way nobody would predict from the phrase itself: And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (17:3). Not a location, not a duration, not a reward scheme. Knowing a person. Everything else in the promise follows from that and none of it comes first.

And the tense is the thing to hold on to. May have — present. Not will receive at death, not will be awarded at the judgement. This Gospel will keep saying it in the present tense until there is no way to miss it: whoever believes has eternal life (6:47); whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life (5:24). Passed. Already. The tense is doing pastoral work — it means that for anyone in Christ, death is not the doorway into eternal life but an interruption in the middle of it.

Notice too what the requirement is, because verse 14 has just set the terms and this verse keeps them. Whoever believes. Not whoever understands — Nicodemus is proof that understanding is not the entrance. Not whoever qualifies. The dying Israelite did not have to comprehend the metallurgy of the bronze snake; he had to trust that the God who told him to look meant it.

Here is the test. Ask what would be true tomorrow morning if eternal life had already started. Most of us, if honest, are living as though the real thing begins later and the present is a waiting room with better or worse furniture. This verse says the substance is already in hand and only the delivery is outstanding — which changes what a bad diagnosis is, and what a good week is, and what is actually at stake in a Tuesday.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So loved' — the adverb points to the manner and degree of the love: in this way, to this extent. 'The world' — not just Israel but the whole of fallen humanity, the object of God's love despite its rebellion. 'His only Son' — the gift is not an angel, not a prophet, not a lesser being but the Father's own eternal Son. 'Whoever believes' — the scope is universal; the condition is faith. 'Should not perish but have eternal life' — the two destinies are perishing and life; the distinction is not natural but covenantal. The Son is sent to save, not to condemn — the condemnation is already there; the mission is rescue.

One practical note, since a reader may have noticed it and wondered. Is Jesus still speaking here, or has John taken over? Bibles disagree visibly: some close the quotation marks at the end of verse 15, which makes the best-known sentence in the Bible John's own comment rather than a saying of Jesus; others run the speech on to verse 21. In a red-letter edition the verse may be printed in red or in black depending on which publisher you happen to be holding.

The honest answer is that we cannot be certain, because the earliest manuscripts have no quotation marks at all — punctuation is the editor's judgement, not the apostle's. There are reasons for thinking John is now reflecting: the tense shifts to the past, God's giving of his Son is spoken of as a completed thing, and the phrase 'only Son' is one John uses in his own voice elsewhere (1:14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Others reply that nothing in the passage signals a change of speaker and the thought runs on unbroken from the serpent in the wilderness.

What is worth saying plainly is that nothing whatever hangs on it. If John wrote it, it is the Spirit-carried testimony of the apostle who leaned on Jesus's chest, and it is Scripture. If Jesus said it, it is Scripture. The words are not more true in red ink. And either way they are the settled summary of what the man in front of Nicodemus had come to do.

Now the harder problem with this verse, which is not textual at all. It is the best-known sentence in the world, and familiarity has worn it smooth. It is on placards at football matches and on the bottom of paper cups. A verse can be worn out the way a coin is worn out — still legal tender, and the face rubbed off. So it is worth taking the words apart, slowly, as though they had not been heard before.

So loved. The word is houtos, and here the commonly preached sense needs correcting without losing anything. It is not primarily an adverb of degree meaning so much. It is an adverb of manner: in this way, thus, like this. The sentence is not measuring the love and pronouncing it enormous. It is pointing at something and saying: that is how. God loved the world in this way — he gave his Son. And of course the degree comes flooding back in the moment the manner is stated, which is why the traditional reading is not wrong in its instinct. But the grammar puts the emphasis where the verse puts it. The size of the love is not asserted. It is demonstrated, and then left standing.

The world. This is the word that has been quietly sentimentalised. In this Gospel kosmos is almost never a neutral term for the population of the planet. It is humanity organised against God — the world that did not know him (1:10), that cannot receive the Spirit (14:17), that hates Christ and will hate his people (7:7; 15:18-19). That is the object of the love. Not a world that was lovable and therefore loved; a world that was hostile and loved anyway. Take the sentimental reading and the verse says God cared about a rather nice planet. Take John's own vocabulary and it says God set his love on the very thing that was set against him.

He gave. Not sent, though he did send. Gave. To give a thing is to part with it, and the whole weight of the verse rests on the fact that the giver did not keep what he gave.

Should not perish. The alternative is stated without softening, and modern ears want it softened. Perish is a real word about a real outcome, and Jesus uses it more than anyone else in the New Testament. This is not a verse about improving people's lives. It is a rescue verse, and rescue implies something to be rescued from.

Then verse 17, which needs a guard, because it is regularly used to cancel the rest of the paragraph. God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world. That is gloriously true and it is a statement of purpose, not a statement that judgement does not exist — as the very next verse proves, since it says outright that those who do not believe are condemned already. The two sit together without strain. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anybody. That the drowning is real is precisely why it was launched.

Here is the test, for a verse most readers can say from memory. Try saying it about yourself, out loud, with your own name where the world stands, and notice whether anything in you flinches. Most people can affirm the sentence as a general truth for years without ever once letting it be true in the particular. It was not written to be agreed with. It was written to be believed by somebody.

He gave. That is the verb, and it is not a lending or a risking or a dispatching on a mission with a fair expectation of return. The Father had one Son — eternally his, the delight of him before there was a world to be delighted in — and put him into the hands of a race that this Gospel has already described as not knowing him and not receiving him.

And the world he loved was not lovely. That is the whole scandal of the sentence. Nothing on this side was the reason for it. The love came entirely from the side of the one who was doing the loving, and it has never needed anything here to keep it going.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Condemned already' — the natural state of humanity apart from Christ is not neutral; it is already under judgment. The coming of Jesus does not introduce condemnation; it introduces the possibility of escape from a condemnation that was already in place. 'People loved the darkness' — the judgment is not arbitrary; it reflects the settled preference of the human heart. The darkness is comfortable because it conceals the evil of human works. The light is unwelcome because it reveals them. The verdict of the last day is simply the disclosure of the verdict already present in each person's response to Christ.

Everything turns on one word, and it is the word that frightens people: already.

Take it slowly, because it is more merciful than it sounds. The verse is not saying that a sentence is passed on people the moment they hear about Christ and decline. It is saying the sentence was passed long before, and that the arrival of Christ is not what put anyone in danger. He walked into a situation that was already lost. Nobody was standing in neutral territory waiting to see how they felt about him.

Which means the gospel is not an examination that a person might fail. It is a rescue that a person might refuse — and those are entirely different things, though they feel similar from the inside. In the first, Christ increases the risk. In the second, he is the only reason the risk has an exit.

Now the guard, because this verse does real damage in the hands of the wrong reader. There are people who read condemned already and immediately begin auditing themselves for whether they have believed hard enough or sincerely enough to have crossed the line. Read the sentence again. The condemnation attaches to one thing only: because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. It is not measuring the quality of anyone's faith. It is distinguishing between those who have come to him and those who have not. A weak hand on a strong rope is not the same as no hand at all, and this verse is about which rope, not about the strength of the grip.

Then verse 19 does something startling, and it is easy to read past. It defines the judgement — this is the judgement — and the definition is not what anyone would write. Not a throne, not a book opened, not a sentence pronounced. The light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light.

The judgement, in other words, is not primarily something done to people at the end. It is something disclosed about them now. God's verdict turns out to be the publication of a preference that was already there and already operating. That is why the last day can be perfectly just without anybody being surprised by it: the evidence will be what each person actually loved, and every one of them chose it themselves, in daylight, repeatedly.

And note the verb, because it is stronger than the one we would use. Not tolerated the darkness, not drifted into it, not failed to escape it. Loved it. The problem the Bible describes is not that people cannot find their way to the light. It is that when the light arrived, in person, in a country prepared for him, something in the human heart preferred the alternative — and preferring is an act of love, however unflattering the object.

Which locates the real difficulty exactly where Nicodemus has been told it is. If unbelief were an information problem it could be solved by teaching, and he of all people would already be safe. It is an affection problem. And affections are not argued into place; they have to be born.

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The movement toward or away from Christ is morally diagnostic: it reveals the orientation of the heart. Those whose works are evil flee the light instinctively, not because the light is bad but because exposure is unwelcome. Those who 'do what is true' — who are oriented toward reality and God — come to the light, because they want their works to be seen as what they are: carried out in God. This is not a works-righteousness system but a description of the spiritual trajectory of genuine faith versus settled unbelief.

The reason given for avoiding the light is worth stating plainly, because it is one of the most accurate sentences ever written about human beings: lest his works should be exposed.

The verb is a courtroom and workshop word — to bring to light, to test, to show a thing up for what it is. And the instinct it describes is universal and immediate. Nobody has to be taught it. A child who has broken something goes quiet and moves toward the door. The whole apparatus of adult life — the edited version we give at dinner parties, the tone we adopt in an email that is covering for something, the friendships that stay carefully shallow — is a very sophisticated development of the same reflex, which is to stay where the lighting is favourable.

And this is where the verse becomes uncomfortable rather than merely true, because avoidance of the light is not usually experienced as avoidance. It is experienced as being busy. It is felt as not having time to pray, or as finding a particular book of the Bible dull, or as a sudden strong preference for reading about the faith rather than sitting still in front of God. The man in this verse is not shaking his fist. He simply does not come.

Then the other side, and the phrase in it is a Hebrew idiom that English flattens: whoever does what is true — literally, whoever does the truth. In Scripture truth is not merely a property of statements. It is something a person can do, or fail to do; it means integrity, faithfulness, being in reality the thing one appears to be. So the two groups are not the clever and the stupid, or the religious and the irreligious. They are those who will come out into the open and those who will not.

Keep the guard the note above puts in place, and make it sharper, because this pair of verses can be read as saying that good people come to Christ and bad people avoid him — which would undo the whole chapter. Read the last clause: he comes to the light so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God. The works were done in God. Whatever is found in the light was put there by the one holding the lamp. Nobody in this passage brings his own goodness to the light for inspection and passes. The new birth stands behind every honest thing a person has ever done, which is exactly why coming into the light is not the terrifying act it looks like from outside.

Here is the test, and it is easy to run. Notice what happens in the first few seconds after somebody criticises you accurately. Not what you eventually conclude after a day of turning it over — the first movement, before the reasoning starts. If it is a scramble for cover, an immediate counter-example, a mental list of the critic's own faults, that is the reflex of this verse, and everyone has it. The question this chapter asks is not whether the reflex is there. It is whether anything has been born in a person that is capable of overriding it and walking toward the lamp.

The remarkable thing about the Christian life is that it makes exposure survivable. The light that shows everything up belongs to the one who came not to condemn but to save — which means the worst that can be found has already been dealt with, and there is nothing left in the file that can be used.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John the Baptist's final testimony in this Gospel is the most beautiful articulation of humble submission in the New Testament. When his disciples come to him alarmed that Jesus's ministry is drawing larger crowds, John does not feel threatened. He feels fulfilled. 'He must increase, but I must decrease' — eight words that define the entire posture of the genuine servant of God. John is the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom; his joy is complete when he hears the bridegroom's voice and can step aside. The one who comes from above is above all; what he testifies to is true; whoever receives his testimony has set their seal to this: God is true.

The setting is easy to skip and John supplies it carefully. Jesus is in the Judean countryside and his disciples are baptizing — the narrator will tighten this a page later to say Jesus himself did not baptize (4:2) — while John is at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there (vv. 22-23), a logistical note rather than a theological one. Two ministries run side by side for months, and no other Gospel records the period at all. The reason we have it is the bracket at verse 24: for John had not yet been put in prison — an aside from a writer who knows the other accounts begin the Galilean ministry after that arrest, and who stops to steady a reader who would otherwise be confused.

What triggers the testimony is a dispute over purification (v. 25) — whose washing counted — which is the question this Gospel has been circling since six stone jars for the rites of purification stood at a wedding in chapter 2. The disciples' complaint is the language of a threatened camp: he who was with you, to whom you bore witness, and then all are going to him (v. 26), which is not true and which they know is not true. All is what anxiety says.

John's first answer is the root of everything that follows and is easily the most overlooked verse in the section: a person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven (v. 27). Not most things — not one. If Jesus has the crowds, heaven gave them; if John's are thinning, heaven arranged it; and if John ever had a crowd, that was given too, which removes any basis for treating it as his to lose. He then repeats for the third time in this Gospel that he is not the Christ (v. 28) before reaching for the wedding.
verseByVerse.theology:
John the Baptist's final words in this Gospel are also its most concentrated theological summary: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God's wrath. There is no middle ground: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

Verse 30 contains a word that is usually missed: both verbs carry must. Not I ought to step back graciously but a divine necessity — the same word Jesus used at verse 14 of the Son of Man being lifted up. The rise of one and the waning of the other are a single arrangement, and it was not the Baptist's to negotiate. These are also his last recorded words in this Gospel; he does not appear again except in the past tense.

The closing verses hold eternal life and wrath in the same frame, and the pairing at verse 36 is deliberately asymmetrical: not believes against does not believe, but believes against does not obey (apeitheo, refuses to be persuaded). The unbelief in view is not doubt politely held but the refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed.

And the final verb is this Gospel's own great word. The wrath of God remains on him is menei, from meno — the abiding word, whose first appearance was the Spirit coming down and remaining on Jesus (1:32-33), which reappeared when the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed (1:38-39), and which carries the whole of chapter 15. Something abides on everyone. On Christ the Spirit rests and does not lift; in his people he himself abides; and on the one who refuses him the wrath he was already under simply stays, because nothing has happened to move it. Nothing arrives — which is the same truth as condemned already at verse 18, said with a different verb, and which is also where the mercy lies: what remains can be lifted, and this chapter has already said how.
verseByVerse.examples:
Keller notes that 'he must increase, I must decrease' is the defining characteristic of all genuine ministry — the minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ's has misunderstood the calling. Stott observes that the image of the friend of the bridegroom captures perfectly the joy of the one who serves another's marriage rather than his own: he is not jealous, not diminished, but fulfilled in the fulfillment of the one he loves.

The friend of the bridegroom is sharper than a general lesson in humility once the role is understood. He arranged the marriage, carried the messages between the families, handled the negotiations, and on the night stood outside the chamber on guard. The wedding was in a real sense his project — and the moment the bridegroom's voice was heard inside, his work was finished and his job was to go home. The Greek doubles the joy for emphasis: he rejoices with joy, and the perfect tense of verse 29 says that joy is now standing complete, at the exact moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life. And if Jesus is the bridegroom there is a bride, and she is not the audience at the wedding — she is the one being married.

Verse 30 must not be left sentimental, because of what it cost. Within months John was arrested for telling the truth about a marriage, and from that cell he sent to ask whether Jesus was after all the one who was to come (Matt. 11:2-3) — not the question of a serenely fulfilled man, but of one whose decrease had gone further than he bargained for. He was beheaded without trial to settle a promise made in front of dinner guests. And Jesus' verdict, delivered while he was in that cell doubting, was that among those born of women no one greater had arisen (Matt. 11:11).

This is the passage for anyone being replaced — the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the retirement that arrived before the sense of usefulness did, the body doing less than last year. The world has no account of those except loss. Note where the weight of the sentence actually falls: he must increase is doing all the work, and the second clause is only its shadow. Nobody in Scripture is asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking; the decrease is bearable, and is even a completed joy, solely because of who fills the space.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallel ministries of Jesus (through his disciples, as 4:2 clarifies) and John in the Judean countryside create the occasion for the Baptist's final great testimony. Both are baptizing, both are drawing crowds — yet they are not rivals. John's ministry at Aenon near Salim (the exact location is uncertain but Samarian) continues its appointed function: preparing people through repentance and washing. The geography of grace is generous; the Spirit was moving simultaneously in multiple places through multiple servants.

One correction the narrator himself supplies a page later, and it saves a false impression: although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples (4:2). John records the fact and then goes back and tightens it. There is no record anywhere in the New Testament of Jesus baptizing a single person with his own hands — which is worth noticing in a chapter about water, and which Paul echoes when he thanks God he baptized almost nobody at Corinth, precisely so that no one could attach themselves to the man who did it (1 Cor. 1:14-17).

Then a detail so ordinary it is usually skipped: because water was plentiful there. Not a theological remark — a logistical one. Aenon means something like springs, and the note tells us why a preacher pitched at that particular spot: there was enough water. Which quietly settles a question people argue about, since a man who only needed to sprinkle would not have to go looking for abundant water.

What matters more is the picture of two ministries running at once, in the same region, doing overlapping work, without either man treating the other as competition. Jesus is in the Judean countryside. John is thirty or forty miles off at Aenon. Both are drawing crowds. Neither has issued a statement about the other. The only people in this passage who are worried about the arrangement are the followers, which is how it usually goes.

There is something worth learning from a scene in which nothing happens. Two men are doing overlapping work in the same country at the same time, and the text records no meeting, no agreement, no division of territory, and no comment from either about the other. They simply get on with it.

That is not indifference; John will speak about Jesus in a moment with more warmth than anyone in the Gospel. It is that neither of them experienced the other's existence as a problem requiring management. The absence of a strategy here is itself the point. Where two works are genuinely God's, they do not need a treaty.

And notice who is where. Jesus has left Jerusalem — the temple, the council, the centre — and gone out into the Judean countryside. He was in the capital for a feast, had the attention of a member of the Sanhedrin, and could have stayed and built on it. He goes to the fields instead, where the water is, and works there for months that no other Gospel records.

Here is the test, and it is for anyone who has a work of their own, however small. When another church in your town does well, or another department, or another parent's child, what is the first thing that happens in you before the correct response arrives? Not what you say — what happens. These verses describe two ministries running side by side with no anxiety in either of them, and the only unease in the passage belongs to men who were not doing either.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This parenthetical note anchors John's gospel chronologically in relationship to the Synoptics, where John's imprisonment marks the beginning of Jesus' Galilean ministry (Mark 1:14). Here the two ministries overlap — a period the Synoptics pass over quickly but John lingers on, because this overlap produces John's most profound testimony about the relationship between the herald and the bridegroom. The parenthesis is not editorial fussiness; it is a temporal marker that helps readers locate this climactic testimony in redemptive history.

It is worth sitting with what this little bracket implies about the writer. He is aware that other accounts of Jesus exist. He knows they open the Galilean ministry with the sentence after John was arrested (Mk. 1:14), and he knows a reader coming from those accounts will be confused to find John still at liberty and still baptizing. So he stops the narrative and puts in a note.

That is not the behaviour of a man inventing. It is the behaviour of an old eyewitness filling in what the earlier accounts left out, aware of where his readers may trip, and taking the trouble to steady them. This whole stretch — the months when the two ministries overlapped, before the arrest — is a period the other Gospels simply pass over. John was there for it, and it is the reason we have the finest words on humility ever spoken by a human being, which would otherwise have been lost entirely.

And there is a shadow across the parenthesis. Not yet put in prison. The reader is being told, in advance and in passing, how this ends. The man about to say the loveliest sentence in the Gospels is a few months from a cell, and rather less than that from an executioner sent to settle a promise made at a birthday party. He says I must decrease without knowing the half of what it will mean, and it turns out he meant it anyway.

Which is worth stopping over, because it describes a position most people occupy at some point. John says the finest sentence of his life in a stretch of months when things are visibly going against him — his crowds thinning, his best men transferring, and a prison he cannot see yet already waiting. The words were not spoken from a settled retirement. They were spoken on a downward slope, by a man who could feel the gradient and did not yet know where it went.

Almost nobody gets to say he must increase, but I must decrease from a position of strength. It is said, when it is said at all, by people whose decrease has already started and is not going to be reversed — and that is precisely when it counts, and precisely when it is hardest to mean.

The bracket also does something quietly generous to the reader. It tells the end of the story before the story is told. There is no suspense left about whether the Baptist's humility will be rewarded with a comfortable old age; the arrest is announced in advance, in a parenthesis, almost apologetically. What follows has to be read knowing how it turns out — which is exactly the position everyone reading it is in about their own life, minus the parenthesis.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' report is tinged with jealousy on their master's behalf: all are going to him. They expect John to be troubled by the competition. The dispute over purification rituals provides the occasion for the question of authority — whose baptism counts, whose ministry is authentic? The disciples are thinking in terms of religious competition; John is thinking in terms of divine purpose. Competitive ministry — measuring one church against another, one preacher against another — always misunderstands the nature of service to Christ.

Notice what triggers the whole thing, because John records it as an aside and it is not an accident: a discussion arose… over purification. The argument that produces the New Testament's greatest statement about humility began as a dispute about ceremonial washing — whose water counted, which rite was valid, who had the authority to administer it. This Gospel has been circling that question since chapter 2, when six stone jars for the Jewish rites of purification were standing empty at a wedding and were filled with something else entirely.

And look at how the complaint is put, because every word of it is the language of a threatened camp. He who was with you across the Jordan — the phrasing puts Jesus in a subordinate position, the junior figure who used to be part of John's operation. To whom you bore witness — with the implication that he owes his standing to their master, and is now trading on a reference. And then the sentence that gives the game away: look, all are going to him.

Which is not true, and they know it is not true, since John is standing in front of a crowd big enough to require a spring. All is what anxiety says. It is the arithmetic of a man watching numbers move in the wrong direction, and it is one of the most reliable symptoms of the disease: nobody who is genuinely at peace about a comparison ever needs to reach for a total.

The saddest thing in the verse is that they are being loyal. They are not attacking their master; they are defending him, and they have come to him with what they take to be bad news out of real affection. That is worth naming, because this is how the ugliest instincts in church life usually present themselves. Almost nobody is consciously jealous. They are concerned. They are concerned about standards, about where things are heading, about a church down the road that seems to be doing rather well.

There is one more thing in the report that gives it away, and it is the smallest word in the sentence. Look — ide, an imperative. They are not informing him. They are directing his attention, the way one does when a person is failing to be as alarmed as the situation warrants. They want him to see what they see.

And he will not look at it, because he is looking at something else. That is the whole difference between the disciples and the master in this passage, and it is not a difference of temperament. They are measuring one ministry against another, which is the only arithmetic available to a man who does not know who Jesus is. John is measuring nothing, because he settled the question at the Jordan and has not reopened it since.

Here is the test, and it is not about ambition. Notice which facts about other Christians you retain. Most people can recall, without effort and often for years, the numbers, the growth, the invitation someone else received. Facts of that kind do not stay in a memory by accident; they are kept because something in us is keeping accounts. It is possible to be entirely sincere, and loyal, and generous in speech, and still be running a ledger that God never opened.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John's first answer cuts to the root of all ministry theology: everything is gift, nothing is earned or accumulated. If Jesus is drawing more followers, it is because heaven has given it. If John's crowds are diminishing, it is because heaven has arranged it. Sovereignty over ministry success belongs entirely to God. This single sentence dismantles every form of ministerial envy, rivalry, or pride. The one who understands that everything comes from heaven has no reason to be threatened by another's abundance, because he knows his own abundance (and shortage) comes from the same source.

It is worth weighing how absolute the sentence is, because the temptation is to hear it as modesty and move on. A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven. Not most things. Not the important things. Not one.

Applied to the case in hand it is devastating in both directions at once. If Jesus is drawing the crowds, heaven gave him the crowds — so envying him is a complaint against God. If John's numbers are falling, heaven arranged that too — so the decline is not a failure to be fought but an allocation to be accepted. And if John ever had a crowd in the first place, that was given as well, which removes at a stroke any basis for regarding it as his to lose.

That last move is the one that does the work, and it is the reason this single sentence dismantles ministerial envy at the root rather than merely scolding it. Envy always requires a sense of ownership somewhere — the assumption that a thing was mine, or ought to have been. Take away the ownership and there is nothing left for the envy to attach to. A man cannot be robbed of what he was only ever handed.

It also cuts the other way, against the reflex to take credit. Whatever gift a person has for teaching, or organising, or listening well, or making a room feel safe — none of it was manufactured. The intelligence was issued. The temperament was issued. Even the capacity to work hard, which feels more like an achievement than anything else on the list, was issued.

Here is the test, and it is quick. Think of another Christian, or another church, whose fruitfulness has cost you something to look at. Now try saying about them, in plain words and meaning it, that heaven gave them that. Most of us can manage the sentence. Rather fewer can manage it without immediately adding a qualification — although, of course… The qualification is the thing to notice. It is the sound of a man who has not quite conceded that the giving was God's to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John reaches for the wedding metaphor to describe his relationship to Jesus. The bridegroom is Christ; the bride is the people of God; John is the best man — the shoshben in Hebrew tradition who arranges the marriage and stands with the groom. The best man's joy is complete when he hears the bridegroom's voice speaking to the bride. This is the purest description of gospel ministry: arranging the encounter between Christ and his people, then stepping back in joy when the meeting happens. Joy that is complete is joy that has achieved its purpose.

Two details make the image sharper than a general point about humility.

The first is what the friend of the bridegroom actually did. He was not a decorative figure. In Jewish custom he arranged the marriage, carried the messages between the families, handled the negotiations, and on the night itself stood outside the bridal chamber on guard. The wedding was, in a real sense, his project. He had worked at it for months and it was the most important thing he had done that year. And the moment the bridegroom's voice was heard inside, his work was over and his job was to go home.

The second is the grammar of the joy, which the Greek doubles for emphasis in a way English cannot: he rejoices with joy at the bridegroom's voice. It is not resignation dressed up. It is not a man being gracious about a disappointment. And it is not the joy of a spectator — it is the specific gladness of somebody whose own work has just succeeded, and whose success takes the form of being no longer required.

Which is why the tense in the last clause matters: this joy of mine is now complete — a perfect tense, a thing brought to fullness and standing full. Not will be complete one day when I have made my peace with this. It is finished, now, at the exact moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life.

Note also what he is not in this picture, and he says it himself for the third time in this Gospel: I am not the Christ. He has been saying it since chapter 1, to delegations and to disciples, and it has never once sounded like a disappointment. The reason he can watch the crowd leave without panic is that he never mistook himself for the reason they came.

And there is a quiet largeness in the metaphor that should not be walked past. If Jesus is the bridegroom, there is a bride — and she is not an afterthought or an audience. The people being baptized in that river, and the ones who would follow for two thousand years, are not the crowd at the wedding. They are the one being married.

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most profound ministerial theology in Scripture, in seven words. Must increase, must decrease — both are divine necessities, not human preferences. John does not choose to decrease as a pious gesture; the must signals that this is the appointed order of redemptive history. Jesus' glory is not competitive with John's; it is its completion. As Stott observes, any preacher, teacher, or leader who does not have this as their conscious ambition has confused themselves with the one they serve. The herald's glory is to become unnecessary once the King has arrived.

These are the last recorded words of John the Baptist in this Gospel. He does not appear again except in the past tense. Whatever else is true of the man, this is the sentence he goes out on, and it is worth reading as a final statement rather than a devotional maxim.

Both verbs carry the same small, hard word: must. It is not I ought to try to decrease, or I have decided to step back graciously. It is the language of necessity — the same word Jesus used four verses earlier about the Son of Man being lifted up. The rise of one and the shrinking of the other are not two separate events, one admirable and one regrettable. They are a single arrangement, and it was not John's to negotiate.

The two verbs come from the world of measurement and light. To increase is to grow, to spread, to become more; to decrease is to be made less, to wane, the word used of a river dropping in the dry season or the moon going down. And that image is the right one, because it is exact: the moon has no light of its own, its whole business is to shine when the sun is not there, and its going is not a tragedy but the arrival of morning.

Now the part that turns this from a fine sentiment into something costly. He said it, and then it happened — and not gently.
