Within months he was arrested by Herod for telling the truth about a marriage. He spent the rest of his short life in a fortress cell. From there, in the dark, he sent messengers to ask Jesus whether he was in fact the one who was to come, or whether they should look for someone else (Matt. 11:2-3) — which is not the question of a man serenely fulfilled, but of a man whose decrease had gone considerably further than he had bargained for. And he was beheaded, without trial, to settle a promise made in front of dinner guests.

That is what I must decrease came to. It is worth knowing, because it stops the sentence being sentimental. He was not describing a manageable step backwards into a supporting role. He was describing, without knowing it, the whole remainder of his life.

And Jesus' verdict on him was delivered while he was in that cell, doubting: among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist (Matt. 11:11). The greatest man who ever lived, on the assessment of the only person qualified to make it, is the one who arranged his entire existence around becoming unnecessary — and who wobbled at the end, and was called the greatest anyway.

This is the verse for anyone being replaced. The younger colleague who is plainly better at it. The role handed on. The children who no longer ring. The retirement that arrived before the sense of usefulness did. The body that is simply doing less than it did, and will do less again next year. Every one of those is a decrease, and the world has no account of them except loss.

Here is the test, and it is a hard one to fail honestly. Think of the thing you are most afraid of losing — not possessions; standing. Being needed, being consulted, being the one who knows. Now ask what would be left if it went. If the answer is nothing much, then the thing has quietly become the self rather than the service. John's answer to that question was a person, standing in a river a few miles away, and it was enough to make the losing of everything else a joy rather than a bereavement.

He must increase. That clause is doing all the work, and the second clause is only its shadow. Nobody in Scripture is ever asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking. The decrease is bearable — is, in fact, a completed joy — solely because of who is filling the space.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether these are John the Baptist's words or the Evangelist's reflection (the transition is debated), the theology is clear: origin determines authority. He who comes from above speaks with heavenly authority; he who is of the earth — even the greatest prophet — speaks from earthly perspective. Jesus' testimony is heavenly because his origin is heavenly. Yet no one receives his testimony: the most authoritative witness in history is the most rejected. This is the scandal of the incarnation — God speaks and the world stops its ears.

That parenthesis about the transition is the same question raised at verse 16, and for the same reason: the Greek has no quotation marks, so where the Baptist's testimony stops and the Evangelist's reflection begins is the editor's decision rather than the apostle's. It happens twice in this one chapter, which tells you something about how John writes — he moves from reporting a voice to adding his own without seam or announcement, because in his mind the two are saying the same thing. And as at verse 16, the authority of the words is unaffected either way.

One thing more, on the sentence that ends the verse: yet no one receives his testimony.

Taken flatly it cannot be right, since the next verse begins whoever receives his testimony — so somebody plainly does. This is the Bible's ordinary way of speaking about a general refusal, the same idiom as a man saying nobody came about a poorly attended meeting where in fact eleven people came. It is not a statistic. It is a lament.

And it is the same note the Prologue struck: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11). The testimony is perfect. The witness has seen and heard what he is describing, at first hand, which is more than can be said for any other teacher who has ever lived. The evidence is not the problem, and it never has been.

The first half of the verse is the one to hold on to, though, because it states the principle underneath everything in this chapter: he who comes from above is above all.

Origin decides authority. And the sentence in the middle is unexpectedly humbling about the alternative: he who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. That is John the Baptist describing himself — the greatest man ever born of women, according to the only assessment that counts, filing himself under earth without complaint. He is not being falsely modest. He is being accurate about the one distinction that matters, which is not between a great man and a small one but between everyone born here and the one who came from somewhere else.

Which is why no amount of religious excellence closes the gap, and why Nicodemus at the start of this chapter and the Baptist at the end of it are in the same category and know it. The best teacher in Israel and the last of the prophets are both of the earth. Only one person in the passage came down, and he is the only one with anything to report.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To believe Jesus is to certify God's truthfulness. Faith is not merely personal benefit; it is a public declaration about God's character. The one who trusts Christ affixes a seal — a legal metaphor — attesting that what God has said is true. Conversely, to reject Christ's testimony is to call God a liar (see 1 John 5:10). Faith and unbelief are not merely personal choices; they are theological positions about the integrity of God. The gospel stakes everything on the truthfulness of the Father who sent the Son.

The picture behind the word is worth having. A seal was pressed into wax or clay by a signet ring, and it was the ancient equivalent of a signature on a contract — it meant this is mine, I stand behind it, and it can be produced against me later. Setting a seal was not an opinion. It was a commitment with legal teeth.

So faith, in this verse, is not first a feeling or even first a benefit received. It is a signature. To believe Christ is to put one's name to the claim that God tells the truth — and to do it in advance of most of the evidence, since a great deal of what God has said has not happened yet.

The reverse is stated elsewhere with a bluntness that stops the breath. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar (1 Jn. 5:10). That is not rhetorical overreach. If God has testified about his Son and a man declines the testimony, there is no third position available; he has, in effect, filed a statement that God's word cannot be relied upon.

Which quietly disposes of the idea that unbelief is a modest, humble posture — the reasonable caution of someone who simply has not seen enough. It is a verdict, and it is a verdict about somebody's character.

And there is comfort in the same image, on the other side. A seal works both ways in Scripture. Believers are told they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Eph. 1:13). The one who signs his name to God's truthfulness discovers that God has already signed his name to him.

Here is the test, and it is a way of finding out what has actually been signed. Think of a promise of God that your circumstances currently contradict — that he works all things for good, that he will never leave, that the light is not overcome. Now ask which of the two you are treating as the fixed point: the promise, or the circumstance. Everybody has one of them as the constant and the other as the thing to be explained. Faith is not the absence of the contradiction. It is which side of it a man puts his name to while the contradiction is still standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one God sent speaks God's words — not in the partial, mediated manner of the prophets who received the Spirit for specific occasions — but without measure. The Spirit's fullness in Christ is qualitatively different from every previous anointing in Israel's history. And the foundation of all this is the Father's love for the Son: the mission of the Son flows from the eternal love of the Trinity. The Father gives all things into the Son's hand because he loves him. Mission is always downstream of the eternal love within the Godhead.

There is a genuine ambiguity in the middle clause, and both readings are true, so it is worth naming rather than smoothing. He gives the Spirit without measure — the Greek does not supply the subject. It can mean the Father gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, which fits what the Baptist saw at the Jordan when the Spirit came down and remained on him (1:32-33). Or it can mean the Son gives the Spirit without measure, which is what he is said to do from chapter 7 onwards, and what the Baptist announced at the very beginning: this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.

The two hold together, and the order between them is the point. The Spirit rests on the Son without limit, and out of that fullness the Son gives — which is why what reaches the believer is not a diluted portion. Israel's prophets had the Spirit for a task and a season; a measure was issued, and it was withdrawn. The one speaking here holds him without a ceiling.

Then the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand, and the two halves belong together as cause and consequence. The handing over of all things is not an administrative arrangement. It is what love does: the Father withholds nothing from the Son because he loves him.

And a phrase worth holding on to, for later in this Gospel. All things into his hand — the same hand out of which, in chapter 10, Jesus will say no one is able to snatch his sheep (10:28-29). What has been put into that hand includes people, and nothing has ever been taken out of it.

The Father loves the Son. Before there was anything made, or anyone to save, or a world to be given up for, that was already the case — and it is the oldest fact in existence. Everything in this chapter runs downstream of it. The Son was given because the Father loves him and would share him. All things were put into his hand because the Father loves him and would deny him nothing.

The love that holds the universe together is not a policy God adopted toward creatures. It is what was going on between the Father and the Son before there were any creatures — and the gospel is the announcement that it has been opened, and that there is room inside.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter that began with new birth ends with the sharpest possible alternative: eternal life or the abiding wrath of God. The symmetry of "believes" and "does not obey" reveals that saving faith is not mere intellectual assent but covenantal allegiance — it includes obedience. The wrath of God is not a future threat but a present condition: it remains on those who reject the Son. Calvin is clear that this wrath is not God's caprice but his settled, holy displeasure against all that contradicts his character. The only escape is the Son — precisely because the Son bore that wrath in his body on the tree.

The verb at the end of this chapter is the one this Gospel began with, and the effect of noticing it is chilling.

The wrath of God remains on him. The word is menei — from meno, the abiding word, the great verb of the fourth Gospel. Its first appearance was in chapter 1, when the Baptist watched the Spirit come down and remain on Jesus, and knew by that sign who he was (1:32-33). Its next was two verses later, when the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed with him (1:38-39). It will run all the way to chapter 15 and the vine: abide in me, and I in you.

And here is the same verb, at the close of the chapter, describing what settles on a man who will not have the Son. Something abides on everyone. On Christ, the Spirit rests and does not lift. On those who are his, he himself abides. And on the one who refuses him, the wrath he was born under simply stays where it was, because nothing has happened to move it.

Which is exactly the point the verse is making, and it is easy to miss because we hear wrath and picture something arriving. Nothing arrives. The wrath is not sent as a punishment for unbelief; it remains, in the present tense, as the condition that was already in place — the same truth as condemned already in verse 18, said now with a different verb.

Note also the pairing, which is deliberately asymmetrical. Not believes against does not believe, which is what we would expect, but whoever believes against whoever does not obey. The word is apeitheo — refuses to be persuaded, will not comply. John is not smuggling works into salvation. He is saying that the unbelief in question is not an intellectual position politely held but a refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed. It is closer to insubordination than to doubt.

Now the guard, because this verse frightens people and some of them are the wrong people. It is not addressed to the Christian who has bad days, or doubts, or a faith that feels thinner than he wishes. The one described here is not struggling with the Son; he is declining him. And the whole sentence turns on a present-tense contrast — has eternal life against remains — which means the two conditions are not being weighed at some future assize. They are the two states people are in this evening.

Which is also where the mercy is, and it is enormous. If wrath remains rather than arrives, then it can be lifted rather than merely postponed — and this chapter has already said how. It was lifted the way the poison was lifted in the desert: not by the dying man's exertion but by his looking at something raised up on his behalf.

The chapter opened with a man who came in the dark because he did not want to be seen. It closes with a sentence about what is resting on people. And between them stands the Son of Man lifted up, and the announcement that God gave him, and the promise that whoever looks will live.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus's conversation with the Samaritan woman is the longest one-on-one dialogue in the Gospels. Every element of the encounter crosses a boundary: Jesus crosses from Judea to Samaria, from Jewish to Samaritan territory; he speaks to a woman alone at a well, violating social convention; he engages with someone of scandalous personal history; he reveals himself as the Messiah to an outsider before he does so publicly to his own people. The conversation moves from physical water to living water, from the woman's five husbands to the question of true worship, from worship in Jerusalem or Gerizim to worship in Spirit and truth. The woman who came alone to the well in the midday heat returns to her village as the first evangelist in John's Gospel.

The journey is an appointment, not a shortcut. John says Jesus had to pass through Samaria (v. 4) — edei, the same little word used of the new birth at 3:7 and of the Son of Man being lifted up at 3:14 — and the geography flatly contradicts it, since Jews routinely took the longer road down the Jordan valley to avoid Samaritan territory. The necessity was not topographical. What sets him on that road is the same necessity that sets him on the cross. And what prompts the departure is the report from the end of chapter 3: the Pharisees hear that he is baptizing more disciples than John (vv. 1-3), the very news that had troubled the Baptist's own followers.

He arrives exhausted (vv. 5-6) at ground layered with covenant memory — Jacob's field, Joseph's burial place, the mountains of the blessing and the curse — and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, which by strict opinion meant drinking from an unclean vessel (vv. 7-9). She hears living water in its ordinary sense of running water and objects, sensibly, that he has no bucket and that the well is deep, and asks whether he is greater than Jacob (vv. 11-12) — a rhetorical impossibility that happens to be the question of the chapter. She asks for the water for entirely practical reasons (v. 15), and Jesus does not correct the motive; he changes the subject to her husband (vv. 16-17), the point at which the conversation stops being about a topic and acquires a particular life.

Told about worship, she calls him a prophet (v. 19) and raises Gerizim — a mountain visible from that well, still carrying the rubble of the temple a Jewish ruler had destroyed about 128 BC. Jesus abolishes the dispute rather than settling it, and then says the thing that stops this being a story about tolerance: salvation is from the Jews (v. 22). The Samaritans expected not a king but a teacher who would tell us all things (v. 25), which is precisely what he then does — I who speak to you am he, the first plain self-disclosure in the Gospel and the first of its I am sayings.

The disciples return and marvel, and John records the two questions nobody asked (v. 27) — one of them the very question Jesus had put to his first followers at 1:38. The woman leaves her jar (v. 28) and the town comes out (v. 30). Then the harvest discourse the section is usually cut short of: his food is to do the Father's will and finish his work (vv. 31-34); the fields are white already, not in four months (vv. 35-36) — he is pointing at Samaritans crossing the fields; and the reapers are entering labour that was not theirs (vv. 37-38). He stays two days in a Samaritan town, eating their food under their roofs (vv. 39-40), and it ends with the townspeople telling the woman they no longer believe on her word but their own (v. 42), and with the title that closes the episode: the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious program or a moral reformation; it is himself — the inexhaustible source of eternal life. 'The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' Jesus does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. The worship in Spirit and truth for which the Father seeks is not worship in a particular location but worship in the reality of who God is (truth) and by the power of God's own Spirit — the worship that the new covenant makes possible through the regeneration that Nicodemus could not understand.

The living water is explained by John himself later in the book. Standing in the temple Jesus cries out about rivers of living water, and the narrator adds the interpretation — this he said about the Spirit (7:38-39). So the gift offered at the well is the indwelling Spirit, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp one chapter earlier, now pictured as a spring rather than a well. The distinction matters: a well is a store that must be gone to, lowered into and hauled from; a spring is water arriving from underneath under its own pressure, and the verb for welling up means to leap. What Jesus gives does not merely satisfy the drinker — it turns the drinker into a source.

Worship in spirit and truth is not sincerity set against ritual. Spirit is the Holy Spirit who enables it, and truth in this Gospel is a person before it is a quality (14:6) — so both halves are gifts rather than techniques. What is ruled out is worship that is correct and dead, and worship that is warm and invented: truth without Spirit is a corpse, Spirit without truth is a mood. And God is spirit (v. 24) does not mean God is vague or impersonal — the God described here speaks, seeks, loves and sends — but that he has no body and no location, and therefore cannot be arrived at or run out of.

The decisive clause is the Father is seeking such people to worship him (v. 23). Worship is ordinarily conceived as the search conducted from this end; here God is the one out looking, which is precisely what the chapter has been narrating since verse 4. A woman went to a well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come three days out of his way. Note too that salvation is from the Jews is from, not for: the privilege was a channel and never a possession.
verseByVerse.examples:
Keller notes that Jesus's method with the Samaritan woman is a model of contextual evangelism: he begins with her felt need (water), moves to her deeper need (the living water), exposes the root issue (her relationships), and leads her to the question of worship and the identity of the Messiah. He does not condemn; he illumines. Calvin observes that the woman's testimony — 'Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did' — is the most basic form of Christian witness: here is someone who knows me completely and has not rejected me.

The five husbands deserve more care than they usually get. John never calls this woman immoral; Jesus never mentions sin to her, never calls her to repent, and never says go and sin no more — which he does say to the woman of chapter 8 and the man of chapter 5. A woman could not divorce in that world, so five marriages behind her means five times widowed or five times dismissed, or some mixture — things done to her at least as readily as by her. The town does not behave as a town behaves toward someone it has cast out: she speaks, they listen, they come (vv. 29-30, 39). The honest answer is that we are not told, and it matters that it be said, because women have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. (The old reading of the five husbands as an allegory of the five nations resettled in Samaria in 2 Kgs. 17 should also be resisted: it dissolves a real woman into a diagram, which is the one thing this passage refuses to do to her.)

Her testimony is instructive precisely because it is so poor by our standards. One fact, about herself; overstated (all that I ever did, when he had named one arrangement); no doctrine; and a closing line phrased in Greek to expect the answer no — nearer to this couldn't be the Christ, could it? And the town emptied. What travels is not the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Notice what her sentence leaves out: she never says and he did not despise me, because that is the tone of the whole remark. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted — which is the thing most people are most afraid of.

The harvest section is for the discouraged sower, and there are many. One sows and another reaps contains no promise that the sower sees it; the parent who prayed for thirty years, the teacher whose class drifted, the missionary who left with nothing to report are all inside that saying. The promise is in the verse before: sower and reaper rejoice together. In ordinary farming the reaper takes the visible result; here the arrangement is deliberately made so that neither can celebrate without the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees are tracking the growth of Jesus' ministry with the metric of discipleship numbers — a measure John's gospel immediately qualifies: Jesus himself did not baptize. The clarification matters: the growth is not a personal empire-building project but the movement of the Spirit through servants. When religious authorities begin measuring ministries by numbers, they have already confused the kingdom of God with institutional competition. Jesus does not flee Jerusalem because he fears the Pharisees but because his hour has not yet come — everything is governed by divine timing.

Read this straight on from the end of chapter 3 and it stops being a bare travel note. Three verses earlier, John's disciples came to him upset and said all are going to him. Now the same report reaches the Pharisees — and John words it with deliberate care: the Pharisees heard, and Jesus learned that they had heard. The same piece of news travels to two different sets of ears, and the reactions could not be further apart. In one camp it produces a jealousy their master will not share. In the other it produces surveillance.

It is worth noticing what the news actually was, because it was numbers. Not doctrine, not a healing, not a claim he had made — a count of disciples. The first recorded reason the religious authorities began taking an interest in Jesus is that he was growing faster than the competition.

Then the correction in the bracket, which the narrator has come back to add: although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples. John has already told us in 3:22 that Jesus was baptizing, and here he tightens it. There is no record anywhere in the New Testament of Jesus baptizing a single person with his own hands.

That is not a trivial tidy-up. It removes, at a stroke, any possibility of a class of Christians who could say they were baptized by Jesus personally. Paul saw the same danger at Corinth and was relieved to have baptized almost nobody, precisely so no one could form a party around the man who did it (1 Cor. 1:14-17). Whatever divides the church, it was never going to be a hierarchy of who had the better officiant.

And what does he do about the surveillance? He leaves. Not in fear — this is a man who had recently cleared the temple courts with a whip in front of these same authorities. He goes because a collision now would be premature, and everything in this Gospel runs on an hour that has not yet come. There is a kind of courage that consists of walking away from a fight you could win, at a moment of your own choosing, because the fight is not the point.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The geographical had to is not topographical necessity — a Jewish traveler could go around Samaria — but divine compulsion. The Spirit was driving Jesus through territory Jews typically avoided: Samaritans were considered half-breed apostates, the unclean residue of Assyrian deportations mixed with foreign settlers. That Jesus had to go through Samaria is John's announcement that the gospel will not respect the ethnic boundaries that religious tradition has erected. Every human barrier that excludes the seeker from the Savior is, for Jesus, an occasion for crossing.

The word is edei, and it is worth pressing, because the geography flatly contradicts it. There was a perfectly good road that avoided Samaria — down the Jordan valley through Perea and up again — and Josephus tells us Galileans used it routinely. Devout Jews took the long way round as a matter of course. Going through Samaria saved perhaps three days; it was the quicker road, not the compulsory one. So when John writes that Jesus had to pass through Samaria, he is not reporting a fact about maps.

It is the same little word this Gospel keeps using for things that are settled in heaven. You must be born again (3:7). So must the Son of Man be lifted up (3:14). And now: he had to go through Samaria. The necessity that put him on that road is the same necessity that put him on the cross.

Which means the whole chapter is an appointment. A woman is going to walk out to a well at the hottest hour of the day, on an errand she has run a thousand times, and find that the shortest route between Judea and Galilee has been redrawn in heaven so that a tired man would be sitting on the wall when she arrived.

And it is worth being honest about who the Samaritans were, since half-breed apostates is how their neighbours described them rather than a neutral account. When Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC it deported the leading families and resettled foreigners in the land, and the population that resulted was mixed in blood and in religion (2 Kgs. 17:24-34). By Jesus' day they held to the five books of Moses and nothing else — no prophets, no psalms — and they worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem.

The hostility was not ancient prejudice looking for a cause. It had recent history in it: around 128 BC a Jewish ruler, John Hyrcanus, marched north and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim. That ruin was still visible from the well. When the woman raises the mountain in a few verses, she is not opening an abstract debate about liturgical geography. She is pointing at rubble that Jews had made.

Here is the thing to take from a verse about a road. Most people can look back and find a detour in their own life that made no sense at the time — the job that fell through, the move nobody wanted, the illness that emptied a diary. This verse does not promise that every such thing has a well and a waiting woman at the end of it. It does say that the one who arranges routes is not confined to the ones that look sensible, and that at least once in history the pointless-looking detour was the whole plan.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The geography is thick with covenant memory: Sychar near Shechem, the field of Jacob's inheritance, the well that Jacob dug. Jesus sits at the intersection of Israel's patriarchal past. And he is weary — genuinely, physically tired, the weariness of a man who has been walking in the midday heat. The incarnation is not a divine costume; Jesus' exhaustion is real. The one through whom all things were made (1:3) now rests at the well his ancestor dug, waiting for the Father's appointment with a woman no one expected.

Stand at that well for a moment, because almost everything in the paragraph is doing work.

The ground is Jacob's, and John says so twice. This is the field Jacob bought outside Shechem when he came back from Paddan-aram, the first piece of the promised land any patriarch ever owned outright (Gen. 33:18-20). It is the plot he willed to Joseph (Gen. 48:22), and it is where Joseph's bones were finally buried after being carried out of Egypt and round the wilderness for forty years (Josh. 24:32). It is also where Israel stood between the mountains and swore they would serve the LORD (Josh. 24), and where the kingdom tore in half a few generations later (1 Kgs. 12).

There is no square yard of ground in Israel more layered with covenant memory, promise, oath-taking and failure — and it is in Samaria, in enemy country, and a Jewish traveller has just sat down on the wall of the well with nothing to draw with.

The well is real and it is still there; it goes down something over a hundred feet through rock. It was not a spring. Somebody had to lower a vessel a hundred feet and haul it up, twice a day, for as long as the family lasted.

Then the two words the paragraph turns on. He was wearied — the verb means worn out by labour, the exhaustion that comes from work rather than from lack of sleep. And the sixth hour, which is noon: the sun directly overhead, the worst part of the day to be walking and the worst part of the day to be fetching water.

This is the Gospel that opened by saying all things were made through him. Twenty verses in, he cannot walk any further and has to sit down. The two facts are placed in the same book by the same author without any sense that they need reconciling, and any account of Christ that finds one of them embarrassing has stopped reading somewhere.

And there is a line running from this well to the end of the book, which is worth having in view early. The man sitting here with no bucket is about to offer a stranger water that ends thirst permanently. Fifteen chapters later he will be hanging on a cross, and the last thing he says before it is finished is I thirst (19:28). He ended thirsty. That is how the offer was paid for.

Say a word to the reader who is simply tired, because this verse is one of the few places in Scripture that meets him without instruction. Not spiritually dry — tired: the kind where the body has stopped cooperating and the day still has eight hours in it. There is no rebuke here and no encouragement to push through. The Son of God sat down on a wall in the heat because he could not go on, and the most important conversation in the chapter happened while he was in that condition. Being exhausted is not a lapse in discipleship, and God is not obliged to wait until a person is at their best.

The one through whom the springs were made sat down beside a hole in the ground that somebody's great-grandfather had dug, because he was too tired to walk, and waited in the midday heat for a woman who was not coming to meet him.

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything about this encounter violates convention. The hour is wrong (noon, when respectable women did not come to the well), the gender is wrong (a Jewish man does not address an unknown woman), the ethnicity is wrong (no dealings between Jews and Samaritans). Jesus violates every protocol without apology. The request — Give me a drink — opens the conversation from a position of need; he asks her for help before offering her anything. This is grace approaching the outcast without condescension: he who has everything presents himself as needy in order to create the space for encounter.

Count what is wrong with this scene by the standards of the day, because the list is longer than we feel it.

He is a man, alone, speaking to a woman, alone, in an isolated place. Rabbinic caution about this was severe to the point of comedy; there were teachers who held that a man should not greet a woman in public, and some who took pride in never having looked at one. He is a Jew asking a Samaritan for water — which raises a question of ritual cleanness the woman will name herself in the next verse, since the vessel she draws with is hers. And he is asking a favour of somebody with nothing, which is not how benefactors behave.

He breaks all of it in four words and offers no explanation for any of it, then or later.

But the four words are the thing. Give me a drink. The first thing the Son of God says to this woman is a request for help — and it hands her, for the length of one sentence, the position of the one who has something the other needs. She is not approached as a case, or a project, or a problem to be addressed. She is approached as the person by the well with the rope.

That is not a technique, and it would be a poor one if it were, since a favour asked in order to open a conversation is a manoeuvre and people can smell it. He was genuinely thirsty. He had walked since morning and had nothing to draw with. The request was true, and being true it did what no strategy could have done.

There is something in this for anyone who has tried to speak to a neighbour about Christ and found the whole thing artificial. Nearly all our discomfort comes from arriving as the one with the answers, which sets up a transaction where one party is deficient and both of them know it. This conversation starts from the opposite end. The most common ground between any two human beings is not that one of them is right; it is that both of them need things, and one of them is thirsty now.

And notice what he does not open with. Not her history, which he already knows in full. Not her theology, which is defective. Not her nationality. Those all come up, and every one of them comes up later, and not one of them is the doorway.

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parenthetical explanation for Gentile readers (and the woman's own surprise) confirms that Jesus has crossed a major social boundary. The disciples' absence is providential: this conversation happens precisely because Jesus is alone. The woman's question is not hostile but genuinely puzzled — she has enough experience of Jewish contempt to be surprised by a Jewish request. Her surprise is the crack through which grace enters. When the wall of expected contempt does not appear, the heart opens a little, and Jesus speaks into that opening.

John explains the situation twice in one verse, in two brackets, which tells us he is writing for people who would not otherwise follow. The disciples are away buying lunch — which is itself worth a glance, since a party of Jewish men buying food in a Samaritan town is a small sign that this group's boundaries were already looser than the custom.

The second bracket is the famous one: For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. The verb is unusual and may be narrower than the English suggests — some understand it as do not use vessels in common, which would fit the situation exactly. A Samaritan woman was regarded by strict opinion as ritually unclean, and so was anything she handled. If that is the sense, her surprise is precise: it is not that a Jew has spoken to her, but that he is proposing to drink from her jar.

Her reply is not a rebuff and it is not bitterness. It is astonishment, and it is worth hearing the arithmetic in it: you, a Jew — me, a woman of Samaria. She names both barriers in one breath, and she names them in the order that puts the greatest distance between them. She has spent her life on the wrong side of a line she did not draw, and here is somebody standing on the other side of it asking for a drink.

The note above is right that her surprise is the crack through which grace enters, and it is worth pressing why. Contempt she could have handled; contempt is familiar and there are ways of standing that absorb it. What she has no defence against is a Jewish man asking her for a favour. The wall she has braced against did not arrive, and the bracing is now doing nothing, and she is off balance and talking.

Which is a plain observation for anyone who wants to be useful to a person outside the faith. Most people who are not Christians already know exactly what they expect from Christians — they have an idea of the disapproval and they have arranged themselves against it. The single most disarming thing available is not a better argument. It is the disapproval failing to turn up.

And there is a sting for the church in the bracket. Jews have no dealings with Samaritans is stated as a simple fact of the world, with no comment attached. John does not editorialise. He simply records the rule, and then records the Son of God ignoring it, and lets the reader work out which of the two is going to last.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus pivots from her water to his water, from his need to her need. If you knew — the condition points to the epistemological gap between them. She does not yet know who she is speaking with, and that ignorance is her poverty. The gift of God: living water is not earned, not bartered, not purchased at the noon-hour well of ordinary religion — it is gift. The one asking for a drink is the one who can give what no well contains. This is the pattern of all evangelism: begin with the human's ordinary need, move to the divine gift that satisfies the need beneath the need.

The phrase "living water" is doing the same work here that "born again" did with Nicodemus, and the woman's puzzled reply only makes sense once you see it. The words (in Greek, hudor zon) have an ordinary meaning before they have a spiritual one: living water is running water — a spring or a stream, water that moves — as opposed to the still, stored water of a cistern or a well. It was the better water, the kind everyone preferred. So the woman hears a claim about plumbing, not salvation: this stranger, who has no bucket and no rope, is somehow offering her fresh running water instead of Jacob's standing well — and she asks the only sensible question, "Where do you get that living water?" (v. 11). She is not being dull. She is hearing the plain sense of the word, exactly as Nicodemus heard "again."

Jesus means the other sense, the water that is life itself, and he lets her literal question carry the conversation up toward it. John will eventually tell us in so many words what this water finally is: standing in the temple, Jesus cries out again about "rivers of living water," and John adds the interpretation — "this he said about the Spirit" (7:38-39). The gift Jesus offers the woman at the well is nothing less than the indwelling Spirit of God, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp, now pictured as a spring that never runs dry.

Two ignorances are named in the first clause, and it is worth separating them: if you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, Give me a drink. She does not know what is on offer, and she does not know who is offering it. Both would have to be corrected for her to ask, and the second is the one that does the work — because a gift is only as good as the giver is able, and she is looking at a tired man with no bucket.

Then the clause that ought to stop anybody: you would have asked him. That is all. Not you would have qualified, or you would have made amends first, or you would have got the mountain question right. The only thing standing between this woman and living water, on Jesus' own account, is that it had not occurred to her to ask — and the reason it had not occurred to her is that she had no idea who she was talking to.

Which locates the problem exactly where this Gospel keeps putting it, and it is not where most people look for it. Her difficulty is not that she is unworthy; her history is about to be laid out and it changes nothing. It is not that she is a Samaritan; the barrier has already been crossed by the man sitting on the wall. It is that she does not know who he is. Ignorance, not unworthiness, is what is keeping her poor — and he does not lecture her about it. He tells her, in stages, until she asks.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman is practically minded: he has no bucket. She invokes Jacob — their shared patriarch — to challenge his implied superiority. Are you greater than Jacob? It is one of the great dramatic ironies of the gospel: yes, infinitely greater. The one who created Jacob, who named Israel, who watched over the patriarchs in every generation stands before her asking for a drink. She is asking the right question without knowing how right it is. Jesus never rebukes these questions; he uses them as stepping stones toward revelation.

Her two objections are both perfectly sensible, and they are the objections of a competent person. You have nothing to draw water with — literally, no bucket; the well is over a hundred feet deep and there is a stranger sitting on it with empty hands. The well is deep. She is not being obtuse. She is stating the facts of the situation to a man who appears not to have noticed them.

Then our father Jacob, and the possessive is the interesting word. Samaritans traced themselves to Joseph, and claimed the patriarchs as their own, which Jews disputed. In one phrase she has answered the whole boundary problem she raised two verses earlier: whatever else divides them, they have the same great-grandfather, and she is standing on his land.

And the question she asks is the question of the chapter, asked by somebody who thinks she already knows the answer: Are you greater than our father Jacob?

John loves this. It is exactly the shape of the question the crowd will ask about Abraham in chapter 8 — Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? — and to which Jesus will reply before Abraham was, I am (8:53-58). The Gospel keeps putting the true answer in the mouths of people who intend it as a rhetorical impossibility. Yes, and not by a margin that can be measured. Jacob dug a hole and it was a good hole and his descendants were still hauling out of it seventeen hundred years later. The man she is talking to made the water.

Notice what he does with the objection, because it is instructive. He does not correct her about the bucket, and he does not answer the question about Jacob — not for another fourteen verses, when he answers it far more completely than she asked it. He takes the practical difficulty she has raised and uses it as the next step up. Her literalism is not an obstacle to the conversation; it is the staircase.

Which is worth remembering when someone raises what feels like a frustrating objection to the faith — the one that seems to miss the point so completely that there is nowhere to go. Very often it does not miss the point. It is the point, held at the only end the person can currently reach.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The observation is both literal and spiritual: Jacob's well, however ancient and deep, cannot permanently satisfy. All the waters of natural provision — comfort, relationship, achievement, religion — eventually run dry. The human soul is constitutively thirsty in a way that no earthly well can quench. Augustine's prayer is the theological framework for this verse: our heart is restless until it rests in thee. Jesus does not despise the well; he identifies its limitation in order to direct her attention to what lies beyond it.

It is a strange thing to say to a woman with a jar in her hand, and it is worth hearing how mild it sounds and how total it is. He does not say Jacob's well is bad water. He says: whoever drinks this will be thirsty again. It is a statement about the mechanism, not the quality.

And it is simply true, of the well and of everything the well stands for. Every good thing available to a human being works on the same cycle: it satisfies, and the satisfaction wears off, and the need returns at full strength and slightly sooner than last time. The meal, the holiday, the promotion, the applause, the relationship. None of them fails. They all work exactly as advertised, and then they stop working, and the stopping is not a fault in them.

Say it plainly to the reader who keeps going back to the same well and hates himself for it — and the well may be a bottle, or a screen, or a person he should have stopped calling, or simply the approval of somebody whose opinion he cannot get out from under. The verse is not a rebuke of the thirst. Thirst is not a sin; it is a design feature, and the ache is not evidence that something has gone wrong with a person. What the verse says is that the well he is returning to has never once promised what he keeps arriving with. It gives what it has. It gives it every time. And the interval between drinks gets shorter, which is the whole mechanism of every addiction there has ever been.

Here is a test that can be run without any spiritual vocabulary at all. Think of the thing you were most sure would settle you — the one you honestly believed, five or ten years ago, would mean you had arrived. Suppose you got it. Did the wanting stop? For almost everybody the answer is that the wanting moved. It did not diminish; it changed address. That is not cynicism about good gifts. It is data, gathered from your own life, about what kind of creature you are.

Note that he does not despise the well. He asked for a drink from it four verses ago and presumably got one. There is nothing in this chapter against ordinary water, ordinary marriage, ordinary bread. The problem was never that people love things too much. It is that they ask of them what they were never built to carry.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Never be thirsty again' — the desire Jesus satisfies is not cyclical (satisfied then hungry again) but permanently resolved. The image shifts from drinking water to becoming a spring: what Jesus gives transforms the recipient into a source. The woman's response is still literal — she wants not to have to make the daily trip to the well. But her desire for this water, however misconceived, is the beginning of genuine need expressing itself. Jesus does not correct her literalism immediately; he proceeds to expose the deeper need.

The Greek behind will never be thirsty is emphatic to a degree English cannot manage — a double negative stacked on a future, something like will certainly not ever thirst, not for eternity. It is not a mild reassurance. It is a door closing on the whole cycle described in the previous verse.

And then the image changes in a way that should stop the reader, because it stops being about drinking at all. He does not say the water will keep her topped up, or that she may come back to him whenever she runs low. He says the water he gives becomes in him a spring. The one who drinks turns into a source.

That is the difference between a well and a spring, and it is the whole point of the picture. A well is a hole where water is stored; it has to be gone to, lowered into, hauled out of, and it is finite. A spring is water arriving from underneath, under its own pressure, without anybody's effort, and the word John uses for welling up means to leap — it is used elsewhere of a lame man jumping to his feet. The picture is not of a reservoir carefully managed. It is of something that will not stay down.

Which is why the daily trip to this well is about to end for her, though not in the way she means. She is standing beside a hundred feet of rope and stone, at noon, because that is what getting water costs. He is offering her the end of the errand.

Her reply is still entirely literal — so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water — and it is easy to smile at. It is worth not smiling. She has heard an offer she does not understand and she has asked for it anyway, which is more than Nicodemus managed with a far better education and every advantage of background. Her theology is wrong and her hand is out. In this Gospel that combination does considerably better than the reverse.

And notice that Jesus does not correct the misunderstanding. He could have said: no, you have misheard me, let me define my terms. He lets her ask for the right thing for the wrong reason, and simply goes on. There is a lesson buried there for anyone who has ever wanted to withhold the gospel from somebody until their motives were properly sorted out. Nobody's motives are properly sorted out. Every person who has ever come to Christ came for a tangle of reasons, at least half of them self-interested, and he has never yet sent one of them away to think it over.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conversation about spiritual water has reached its limit; Jesus goes deeper. Go, call your husband: the command moves the conversation from thirst to the source of her thirst. Her answer — I have no husband — is technically true and practically evasive. Jesus receives it with neither condemnation nor evasion: "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband.'" He honors the partial truth. This is pastoral wisdom: acknowledge what is true before addressing what is hidden. The gospel does not begin with exposure; it begins with acknowledgment and moves gently toward full disclosure.

The turn in this conversation is so abrupt that it is worth asking why he makes it. They have been talking about water and eternal life; she has just asked for the gift. And instead of giving it, he says: go and fetch your husband.

It is not a change of subject. It is the point at which the conversation stops being about a subject at all. Everything up to here could have been had in the abstract — thirst in general, life in general, a gift available to whoever wants one. The moment he mentions her husband, the conversation acquires a particular person with a particular history, and it can no longer be conducted from a safe distance.

That is nearly always where the difficulty lies. It is not hard to be interested in Christianity. Enormous numbers of people are genuinely interested in it, read about it, find it beautiful, and are never once cornered by it — because the whole thing is conducted in the third person. The sentence that changes the temperature is never a doctrine. It is always something like go, call your husband: a request that cannot be answered without bringing one's actual life into the room.

And note what he does with her answer. I have no husband is three words that are entirely true and are being used to hide something, which is a manoeuvre most of us could perform in our sleep. It is not a lie. It is an accurate sentence deployed as a wall.

He does not knock it down. He agrees with it — you are right in saying, I have no husband — and then, in the next breath, says the thing the wall was built to keep out. He takes her own words and hands them back with the rest of the sentence attached.

There is something worth learning in that, and it is not a technique for winning arguments. He begins with what she got right. She said a true thing under pressure, and he acknowledged it before he said anything else. Most exposure in human hands leads with the discrepancy; this leads with the accuracy and lets the discrepancy follow. The difference in effect is enormous, and it is the difference between a person who is being caught out and a person who is being told the truth by somebody who is plainly on their side.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five husbands, and a current companion who is not a husband: a history of broken covenants, failed relationships, social shame. Jesus knows it all and says it without cruelty, without the sneer of the moralist. What you have said is true — he does not dwell on the failure; he confirms the truth and moves on. This is divine mercy in action: total knowledge combined with total gentleness. The woman's thirst for living water now has a name — the thirst of a soul that has looked for love in every wrong place and found only diminishing satisfaction.

That is the reading this passage has almost always been given, and it may well be right. But it is worth telling the reader honestly how much of it the text actually supplies, because a great deal has been built on very little. John never calls this woman immoral. Jesus never mentions sin to her, never calls her to repent, and never tells her to go and sin no more — which is striking, since he says exactly that to the woman in chapter 8 and to the man at the pool in chapter 5. The one irregularity he names outright is the present arrangement: the man she has now is not her husband.

And about the five, consider how such a marriage ended in that world. A woman could not divorce her husband; a husband could dismiss a wife, and for very little. So five marriages behind her means five times widowed, or five times sent away, or some mixture of the two — a life of things done to her at least as easily as things done by her. The detail about the hour is likewise thinner than it looks: John simply says it was the sixth hour, and he gives us the time of day elsewhere without any suggestion of scandal (1:39; 19:14). Nor does the town behave as a town behaves toward a woman it has cast out — she speaks, and they listen, and they come out to see (vv. 29-30, 39).

The truthful answer is that we are not told, and it matters that we say so. There are women who have sat through sermons on this chapter and heard themselves described — divorced not by their own choosing, or widowed young, or long ago abandoned — and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. What the passage does assign is this: Jesus knew every year of her history before she said a word, stayed and asked her for a drink anyway, gave her the plainest statement of his identity recorded anywhere in the Gospels, and sent her back to her town as the first person in this book to tell anyone who he was.

One more possibility deserves a mention and then a firm hand, because it turns up in commentaries and it is worth knowing why this one does not follow it. Some have read the five husbands as an allegory: Assyria resettled Samaria with people from five foreign cities, each bringing their own gods (2 Kgs. 17:24-31), so the five husbands are said to represent the five false worships, and the sixth companion the corrupt Samaritan religion. It is ingenious, and there is a certain neatness to it. But John gives no hint of it, the numbers do not in fact work cleanly.

Above all it has the effect of dissolving a real woman into a symbol — which is the very thing this passage refuses to do to her. She is not a diagram of Samaria. She is somebody with five marriages behind her and a man in the house now, standing in the heat with a jar.

And hold on to the one thing the passage states outright, because it is the thing to say to anybody who has ever dreaded being fully known. He knew all of it before she spoke — every year, every name, every ending — and he had already asked her for a drink. The knowledge came first and the kindness was not adjusted by it.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exposed by supernatural knowledge, the woman correctly identifies Jesus as a prophet — a significant upgrade from "a Jew" (v. 9). And she immediately raises the great theological controversy between Jews and Samaritans: Mount Gerizim versus Jerusalem. This is often read as deflection — changing the subject from her personal history — but it may also be genuine: a woman who has failed at love is now asking about true worship. Jesus does not dismiss the question as evasion; he answers it, because true worship is exactly what her soul needs.

Both readings are available and the honest thing is to hold them together, because the same words can be spoken by two very different people.

It may be deflection. It has all the marks. A man has just named the most painful arrangement in her life, and within one sentence she is discussing comparative liturgy. Anyone who has ever tried to talk to a friend about something real knows the manoeuvre: the sudden availability of a large, interesting, impersonal question at exactly the moment the small personal one became unbearable. Religion is uncommonly good for this. There is always a doctrine to argue about, and arguing about it is a great deal easier than being known.

And it may be entirely genuine. Here is a woman whose life has gone wrong in the area where people look hardest for happiness, standing in front of somebody who has just proved he can see. If she has ever wanted to ask where God can actually be found — and a person with five endings behind her may have wanted that badly — this is the only chance she will ever get, and she takes it with the first question that comes.

The reason not to force a verdict is that Jesus does not. He answers the question. He does not say we were talking about your husband. He takes what she asks and gives her the fullest teaching on worship anywhere in the Gospels — which is what he would do if it were sincere, and is also, as it happens, the only thing that would ever have helped if it were not.

Now the mountain, and it is not an abstraction. Gerizim rises directly above that well; she could have pointed at it while speaking, and the phrase is this mountain. Its history is layered. It is where Israel was told to stand to pronounce the blessings when they entered the land (Deut. 11:29; 27:12) — the Samaritans' whole case rested on that. Their own copy of the law of Moses even carried a command to build the altar there. And on its summit, when this conversation took place, lay the rubble of the temple they had built, torn down by a Jewish ruler about a hundred and fifty years earlier.

So the disagreement she raises is not a seminar topic. It is a ruin she can see from where she is standing, and the people who made it are the people this man belongs to. That is what makes his answer so remarkable: he is about to tell her that the argument is over, and that neither side won it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus dissolves the geographic controversy with an eschatological announcement: neither mountain matters anymore, because the hour is coming. The hour — always in John connected to Jesus' glorification and the gift of the Spirit — will make all temple-locations obsolete. Worship is about to become radically portable, radically internal, radically personal: not a place but a relationship, not a mountain but a Person. The Jerusalem/Gerizim debate was about the correct address for God; Jesus announces that God will no longer be addressed at any address but encountered in Spirit and truth.

Three small things in the opening words, easily passed over.

Woman — the same address he used to his mother at Cana and will use to her from the cross (2:4; 19:26). In English it lands cold; in that setting it is formal and respectful, and it is worth noticing that he speaks to a Samaritan at a well in precisely the same register in which he speaks to his own mother.

Believe me. This is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus says those two words to anybody. Elsewhere he says truly, truly and lets the authority stand on its own. Here, to a woman who has every reason to expect a Jewish man to be arguing with her rather than levelling with her, he asks for her trust directly, as one person to another, before he says the thing that will cost her her side of the argument.

And the Father — the first time in this conversation he uses the name. She asked where people ought to worship. He answers by telling her who it is that is worshipped, and the name he chooses is the domestic one.

Then the announcement, and its scale is easy to miss because it is so calmly put. Neither mountain. Not your mountain is wrong and ours is right — which was the entire content of the dispute, and which he could have said with complete justification, and half of which he is about to say. Neither. The argument she has raised is not going to be settled. It is going to be made obsolete, and within about forty years both buildings under discussion would in fact be gone.

What is being dismantled here is older and more stubborn than the Samaritan question. It is the assumption, which every religion in history has held and which sits very deep in ordinary human instinct, that God is more available in some places than others. That there is a spot, and the spot has to be reached, and getting there is most of the work.

It is worth admitting how much of that survives in people who would deny holding it. The sense that prayer counts more in a church building than in a car. The suspicion that a quiet time before six in the morning is worth more than the same words said at eleven at night. The holiday to a place where God seemed close, and the low-grade grief of coming home.

None of that is wicked, and some of it is simply the way memory and attention work. But this verse says the mountain has been closed, and that everyone who has ever been unable to get to the holy place — the housebound, the shift worker, the mother of small children, the prisoner, the woman who cannot show her face in town before dark — has not been kept away from anything at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus affirms Jewish priority in salvation history — salvation is from the Jews — while announcing its transcendence. The Samaritan worship is defective not because of its location but because of its content: they worship what they do not know, having severed themselves from the prophetic scriptures. But the coming hour transcends even correct Jewish worship: true worshipers will worship in spirit and truth, where spirit indicates the Holy Spirit's enabling presence and truth indicates the revelation brought by Jesus himself. The Father is seeking such worshipers — the seeking is divine, which means this worship is a gift before it is a duty.

One clause in this verse stops the whole passage from becoming what it is most often made into, and it should not be softened: salvation is from the Jews.

Everything else here is so generous — the barriers down, the mountain abolished, a Samaritan woman receiving the finest teaching on worship in the Bible — that it is tempting to conclude Jesus is indifferent to the disagreement. He is not, and he says so with a bluntness that would end most modern conversations: you worship what you do not know; we worship what we know. He puts himself unmistakably on one side. The Samaritans had cut themselves off from the prophets and kept only the five books of Moses, and the result was a real impoverishment — a God known in outline. He does not call that a different route up the same mountain. He calls it worshipping what they do not know.

And then the same sentence takes away any possibility of using that as a boast. Salvation is from the Jews — from, not for. The privilege was never a possession; it was a channel. Israel was the well the water came through, and a well does not congratulate itself on the water. The Jew hearing this is told his heritage is genuine and is told, in the same breath, where it was always headed.

Then the hinge of the chapter: the hour is coming, and is now here. He has used the hour is coming twice; only now does he add the second half. Something has already started. The new worship is not entirely future — it is beginning at this well, in this conversation, with this woman, who is about to become the first person in the book to tell a town who he is.

And the last clause is the one to take away, because it turns the whole subject round: the Father is seeking such people to worship him.

Every word of that is the wrong way up by ordinary religious instinct. Worship is what we do to find God; here God is the one out looking. She came to this well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come three days out of his way. That is not an illustration of the verse — it is the verse, happening while it is spoken.

Say it to the reader who has spent years with the low background sense that he is not much of a worshipper — that the singing does not move him, that his prayers are dutiful, that other people plainly have something he does not. This verse does not tell him to try harder to find God. It says the Father is out looking for worshippers, which means the search that matters is not the one being conducted from this end, and it has a considerably better record.

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is spirit: not that God has no reality or substance, but that God is not limited by physicality, not confined to temples, not locatable on mountains. The implication for worship is total: since God is spirit, worship that is merely external — correct location, correct ritual, correct calendar — misses the point. Spirit-and-truth worship engages the whole person, animated by the Holy Spirit, in response to the full self-revelation of God in Jesus Christ. Reformed theology has always insisted that authentic worship is God-initiated and God-enabled: we worship because he has sought us, in the mode he has prescribed, through the Son he has given.

Three words, and they need unpacking rather than admiring, because God is spirit is one of those sentences everybody nods at and few could explain to a child.

Start with what it does not say. It does not say God is a spirit, one item in a category of ghostly beings — the Greek has no article, and the point is not to classify him. It does not mean God is vague, or that he is an atmosphere, or a force, or an impersonal energy behind things. The God being described here talks, seeks, loves, sends and is called Father in the same breath.

What it means is that God has no body and is not located. He cannot be run out of, or run to. He does not occupy a spot that another spot lacks. A statue can be stolen; a temple can be burned; a mountain can be captured, and Gerizim had been. None of that touches him, because he was never on it.

Which is why the conclusion follows as it does: those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. If God had been a local deity, worship would be a matter of arriving. Since he is not, worship is a matter of being a certain kind of person in his presence — and every person is already in his presence, all the time, which is the part that makes this comfortable and uncomfortable at once.

Now the phrase itself, because it is regularly misread as a contrast between heartfelt and formal — sincerity against ritual. That is not quite it. Spirit here is almost certainly the Holy Spirit, the one Jesus has just been describing to Nicodemus as the agent of the new birth and picturing here as a spring welling up inside a person. And truth is not sincerity either; in this Gospel truth is a person before it is a quality — I am the way, and the truth (14:6). So worship in spirit and truth means worship enabled by God's own Spirit and shaped by God's own self-revelation in his Son. Both halves are gifts. Neither is a technique.

Which cuts two ways, and it needs to cut both. It rules out worship that is correct and dead — the right words in the right order with nobody home, which is what the Samaritans' neighbours in Jerusalem were increasingly good at. And it rules out worship that is warm and invented — deeply felt, powerfully moving, and directed at a God assembled from preference. Truth without Spirit is a corpse. Spirit without truth is a mood.

Here is the test, and it is a plain one. Ask what happens to your worship when the music stops — when the service is dull, the preacher is poor, the room is cold and nothing at all is being generated for you. Something is left, or nothing is. That residue is the part that was in spirit and truth. The rest was the building.

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'I who speak to you am he' — the most direct messianic self-disclosure in the Synoptic period of Jesus's ministry, and it is made to a Samaritan woman at a well. Not to the high priest, not to the scribes, not even to the disciples yet — but to this woman, whose combination of social marginalization and spiritual hunger makes her the perfect first recipient of the full revelation. The conversation that began with 'give me a drink' ends with 'I am the Messiah.' This is the grammar of grace.

Two things make this moment larger than it looks.

The first is what she was actually expecting, because the Samaritans did not use the word Messiah in the way Jerusalem did. Having only the five books of Moses, they had no royal prophecies of David's line to build on. What they looked for came out of Deuteronomy 18 — a prophet like Moses whom God would raise up and into whose mouth he would put his words. They called him the Taheb, roughly the restorer, and what they chiefly expected of him is exactly what she says here: when he comes, he will tell us all things. Not a king who would reign. A teacher who would settle everything — including, presumably, the argument about the mountain she has just raised.

Which makes her sentence quietly poignant. She has been told something enormous about worship, and her response is essentially: one day somebody will come who can sort this out. She is deferring the whole matter to a figure in the future, standing three feet from him.

The second is the form of the answer. In Greek it is ego eimi — I am — with the participle following: literally I am, the one speaking to you. It is the first time in this Gospel that Jesus applies those two words to himself, and John will use them again and again until, in chapter 8, the crowd picks up stones at before Abraham was, I am. Here the phrase is doing ordinary work — it is a perfectly normal way of saying that is me — and it is also the beginning of the most loaded formula in the book, and the phrase God gave Moses at the bush.

Now hold the whole scene together, because it is the most improbable arrangement of facts in the chapter. He has been in Jerusalem for a feast. He has spoken with a member of the ruling council by night and told him a great deal without ever saying this. He has a group of disciples who have been with him for months and have not heard it. And the first bare, unhedged declaration of who he is goes to a Samaritan woman with an irregular household, alone, in the heat, with nobody there to write it down.

She had said that one day someone would come and tell them all things. He said: I am he, the one talking to you now. It is the shortest distance between a longing and its object in the whole of Scripture.

The first time in this Gospel that Jesus says plainly who he is — no parable, no sign, no delay — he says it in a foreign country, at midday, sitting on the wall of a well, with nobody present but one woman whose name is never recorded. Not in the temple. Not to the council. Not even to the twelve, who are in town at that moment buying lunch.

He had been in Jerusalem a few weeks earlier and told them nothing. He tells her everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples' silence is eloquent: they are shocked but have learned not to challenge Jesus. The woman leaves her water jar — the emblem of her original errand — abandoned at the well. She came for water and leaves with something so much more that the original purpose is forgotten. This is the pattern of every true encounter with Christ: what we came for is superseded by what he gives. The abandoned water jar is a small monument to transformed desire. She no longer needs Jacob's well; she has found the spring that Jacob's well was always pointing toward.

John records something that did not happen, which is unusual, and the wording is very exact. They marvelled — but no one said, What do you seek? or, Why are you talking with her?

Two questions nobody asked. And the first of them is the question Jesus himself asked at the very beginning of this Gospel, when two men were trailing him down a road and he turned round: What are you seeking? (1:38). It is the same verb. The disciples have the question available to them, and they do not use it — not on him, and not on themselves.

What is being described is a room full of men who are shocked, who have a perfectly reasonable enquiry to make, and who say nothing. Whether that is reverence or awkwardness John does not say, and it is probably both. But the effect is a silence with a shape: they have already learned that he does things they would not have advised, and they have not yet learned to ask why.

It is a familiar silence. There is a way of following Christ for years while carefully never bringing him the question that is actually there — the one about the prayer that was not answered, or the person he did not heal, or the passage that troubles rather than comforts. It is possible to mistake that for reverence. This Gospel is full of people who asked him bad questions and got somewhere; it has rather fewer examples of people who asked nothing.

Then the jar. She had walked out to that well for one reason, in the heat, carrying an empty vessel, and she goes back to town without it. John did not have to tell us that. It is the kind of detail that survives only because somebody saw it.

It is not a symbol she intended. She simply left it — the way people leave things when something has happened that makes the errand irrelevant. And there is a practical edge in it that is easy to sentimentalise away: the jar was not hers to abandon. She would have to come back for it. Whatever had just happened to her, it did not remove the daily walk, or the hundred feet of rope, or the heat. It removed the reason she had been coming alone.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman becomes the first evangelist in John's gospel — and she evangelizes her own community, the community from which she had apparently been excluded (hence drawing water alone at noon). Her testimony is an invitation, not a proof: Come and see. Her question — Can this be the Christ? — is rhetorically humble but evangelistically effective: the townspeople come. God uses the testimony of the broken and the restored, not merely the credentialed and the respectable. The gospel frequently travels its first miles through the most unlikely messengers.

Look at what her testimony actually consists of, because it is a remarkably poor piece of evangelism by any standard we would apply.

She has one fact, and it is about herself. She overstates it — all that I ever did, when in truth he had named a single arrangement. She cannot explain the living water, she has no doctrine of the incarnation, she got the mountain question wrong twenty minutes ago, and her closing line is not even a claim.
