Passover is the feast of bread: unleavened bread eaten in haste, a lamb killed, and behind it the memory of a nation fed in a desert with bread that came down every morning for forty years. Everything in this chapter — the wilderness setting, the bread, the manna argument, the flesh given for the life of the world — is standing inside that feast, and John tells us so before a single loaf is broken.

Then the question, and there is a small detail in it that repays knowing. Jesus turns to Philip — and Philip, John told us back in chapter 1, was from Bethsaida (1:44), which is the town they are nearest to. He asks the local man where to buy bread. It is exactly the question one would put to somebody who knows the district, and it is asked of the one person present who could be expected to have an answer.

And note the pronoun: where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat? He does not say they. He includes Philip in a responsibility Philip has not accepted and could not discharge. That is how the test is set — not by asking Philip to do the impossible, but by quietly making the crowd's hunger his problem too.

And note who moves first. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him — he sees them, and the question about bread is out of his mouth before anybody has asked him for anything.

Nobody in this story requests a meal. There is no petition, no crowd complaining of hunger, no disciple raising a concern; in Matthew and Mark the disciples eventually suggest sending everyone away to fend for themselves. The initiative is entirely his, taken while the crowd is still walking toward him and has no idea it is about to be fed.

verseByVerse.quote: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip's economic analysis is accurate: two hundred denarii — roughly eight months' wages — would not feed this crowd adequately. He has done the math and found the situation impossible. But his calculation excludes the one standing beside him. When we measure our resources against the need without factoring in Christ, we will always conclude that it cannot be done. Philip's answer is not faithless cynicism; it is the honest response of a man whose categories have not yet expanded to include the miraculous provision of the Son of God. Faith is the expansion of the denominator.

John's bracket is one of the kindest in the Gospel: he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.

Which means the outcome was never in question. The bread was going to arrive whatever Philip said. The test was not an audition Philip could fail in a way that would cost the crowd their dinner — it was a question asked by somebody who had already decided, in order that the man being asked might find out what was in him.

That is worth holding on to when a situation feels like a test. The tests God sets are not entrance examinations with the result pending. He knows what he will do. The examination exists so that the person taking it discovers where his own arithmetic runs out — which is information he needs and cannot get any other way.

And Philip's answer is a good one. It deserves to be said clearly, because he is often treated as the failure of the passage. Two hundred denarii is roughly eight months' wages for a labourer; he has evidently made a rapid estimate of the crowd, the price of bread, and the size of the common purse, and concluded that even that sum would not give each person a little. The sum is correct. The conclusion follows from the premises.

His problem is not his arithmetic. It is that he was asked where and answered how much. The question was about a source; he replied with a budget. And a man who converts every question about God's provision into a question about available resources will always arrive at the same answer, and the answer will always be right, and it will always be beside the point.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, said to him, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Andrew's contribution is to bring what exists to Jesus' attention — five barley loaves (the food of the poor) and two fish. Then he adds the disclaimer: but what are they for so many? He brings the resource but cannot imagine its sufficiency. This is the beginning of the right posture: bring what you have to Jesus, even when you cannot see how it is enough. The miracle does not begin with abundance but with offering. Every great work of God in history has begun with someone placing an inadequate offering into the hands of the one who multiplies.

There is an Old Testament story sitting directly underneath this, and once it is seen the whole scene changes shape.

A man came to Elisha with twenty loaves of barley and fresh ears of grain, and Elisha said: give it to the men, that they may eat. And his servant objected — How can I set this before a hundred men? — and Elisha said they would eat and have some left. And they did, and there was some left over (2 Kgs. 4:42-44).

Barley loaves. An objection about the ratio. A command to distribute. Food left over. Andrew's sentence is almost word for word the servant's sentence, and any Jew who knew his Scriptures would have felt the echo. What is different is the scale: Elisha fed a hundred from twenty loaves; here it is five thousand from five. Elisha's servant was out by a factor of five. Andrew is out by a factor of a thousand.

And the loaves themselves say something. Barley was the poor man's grain — cheaper than wheat, coarser, what you ate when wheat was beyond you. This is a child's packed lunch of the plainest kind, and it is the only food in the story.

Notice what Andrew actually does, because he is easy to patronise for the second half of his sentence. He is the only person in the passage who has gone and looked. Philip did the sum; Andrew went through the crowd and found out what was actually there. And he brings it — knowing it is absurd, saying so out loud, and bringing it anyway.

That is not weak faith. It is the exact posture the chapter requires: hands out, holding something insufficient, with no idea what will happen. Nothing in the Gospels suggests Jesus wanted the disciples to feel confident. He wanted the loaves.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Have the people sit down." Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover grass, the five thousand reclining as at a banquet, the giving of thanks (eucharisteo — the word from which "Eucharist" derives) — every element points forward to the Lord's Supper and backward to the Exodus manna. As much as they wanted: not rationed grace, not measured mercy, but abundance beyond need. The feeding of the five thousand is a enacted parable of the inexhaustible provision of the one who is himself the bread. He does not merely supply bread; he is the bread that gives life to the world.

Now there was much grass in the place. It is the sort of detail nobody invents, and it does two things at once. It dates the scene — grass in Galilee means spring, which fits the Passover of verse 4 — and it turns a hillside into a dining room. Five thousand men, and Matthew adds women and children beyond that, told to recline on green grass while somebody brings food to them.

Anyone raised on the psalms would feel where they were: he makes me lie down in green pastures (Ps. 23:2). Mark, telling the same story, says they sat down in groups on the green grass, and adds that Jesus had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mk. 6:34). The shepherd sits his flock down on the grass and feeds them. Four chapters later Jesus will say I am the good shepherd, and this hillside is where the picture was first acted out.

Then the verb over the loaves: when he had given thanks — eucharistesas, the word the church would take for its central meal. He does what any Jewish head of a household did before eating, and says what they said: blessed are you, LORD our God, king of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth. It is the most ordinary sentence in Jewish life. He says it over five loaves in front of five thousand people, and then it turns out to be true in a way it had never been before.

And the last phrase is the one to sit with: as much as they wanted. Not enough to go round. Not a small piece each, which is precisely what Philip had calculated could not be managed. As much as they wanted — every person on that hillside eating until they stopped wanting more, which almost none of them would have done at home.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost." So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gather up the fragments, that nothing may be lost: the concern for the remnants after abundance is itself a sign. Twelve baskets — one for each tribe, one for each apostle — overflow with what remained after full satisfaction. Divine generosity always exceeds the need; the miracle does not produce just enough but more than enough, and then more still. The twelve baskets of abundance are a sacramental surplus: God's provision is not stingy. And the words nothing may be lost echo forward to Jesus' promise about his sheep (6:39; 10:28): in the economy of grace, nothing given to him is ever wasted.

This is the strangest instruction in the story and it is the one that tells you most about him.

He has just produced food out of nothing. There is no reason of scarcity to save the scraps; the man who made the meal could make another one. And the first thing he says after five thousand people have eaten to satiety is: pick up the bits, so that nothing is lost.

Extravagance and carefulness are not opposites in him. The same person who gave them as much as they wanted will not have a fragment of it trodden into the grass. That is worth knowing about God, because we tend to assume that generosity implies indifference to detail — that a being who can make more will not much mind what happens to this. He minds.

And the phrase is deliberate. That nothing may be lost — the verb is apollymi, to be destroyed or lost, and it is the word that will run through the rest of this chapter and out into the Gospel. In a few verses Jesus will say the Father's will is that of all he has given him he should lose nothing (v. 39). In chapter 10 he will say no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand. In chapter 18, when the soldiers come and he tells them to let the disciples go, John says this fulfilled the word of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (18:9).

So the barley crusts in the grass are the first instalment of a promise about people. The one who sends men round a hillside to make sure a scrap of a poor child's lunch is not wasted is the same one who says he will not lose a single person the Father has given him — and the second sentence is easier to believe once the first has been watched.

Twelve baskets, and the number is not accidental in a country with twelve tribes and a teacher with twelve disciples. The leftovers exceeded the original supply by a considerable margin. They began with five loaves and finished with twelve full baskets, which is the arithmetic of the kingdom: what is handed over comes back larger than it went in, and the surplus is not the point but it is never absent.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd's response to the feeding is correct theology wrongly applied: yes, he is the Prophet (Deut. 18:15) — but they want to make him a bread-king, a political messiah who will supply daily needs and overthrow Rome. Jesus refuses the crown as forcefully as he refuses the devil's shortcut in the wilderness temptations. A king who gives bread but does not give himself is not the King the world needs. Jesus withdraws to the mountain precisely to refuse the popularity that would distort the mission. The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom.

The verb in verse 15 is violent and it is easy to miss under the polite English. They were about to come and take him by force — harpazein, to seize, to snatch, the word used of a wolf carrying off a sheep (10:12) and of the Spirit catching Philip away (Acts 8:39). This is not a crowd offering him a crown. It is a crowd intending to make him take one.

Which is a strange sentence to have to write about the King of the universe, and it is the point. He is in real danger here — not from the authorities, who will get their chance, but from an adoring mob who have decided what he is for. It is the same offer the devil had already made in the wilderness, and it is being made again by people who love him.

And what he refuses is not the kingship. He is the King, and he will say so to Pilate. What he refuses is a kingship on their terms — a bread-king, installed by acclamation, who solves the food problem and then the Roman problem, and who never gets anywhere near a cross. Given what he had come to do, the most dangerous thing available to him that afternoon was popularity.

So he leaves. He withdrew again to the mountain by himself, and Mark tells us what he did there: he went up to pray (Mk. 6:46). The largest crowd of his ministry wanted to make him king, and he walked away from them up a hill in the dark to talk to his Father.

Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable for anyone doing anything for God. Think of the response you would most like your work to receive. Now ask whether that response, if it came, would help or hinder what the work is actually for. There are successes that are indistinguishable from failure at the level that matters, and the ability to recognise one and walk away from it is very rare and is not natural to anybody.

Note finally that their theology was right. This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world — Moses had promised exactly that (Deut. 18:15), and they had correctly identified the man. Being right about who Jesus is and wrong about what he is for is not a small error corrected by more information. It sent five thousand people up a hill with a crown and no idea what they were doing.

verseByVerse.quote: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples are in the boat, heading across the lake in the dark, without Jesus. John's darkness is never merely chronological — it is spiritual disorientation, the condition of those who are doing the right things (following Jesus' instructions) but in the absence of his presence. It was dark, and Jesus had not yet come. The disciples are not lost; they are faithful but not yet accompanied. Every Christian knows this experience: the obedient life in the night of divine hiddenness, doing what was commanded while waiting for the presence to become visible again.

Two facts sit side by side in this sentence and the Gospel does not soften either. They are exactly where they should be, doing exactly what they were told — Mark says he made them get into the boat and go ahead of him (Mk. 6:45). And it is dark, and he is not there.

The order of the clauses is the thing. John does not write Jesus had not come to them, and it was dark, as though the darkness were caused by the absence. He writes: it was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them. Two separate facts, laid down flat, with no explanation offered for either.

That is worth having, because most Christian accounts of a dark stretch reach immediately for a reason. There must be sin in it, or a lesson in it, or a failure of faith somewhere. Sometimes there is. Here there is nothing of the kind, and John does not supply one. They obeyed an instruction, night fell, and he had not arrived yet.

And the last three words of the verse are what makes it bearable: not yet. John is writing sixty years later and knows perfectly well how the night ended. He puts the yet in deliberately, and it is the only comfort available in the sentence — not that the darkness is short, or that it means something, but that his absence has a term on it.

They are also, it is worth remembering, coming down off the best day of their lives. Five thousand people fed from a boy's lunch, twelve baskets of surplus, a crowd trying to crown their master. And that evening they are alone on black water with the wind against them. The distance between those two experiences is about six hours, and anyone who has had a high Sunday followed by a Monday will recognise the geography.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The storm arises while the disciples are being obedient, in the middle of doing exactly what they should be doing. This is a crucial corrective to the prosperity theology that measures obedience by the smoothness of the journey: faithful disciples face rough seas. The wind that opposes them is not evidence of divine disfavor but of natural reality — and the occasion for a revelation of divine power. God uses the storms of the obedient life not to punish but to display who is walking toward us on the water. The resistance is the setup for the revelation.

It is one sentence and it says everything by saying almost nothing. The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing. No dramatics, no cry for help, no sense that the writer thinks this needs explaining.

The Sea of Galilee sits about six hundred feet below sea level in a bowl of hills, and cold air spilling down the ravines from the heights meets the warm air over the water and produces squalls with very little warning. Fishermen who had worked that lake their whole lives knew it and were still caught by it. This is not a supernatural assault. It is the weather, and the men rowing into it were professionals.

Which is exactly why it is worth stating plainly what the verse does not say. It does not say the storm came because they had done something wrong; they had done what they were told. It does not say the storm came to teach them a lesson; John draws no such moral. It says the wind was blowing.

A great deal of harm is done by the assumption that adverse conditions in a Christian life are always messages. Sometimes the wind is simply the wind. Living in a world that is running down means that things break, and bodies fail, and boats get caught out on lakes, and the fact that a person was in the middle of obeying God when it happened is not evidence of anything at all.

What the storm does supply is the occasion. Nothing is being punished here and nothing is being corrected. But the men in that boat are about to see something they could not have seen on land in daylight, and it is not incidental that the revelation comes to people who are wet, frightened, and several hours into work that is getting them nowhere.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is I: in Greek, ego eimi — the divine Name, the same words by which God identified himself to Moses (Ex. 3:14). Jesus walking on the water is a theophany — a visible manifestation of the one who in Job 9:8 "trampled the waves of the sea." Do not be afraid: the angels' announcement at every divine appearance in Scripture. The disciples' terror is appropriate, because they are in the presence of the Almighty. The comfort is not "relax, it's just me" but "be at peace — the Lord God is with you in this boat, in this storm, in this night." The fear is transformed, not dismissed.

Take the geography first, because it fixes how alone they were. Three or four miles — John gives it as twenty-five or thirty stadia — puts them at the widest part of the lake, as far from either shore as it is possible to be. They had been rowing for hours into a headwind and had covered perhaps half the crossing.

And then a man is walking towards them on the water.

It is worth resisting the instinct to hurry to the comfort, because their terror was the correct response and John records it without embarrassment. Whatever they thought they were seeing, it was not a reassuring sight, and Mark says outright that they took him for a ghost and cried out.

Now the sentence he says to them, which every English Bible renders as It is I and which in Greek is ego eimi. It is a perfectly ordinary way of saying it's me, and translators are right to render it so. It is also the two words that stood behind the burning bush — I AM has sent me to you (Exod. 3:14) — and the two words this Gospel will build seven declarations on, starting later in this very chapter. John knows both senses. He has just written that the man saying it is standing on top of a lake in a gale.

Because there is nothing ambiguous about what walking on the sea means in Israel's Scriptures. The sea is the untamed thing, the domain of chaos that only God has authority over. Job says of God that he alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea (Job 9:8). A psalm says of the Red Sea crossing, your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters, yet your footprints were unseen (Ps. 77:19). Mark, describing this same night, says something stranger still: he meant to pass by them (Mk. 6:48) — which sounds like indifference until you know that passing by is the technical language of a theophany, what God did to Moses in the cleft of the rock and to Elijah at the mouth of the cave.

So this is not a display of power laid on to impress fishermen. It is a man doing, in front of witnesses, the specific thing the Old Testament says God does — and identifying himself with the two words God used at the bush.

And the comfort is not what we would have written. Do not be afraid comes attached to the most frightening statement available. They are not told there is nothing to fear. They are told who it is, and the reason to stop being afraid is that the one on the water is the one whose sea it is.

A man walked across the top of a storm in the middle of the night to reach a boat containing twelve tired people, none of whom had asked him to come.

The waves that Job says God tramples were, that night, under a pair of ordinary feet with the dust of a Galilean hillside still on them. And the first thing the voice out of the dark said was not a command, or a rebuke, or a claim. It was his name, and then: do not be afraid.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were glad to take him into the boat: joy as the specific response to the presence of Christ in the storm. And immediately — the same word used for the instantaneous healings throughout the gospels — the boat is at the shore. The journey that was laborious (three or four miles of hard rowing against the wind) is completed instantaneously when Jesus is in the boat. This is not merely a miracle of speed; it is a parable: what we cannot accomplish through all our straining, Christ accomplishes immediately when he takes his place among us. His presence changes everything.

There is one more Old Testament echo here and it completes the set, so it is worth having.

Psalm 107 describes men who go down to the sea in ships, who see the works of the LORD in the deep, who are lifted up to heaven and down again to the depths until their courage melts away. They cry to the LORD in their trouble, and he stills the storm — and then the last line: and he brought them to their desired haven (Ps. 107:23-30).

That is this verse. The rowing, the terror, the crying out, the calm, and the arrival. John does not quote the psalm; he simply narrates it, and any reader who knew the psalter would hear the whole thing.

And the detail that everyone stumbles over — immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going — is left exactly as it stands. John does not explain whether the remaining distance was covered miraculously or whether they were nearer than they thought. He reports that the moment he was aboard, they were there.

What is worth taking is the shape of it rather than the mechanics. They had rowed for hours against the wind and covered half a lake. He steps in, and the journey is over. Everything they had achieved by straining was real and was not enough; what finished it was his presence in the boat, and it took no time at all.

Say that carefully, though, because it can be turned into a promise that difficulties evaporate when a person is spiritual enough. They do not. This crossing had a storm in it, and hours of useless rowing, and real fear, and none of that was cancelled retrospectively. The rowing still happened. What the verse says is that the arrival did not finally depend on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–71 — The Bread of Life Discourse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The discourse on the Bread of Life is the longest and most difficult teaching in John's Gospel. It begins with the crowd seeking Jesus after the feeding miracle, and Jesus cuts through their motive immediately: they seek him for the bread, not for the sign. He redirects them: do not work for food that perishes but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give. The discourse then moves through a series of exchanges, each one going deeper: I am the bread of life; he who comes to me will not hunger; he who believes in me will not thirst. Then the most scandalous statement: 'Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.' The discourse ends with mass defection among the disciples and Peter's great confession: 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.'

The label above covers fifty verses and the summary reaches perhaps a fifth of them, so the rest is set out here and treated in full in the verse track. The crowd's question what must we do, to be doing the works of God? (vv. 28-29) is answered with a plural turned singular: one work, and it is to believe — which is both the easiest thing he could have required and the hardest, since it offers nothing to measure. They then demand a sign (vv. 30-31), having eaten one the day before, and quote the manna at him as the standard. He takes their quotation apart in the grammar rather than the vocabulary (vv. 32-33): not Moses but the Father, not gave but gives, and the bread is not an it but a he.

Three sayings then run in parallel and should be read together rather than played against each other. All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out (v. 37) — the second half emphatic in Greek, and the only condition in it is coming. Everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him (v. 40) keeps the door as wide as language allows. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (v. 44) states an inability, using a verb that means to haul rather than to woo — and the same verb is used of what the cross does to all people (12:32). Verse 45 glosses the drawing as a teaching, quoting Isaiah's new-covenant promise that all God's people will be taught by him (Isa. 54:13), with the immediate qualification that no one has seen the Father directly (v. 46). And I will raise him up on the last day is attached to each of these in turn, four times in the chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54).

The grumbling of vv. 41-42 uses the word the Greek Old Testament reserves for Israel murmuring in the wilderness, and the objection — is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? — is unanswerable from inside the information they have. The manna argument closes with four cold words: your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died (v. 49). It was a magnificent arrangement for keeping alive people who were going to die anyway.

Verse 51 is the pivot of the whole discourse and the tense changes to mark it: the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh. Something has not happened yet, and it is a death. The scandal of vv. 52-53 is sharper than modern readers feel, since drinking blood was not merely distasteful but the one thing the law forbade on pain of being cut off (Lev. 17:10-14). The language then moves from feeding to abiding, and for the first time in the Gospel it runs both ways — abides in me, and I in him (v. 56) — before verse 57 sets out the chain: the living Father, the Son who lives because of the Father, and the believer who lives because of the Son.

The setting of all this was the synagogue at Capernaum (v. 59), and the word his disciples use of the saying is not difficult but harsh (v. 60) — they are not saying they cannot follow it but that they cannot stomach it. His reply raises the ascension (v. 62), which either intensifies the offence or dissolves it, since a body that goes back up is not a body that gets eaten. Then the interpretive key, given to his own people at the point they ask: it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all; the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (v. 63) — the clarification arriving exactly where a reader wants it, and pointing away from physical eating. Verse 65 restates verse 44 with one word changed, from draws to granted, at the moment the doctrine is being demonstrated.

The chapter ends in three movements. The defection is the event the Gospel has been warning about since 2:24, and nothing caused it but a sermon (v. 66). The question to the twelve — do you want to go away as well? (v. 67) — is the most exposed thing Jesus ever says, asked by a man with nothing left to hold anybody with but himself. Peter's reply is a question rather than a creed, and confesses no new understanding, only that there is nowhere else (v. 68). And the title he reaches for, the Holy One of God (v. 69), had already been shrieked at Jesus by an unclean spirit in this same town (Mk. 1:24). Jesus will not let the confession stand as a headcount: one of you is a devil (v. 70), and John names him (v. 71). Judas heard the hard saying and stayed — which is the most frightening fact in the chapter, and the standing proof that proximity guarantees nothing.
verseByVerse.theology: The Bread of Life discourse is simultaneously eucharistic (the language of eating and drinking Jesus's flesh and blood points to the Lord's Supper) and spiritual (the key interpretive statement is 'it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all'). The flesh and blood Jesus speaks of is not a literal cannibalism but the reception of his atoning death: to eat his flesh and drink his blood is to appropriate by faith the benefits of his sacrifice. No one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws them; all who are given to the Son by the Father will come; all who come will be raised up on the last day. The sovereignty of grace and the necessity of faith are held together throughout.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin sees the Bread of Life discourse as the most complete exposition of the doctrine of the Lord's Supper in the New Testament: the supper is a spiritual feeding on Christ himself, received by faith, not a physical re-sacrifice. Sproul notes that the mass defection at the end of the discourse — 'many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him' — is the most important event in John 6: it reveals that the crowd's 'belief' was not genuine, and that the true disciples are known not by enthusiasm but by perseverance. Keller observes that Peter's confession — 'you have the words of eternal life' — is the greatest response to a hard teaching in the Gospels: when you cannot understand what Jesus is saying, you remain because of who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd is doing detective work: they know there was one boat, they know Jesus did not get in it, and they cannot account for his disappearance. Their puzzlement about his location is the occasion for the bread of life discourse — a discourse that will expose the shallowness of bread-seeking and call them to the seeking that satisfies. John notes that the additional boats arrive near where the Lord had given thanks — a liturgical phrase that reminds the reader that the feeding was not mere food-distribution but a foretaste of the Eucharistic feast of the new covenant.

What John records here is a piece of reasoning, and it is worth watching because it shows how close a person can get to the truth by pure logic and still miss it entirely.

They had counted the boats. They knew there had been one, and they knew the disciples had taken it, and they knew Jesus had not been in it. Their deduction is faultless: he cannot have crossed the lake. So they get into the boats that have since arrived from Tiberias and go looking for him on the other side — and find him there.

Nobody asks the obvious question. A man they last saw on the eastern shore, who could not have taken a boat, is standing in Capernaum the next morning. That is not a puzzle about logistics; it is a fact that ought to have stopped them where they stood. They notice the anomaly, cross the lake to resolve it, arrive, and open with a question about his timetable.

It is possible to be extremely observant about Jesus and entirely incurious. These people were paying close attention — closer than most — and every scrap of it was directed at the surface.

There is one odd phrase in these verses that most readers slide over: the boats came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.

It is John's own aside, not part of the narrative, and it uses a title — the Lord — that he almost never uses of Jesus during the ministry. He is writing decades later to churches who broke bread every week and said thanks over it, and for a moment his own vocabulary slips into theirs. The hillside is being remembered by a man who has since watched the same action performed ten thousand times in an upper room.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeking Jesus: the crowd's search is persistent, energetic, and ultimately misdirected — as Jesus will expose in the next verse. They are seeking him because their physical hunger was satisfied, not because they have understood who he is. Their seeking is real (they cross the lake to find him) but its motivation is deficient. The difference between seeking Jesus for what he gives and seeking Jesus for who he is is the difference between using God and worshiping God — a distinction that runs through every era of church history and every human heart.

Give them their due first: they got into boats. It is several miles across that lake and they had already walked round part of it once. Nobody in this verse is casual. The seeking is strenuous, organised, and expensive, and it is the sort of effort most of us would be pleased to see in ourselves.

And Jesus is about to tell them it was aimed at the wrong thing.

Which is the uncomfortable possibility this verse opens and it should not be closed too quickly. Effort is not evidence. It is entirely possible to work hard at religion — to travel, to give, to attend, to serve, to arrange a life around it — and for the whole apparatus to be in pursuit of something other than God. The energy proves the wanting. It says nothing about what is wanted.

Here is the test, and it takes some honesty. Suppose the specific benefit you associate with your faith were removed — the community, the sense of purpose, the moral framework that keeps your life in order, the hope of things going well. Suppose only Christ were left. Would you still cross the lake?

That is not a question anyone answers well, and it is not asked to produce despair. It is asked because these people crossed a lake and the answer, for them, turned out to be no — and they had no idea until he told them.

It is worth noting where they end up: Capernaum. That is his own base, the town of the synagogue in verse 59, the place he had made his home. They cross a lake to find him and arrive at his address.

Which supplies the small, bleak irony the verse runs on. They looked in the right place, they found the right man, and the search was still a failure — because finding Jesus and receiving him are two different things, and this Gospel said so on its first page: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (1:11).

verseByVerse.quote: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not answer their question about timing; he answers their question about motivation — which they have not asked but most need to hear. You are seeking me not because you saw signs but because you ate your fill. The crowd experienced the miracle as provision, not as revelation; as satisfaction of appetite, not as pointer to the true bread. They consumed the sign without reading it. This is the danger of every experience of divine blessing: receiving the gift without receiving the giver, being satisfied by what God gives without being drawn to who God is.

He does not answer the question they asked. They want to know when he arrived; he tells them why they came. And the diagnosis is delivered with a bluntness that would end most pastoral conversations: you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.

Note the strangeness of that first clause. Not because you saw signs — but they had seen the sign; five thousand of them had eaten it. What he means is that they had not seen it in the sense the word carries in this Gospel. A sign is a signpost. They had eaten the signpost.

And the verb for their eating is worth having, because it is faintly rude. Echortasthete comes from the word for fodder; it is what you say of animals fed to satiety. He is not being cruel — he had given them the meal himself, and given it lavishly. But the description is exact: they had been filled up, and being filled up was the whole of what had happened to them.

Which is the danger of every good thing God gives, and it is not a danger that announces itself. Nobody decides to want the gift more than the giver. It happens by the ordinary operation of appetite: the bread was real, the hunger was real, the satisfaction was real, and a person can live for years on that circuit without ever once turning to look at where the bread came from.

He tells them so to their faces, on the morning after feeding them, having watched them row across a lake to find him. It is one of the most bracing sentences in the Gospels and it is spoken by somebody who has just spent an afternoon meeting their needs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Work for the food that endures: not a contradiction of grace (as if eternal life were earned) but a call to reorder desire and effort. The crowd is laboring across the lake in boats, exerting great energy in the pursuit of perishable bread. Jesus calls them to direct that same energy toward what lasts. The Son of Man will give this food — it is gift, not wages — but they must actively receive and pursue the giver. God the Father has set his seal on Jesus: the divine authentication is complete, the credentials are established. The question is whether they will receive the one the Father has certified.

Two things in this verse repay attention, and the first is a paradox that has troubled careful readers.

Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures — and then, in the same breath, that this food is what the Son of Man will give to you. Work for a gift. It sounds like a contradiction and it is not: the working is not the purchasing. A man may labour hard to get to where something is being handed out without in any sense having earned it. What is forbidden is not effort but effort aimed at the wrong provision.

And the contrast is sharpened by the word perishes — the same verb from the twelve baskets, where nothing was to be lost. Ordinary bread perishes; that is its nature, and the loaves they ate the day before were already going stale. The food he is describing does not.

The second thing is the image at the end: on him God the Father has set his seal. A seal was pressed into wax or clay by a signet ring and meant ownership and authentication — this is mine, this is genuine, and I stand behind it. Merchants sealed sacks of grain. The picture is deliberately commercial and deliberately unglamorous: the Father has stamped his Son the way a supplier stamps a consignment, and the stamp is the guarantee that the contents are what they claim to be.

Which means the question in front of the crowd is not whether the bread is good. It is whether they will accept certification from the only authority competent to issue it — and they will spend the next verse asking for further evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they said to him, 'What must we do, to be doing the works of God?' Jesus answered them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
'What must we do?' — the works-righteousness instinct: give us a task list, a moral program, a set of religious duties. Jesus's answer is simultaneously the simplest and the most demanding thing he could say: the one work God requires is faith in the one God has sent. Faith is not nothing — it is the total orientation of the self toward Christ in trust and dependence. But it is not a work in the sense of a human achievement; it is the reception of a gift. And yet it must be done, and those who do not do it will perish.

Watch the plural become singular, because the whole exchange is in it. They ask what they must do to be doing the works of God — plural, a programme, a list of items to be worked through. He answers with the work of God, singular, and there is one item on it.

Their question is the most natural religious question there is, and every religion on earth has an answer to it. Give us the list. Tell us the observances, the disciplines, the standard, and we will apply ourselves — and there is real sincerity in it, because a list can be worked at and progress can be measured and a person can know where he stands.

What he gives them instead cannot be worked at in that way at all. This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.

And there is a deliberate ambiguity in the phrase which the older commentators loved. The work of God can mean the work God requires, and it can mean the work God does. Both are true here and neither should be dropped. It is required — he says so, and unbelief is not a misfortune but a refusal. And it is God's own doing, as verse 44 will say with a bluntness that offends people to this day: no one can come unless the Father draws him.

Which is why the answer is simultaneously the easiest and the hardest thing he could have said. Easiest, because a man on his deathbed with no strength for a list can do it. Hardest, because it cannot be part-done, cannot be got up to gradually, and offers nothing to measure. A list lets a person keep control of the transaction. Faith hands the transaction over.

Here is the test. Notice what happens inside you when a sermon ends without an application — no steps, nothing to implement. If the response is a mild frustration, that instinct is the one in this verse, and it is worth knowing it is there. It is not a bad instinct. It is simply the one Jesus declined to satisfy.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having just eaten five thousand people's worth of bread from five loaves, the crowd demands a sign. The audacity is breathtaking and humanly predictable: yesterday's miracle is already insufficient; today requires new evidence. They invoke the manna — Moses gave them bread from heaven daily for forty years. Implied comparison: what Moses did for decades, you did once. The manna becomes the standard against which Jesus is measured and found wanting in their accounting. They are using Scripture to resist the one Scripture points to — the classic move of those who love the text but not its subject.

The audacity is worth stating in its full size. Yesterday afternoon they ate bread that came out of nothing, in a quantity that left twelve baskets over, and this morning they are asking what sign he intends to perform so that they may believe.

Not another sign. They ask what sign do you do, as though the account were empty.

And the manna is the standard they are measuring by, which tells you exactly what they want. Moses, they say, gave bread from heaven — daily, for forty years, to a whole nation. One hillside meal, however impressive, is a single afternoon. The implied challenge is not prove yourself so much as can you keep it up? They are negotiating for a supply.

There is something almost comic and entirely recognisable in it. A miracle yesterday secures nothing today. Gratitude has a shorter half-life than anybody expects, and it is not cured by the size of the mercy — the generation that walked out of Egypt through a parted sea were complaining about the catering within about six weeks.

Note also what they do with Scripture: as it is written, he gave them bread from heaven to eat. They quote it correctly — it is Psalm 78:24, or close to it — and they use it as a weapon against the man standing in front of them. Jesus is about to take the same sentence apart word by word and show that they have misread the subject of it, which is the same operation he performed on Moses at the end of chapter 5.

And the little clause at the front of their demand gives the whole game away: that we may see and believe you.

It sounds reasonable and it is the reversal of everything this chapter teaches. They are proposing terms — produce the evidence, and belief will follow — which puts the sign in the position of proof and themselves in the position of assessors. Jesus never accepts that arrangement from anybody. He will tell Thomas that those who have not seen and yet believe are the blessed ones, and here he simply talks past the offer.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus corrects their misreading: Moses did not give the manna — the Father did. And the manna was not the true bread but a type, a shadow, a foretaste. The true bread from heaven is a person, not a substance: he who comes down from heaven. This is the great typological argument of the discourse: everything in Israel's Exodus experience was pointing forward to Jesus. The manna fed bodies in the wilderness for forty years; the true bread gives life to the world permanently. The shadow has given way to the reality, and the reality infinitely exceeds it.

He corrects their quotation in two places, and both corrections are in the grammar rather than the vocabulary.

First the subject. They said Moses gave them bread; he says it was not Moses. That is simply true — Exodus records God saying I am about to rain bread from heaven for you (Exod. 16:4), and Moses himself told the people that their grumbling was against the LORD and not against him. The manna was never Moses' to give. He was a man who woke up to it on the ground like everybody else.

Second the tense, and this is the sharper one. They said God gave — past, finished, a thing that happened to their ancestors. He says the Father gives, present. The action is not over. It is happening in the room.

Then the sentence that turns the whole discourse: the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world. Not it — he. Up to this point every hearer has assumed they are discussing a substance, and the substance has simply become a person without warning.

And the manna was always going to be too small a picture, which is worth saying since Israel remembered it as the golden age of provision. It fell six mornings a week for forty years and it kept a nation alive in a place where nothing grows. It also had to be gathered again the next day, went rotten if hoarded, stopped the moment they reached the land, and did not prevent a single one of the people who ate it from dying in the desert.

And the last phrase of verse 33 is the one to carry forward, because it is the first time in this Gospel that the bread is given a scope: he gives life to the world. Not to Israel, not to the crowd on the hillside, not to the people who ate yesterday. It is the same word John has been using since the prologue for the world that did not know him — and it is put here, in an argument with hostile men, as the stated purpose of the bread.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Sir, give us this bread always." Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give us this bread always: like the Samaritan woman's "Sir, give me this water" (4:15), the request is sincere but still thinking in physical categories — a supply that never runs out, an inexhaustible provision. Jesus' response is the first great I AM saying of the gospel: I am the bread of life. Not I give bread; I am bread. The provision and the provider are identical. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger, whoever believes in me shall never thirst: hunger and thirst are the deepest metaphors for existential need — and Jesus claims to satisfy both, permanently. This is not a program or a resource; it is a Person.

This is the first of the seven great declarations that give this Gospel its shape, and it is worth naming the set here since the rest of the book keeps returning to them. I am the bread of life (6:35). I am the light of the world (8:12). I am the door (10:7). I am the good shepherd (10:11). I am the resurrection and the life (11:25). I am the way, and the truth, and the life (14:6). I am the true vine (15:1).

Seven, and each takes something ordinary — bread, a lamp, a doorway, a shepherd, a road, a vine — and says: that is not a picture of me, I am the thing itself and every example you have ever met was the picture.

And notice which one comes first, and where. Not light, which would have been grander. Bread — the plainest, cheapest, most daily thing in the world, the item nobody notices until it is missing. Said in a synagogue, to people who had eaten the day before, in a district where a bad harvest meant a funeral.

Then the two halves of the promise, and they are not the same. Whoever comes to me shall not hunger — the coming answers the hunger. Whoever believes in me shall never thirst — the believing answers the thirst. Coming and believing are set side by side as the same act described twice, which is how this Gospel always speaks of faith: it is not an inward opinion but a movement toward a person.

What is being claimed is easy to nod at and enormous. Every human being alive is running an experiment on the question of what will finally satisfy, and every one of us has already found that the answers are temporary. He is not offering to improve the supply. He is saying the appetite terminates in him, and that anyone who arrives will find the search over.

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The indictment is precise: they have seen — they were there at the feeding, they witnessed the sign — and they do not believe. Seeing is not sufficient for belief. The problem is not a lack of evidence but a failure of will and heart. This is the Reformed doctrine of total depravity applied to epistemology: natural sight, however clear the object, cannot produce saving faith. The eyes must be opened by the Spirit; the heart must be renewed by grace; the will must be freed by the Father's drawing (v. 44). Unbelief in the face of evidence is not rational; it is moral failure at the deepest level.

The sentence is short and the sadness in it is easily missed: you have seen me and yet do not believe.

Not you have seen my works, though they had. Not you have heard my teaching. You have seen me. The thing that ought to have settled it is not an argument or a miracle but the person, and they have had him in front of them at close range, for a whole day, with a meal in between.

Which closes off the assumption almost everybody makes at some point: that if we could only have been there, it would all have been obvious. It was not obvious. Being present was not sufficient. The people who watched him make bread out of nothing and then followed him across a lake are the same people he is describing as unbelieving.

And it is worth saying gently to anyone who has ever wished for more evidence — the sign, the confirmation, the unmistakable thing that would settle the matter for good. This chapter contains five thousand people who were given exactly that, and it is not recorded that a single one of them was still following him by the end of it.

The opening words are worth a moment: but I said to you. He is quoting himself, and the reference is probably to verse 26 that same morning — you seek me because you ate your fill. The conversation has run twelve verses and he is already having to repeat a diagnosis they did not accept the first time.

Which is its own quiet evidence for the point he is making. A man who could produce bread from nothing cannot, by any amount of saying it, make a person see what is in front of him. That takes something else, and the next verses name it.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father gives me will come to me: the great double comfort of Reformed soteriology — the Father's election guarantees the Son's reception. No one the Father gives to Jesus will be lost in transit; no one who comes will be turned away. These two promises (all shall come; none shall be cast out) are the foundation of perseverance: the security of the believer rests not on the strength of his coming but on the certainty of the Father's giving. And the Son's mission is defined entirely by the Father's will: he has not come to run his own agenda but to accomplish the Father's saving purpose.

Verse 37 has two halves and each one has rescued more people than can be counted. They should be taken slowly and in order.

All that the Father gives me will come to me. The direction is worth noticing: this is a statement about the Father's giving and the Son's certainty, and there is not a word in it about the strength of anybody's grip. It is also, incidentally, an answer to the situation Jesus is standing in. He has just been abandoned by a crowd of five thousand and will shortly be abandoned by most of his disciples, and what he says about it is not that his ministry has failed but that everyone the Father has given him will arrive. He is not counting the room.

Then the second half, and it is the sentence to give to anybody who is afraid: whoever comes to me I will never cast out.

The Greek is emphatic in a way English cannot quite reach — a double negative with a future, something like I will certainly not, ever, under any circumstances, throw out. And the verb is physical. To cast out is what you do to somebody at a door: it is used of the man born blind being put out of the synagogue (9:34), of the traders driven from the temple. It is the language of being shown off the premises.

So the promise is not I will be tolerant of your failures, which is a smaller thing. It is that there is no version of the story in which somebody who came to him is put outside afterwards.

And note what the promise does not depend on. Not on how the person came — well or badly, early or late, from conviction or desperation or sheer exhaustion. Not on what they brought. Not on what they have done since. The only condition in the sentence is whoever comes, and it is stated so broadly that no one can be excluded by a technicality.

Here is the test, and it is for the anxious rather than the casual. Ask what you are secretly afraid would get you thrown out — the particular thing, not sin in general. Now read the verse again and notice that it does not have an exceptions clause, and that the man who said it knew everything about you before you came and issued the promise anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I should lose nothing of all that he has given me: the Son pledges to keep what the Father has given him — not because the sheep are strong enough to hold on but because the Shepherd's grip is stronger than every enemy. The final resurrection — raise it up on the last day — is the ultimate proof of the security: not only preserved in this life but raised in the next. The perseverance of the saints is not an achievement of saintly willpower but the consequence of the Father's election, the Son's keeping, and the Spirit's sealing. God finishes what God begins.

The Son is here quoting his job description, and it is worth registering that it is stated as the Father's will rather than the Son's intention. This is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me.

Which means that if a single person given to Christ were finally lost, the failure would not be a disappointment to the Son. It would be a failure of the Son to do what the Father sent him to do — and this Gospel has spent two chapters establishing that he does nothing on his own and always does what he sees the Father doing.

The verb again is the one from the twelve baskets: lose, apollymi. He would not have barley crusts trodden into the grass. He is now applying the same care to people, and John will close the circle in the garden when the soldiers arrive and Jesus negotiates the release of his disciples, adding the note that this fulfilled the word of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (18:9).

And the guarantee is not left at preservation. But raise it up on the last day — the same phrase four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54), which is unusual enough to be deliberate. Keeping somebody safe through this life is not the promise; anybody can be kept safe until they die, and everybody dies. What is promised is that the keeping extends through the grave and out the other side.

There is a plain comfort in the fact that this is stated as a determination rather than a hope. He does not say he will do his best.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The will of the Father is not hidden or arbitrary; it is publicly proclaimed: everyone who looks to the Son and believes has eternal life. The democratic offer — everyone — stands alongside the sovereign purpose — the Father's will. Reformed theology does not resolve this tension by denying either side but holds both: the offer is genuine and universal, the will is sovereign and effective. Those who look and believe discover, on looking back, that the Father had been drawing them all along. The looking and believing are real human acts; they are also the Father's gift.

Verse 39 gave the Father's will from the side of the Son's keeping. Verse 40 gives the same will from the side of the sinner's looking, and the two sentences are deliberately laid one on top of the other so that neither can be read alone.

And the verb in this one is worth having. Everyone who looks to the Son — the word means to gaze at, to contemplate, to keep one's eyes on. It is not a glance. It is the posture of somebody watching.

Which sends the reader back to the bronze serpent three chapters ago, where the dying were told to look and live, and forward to the cross, where John will quote Zechariah: they will look on him whom they have pierced (19:37). Looking is the one thing required, and it is required because it is the one thing a person with nothing left can still do.

Then the word that keeps the door as wide as it will go: everyone. Held next to verse 44's no one can come unless the Father draws him, it produces the tension that has divided the church for centuries — and the two verses are eleven apart in a single speech, so whatever the resolution is, Jesus evidently did not experience them as in conflict.

The pastoral order matters more than the systematic one. Nobody has ever been kept out by the doctrine of election; the door has everyone written over it, and no one who looks to the Son will be turned away on the grounds that they were not on a list. What the drawing explains is not who may come but why anybody does — and it is a question asked afterwards, looking back, by people already inside.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." They said, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, 'I have come down from heaven'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grumbling echoes Israel in the wilderness — the same word used in the Septuagint for the people's complaint against Moses. They know his parents: the Galilean hometown logic that makes divine origin impossible. They have the facts right (his mother is Mary, his father is thought to be Joseph) and draw the wrong conclusion (therefore he cannot have come from heaven). The incarnation is precisely this scandal — God in human particularity, the eternal Word with a known address and a recognizable family. Familiarity with Jesus' humanity becomes the barrier to recognizing his divinity.

The word for their grumbling is the one that runs through the wilderness story like a refrain. Gongyzo is what the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel murmuring against Moses at the bitter water, at the lack of meat, at the report of the spies — a low, sustained complaining that never quite becomes open revolt.

So the picture is now complete and John has built it carefully. There is bread from heaven, a crowd in a wilderness, a demand for a sign, an appeal to Moses — and now the murmuring. The generation Jesus is standing in front of is behaving exactly like the generation their argument depends on, and every one of them would have said the failure of that generation was the great cautionary tale of their history.

And their objection is unanswerable on its own terms. Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? They are not making anything up. They knew the family. They could probably have named the street. There is no way, from inside that information, to get to the conclusion that the man came down from heaven.

Which is the permanent scandal, and it has not weakened with time. God did not arrive in a form that made the conclusion easy. He arrived as somebody's son, in a documented family, from a town people could point to — and the very facts that make the story checkable are the facts that make it incredible.

There is also a warning here for anyone who has known Christian things a long time. The obstacle in this verse is not ignorance. It is familiarity — the settled sense that one already knows what there is to know about him, which is the most effective barrier there is, because it never feels like resistance. It feels like being well informed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can come to me unless the Father draws him: the most explicit statement of prevenient grace in John's gospel. The inability is absolute: natural humanity, left to its own capacity, will not come to Jesus. Coming requires drawing — the active, initiating grace of the Father that overcomes the will's resistance and brings the sinner to the Son. This is not divine coercion but divine liberation: the will that has been enslaved by sin is freed to do what it most deeply wants to do. The drawing creates the coming; the election produces the faith. All the praise belongs to the one who drew.

The verb is stronger than the English lets on and it should not be softened into persuasion. Helkyo means to drag or haul: it is used of hauling a net full of fish up the beach (21:6, 11), of drawing a sword from its sheath (18:10), and of Paul and Silas being dragged into the marketplace (Acts 16:19). It is not a word for gentle wooing.

And yet it is not a word for coercion either, because the same Gospel uses it of what the crucifixion does: and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (12:32). Whatever the drawing is, it operates through a cross rather than against a will — and nobody has ever been hauled to Christ against their inclination, because the drawing works by changing what a person wants.

Now the hard clause, and it should be stated rather than managed. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. Not no one will; no one can. It is an inability, and the whole of this Gospel has been demonstrating it — a teacher of Israel who could not follow a sentence about birth, a crowd who ate the sign and asked for another, men with every witness heaven could produce who would not come.

What that doctrine is for is worth being clear about, because it is regularly deployed as a weapon and it is not one. It is not a means of sorting other people into categories; nobody has been given the list, and this chapter shows Jesus preaching to a room he knows contains both. It is not a reason to stop pleading with anybody, since he is pleading with them as he says it.

It is an explanation offered to people who are already believing, and it answers one question: why me? Why did this land, when it did not land on the man beside me who had the same information and more sense? And the only answer this chapter permits is that somebody came and got me — which removes the last possibility of taking any credit for it, and removes at the same time the fear that a faith I produced could be one I might fail to maintain.

And then the same promise a third time, attached to the drawing like a receipt: and I will raise him up on the last day. The one who does the hauling also does the raising. Nothing in the sequence is left to the one being drawn.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus grounds the drawing in Isaiah 54:13 — the new covenant promise that all God's people will be taught directly by God. The Father teaches by drawing — by the internal work of the Spirit that opens the mind, warms the heart, and directs the will toward the Son. Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me: the teaching and the coming are inseparable. No one sees the Father directly — only the Son, who is from God, has that vision. The Son is the only authorized revealer of the Father; to know the Father, you must receive the Son's revelation of him.

The quotation is from Isaiah 54:13, and it sits in a chapter about a barren woman being told to enlarge her tent because she is going to need the room. All your children shall be taught by the LORD, and great shall be the peace of your children. It is a promise of the new covenant, in which instruction stops being something passed down through an institution and becomes something God does directly in every member of it.

Which is how Jesus glosses the drawing of verse 44, and the gloss makes it warmer without making it weaker. The Father's drawing is a teaching. Not a mechanical operation performed on an inert object — a person being taught something by God, and coming as a result of having learned it.

And the sequence is worth having in order: everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. Heard, learned, comes. Nobody arrives at Christ without having been taught, and nobody who has been taught fails to arrive. The teaching is effective, which is what distinguishes it from every other kind.

Then the qualification in verse 46, which is put in almost as an aside and is not one. Having said that everyone is taught by God, he immediately blocks the obvious misreading: this does not mean anyone has direct unmediated access to the Father. Not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God. The teaching happens; the seeing does not. Whatever a person learns of God, they learn it through the Son — which is precisely what 1:18 said, and it is why the drawing always terminates in the same place.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes has eternal life — already possessed, not waiting for death to begin. Eternal life is the quality of the life of God shared with those who trust in the Son; it begins the moment faith is born and continues through death and resurrection into the age to come. I am the bread of life: the great I AM declaration is repeated, intensified. Jesus does not merely provide what keeps people alive; he is himself the substance of that life. Union with Christ is not a metaphor for spiritual benefit; it is the substance of salvation itself.

Two sentences, and the second is the same sentence he said twelve verses ago. Repetition on that scale in a short speech is not accident; it is a preacher who has been interrupted, argued with, and grumbled at, going back to the point.

And the first one is worth weighing for what it leaves out. Whoever believes has eternal life. There is no object supplied. Not believes in me, though that is plainly meant and is said elsewhere in the chapter; here the verb simply stands. It is the barest statement of the terms anywhere in John, and it is put barely on purpose.

What it does not contain is any of the machinery a person might expect. Nothing about how much is believed, or how well, or for how long, or with what accompanying feelings. No mention of understanding — which is significant in a chapter where nobody understands anything. And the tense is present: has, now, in hand.

Which is the answer to a particular kind of Christian anxiety, and it is worth naming because it is common. There is a way of hearing the strong doctrine of the preceding verses — the drawing, the giving, the Father's will — and concluding that everything depends on whether one is inside a decision made before the world began, and then attempting to audit oneself for evidence of it. That way lies misery, and it is not what the verses are for.

The instruction never changes and it is not complicated: whoever believes has. The looking is the looking of a man on a mat, or a dying Israelite in a desert turning his head. It has never once been made harder than that.

The verse opens with the double amen — truly, truly — which is peculiar to this Gospel and occurs twenty-five times in it. Elsewhere in the Gospels Jesus says amen once; John always records it doubled.

The word normally goes at the end of somebody else's statement: it means so be it, that is reliable. He puts it at the front of his own. Nobody else in Jewish literature does this. It is a man endorsing his own words in advance, on his own authority, with the formula ordinarily used to endorse the words of God — and he does it here to introduce the simplest sentence in the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast is stark: manna sustained physical life for a generation in the desert — then those who ate it died. Every provision short of Christ is ultimately insufficient: it sustains for a season and then the body fails. The bread that comes down from heaven is qualitatively different: eating it means not dying. The death in view is the second death — the final separation from God. Physical death remains; spiritual death, eternal death, is overcome by the one who himself died and rose. The manna was grace for the wilderness; this bread is grace for eternity.

Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. It is one of the coldest sentences in the Gospels and it is aimed straight at the argument they opened with.

They had produced the manna as the gold standard: God fed a nation for forty years, and what have you done to compare with that? He takes the whole of it and adds four words. And they died. Every one of them. The bread came down out of heaven six mornings a week for four decades, and the entire generation that ate it was buried in the sand between Egypt and the land — which is the one part of the story they were not quoting.

So the argument turns round completely. The manna is not the standard Jesus has to match. It is the demonstration that a provision of that kind, however miraculous and however sustained, does not solve the actual problem. It was a magnificent arrangement for keeping people alive who were going to die anyway.

And that is a fair description of everything else too, which is the wider point and worth stating without cynicism. Medicine, food, safety, all the ordinary mercies — every one of them is real, and every one of them extends a life rather than saves it. The best possible outcome of all our arrangements is a longer wait.

Against which: this is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die. Not eat and live longer. Not eat and die comfortably. Not die.

Which requires the plain word, since Christians are buried like everybody else. The death he is speaking of is the one that is final, and the promise is not that a believer's body will be spared — this Gospel will shortly have him standing at a friend's tomb weeping — but that what happens at the graveside is no longer the end of the sentence. The manna could not stop a single funeral. This bread does not stop them either. It stops them being the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the bread that I will give is my flesh: the discourse pivots to the cross. The bread of life is not merely Jesus' teaching or presence; it is his sacrificed body. The feeding of the five thousand pointed here; the Passover setting confirmed it; now the language becomes explicitly incarnational and sacrificial. For the life of the world: the atonement is cosmically universal in its scope, particular in its application. He gives his flesh — a voluntary self-giving that anticipates Gethsemane and Calvary. The bread of life is a crucified Lord; there is no eating without his death.

This is the sentence the whole discourse has been walking toward, and it lands with a change of tense that is easy to miss. Everything so far has been present: I am the bread, whoever comes, whoever believes. Now: the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh. Future. Something has not happened yet.

Up to this point a hearer might have taken the bread as his teaching, or his presence, or his company. He now names it, and it is his body, and it is going to be handed over.

And the preposition is the one the church has built its doctrine of the atonement on: for the life of the world — hyper, on behalf of, in place of. It is the word used at the Last Supper of the body given for them, and the word Caiaphas will use without knowing what he is saying when he observes that it is expedient for one man to die for the people (11:50).

So the bread is not a metaphor for spiritual sustenance in general. It is a specific man, on a specific afternoon, dying in place of others — and the reason a person can be fed by him at all is that he was broken up first. That is why the crowd cannot follow it. They came for bread and are being told that the bread is a corpse.

And the scope in that phrase should not be quietly narrowed. For the life of the world — the same word that has been running through this Gospel since chapter 1, the world that did not know him and does not receive him. Whatever is settled about the extent of the atonement, this sentence was said to a hostile crowd in a Galilean synagogue and it did not have their names on it or anybody's.

He is standing in a synagogue in Capernaum, telling people who ate his bread yesterday that the meal he actually came to serve is himself, and that it will be served in pieces.

Nothing compelled it. He had made the loaves out of nothing the previous afternoon and could have gone on making them for forty years, as the manna had come, and kept a nation alive and been crowned for it. He declined the crown, walked away up a hill in the dark, and came back to say that what he intended to give was his flesh.

The bread of God is not something he carries. It is what he is, and it had to be broken before anybody could eat.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
