The Jews dispute — the same verb used for their grumbling, now sharpened into outright controversy. They understand Jesus literally and are scandalized: eating flesh violates Jewish law. Jesus does not soften the offense but intensifies it: unless you eat and drink, you have no life. The language of eating and drinking is the language of intimate participation, of taking into oneself what nourishes. To eat Christ's flesh and drink his blood is to receive the full benefit of his atoning death — to appropriate by faith everything he accomplished on the cross for the life of the world.

It is worth stating plainly how appalling this sounded, because familiarity has taken all the edge off it and the crowd's reaction is otherwise unintelligible.

Eating human flesh is horrifying in any culture. But drinking blood was, to a Jew, in a category of its own. The prohibition is absolute and repeated: If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood, I will set my face against that person who eats blood and will cut him off from among his people (Lev. 17:10). The blood was the life, and the life belonged to God; it was poured out at the altar and never consumed. A Jew did not eat a properly killed animal until the blood had been drained from it, and observant Jews still do not.

So what he has said is not merely strange. It is the naming of the one thing their law forbade on pain of being cut off — and he says it in a synagogue, and then says it three more times.

Which is why disputed among themselves is exactly right. The verb has moved on from the low murmuring of verse 41 to open argument; the room has split and they are shouting at each other about him.

And notice that he does not de-escalate. Their question — how can this man give us his flesh to eat? — is a fair one, and a teacher who wanted the room back would have answered it. He answers by raising the stakes: not only is it possible, it is necessary, and without it you have no life in you.

The reason he does not soften it becomes clear eleven verses later, when he tells his own disciples that the flesh is no help at all and that his words are spirit and life. He is not being obscure for effect. He is describing something that cannot be said any other way — a union with a dying man so complete that the nearest available picture is taking him into yourself and living on him — and the picture is offensive precisely because the reality is so total.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The positive side of the previous verse's negative: those who do eat and drink — who receive Christ's sacrificial death by faith — have eternal life and the certainty of resurrection. Whoever: the universality of the offer stands alongside the particularity of the reception. This is the Eucharistic theology of the gospel: not that bread and wine become flesh and blood in a physical sense, but that the Lord's Supper is the ongoing enacted proclamation of the death that gives life, and the faithful reception of it is the ongoing feeding on the crucified and risen Christ by which spiritual life is sustained and deepened.

That denial should not be left bare, because this chapter is one of the principal texts on which the Roman Catholic Church rests its teaching that the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ. The reading deserves to be stated at its strongest rather than waved away. Rome points out that the crowd plainly took Jesus literally — how can this man give us his flesh to eat? — and that instead of correcting them he pressed harder, moving from a general word for eating to a blunter one that means to gnaw or chew. He says his flesh is true food and his blood true drink. And when disciples found it intolerable and walked away, he did not call them back to explain that he had meant it as a figure. He let them go. If ever a speaker had reason to clarify a misunderstanding, it was here, and he did not.

That is a serious argument and it deserves a serious answer, which the passage itself supplies nine verses later. When his own disciples say the saying is hard, Jesus tells them what the saying was: it is the Spirit who gives life, the flesh is no help at all; the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life (v. 63). That is the clarification, given exactly where a reader would want it — and it points away from physical eating, not toward it. Notice too what he offers as the parallel: whoever feeds on him abides in him, and abiding is the word John uses throughout for a relationship held by faith, not by digestion. And there is the plain matter of timing. Jesus is speaking a year before the Last Supper, to a crowd who had no sacrament to think of and could not have understood a reference to one. Whatever this chapter is doing, it cannot be describing a rite that did not yet exist; it is describing how a person receives a crucified Saviour, which is by believing in him — the very thing Jesus said outright at verse 35, that the one who comes to him will never hunger and the one who believes will never thirst.

None of which makes the Lord's Supper a bare memorial or an optional extra. The Reformed churches have always taught that Christ is truly given to his people at that table and truly received — really, spiritually, by faith, through the Spirit — so that the feeding is no metaphor even though the flesh is not chewed. The disagreement with Rome is not about whether Christ gives himself to us there. It is about the mechanism, and about whether the once-for-all sacrifice can be re-presented. On this chapter's own terms the answer is that the eating is believing, and the life comes through the Spirit.

One further note on the fourfold refrain, since this is its third appearance: and I will raise him up on the last day. Four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54), attached in turn to the Father's will, to the one who looks, to the one who is drawn, and now to the one who feeds. Whichever way the promise is approached, it terminates in the same sentence — which is a preacher hammering one nail.

verseByVerse.quote: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
True food, true drink: as the true bread surpasses the manna, so the feeding on Christ surpasses all ordinary nourishment. The language moves from sustaining to abiding: whoever feeds abides in me, and I in him. Abiding — the great Johannine word for the mutual indwelling of Christ and his people — is the consequence of feeding. Every act of genuine faith in the crucified and risen Lord deepens the union between the Savior and the saved. This is not mystical absorption but covenantal union: the believer and Christ inhabit each other in the intimacy of the Spirit-mediated relationship that the Father and Son share.

The word that changes here is abides, and it is the one this Gospel has been carrying since chapter 1. Meno first appeared when the Spirit came down on Jesus and remained (1:32); it turned up as a domestic detail when the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed (1:38-39); it will carry the whole of chapter 15 — abide in me, and I in you; and it will name what rests on the unbeliever at the end of chapter 3.

Here it does something new. Up to now the abiding has been one-directional. This is the first time in the Gospel that it runs both ways: abides in me, and I in him.

That mutuality is worth pausing over because it is a strange thing to claim. Ordinary eating is entirely one-directional — the bread goes into the man and the man is unchanged in kind by it. Here what is taken in also takes in. The one being fed ends up inside the food.

Which is the answer to anyone who reads the eating and drinking language as a transaction — as if Christ were a commodity to be consumed for benefit. The whole vocabulary of the discourse has been building toward a relationship rather than a supply, and abide is where it arrives. Not a substance taken, but two persons who come to be in each other.

And true food, true drink — the same word used of the true light in chapter 1 and the true bread a few verses ago. It does not mean genuine as opposed to fake. It means the real thing of which every other example is a copy. Every meal anybody has ever eaten was an approximation of this.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chain of life: the Father is the living source; the Son lives because of the Father; the believer lives because of the Son. Life flows from the Father through the Son to those who receive him. This Trinitarian chain of life-giving is the inner logic of salvation: the Father sends, the Son gives himself, the Spirit applies. The contrast with the manna is now complete: your fathers ate the manna and died; whoever feeds on this bread will live forever. The wilderness generation received physical sustenance; the church receives the life of God himself — and cannot die.

The chain in this verse is the clearest statement in the chapter of how life actually travels, and it is worth setting out link by link.

As the living Father sent me — the Father is described by the one adjective that matters here: he is the living one, the source, the only being who has never had life handed to him. And I live because of the Father — the Son's life is described as derived, which is exactly what verse 26 of the previous chapter established: the Father granted the Son to have life in himself, eternally and without beginning. So whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.

Three links, and the preposition is identical in the last two. The believer lives because of Christ in the same way Christ lives because of the Father. That is a startling comparison and it is Jesus who makes it. The relation between a Christian and Christ is being described in the same grammar as the relation within the Godhead — not the same in kind, since one is eternal and the other is a gift to a creature, but running along the same line and out of the same source.

Which is why the manna comparison can now be closed for the last time. Not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. The manna came from heaven but it did not come from the Father's own life; it was a substance, and substances sustain and then stop. What is on offer here is not a better grade of provision. It is a place in a chain that begins in the life of God and has no terminus.

He has now said it four ways in twenty verses — the bread of life, the living bread, the true food, and now the chain of living. The crowd will say in a moment that this is a hard saying, and they are right, though not for the reason they think. It is not hard to follow. It is hard to want.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bread of life discourse is delivered in the synagogue — the official teaching space of Jewish religious life — and it produces the opposite of the crowd's earlier enthusiasm. This is a hard saying: not difficult to understand but difficult to accept. The disciples (the wider circle, not just the twelve) are scandalized by the demand for exclusive, total dependence on Jesus. Hard sayings are tests of faith: will we receive what we cannot fully comprehend because we trust the one who says it? The question "who can listen to it?" is the question every generation asks when the gospel's demands exceed their comfort.

John locates it precisely: in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. Not on a hillside with a crowd, but in the building where the community met to hear the Scriptures read — his own town, his own people, the room where he had probably been sitting since he was a boy.

And the word for hard is not the word for difficult. Skleros means harsh, rough, unyielding — it is used of a stiff wind, of a harsh master, of a cruel word. They are not saying they cannot follow the argument. They are saying they cannot stomach it.

That distinction matters, and it should be pressed, because it is the difference between two kinds of objection to Christianity that get mistaken for each other constantly. There is genuine intellectual difficulty, and it deserves patient work; this commentary spends a good deal of its length on it. And there is the objection that has nothing to do with comprehension — where the thing is understood perfectly well and is found intolerable. This is the second kind, and Jesus treats it as such: his reply says nothing whatever to clarify the content.

Note also who is speaking. Not the Jews, who have been grumbling since verse 41. Many of his disciples. These are people who had attached themselves to him, travelled with him, called him teacher. The crowd's objection was hostility; this is desertion forming in the ranks.

And their question is worth hearing as it was asked: who can listen to it? — not who can understand it, but who can go on sitting here while this is being said. They are already halfway out of the building.

The building is worth picturing, because it can still be visited. Under the fine white limestone synagogue that stands at Capernaum today — fourth or fifth century — archaeologists found the black basalt foundations of an earlier one on the same footprint, from the first century. That is the floor this was said on.

Luke tells us who paid for it: a Roman centurion built it for the town (Lk. 7:5). So the room where the crowd finally turned away was a room a Gentile soldier had given them, and it stood about thirty yards from Peter's house.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus perceives the murmuring without being told and asks the probing question: you are offended by my teaching about eating my flesh — what will you do when you see the Son of Man ascending? The ascension will be more scandalous than the discourse, not less. Jesus is preparing them for the cross and resurrection by which he will return to where he was before — to the pre-incarnate glory he had with the Father. The word made flesh will become the flesh that dies, rises, and ascends. Each stage of the revelation is harder than the last; saving faith must be capable of receiving all of it.

The question he asks back is genuinely puzzling until you see what it is doing. They are scandalised by his talking about eating his flesh — so he raises the ascension, which sounds like an answer to a different objection entirely.

Two readings are available and both are worth having, because they pull in opposite directions and the sentence is probably designed to hold both.

On the first, it is an intensification. If this offends you, wait. The Son of Man going back up is a larger claim than the Son of Man being eaten, and everything from here to the end of the book gets steeper. Faith that cannot take this saying will not survive the next.

On the second, it is a clue offered in mercy. If they were to see him ascend — to watch the flesh he is talking about leave the earth and go back where it came from — they would understand at once that he cannot have meant a butcher's transaction. The body that ascends is not a body that gets eaten. The ascension is the fact that makes the literal reading impossible.

Either way, the phrase where he was before is the hinge, and it is the thing the objectors in verse 42 had denied. They said they knew his father and mother and therefore he could not have come down. He answers by referring, without argument, to the place he came from and is going back to.

And John's note is worth registering too: Jesus knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling. Nobody reported it. This is the same faculty that read the woman at the well and saw Nathanael under the fig tree, and here it is turned on his own people, in the moment they are quietly deciding to leave. He watched them go before they went.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Spirit who gives life: the key to receiving the bread of life discourse rightly. The eating and drinking are not physical but spiritual — received by faith through the Spirit's illumination. The flesh — natural human understanding and appetite — cannot produce the life that Jesus offers. His words are spirit and life: they do not merely describe spiritual realities but communicate them, carrying the life they announce to those who receive them in faith. Yet Jesus knows from the beginning who does not believe — divine foreknowledge encompasses both the elect and the apostate without being the cause of either's choice.

This is the interpretive key to the chapter and it should be read slowly, because it is where Jesus tells his own disciples what the previous twenty verses were about.

It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all.

Notice the word he chooses. He has just spent ten verses telling them to eat his flesh, and he now says that flesh is of no use whatever. That is not a contradiction; it is a signal, and it is placed exactly where a hearer needs it. The category they have been reasoning in — the physical, the literal, the butcher's shop — is the wrong category, and no amount of it will produce what he is offering.

Then: the words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Not describe spirit and life. Are. The saying they have just called intolerable is itself the thing that carries the life, which means the way to eat him is to receive what he has said.

And this is why the eating is believing. It is not a Reformed convenience imposed on a difficult text; it is the explanation the speaker gives when his own followers ask, offered before anybody had a doctrine to defend.

Then the sentence that darkens the room: there are some of you who do not believe. Said to disciples. Not to the crowd, not to the authorities — to the people standing closest, some of whom he is telling, to their faces, that they do not believe.

John's bracket is heavier still, and it is the first mention of the betrayal in this Gospel: Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him. From the beginning. Which means that every time Judas was sent out, every meal he shared, every miracle he watched, every time his feet were washed — all of it happened with this known.

It is worth saying carefully that foreknowledge is not the same as causation. John does not say Judas was made to do it. He says Jesus knew. And the terrible thing about the sentence is not what it does to Judas's freedom but what it says about Christ's patience: he kept a man beside him for years, giving him everything he gave the others, knowing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The defection of many disciples is not a surprise or a defeat; it is the confirmation of what Jesus has been saying throughout the discourse. No one can come unless it is granted by the Father: the key word is granted — a gift, a bestowal. Those who remain are those to whom the Father has given this capacity; those who leave are those to whom it has not been granted. This is not fatalistic resignation but theological precision: the foundation of perseverance is divine election, not human resolve. The ones who stay will discover, on reflection, that they stayed because they were kept.

He is quoting himself — this is why I told you — and pointing back to verse 44. The doctrine is being restated at the precise moment it is being demonstrated, which is the reason it is in the chapter at all.

And the wording has shifted very slightly, in a direction worth noticing. In verse 44 no one can come unless the Father draws him. Here, unless it is granted him by the Father — a word of gift, of something handed over freely. The drawing of verse 44 emphasised the power required; the granting here emphasises that it was a present.

Which is the sentence to have in mind for what happens next, because the alternative explanations are all worse. The disciples are about to walk out in numbers, and there are only so many accounts available. Either the teaching was a failure of communication, or the crowd were unusually hard-hearted, or something is going on that the visible facts do not disclose. Jesus offers the third, and he offers it in a form that removes the possibility of anyone remaining feeling superior about it.

Because that is the effect of this verse on the eleven who stay. Whatever separates them from the ones leaving, it is not insight, or loyalty, or a better grasp of the argument — it was granted them. The only people in the building entitled to feel any pride are told, before the doors have even swung, that they have nothing to be proud of.

And there is a comfort in it that only becomes visible later, which is worth naming for anyone who finds the doctrine cold.

If staying were a matter of resolve, then every Christian would be one bad season away from the door — and most of us know our own resolve well enough to find that terrifying. What Jesus says here removes the whole question from that ground. The eleven did not out-endure the others. They were given something, and the giving was not conditional on their performance that evening or any evening afterwards, which is fortunate, since within a year every one of them would run away and one would deny knowing him.

They came back. That is the part the doctrine explains and self-confidence cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many turned back — the great defection at the end of the bread of life discourse. These are not Pharisees or hostile authorities; they are disciples, people who had been following Jesus. The hard saying has done its work: it has separated those who want Jesus' blessings from those who want Jesus himself. And then Jesus turns to the twelve with the most vulnerable question in the gospel: Do you want to go away as well? He will not hold them by diluting the gospel. If the cost is too high, the door is open. Authentic discipleship cannot be coerced; it can only be offered and received.

This is the verse the whole chapter has been building toward, and it deserves to be stated at its full weight rather than hurried past on the way to Peter.

After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.

Count what has happened in about eighteen hours. On the previous afternoon a crowd of five thousand was so convinced that they tried to take him by force and crown him. By the following evening the same movement has collapsed, and the collapse is not partial. Many is John's word, and the rest of the chapter suggests it was very many — by the end there are twelve men left, and one of those is Judas.

And nothing happened. That is the thing to sit with. There was no scandal, no defeat, no failure of nerve, no miracle that went wrong. He did not stop healing people or start behaving badly. He preached a sermon, and the sermon emptied the room.

Which is why this chapter has been standing behind so much of what has gone before. It is the demonstration of what John meant at 2:24 when he said Jesus did not entrust himself to the crowd who believed because of signs; it is what the Galilean welcome of 4:45 was always going to come to; it is the end of the hour in which they were willing to rejoice in the Baptist's light. Every one of those was a warning, and this is the event.

Two phrases in the verse are worth having exactly. Turned back — they went away behind, they returned to what they had been doing. And no longer walked with him, which is not a theological formula but a physical description: they stopped travelling in the same direction as him. Discipleship in the Gospels is mostly a matter of where a person's feet are, and apostasy looks less like a decision than like a road not taken any further.

Say the honest thing to whoever needs it. If you have watched somebody leave — a child, a friend, somebody you led to Christ yourself — this chapter says that happened to him, in his own town, in numbers, on the strength of his own preaching, and that it was not evidence of anything having gone wrong. It is the single most consoling fact in the chapter for a certain kind of grief.

And then the question, which is the most exposed thing he ever says. Do you want to go away as well?

He does not chase the crowd. He does not soften anything, or offer a clarification, or send anyone after them. He turns to the twelve — the last people he has — and offers them the door. The Greek phrasing of the question expects the answer no, but it is a real question, and it is asked by a man who has just watched a room empty and has nothing left to hold anybody with except himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's confession is not triumphant but desperate in the best possible way: Lord, to whom shall we go? Not "we choose you above alternatives" but "there is nowhere else." The disciples have not evaluated the options and selected Jesus as the best; they have discovered that outside of Jesus there is nothing — no words of eternal life, no bread that satisfies, no resurrection on the last day. The confession is born of spiritual destitution discovering its only supply. You have the words of eternal life: not "you have an interesting philosophy" but "your words carry the life of God, and we cannot live without them."

Peter's answer is not a compliment and it is not an affirmation of loyalty. It is a question, and the question is the whole point: Lord, to whom shall we go?

He does not say the teaching has become clear. Nothing suggests the twelve understood the flesh-and-blood discourse any better than the people walking out of the door; they had heard exactly the same sermon. What Peter says is that there is nowhere else — that having been where they have been, the alternatives have stopped being alternatives.

Which is a much stronger position than enthusiasm, and it is worth saying so, because Christians often measure their faith by how they feel about it and conclude that a faith held in bewilderment is a poor one. It is not. There is a kind of holding on that survives everything precisely because it has stopped depending on comprehension: not I understand and therefore I stay, but I have nowhere else to take this, and the words that give life are here.

And it is not resignation either. You have the words of eternal life is a positive claim and a large one. He has just heard the words called a hard saying by men who were leaving over it, and he calls the same words life. The difference between Peter and the departing disciples is not that Peter found the saying easier. It is what he concluded about the speaker.

Here is the test, and it is the one this chapter has been driving at. Think of the doctrine you find hardest — the one that would be a relief to discover was not true. Now ask what your reason is for staying with it. If the honest answer is that it has been explained to your satisfaction, that is a good and stable reason and it will hold for as long as the explanation does. Peter's reason will hold longer, because it does not rest on the explanation at all.

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's confession — the Holy One of God — is the highest title in the gospel yet: Jesus is the one consecrated by the Father, set apart from before time, the one on whom the Spirit remains without measure. And Jesus immediately introduces the shadow: one of you is a devil. The believing and knowing of verse 69 are genuine for eleven; they are false for one. The church has always contained both; the outward community of disciples is not identical with the inner community of the elect. Jesus knows which is which from the beginning — and still chooses to include him, because the betrayal is not an accident but a necessity of the redemptive plan.

The order of Peter's two verbs is worth noticing and it is not the order we would use: we have believed, and have come to know. Believing first, knowing second. We instinctively reverse it — find out, then commit — and this Gospel keeps insisting on the other sequence. The servants filled the jars before they saw the wine; the official walked home before he had news; and these men believed and then, over time, came to know.

And the title is startling once its history is known. The Holy One of God appears only a handful of times in the Gospels, and the other occasion is in a synagogue in this same town of Capernaum, where an unclean spirit shrieked it at Jesus: I know who you are — the Holy One of God (Mk. 1:24). The demon got there first. Peter is now saying, as a confession of faith and after everyone else has left, exactly what the demons had been saying all along under duress.

Which is a quiet reminder that the content of a confession is not the whole of it. The words can be perfectly orthodox and mean two entirely different things depending on who is saying them and why.

Then Jesus does something that must have been very hard to hear at that moment. Peter has just said the finest thing anybody says in the chapter, on behalf of all of them, at the lowest point of the ministry so far — and the reply is: Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.

He will not let the confession stand as a headcount. Eleven of them meant it. He does not correct the substance of what Peter said; he corrects the assumed arithmetic behind the we.

And the word is not a bad man. Diabolos — slanderer, accuser, the term this Gospel uses for the enemy himself. It is the strongest thing Jesus ever says about one of his own, and it is said about a man who at that moment had done nothing publicly wrong and was presumably standing there among the others, having also just stayed.

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John names Judas explicitly where Jesus spoke only obliquely. The identification is not a removal of mystery but an invitation to theological reflection: the one who will betray Jesus was among the twelve, ate the bread with him, heard the words of eternal life, watched the signs — and chose the darkness. Judas is not a cartoon villain; he is a warning about the possibility of external discipleship without internal transformation, of knowing the words of eternal life without being given life by them. The greatest privileges do not guarantee the greatest outcomes; only the Father's gift and the Spirit's work can produce the perseverance that endures.

John supplies the name, and it is worth noticing when he does it. Not at the time — Jesus said only one of you, and there is no indication that anybody in the room worked out who was meant; at the last supper they will still be asking. John names him here, decades later, writing for readers who know how it ends.

Which leaves the reader in a position nobody in the story occupied: watching Judas stay. Because that is what happens in this chapter. The crowd leaves, the wider circle of disciples leaves, and Judas stays. He heard the hard saying and did not walk out. He was standing there when Peter said to whom shall we go?, and by every visible measure he was one of the ones who held on.

That is the most frightening thing in John 6, and it is more frightening than the mass defection. The people who left at least made their position plain. Judas remained inside the twelve for something like another two years, was trusted with the money, was sent out to preach, watched the raising of Lazarus, and had his feet washed by the man he sold.

And it must be handled carefully, because there is a reader who will now begin auditing himself for signs of being a Judas — and that reader is almost certainly not one. Consider the evidence the chapter gives. Judas is never once recorded as troubled about his own state. He does not ask whether it might be him; at the supper, when the others ask is it I?, his question comes last and reads as cover. Anxiety about one's own heart is not the mark being described here. The mark is a man entirely at ease.

What the verse does say, and says without softening, is that proximity guarantees nothing. Three years at close quarters with the Son of God, inside the smallest circle, doing the work and hearing every word, did not produce faith in one man out of twelve. Nothing external can. The chapter has already told us what does — no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father — and Judas is the standing proof that everything short of that is insufficient.

The chapter ends where it began, with a question about bread. Five thousand people ate it and went home hungry the next morning. One of the twelve ate it for three years at the same table as the one who made it, and starved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John 7–8 forms a sustained unit set during and after the Feast of Tabernacles, the great autumn harvest festival that celebrated God's provision in the wilderness. The feast is the setting for Jesus's most public ministry in Jerusalem: teaching in the temple, the sending of officers to arrest him, the debate over his origins, and the great invitation on the last day of the feast: 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.' The feast recalled the water from the rock in the wilderness; Jesus claims to be the fulfillment of that provision. The chapter ends in division — some believe, some want to arrest him, the Pharisees dismiss the crowd as accursed — and Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter 3, makes a quiet stand for due process.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on the question of Jesus's origins and authority. Where is he from? Did he come from God or from himself? The crowd is divided: some say he is a good man; others say he leads the people astray. Jesus's teaching in the temple provokes astonishment: 'How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?' His answer is theological: his teaching is not his own but the Father's, and the one who seeks to do God's will will recognize its divine origin. The authority question and the origin question are ultimately the same question: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: Keller notes that the Feast of Tabernacles is the most eschatological of the Jewish festivals — it looks forward to the final harvest, the ultimate ingathering. Jesus's claim at the climax of the feast ('out of his heart will flow rivers of living water') is the claim to be the fulfillment of Israel's end-times hope. Sproul observes that the officers who were sent to arrest Jesus and returned saying 'no one ever spoke like this man' (v. 46) is one of the most powerful testimonies to the authority of Jesus's teaching in the entire Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Tabernacles was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus moves deliberately, not by fear but by divine timing: he would not go to Judea because the hour had not yet come. The Feast of Tabernacles — the great autumn harvest festival celebrating Israel's wilderness journey — is the theological backdrop for the entire chapter. Tabernacles was associated with water-drawing ceremonies and torch-lighting celebrations, making it the perfect setting for Jesus' declarations about living water (v. 37-38) and the light of the world (8:12). The Son of God chooses his moments; his moves are not reactions but initiations.

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' brothers advise a publicity campaign: go to Jerusalem, perform signs publicly, build a following among the disciples there. Their logic is the logic of worldly ambition and religious marketing: visibility produces influence. They are not entirely wrong in their assessment of how movements grow, but they are entirely wrong about what Jesus' movement is. His kingdom does not advance through staged displays of power for maximum audiences. The Son of Man will not show himself to the world on the world's timetable; he will be lifted up on the Father's timetable — on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The editorial note is sobering: those who grew up in the same house, who shared meals and childhood memories and workshop apprenticeship, did not believe. The incarnation is scandalously particular — God in a specific family, in a specific village — and the particularity is itself a stumbling block to those who know the particular details too well. Familiarity is the enemy of awe. His brothers knew Jesus the man too well to recognize Jesus the Lord. After the resurrection, James and Jude will believe (Acts 1:14; Jas. 1:1; Jude 1). The scandal of unbelief can be overcome — but only by resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary: My time has not yet come: the kairos of Jesus is divinely governed, not socially negotiated. His brothers can go to Jerusalem at any time because the world has no reason to hate them — they belong to it; they share its values and speak its language. The world hates Jesus because he names the truth about it: its works are evil. The world tolerates many kinds of religion and moral teaching, but it cannot tolerate the unqualified claim that its fundamental orientation is sinful and that only grace can save it. The cross is the world's answer to that testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not go up publicly with his brothers but later in private (v. 10) — a distinction between the public display his brothers urged and the quiet, purposeful appearance Jesus chooses. I am not going up: not a false statement (he does go) but a refusal of the method they proposed. His going will be on the Father's terms, at the Father's moment, with the Father's purpose. The remaining in Galilee is not passivity but restraint — the strategic patience of the one who knows that the hour has been set from eternity and cannot be rushed by family pressure or popular demand.

That sentence deserves more than a passing defence, because it has been used for centuries to accuse Jesus of a lie. He says "I am not going up to this feast," and two verses later he goes up to the feast. The charge is old: the third-century critic Porphyry pressed exactly this point, and it is still raised. It should be met head-on rather than waved away.

First, a word about the text, since Bibles differ here. Many manuscripts read "I am not yet going up," and some translations follow them. But the shorter reading, without the "yet," has the better claim to be what John wrote, for the plain reason that it is the harder one: a copyist who found the sentence awkward would add a softening word, whereas no copyist would take a smooth sentence and roughen it into an apparent falsehood. So the honest course is to answer the harder text rather than shelter behind the easier.

And the harder text answers well, because the whole exchange is about a manner of going, not a matter of geography. His brothers were not offering him a lift to Jerusalem; they were urging a campaign — "show yourself to the world" (v. 4), go up publicly, with the crowds, and stake your claim. That is the going up he refuses. And John himself supplies the distinction in the very next sentence: when Jesus did go, he went "not publicly but in private" (v. 10). He did not do the thing he said he would not do. The reason he gives is the reason he has given twice already: "My time has not yet come" (vv. 6, 8). He is not managing his image with a convenient untruth; he is declining a schedule that was not his Father's. The man who would shortly refuse to come down from a cross was not a man who trimmed his words to make an afternoon easier.

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus goes to Jerusalem — but quietly, without the public display his brothers urged. The religious authorities are already on alert, scanning the festival crowds for him. Where is he? — the question that runs through the gospel: where does Jesus come from, where is he going, where is he now? The seekers vary: some seek to kill him, some to learn from him, some to make him king. The question "where is he?" is, beneath the surface, the deepest question — where is God? The answer John is giving across twenty-one chapters is: he is here, in this man, in this moment, in this gift of himself for the life of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The public debate about Jesus is muted by fear: some think him good, some a deceiver, but all are reluctant to say so openly because the institutional authorities have made their displeasure clear. This is the social suppression of the public confession that the gospel requires. For fear of the Jews no one spoke openly: the fear of human opinion is always the enemy of faithful witness. Jesus himself will later warn against it (12:42-43), noting that those who love the glory of men more than the glory of God cannot believe. The crowds who admire in private but will not confess in public are, functionally, on the side of those who oppose.

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews marveled at it, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus appears suddenly in the temple courts — the most public teaching venue in Jerusalem — in the middle of the feast, without warning or introduction. His teaching produces marveling: how does a man without formal rabbinical training speak like this? The question reveals the authorities' category for legitimacy: formal education in recognized schools under recognized teachers. Jesus has no such credentials. He is self-taught in the sense that his teaching comes directly from the Father — which is, of course, a far more authoritative source than any rabbinic lineage. The Son's school was eternal communion with the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary: The teaching is not self-originated but received from the Father — a claim that simultaneously explains the authority (it comes from God) and issues an invitation: if anyone wants to do God's will, he will be able to discern whether this is from God. The test of authentic doctrine is not institutional approval but moral and spiritual alignment: the person whose will is oriented toward God has the capacity to recognize God's word when they hear it. This is the epistemology of discipleship: spiritual receptivity enables theological discernment. The willingness to obey is prerequisite to the capacity to know.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The test of a teacher's integrity is whether he seeks his own glory or God's. Jesus seeks the Father's glory — this is the ground of his truthfulness. Then the counter-accusation: you are proud guardians of the Mosaic law, but you are plotting murder — which the law forbids. The irony is devastating: the very people who criticize Jesus for violating the Sabbath are violating the commandment against murder. They are selective in their law-keeping, rigorous about what is convenient and criminal about what is not.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's accusation — You have a demon! — is their explanation for what seems paranoia: why would anyone be trying to kill this celebrated teacher? They do not know about the authorities' intentions (v. 1) or the decision of 5:18. Jesus does not defend himself against the demon charge; he returns to the Bethesda healing and the Sabbath controversy that began the conflict. I did one work: the healing of a single paralyzed man on a single Sabbath has generated a desire to kill him. One act of mercy has revealed the murderous logic of a religious system that places institutional authority above human restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary: The rabbinical ruling on circumcision — performed on the eighth day even when that day falls on the Sabbath, because the covenant obligation overrides Sabbath rest — becomes Jesus' argument by analogy. If circumcision, which affects one member of the body, overrides the Sabbath, how much more should the healing of the entire body? The argument is from the lesser to the greater, from the partial to the whole. Jesus is not dismissing the Sabbath; he is exposing the inconsistency of those who permit circumcision-on-Sabbath while condemning healing-on-Sabbath. Their application of the law is selective in ways that serve institutional power.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary: Judge with right judgment: Jesus calls for hermeneutical consistency and moral honesty in the application of the law. The surface-level reading (healing on Sabbath = violation) gives way under right judgment to a deeper reading: if covenant mercy overrides Sabbath in circumcision, it overrides Sabbath in healing. The anger of the authorities is not principled; it is politically motivated. They are not defending the Sabbath; they are defending their authority. Jesus' appeal to right judgment is an invitation to read the law as the law intended — as a vehicle for mercy, not a weapon for institutional control.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Jerusalem crowd — more politically aware than the Galilean pilgrims — are confused by the authorities' inaction. They expected arrest; instead, Jesus is teaching publicly in the temple without interference. Their logic is that the silence of the authorities implies recognition — perhaps the rulers have concluded he is the Christ. The reasoning is naive (the authorities have not softened; they are waiting for an opportune moment) but the question it produces is the right one: Can it be that this is the Christ? The right question, born of the wrong reasoning, can still be the beginning of saving inquiry.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary: The popular tradition that the Messiah would appear from nowhere, without known origin, is used to dismiss Jesus: they know his hometown and his family. But their "knowing" is surface knowledge — they know Nazareth and Joseph, not the eternal origin in the bosom of the Father (1:18). The very thing they use to dismiss him — his known humanity — is the miracle of the incarnation. The one through whom all things were made took on a knowable, traceable human history so that the unknowable God might be encountered in human flesh. Their certainty about his origin is the measure of their ignorance of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus's proclamation in the temple is bold and direct: you know my human origins, and you are right. But my ultimate origin — the one who sent me — you do not know. This is the deepest irony of John 7: the very people who think they know most about his origin know the least. They know Nazareth; they do not know the Father. Jesus knows the Father because he comes from him — this is not a claim of spiritual experience but of ontological origin: he is the eternal Son who has come from the Father's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The tension between human hostility and divine protection is explicit: they want to arrest him; his hour has not yet come, so they cannot. Human evil operates within the limits that sovereign providence sets; the cross will come, but only when God appoints it, not when human opposition achieves it. Meanwhile, belief is spreading: many believed, arguing from the signs that no messiah could surpass this record. Their faith is sign-based and therefore fragile, but it is real faith beginning, and Jesus receives it — he does not despise the bruised reed of sign-faith that has not yet grown into cruciform faith.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The institutional response to the spread of belief is administrative: send officers to arrest him. The Sanhedrin — both Pharisees and chief priests — acts with official authority. But they will fail, as the officers will return empty-handed, awed by his teaching (v. 45-46). The attempt to suppress the gospel through institutional force is as old as Pharaoh and as recent as the twenty-first century's persecution of the church. It has never ultimately succeeded, because the hour is always in the Father's keeping. Every attempt to arrest the spread of the word meets with the same result: the word continues.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus announces his departure in the hearing of his would-be arresters — a declaration that reframes the entire confrontation. They are not in control of the timing; he is. He will go — not because they drive him away but because the Father calls him home. Where I am you cannot come: the destination is the Father's presence, inaccessible to those who have refused the Son who is the only way there. The seeking and not-finding is judicial: those who refused to seek him when he was present will seek him when he is absent and discover it is too late. The offer of grace has a closing time.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The irony of the questioners' confusion is exquisite: they wonder if he is going to the Greeks — and in the event, the gospel does go to the Gentile world through the apostolic mission. What they suggest mockingly, the Spirit will accomplish literally. Their literalism about Greek Diaspora communities misses the metaphorical truth Jesus intends (going to the Father) while unknowingly predicting the actual expansion of the gospel. Providence has a habit of putting the right words in the mouths of those who oppose it, words they do not understand but which the Spirit will fulfill.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last day of Tabernacles was the climax of the water-drawing ceremony — a daily ritual in which priests carried water from the Pool of Siloam to the temple altar, celebrating both wilderness provision and eschatological hope. Into this charged ritual moment, Jesus stands and cries out — the posture and volume of public proclamation: If anyone thirsts, come to me. He claims to be the fulfillment of the entire ceremony, the source to which the Siloam water pointed. Rivers of living water — not a trickle for personal refreshment but an overflow for the renewal of the world. The thirst of the world is met by the inexhaustible supply of the Spirit.

Two things here will stop a reader who looks closely. The first is a question of punctuation, the same kind met at 3:16, and translations divide over it. Read one way, the sentence runs: whoever believes in me, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water — the believer is the channel, and the water flows out of the Christian. Read the other way, the invitation ends with believing, and the promise begins fresh: out of his heart, meaning out of Christ's, will flow the rivers. The Greek has no punctuation to settle it, and both readings are held by serious translators. The second reading has a strong claim: it fits the water-drawing ceremony he is standing in the middle of, where the water flows from the temple, and it matches Ezekiel's vision of the river pouring out from under the temple threshold (Ezek. 47:1-12) — with Jesus himself the new temple, as he said in chapter 2. But the difference is smaller than it first appears, since John explains in the next verse that he is speaking of the Spirit, and the Spirit comes from Christ to the believer and then out through him. The spring is Christ either way; the question is only how far downstream the sentence is looking.

The second thing is more likely to trouble someone: he says as the Scripture has said, and a reader who goes hunting for the verse will not find it. There is no Old Testament sentence that reads this way. He is not misquoting; he is doing what the New Testament often does, gathering a theme rather than citing a line. The rock struck in the wilderness poured out water for a whole nation (Exod. 17:6; Num. 20:11). Isaiah promised water on the thirsty ground and streams in the desert (Isa. 44:3; 55:1). Ezekiel saw the river from the temple, deepening as it ran until it healed the Dead Sea itself. Zechariah saw living waters going out from Jerusalem (Zech. 14:8) — and that prophecy is read at the Feast of Tabernacles, which is the very feast being kept as he speaks. He is not quoting a verse. He is telling a room full of people at that feast that the whole river of promise they have been singing about has arrived, and is standing in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's editorial clarification is essential: the rivers of living water are the Holy Spirit, to be given after Jesus' glorification (death, resurrection, ascension). Pentecost is here announced in typological language. The Spirit could not be given in fullness while Jesus remained in the flesh; the glorification — the entire event of cross and resurrection — must first be accomplished. The Spirit is the gift of the glorified Christ to his people, the down payment of the age to come, the one through whom the absent Lord is made present. Every experience of the Spirit is an experience of the glorified, ascended, ever-interceding Son.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd divides over Jesus — a division that is itself a fulfillment of Simeon's prophecy that the child would be "a sign that is opposed" (Luke 2:34). The Prophet and the Christ: two messianic categories competing for the right identification. The third group raises the geographical objection: the Christ comes from Bethlehem (2 Sam. 7:12-14; Mic. 5:2), not Galilee. What they do not know is that Jesus was born in Bethlehem — their objection, based on incomplete information, is exactly wrong. The one they dismiss on geographical grounds fulfills every geographical requirement of the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Scriptural argument — Davidic descent, Bethlehem origin — is correct theology applied in ignorance of the facts. Jesus is both: of David's line through Mary and Joseph's legal paternity, born in Bethlehem by divine arrangement. The irony runs throughout John: those who oppose Jesus consistently state truths about him without knowing they are doing so. The division the crowd experiences is the inevitable result of Jesus' presence: he does not come to bring peace at the cost of truth but to reveal what is in every heart. The gospel always produces both faith and opposition.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary: For the second time in this chapter, the attempt to arrest Jesus fails — this time from within the crowd itself. No one laid hands on him: not because Jesus was hidden or protected by human means, but because the hour had not come. The restraint is invisible and divine; to human observers, Jesus simply continues to teach without interference. This is the pattern of providential protection throughout the book of Acts as well: the apostles are imprisoned and released, threatened and preserved, pursued and protected — not by their own cleverness but by the sovereign hand that governs all things according to the counsel of its will.

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary: The officers sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed, and their explanation is a spontaneous confession: No one ever spoke like this man. Those sent as instruments of institutional suppression become involuntary witnesses to the authority of his teaching. The power of Jesus' words is not rhetorical technique or charismatic delivery but the inherent authority of the one who speaks as the Son of God — words that carry life (6:63), words that the Father himself speaks through him (7:16). Even those hardened by official commission cannot hear Jesus without being arrested by something the arresting officers could not name.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The argument from authority: no official has believed in him, therefore belief is error. This is the appeal to institutional consensus as the standard of truth — and it will eventually be proven spectacularly wrong by the resurrection. Among the authorities, Nicodemus is wavering (v. 50-51), and Joseph of Arimathea is believing in secret (19:38). The Pharisees' sweeping claim — no authority has believed — is both rhetorically convenient and factually incomplete. Institutional consensus has never been a reliable gauge of divine truth; the prophets all had to contend with the official consensus of their day.

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees' contempt for the crowd — the am ha-aretz, the people of the land who lack formal legal training — is a religious classism that the gospel dismantles. Blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the hungry: the very people the Pharisees dismiss as accursed are precisely those whom Jesus calls blessed. And the crowd's instinct about Jesus — that no one has ever spoken like him, that he might be the Christ — is closer to the truth than the scholars' rejection. Knowledge of the law, unaccompanied by love of its Author, produces not wisdom but pride, not discernment but contempt.

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Nicodemus reappears — the man who came to Jesus by night (3:1-2) is now speaking, if not yet confessing, in the daylight of the Sanhedrin chamber. His argument is procedural: the law itself requires a hearing before judgment. He does not yet declare that Jesus is the Christ; he advocates for due process. This is faith in its early, cautious, institutional form — not yet the full confession, but moving toward it. Nicodemus is on a journey: from nighttime curiosity, to procedural advocacy, to standing at the cross with Joseph of Arimathea to bury the Lord (19:39). Grace is patient with slow journeys.

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sanhedrin's dismissal of Nicodemus is the same geographical argument used against Jesus — and it is wrong on the facts. Jonah was from Gath-hepher in Galilee; Elijah from Tishbe; Nahum from Elkosh (possibly Galilee). The sweep of "no prophet from Galilee" is factually false, born of contempt rather than exegesis. The council disperses to their homes, the confrontation unresolved, Jesus unarrested, the word continuing to spread. Chapter 7 ends not with a verdict but with a dispersal — the authorities fragmented, the crowd divided, the officers awed, and Nicodemus quietly beginning to move toward the Light.

One practical note about that closing line, since your Bible has probably done something visible with it. Verse 53 is not really the end of chapter 7 at all; it is the opening sentence of the account of the woman caught in adultery, which runs from here to 8:11 and which most modern translations enclose in brackets or set off with a note, because the earliest manuscripts do not contain it. That is why the bracket in your Bible seems to open in an odd place, mid-scene, at the last verse of a chapter. The passage and the reasons for the brackets are handled where the story itself begins, at the start of chapter 8.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus returns to the Mount of Olives and enters the temple at dawn, where he encounters a woman brought for judgment, declares himself the light of the world, and defends the validity of his testimony with a sustained legal argument about the Father as his witness. The chapter opens with the drama of grace overcoming accusation and closes with 'I am he' — the divine Name — driving his opponents to the ground.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is saturated with the language of witness and judgment (a courtroom), light and darkness (the ceremonial torch-lighting of Tabernacles still in view), and the 'I AM' sayings that claim identity with the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus simultaneously judges (he is the one who judges truly, v. 16) and refuses to judge (he did not come to condemn, v. 15). This paradox is resolved in the cross: all judgment was poured out on him so that those who come to him face no condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: The woman caught in adultery: the accusers depart one by one, beginning with the oldest (the most self-aware of their own sin). Augustine: 'There were left two — misery and mercy.' She goes free not because the law is set aside but because Jesus will shortly bear its full penalty. Every Christian stands where she stood: condemned by the law, set free by the one who alone can say 'neither do I condemn you,' because he bore the condemnation himself.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus spends the night on the Mount of Olives — outside the city, in the open air, while the religious establishment sleeps in comfortable houses. At dawn he returns to the temple and sits to teach: the posture of the seated rabbi with full authority. All the people came to him: the contrast with the institutional leaders who reject him is sharpest here. Those without institutional standing flock to the one who has ultimate authority. The temple, which the establishment has made a place of commerce and politics, becomes once again a house of teaching at the first light of day. A note the honest reader needs: this account of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) is placed in brackets or set off with a footnote in most modern Bibles, because the earliest and best Greek manuscripts do not contain it, and where it does appear later scribes sometimes placed it elsewhere (after John 7:36, or even in Luke). So the manuscript evidence weighs against it being an original part of John's Gospel. And yet many scholars believe the event itself is genuine apostolic memory — it rings true to how Jesus dealt with sinners and their accusers, and the early church treasured it. The wise course, and the one taken here: read it, learn from it, but build no doctrine on it that Scripture does not teach clearly elsewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The staging is a legal trap: if Jesus upholds stoning, he violates Roman law (which reserved capital punishment for Rome) and contradicts his reputation for mercy; if he dismisses it, he violates Mosaic law. The woman is not a person to them but a prop. The Pharisees have used her sin as a tool in their political game — the deepest form of exploitation. Placing her in the midst: publicly exposed, humiliated, no advocate, no escape. This is the human condition before the court of divine justice: no cover, no defense, fully seen.

And now the question every reader asks, which the accusers were counting on nobody asking: where is the man? They say she was caught in the act of adultery. Adultery is not a thing a woman can be caught at alone. He was there; they saw him; and he is not standing in the temple courtyard. The law they are so eager to quote does not permit that. "If a man commits adultery with the wife of his neighbour, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death" (Lev. 20:10); "both of them shall die" (Deut. 22:22). Both. The men who open their mouths with "Moses commanded us" have already broken the commandment they are citing, in the very act of citing it, by leaving half the guilty party at home.

That single missing man tells you what this really is. They are not defending the law; they are using it, and they have chosen the defendant who is easier to drag and cheaper to spend. It is the same selective law-keeping Jesus exposed a chapter earlier, rigorous about what is convenient and silent about what is not (7:19, 23-24). It is also, in the oldest and most familiar way, a woman made to carry in public a shame that a man is quietly permitted to walk away from. Jesus never says a word about the missing man, and he does not need to. He simply declines to complete a sentence that was never being passed honestly, and in doing so he refuses to let the law of God be used as a stone in somebody else's political fight.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary: The writing on the ground is the most mysterious gesture in the gospels — John records it but not its content. The finger writing recalls God writing the law on tablets of stone (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10). Perhaps Jesus is the divine Lawgiver, pausing before he renders a verdict that will surpass Moses. The silence is itself an answer: he does not rush to judgment; he bends toward the earth, toward the dust from which both accusers and accused were formed. The one who is asked to condemn stoops first before he speaks.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary: Let him without sin cast the first stone: Jesus does not dismiss the law but applies it with perfect consistency. The law requires two witnesses (Deut. 17:6-7), and the witnesses were to cast the first stones — and they must be innocent of the same charge. Jesus does not abolish capital punishment; he exposes the pretension of those claiming the right to enforce it. Then he bends down again, writing, giving them time to reckon with their own consciences. The genius of grace is that it does not attack the accusers; it invites them to self-examination.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The departure is telling: beginning with the elders, those with the longest memories of their own sin. Wisdom and age sometimes produce humility; these men are old enough to know that they have no standing. One by one they go — no dramatic confrontation, just the quiet withdrawal of those whose conscience has been touched. Jesus is left alone with the woman: the accused and her only defender. His question — Where are they? Has no one condemned you? — is gentle, almost wondering. The trap has collapsed, and what remains is a woman, a silence, and mercy.

Neither do I condemn you: the most astonishing words in this chapter. Jesus — the only one present who actually has the right to condemn — does not. Go, and sin no more: he takes the sin seriously (he does not pretend it didn't happen) while releasing her from its penalty. This is justification: the guilt is real, the condemnation is real, and it is absorbed by the one who speaks.

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately Jesus declares himself the light of the world — the one who exposes sin (as he has just done) and illuminates the path forward. He is the light that makes both exposure and freedom possible.

The legal challenge: self-testimony is inadmissible (Deut. 19:15; John 5:31). But Jesus distinguishes his case from ordinary self-testimony: the rule applies to human witnesses whose knowledge is limited and whose bias distorts their perception. Jesus knows his origin (the eternal bosom of the Father) and his destination (return to the Father). His knowledge is comprehensive and unbiased. You do not know where I come from: their ignorance of his divine origin disqualifies them from judging the validity of his testimony. To evaluate the witness, you must first know the witness.

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: You judge according to the flesh: surface-level, appearance-based, sociologically conditioned judgment — the judgment of those who cannot see past Galilee and Joseph's workshop. Jesus' judgment is different in kind: rooted in the Father's perfect knowledge, the perspective of eternity, the vision of what is rather than what appears. And yet he came not to judge but to save; the full weight of his judgment will be laid aside until the last day. When he does judge, he judges with the Father — the Trinitarian partnership of perfect judgment that the two-witness requirement in the law was designed to approximate.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus meets the two-witness requirement on its own terms: he is the first witness (the Son testifying to his own divine origin), and the Father is the second witness (testified through the baptism, through the works, through the scriptures). The legal requirement designed to protect against false witness is satisfied at the highest possible level: the testimony of the eternal Father and the eternal Son, witnessed in history through signs and the Spirit. No legal objection to Jesus' identity holds when examined carefully; every objection reveals its own deficiency.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary: You know neither me nor my Father: the most damning verdict Jesus pronounces in this chapter. They claim to know God, to serve God, to enforce God's law — but their failure to recognize the Son is proof that they do not know the Father. Knowledge of God is not available independent of Jesus; the Father is known only through the Son he has sent. The location — the treasury, the most public area of the temple courts — underscores the boldness of the declaration. And still the divine protection holds: his hour has not come. Providence sets the boundary of human hostility.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: I am going away: the departure Jesus announces is his return to the Father through the cross. You will die in your sin: the singular — sin — points to the root sin, the fundamental unbelief that refuses the Son. Every other sin is a fruit of this root. Where I am going, you cannot come: not because the destination is physically inaccessible but because without the Son there is no way to the Father. The crowd's misreading — suicide — is darkly ironic: Jesus will indeed give his life voluntarily, but not in despair; in sovereign love, on his own timetable, for the life of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary: From below / from above: two fundamentally different orders of existence, two different epistemic starting points. They cannot recognize Jesus because they think from within the world-system that is alienated from God. Unless you believe that I am he — ego eimi, the divine Name, without predicate — you will die in your sins. The condition for escaping death-in-sin is not moral improvement but this specific belief: that Jesus is the I AM, the God of the burning bush standing in human flesh. This is the irreducible center of the gospel: not a lifestyle but a Person, not a program but a Name.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Just what I have been telling you from the beginning: Jesus does not produce a new self-identification in response to their question; he points back to everything he has been saying. The answer to 'Who are you?' is not a title but a life — the totality of his words and works constitute the answer. He has much to judge but restrains judgment in deference to the Father's timetable. What he speaks is what he has heard from the one who sent him — complete fidelity to the Father's revelation, without addition or subtraction. This is the prophet's definition: speaking what one has heard from God.
