verseByVerse.quote: They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me."
verseByVerse.commentary: When you have lifted up the Son of Man: the crucifixion will be the ultimate revelation of Jesus' identity. The cross, which they intend as destruction, will be the disclosure. Then you will know that I am he: the resurrection will confirm what the cross demonstrates — that this is the eternal Son, that his death was not defeat but sacrifice, that his authority was real and his claim was true. The crucifixion they plan as the end of his influence will be the event that makes his influence permanent and universal. God's purposes are accomplished precisely through what his enemies intend for destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him." As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: He has not left me alone: the Son's awareness of the Father's constant presence is the foundation of his peace in the midst of controversy. The secret of Jesus' composure under sustained opposition is not stoic indifference but filial certainty: the Father is always with him because he always does what pleases the Father. The perfect obedience that we could not render, he renders on our behalf. And the result of this sustained teaching: many believed in him. Even in the chapter's most contested moments, the word goes out and faith is born. The gospel cannot be ultimately suppressed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–59 — The Children of Abraham and the Great I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses those who believed him about the relationship between discipleship, truth, and freedom. The conversation escalates as Jesus challenges their claim to Abrahamic descent, exposes their murderous intent as evidence of a different father, and climaxes with the declaration 'Before Abraham was, I am' — at which point they take up stones.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage presents two competing genealogies: Abraham's children versus the devil's children. The distinguishing mark is not ethnic lineage but moral resemblance — you are of your father the devil if you do his works (lying and murder). This is not ethnic polemic but spiritual diagnosis: the unregenerate heart, whatever its ancestry, is in bondage to the father of lies. The truth that sets free (v. 32) is not philosophical insight but the person of Christ himself (v. 36). Freedom is not the absence of constraint but the liberation of the will from slavery to sin, accomplished by the Son who is himself free.
verseByVerse.examples: The stoning attempt at chapter's end is the authorities' answer to 'Before Abraham was, I am.' They understand perfectly: this is a claim to be the eternal God, the I AM of Exodus 3. They reach for stones because they reject the claim as blasphemy. For the Christian, reading this from the other side of the resurrection, this is the moment where the curtain is drawn back and the eternal Word stands visible in human flesh, claiming what was always true. The authorities stone the wrong person for the right reason — he is exactly who he says he is.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise is sequential: abide in my word → truly my disciples → know the truth → be set free. Genuine discipleship is not momentary belief but sustained abiding — remaining in the word, not just receiving it. The truth that liberates is not abstract philosophical truth but the specific truth embodied in Jesus himself (14:6: I am the truth). Freedom here is not political or social but ontological: freedom from the slavery to sin that enslaves every unregenerate heart. This is the Reformation's great rediscovery: the truth of the gospel, received by faith, produces the freedom that no law or effort can achieve.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, 'You will become free'?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary: Their denial of enslavement is historically tone-deaf (Egypt, Babylon, Assyria, current Roman occupation) and spiritually catastrophic. They have confused ethnic privilege with spiritual freedom. Jesus defines slavery precisely: everyone who practices sin — who is caught in the ongoing, habitual pattern of it — is a slave to sin. This is not occasional transgression but the condition of the unregenerate will: it cannot stop sinning any more than a slave can simply choose to leave. The slavery of sin is deeper than any political bondage because it is internal, invisible, and self-perpetuating.

verseByVerse.quote: "The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."
verseByVerse.commentary: The household metaphor: slaves can be dismissed; sons cannot be expelled. The Jews claim Abraham's household as their permanent home — but their slavery to sin marks them as servants, not sons. Only the Son — Jesus, who is the eternal Son — has the authority to manumit slaves into sons. If the Son sets you free: the conditional is an invitation, not an accusation. Freedom indeed is freedom rooted in the Son's authority, not merely granted by external circumstance. Roman citizenship could be revoked; adoption into God's family through the Son cannot be undone. The liberated slave becomes a permanent son.

verseByVerse.quote: "I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus acknowledges the ethnic lineage while distinguishing it from spiritual lineage. You seek to kill me: the murderous intent is evidence that Abraham's faith does not live in them, whatever their genealogy. My word finds no place in you — the word cannot enter where there is no room, no receptivity, no prepared soil. The two-father structure is now introduced: Jesus speaks what he has seen with his Father; they do what they have heard from their father. The contest is between two paternal influences, two sources of moral formation. The children of God hear God's word; the children of the other father do the other father's works.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Abraham is our father." Jesus said to them, "If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did."
verseByVerse.commentary: If you were Abraham's children, you would do Abraham's works: the test of spiritual parentage is moral resemblance, not genetic descent. Abraham believed God (Gen. 15:6); these men are seeking to kill the one God sent. Abraham received strangers and entertained angels (Gen. 18); these men interrogate and plot. Abraham is the father of faith; faith is not in them. Jesus' appeal is not to ethnic pride but to moral consistency: be what you claim to be. If Abraham is your father, act like Abraham. The argument is unanswerable, which is why it produces murderous rage.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are doing the works your father did." They said to him, "We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God." Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: If God were your Father, you would love me: the test of genuine love for God is love for his Son. Those who claim to love God while rejecting Jesus have not met the God they claim to love. The messianic logic is airtight: God sent Jesus; God's children recognize God's messengers; you do not recognize me; therefore God is not your Father. The claim 'We have one Father — even God' is the highest religious claim a Jew could make, and Jesus meets it with the highest possible challenge: if it is true, where is your love for me?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of what is own nature, for he is a liar and the father of lies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are of your father the devil: not an ethnic slur but a moral diagnosis. The devil's defining characteristics — murder and lying — are visible in their behavior: they seek to kill Jesus (murder) while rejecting his testimony (lying). The devil does not stand in the truth because there is no truth in him: a total description of the corruption of evil. He is the father of lies — the originator, the patron, the model. Every lie traces its genealogy back to the garden. To be of the devil's family is not a permanent condition but a description of the unregenerate heart that only the Son can liberate.

That first clause cannot be left as a single sentence, because no verse in this Gospel has been put to worse use. These words have been read from pulpits before pogroms, painted on walls, and quoted by the architects of the Holocaust as though Christ had licensed what they intended. A Christian reading John ought to know that, and ought to be able to say why it is a straight inversion of the text.

Begin with who is speaking and to whom. The speaker is a Jew, in the Jewish temple, at a Jewish feast, whose mother is a Jew and whose disciples are all Jews, and who has already said in this same Gospel that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). The Evangelist recording it is a Jew. And the audience is not a race: John tells us at verse 31 that Jesus is speaking to Jews who had believed in him, and the argument develops from there among a particular group in a particular courtyard. When John writes the Jews, he most often means the Judean authorities who had set themselves against Jesus — the same shorthand a modern writer uses in saying the palace denied it, meaning some officials and not a nation.

Then notice what kind of speech this is. A prophet of Israel rebuking the leaders of Israel is not an outsider attacking a people; it is the oldest and most Jewish thing in the Bible. Isaiah called them rulers of Sodom (Isa. 1:10). Jeremiah was hated in his own city for saying worse. Ezekiel and Amos and Hosea are relentless. Nobody has ever thought Isaiah anti-Jewish, and this is the same voice at the same work — a family quarrel conducted from inside the family, over whether the Messiah promised to that family had come.

So the man who takes these words as a weapon against Jewish people has understood nothing. He is siding against the Jewish Messiah, whose own charge here is that his hearers intend murder — and then going out to commit it himself, against his Lord's own kinsmen. The verse condemns him, not them. Paul, who felt the whole weight of this, wrote that he could wish himself accursed for the sake of his brothers according to the flesh (Rom. 9:3), and that God has not rejected his people (Rom. 11:1). That is the settled Christian mind, and anything else is an offence against the one who wept over Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Because I tell the truth, you do not believe me: the paradox of fallenness is that truth is repellent to the heart shaped by the father of lies. The unconvicted conscience and the unbelieving heart are not in logical contradiction; they are in spiritual continuity. Which one of you convicts me of sin? The challenge stands unanswered across twenty centuries: no charge of moral failure has ever been sustained against Jesus. His unimpeachable character is itself a witness to his identity. If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me? The unbelief is not rational; it is moral. They cannot bear what he says because it exposes what they are.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God." The Jews answered him, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Whoever is of God hears the words of God: spiritual perception is a function of spiritual origin. The unregenerate cannot recognize the word of God as the word of God; they lack the spiritual receptor that new birth alone creates. The accusation — Samaritan and demon-possessed — is the opponents' reductio: when the argument is lost, the attack becomes personal. A Samaritan was the worst ethnic insult available; a demon was the worst spiritual accusation. Jesus is accused of the two things he most clearly is not: impure lineage and satanic motivation. The accuser of the brethren always inverts reality.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge."
verseByVerse.commentary: I do not have a demon: the denial is calm and direct, without defensiveness. The evidence against the accusation is his entire ministry: he honors the Father, he does the Father's works, he speaks the Father's words. You dishonor me: the indictment is placed before God's judgment, not before the crowd's verdict. I do not seek my own glory: Jesus' freedom from self-promotion is the mark of his divine authenticity. The one who seeks his own glory is always suspect; the one who deflects glory to God and leaves vindication to the Judge is walking in truth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death." The Jews said to him, "Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: He will never see death: not physical immortality (the disciples will all die physically) but freedom from the second death, the death that is eternal separation from God. The word kept by faith is the life-giving power that overcomes the sting of death. Their counter-argument invokes Abraham and the prophets — the greatest of all died; how can this man promise what they could not deliver? What they do not yet understand is that Jesus will himself pass through death and shatter it from within. He can promise what no one else can promise because he is what no one else is: the resurrection and the life.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?" Jesus answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Are you greater than Abraham? — the rhetorical climax of their challenge, intended as devastating. Jesus' answer: yes, infinitely so, but not by self-proclamation. The Father glorifies him — his glory is not self-generated but bestowed by the one they call their God. The irony is complete: the God they claim as their own is the one who glorifies Jesus. To have God as your God is to honor the one God glorifies. Their claim to theism and their rejection of Jesus are in direct contradiction, which Jesus exposes not with contempt but with the calm logic of a son who knows his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: "But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad."
verseByVerse.commentary: I know him: the verb is ginosko — intimate, relational knowledge, the knowledge of the Son who has been in the Father's bosom from eternity (1:18). Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day: the great patriarch looked forward in faith — perhaps at the binding of Isaac (Gen. 22), where the ram provided was a type of the Lamb of God, or at the covenant of Genesis 15, or throughout his life of faith. He saw it and was glad: the faith of the patriarchs was not hope in the abstract but hope in Christ specifically, however dimly perceived. The saints of the Old Testament believed in the same Christ we believe in, through the promise rather than the fulfillment.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."
verseByVerse.commentary: Before Abraham was, I am: the most explicit claim to divine eternity in the gospels. The grammar is deliberately non-past-tense: not 'I was' but 'I am' — the eternal present of the one who has no beginning and no end, the I AM who spoke to Moses from the burning bush. Jesus does not merely claim to preexist Abraham (which could be said of Melchizedek as a type); he claims to exist in an entirely different mode — not temporal pre-existence but eternal, self-existent being. This is the climax of the whole chapter: the light of the world is the eternal God in human flesh, the one before whom Abraham rejoiced with anticipatory faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary: They understand perfectly. This is not persecution of a misunderstood teacher; this is the response of those who have heard the claim to be the eternal I AM and rejected it as blasphemy. They are right about the claim; they are catastrophically wrong about the conclusion. Jesus does not remain to be stoned — his hour has not come — but hides himself and departs. The temple, from which he will soon be permanently excluded by his own death, lets him go one more time. The stones aimed at him will wait until the day when the Son of Man is lifted up — and the nails will do what the stones here could not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–41 — Sight and Blindness: The Light of the World at Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus heals a man born blind on the Sabbath, triggering an extended investigation by the Pharisees. The healed man's faith deepens progressively as he defends Jesus before the authorities; the Pharisees harden in opposition. The chapter closes with Jesus declaring that those who think they see are blind, and the truly blind (humble seekers) receive sight. It is the sustained enacted parable of spiritual blindness and illumination.
verseByVerse.theology: Physical sight and spiritual sight run in parallel throughout the chapter. The man born blind is a picture of humanity in its natural state — unable to see the Light from birth, requiring an external, sovereign act to receive vision. The Pharisees, who see perfectly with physical eyes, are spiritually blind precisely because they are confident they see (v. 41). This is the paradox of total depravity and spiritual pride: the one who knows he cannot see is the one who can be given sight; the one who insists he sees will remain blind. Spiritual humility is the precondition of illumination.
verseByVerse.examples: The progression of the healed man's confession is a model of growing faith: 'the man called Jesus' (v. 11), 'a prophet' (v. 17), 'from God' (v. 33), 'Lord, I believe' and worship (v. 38). Every encounter with Jesus under pressure produces clearer confession. The Pharisees' investigation — a hostile inquisition — inadvertently drives the man deeper into faith. Opposition to the gospel, when it cannot overcome the testimony of experience, ends by casting out the witness (v. 34) — and Jesus finds the cast-out (v. 35).

verseByVerse.quote: As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. And his disciples asked him, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' question frames suffering within the retributive scheme that Job's friends also represent: suffering is punishment for specific sin. If blind from birth, either prenatal sin or parental transgression must be the cause. This is the natural theological instinct of fallen humanity — connecting suffering to guilt in a neat causal chain that makes suffering explicable and God's justice obvious. Jesus will deny the premise entirely. Not all suffering is punishment for specific sin; some suffering is the occasion for the display of God's glory — a harder theology, but one that consoles more deeply.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him. We must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That the works of God might be displayed in him: suffering reframed as stage-setting for divine glory. This is not divine cruelty but sovereign wisdom — God permits certain conditions so that his power and grace may be visibly manifest. We must work while it is day: Jesus is conscious of his limited time; the cross approaches, the night of his departure draws near. Urgency is not anxiety but faithfulness: the servant who knows his master's return is near does not coast. Every day of Jesus' ministry is a day of light that the approaching darkness makes more precious.

But a parent will read this verse differently from a commentator, and the question they bring has to be met. Did God blind a baby, and leave him blind for forty years of begging, in order to set up a miracle? Put like that it sounds intolerable, and no one should pretend otherwise. Two things need saying.

The first is that the sentence may not be doing what it appears to do in English. The Greek has no punctuation and no sentence divisions, and translators must decide where the purpose clause attaches. Read as most Bibles print it, it points backwards and explains why he was born blind. But the clause can equally be taken as beginning the next thought: neither this man nor his parents sinned — but so that the works of God might be displayed in him, we must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. On that reading Jesus is not assigning a reason for the blindness at all. He refuses the disciples' question, and then turns from cause to calling: never mind why it happened, there is work to be done here, and daylight is short. It is the same kind of decision translators face at 3:16 and at 7:38, and serious readers take it both ways.

The second is that even on the traditional reading, the verse says less than the objection assumes. It does not say God caused the blindness so that he could show off. It says the works of God will be displayed in this man — and the display, when it comes, is that Jesus gives him his sight and then goes looking for him after he has been thrown out, and gives him himself. Whatever the years cost, the man ends the chapter seeing, worshipping, and known by name to the Son of God, which is more than the men who interrogated him ever got. The question the disciples asked was about the past and it had no useful answer. The question Jesus answers is what God intends to do about it, and to that there is an answer, and it walked up the road toward a blind beggar who had not asked for anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world." Having said these things, he spit on the ground and made mud with the saliva. Then he anointed the man's eyes with the mud
verseByVerse.commentary: Mud from spittle applied to blind eyes: the method is deliberately earthy, echoing the creation of man from the dust of the ground (Gen. 2:7). Jesus the Creator is doing a new creation. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world: the declaration and the demonstration are inseparable — the healing is the proof of the claim. The incarnate Lord does not teach about light and leave the blind in darkness; he acts in light, creating sight where none existed. Doctrine and deed are always unified in Jesus: he is what he proclaims.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to him, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam" (which means Sent). So he went and washed and came back seeing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The pool of Siloam — whose name means Sent — points to Jesus himself, the one Sent by the Father. The healing requires obedient action on the man's part: go, wash. Not faith declared but faith enacted. He goes in obedience and returns seeing. The sovereign grace that created the condition for sight works through the means of ordinary obedient action. This is the pattern of the gospel: grace precedes response, but response is real. The man did not heal himself; he received healing through the obedience that faith produces.

verseByVerse.quote: The neighbors and those who had seen him before as a beggar were saying, "Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?" Some said, "It is he." Others said, "No, but he is like him." He kept saying, "I am the man."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the man: the healed man's repeated insistence on his own identity is both comic and theologically charged. He uses the same ego eimi construction as Jesus — I am — to assert continuity of identity. Transformation produces disbelief in observers; people cannot update their categories fast enough to accommodate genuine miracle. The community wants to slot the healed man into their existing grid (he must be someone else) rather than revise the grid. This is the first moment of the chapter's running conflict: the evidence is clear, but interpretation is governed by prior commitment.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then how were your eyes opened?" He answered, "The man called Jesus made mud and anointed my eyes and said to me, 'Go to Siloam and wash.' So I went and washed and received my sight."
verseByVerse.commentary: The man called Jesus: this is the first stage of confessional development — he knows the name but not yet the full identity. His testimony is precise and factual: mud, anointing, command, obedience, sight. He does not speculate about what it means; he reports what happened. This is the irreducible foundation of Christian witness: I was blind, now I see. The argument from experience is not sufficient on its own, but it is not nothing — it is the testimony that drives the investigation, produces the inquisition, and eventually leads to the fullest confession. Experience plus teaching equals mature faith.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is he?" He said, "I do not know." They brought to the Pharisees the man who had formerly been blind.
verseByVerse.commentary: He does not know where Jesus is — and this limited knowledge becomes the occasion for the investigation that will deepen his faith. The neighbors bring him to the Pharisees: the appropriate religious authorities who must evaluate any claimed miracle. What begins as responsible referral will become hostile interrogation. The Pharisees' investigation is not disinterested inquiry but institutional self-protection: if the miracle is real, it validates Jesus' authority, which threatens theirs. The question is not really 'Did the miracle happen?' but 'Can we afford to admit it happened?'

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was a Sabbath day when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. So the Pharisees again asked him how he had received his sight. And he said to them, "He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Sabbath detail: making mud (labor) and performing a healing (medical work) both fell under rabbinic Sabbath restrictions. The miracle is legally problematic for the authorities before it is even examined for its reality. The man's answer to the Pharisees is even shorter than to his neighbors — mud, wash, see — three words. He is learning what is essential. Under interrogation, the irreducible testimony becomes more concentrated: something happened, Jesus did it, I can see. The simplicity is its own form of power; it cannot be argued away because it is just the facts.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of the Pharisees said, "This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath." But others said, "How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?" There was a division among them. So they said again to the blind man, "What do you say about him, since he opened your eyes?" He said, "He is a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary: Division among the Pharisees: the evidence is forcing a split. The Sabbath-violation party has decided in advance; the sign-evidence party is following the evidence. The man's confession escalates: from 'the man called Jesus' to 'a prophet.' He is thinking out loud, pressed by the question, and concluding from the evidence that whoever opened congenitally blind eyes must have God-given authority. The prophets healed; therefore this is a prophet. It is not yet the fullest confession, but it is faith growing under pressure — the characteristic mark of authentic spiritual life.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews did not believe that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of the man who had received his sight and asked them, "Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Unable to dismiss the healed man's testimony, the Pharisees call his parents — hoping to find a conspiracy, a fraud, an explanation that doesn't require acknowledging the miracle. Is this your son, who you say was born blind? The question implies suspicion: perhaps the blindness was not real. This is the investigative logic of institutional unbelief: when the evidence is overwhelming, seek the flaw in the witnesses. The parents are summoned to testify about their own child's congenital blindness — evidence no court could reasonably dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: His parents answered, "We know that this is our son and that he was born blind. But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary: The parents confirm the essential facts: this is their son, he was born blind. But they will not say more, because they know what acknowledgment costs. Ask him — the deflection to their adult son is both pragmatically safe and morally evasive. They will not lie, but they will not testify fully. Their fear of the synagogue is a miniature portrait of the cowardly faith that believes but will not confess (12:42-43). To know the truth and decline to speak it under pressure is not neutral; it is the beginning of a capitulation that ends in denial.

verseByVerse.quote: His parents said these things because they feared the Jews, for the Jews had already agreed that if anyone should confess Jesus to be Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, "He is of age; ask him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Put out of the synagogue: excommunication, the social death of first-century Jewish community life. Loss of the synagogue meant loss of neighborhood, commerce, festival, and identity. The fear of social consequence is the most effective suppressor of public faith in every generation. The parents choose social safety over testimony — a choice that the gospel repeatedly presents as fatal to authentic discipleship. The son will make the opposite choice (v. 34-38) and discover that being cast out by human authority is the occasion for finding the one who sought him out.

verseByVerse.quote: So for the second time they called the man who had been blind and said to him, "Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner." The man answered, "Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see."
verseByVerse.commentary: One thing I do know: one of the great testimonies of Christian experience. He cannot argue theology with Pharisees; he cannot resolve the Sabbath debate; he cannot explain the ontology of the miracle. But he knows what happened to him, and that knowledge is unassailable. This is the irreducible core of Christian witness: personal transformation, before and after, whatever the sophisticated objections. Whether Jesus is a sinner, the man wisely declines to judge. What he will not decline is his testimony. The simplest confession, rooted in personal experience of grace, outduels all the institutional scholarship that has decided its verdict in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?" He answered them, "I have told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The man's growing boldness: he is no longer intimidated. I have told you already — his exasperation is entirely legitimate. And then the counterattack: Do you also want to become his disciples? The 'also' implies that he has already decided for himself. The question is either the boldest piece of evangelism in the chapter or the sharpest irony — addressed to men who have already decided against Jesus. Under pressure, authentic faith does not retreat; it advances. The man who began as a passive recipient of miracle has become an active witness who pushes back against his interrogators.

verseByVerse.quote: And they reviled him, saying, "You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses. We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary: Disciples of Moses: the contrast is intended to be shaming. They plant their flag on the authority they know — Moses, the law, the Sinai covenant — while dismissing Jesus as an unknown quantity. But as Jesus argued in 5:46-47, Moses wrote about Jesus; to be a true disciple of Moses is to come to Jesus. Their pride in Mosaic discipleship while rejecting the one Moses foretold is self-refuting. We do not know where he comes from: they repeat the objection of 7:27, unaware that 'where he comes from' is exactly the point — he comes from the Father, which is why his works are beyond human explanation.

verseByVerse.quote: The man answered, "Why, this is an amazing thing! You do not know where he comes from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why, this is an amazing thing! The healed man turns the Pharisees' argument on its head: you claim not to know where he comes from, but God has clearly acted through him — therefore your theological premise must be wrong. His reasoning is sound: God does not attend to sinners (Ps. 66:18), but God has attended to Jesus in an unmistakable way. Therefore Jesus cannot be a sinner. The man is now doing theology out loud, and doing it better than his interrogators. The wisdom God gives to the humble confounds the wisdom of the self-confident learned.

One sentence in his argument needs a guard, because lifted out of this courtyard it has frightened people badly: "God does not listen to sinners." Read flatly, as a rule about prayer, it shuts the door on every person who most needs it open. And it is worth being clear about what these words are. They are the healed man's, not a formula handed down from heaven. Scripture reports his reasoning faithfully and his reasoning serves him well here, but he is a new believer arguing from the common piety of his day, and what he says is a proverb about God's dealings, not a doctrine of access.

Even the psalm behind it says something narrower than the bare sentence. "If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened" (Ps. 66:18) — the word is cherished. What closes God's ear is not the presence of sin in a man but his fondness for it: the person who hugs his sin and simultaneously demands God's help. That is a different thing altogether from a sinner crying out for mercy.

And the plainest refutation of the flat reading is a story Jesus himself told. A tax collector stood far off, would not lift his eyes, beat his breast and prayed, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner" — and Jesus said that man went home justified (Luke 18:13-14). God listened to a sinner, in the very act of being one, at the precise moment he called himself one. So if you have been afraid that your sin has stopped God's ears, notice which way the fear runs. The man whose sin has closed God's ear is not troubled about it. The trouble you feel is not the evidence that he has stopped listening; it is very often the first evidence that he has already begun to work.

verseByVerse.quote: "Never since the world began has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological argument reaches its climax: congenital blindness healed is unprecedented in human history (it exceeds even the healings of Elijah and Elisha). The inference is airtight: only the power of God can do what has never been done. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing — a conclusion that the Pharisees cannot answer because it is logically sound and evidentiary. The healed man has moved from 'I do not know' in verse 25 to 'This man is from God' in verse 33. His faith has been refined under fire into a clear theological confession.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "You were born in utter sin, and would you teach us?" And they cast him out. Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
verseByVerse.commentary: They cast him out — excommunication, the social death his parents feared and he did not flinch from. And immediately: Jesus heard and found him. The one cast out by human institutions is sought by the Son of Man. This is the gospel pattern: the world's rejection is the occasion for Christ's pursuit. He does not wait for the man to seek him; he seeks the man. Do you believe in the Son of Man? — the question is both a test and an invitation to a fuller confession than anything the man has yet made. Jesus brings the investigation to its proper conclusion: not the Pharisees' verdict, but faith.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "And who is he, sir, that I may believe in him?" Jesus said to him, "You have seen him, and it is he who is speaking to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Who is he, that I may believe? — the perfect posture of receptive faith: I want to believe; tell me the object. The man does not resist the call; he asks for clarity. You have seen him: the irony is exquisite — the man born blind, who has just been given physical sight, has now seen the one in whom he is to believe. And it is he who is speaking to you: the same revelation formula as John 4:26 to the Samaritan woman. Jesus identifies himself directly to those whose hearts are prepared to receive the disclosure. The one who sought the cast-out finds him and reveals himself.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary: Lord, I believe — and he worshiped: the progression of the entire chapter compressed into three words and one action. He began knowing only a name; he ends in worship of the Lord. For judgment I came: not as the primary purpose (3:17) but as the inevitable consequence. The light that illuminates also exposes. The coming of Christ produces a division: those who acknowledge their blindness receive sight; those who insist on their sight are confirmed in blindness. The judgment is not imposed from outside but revealed from within: every person's response to Jesus is the disclosure of what their heart truly is.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary: If you were blind, you would have no guilt: if they lacked the light entirely, their rejection would be excusable. But they have had the light — Torah, temple, prophets, and now Jesus himself — and they have chosen not to see. Culpable blindness is the blindness of those who could see but will not. Your guilt remains: the word used for sin remaining is the same as John 20:23 for sins retained in judgment. The Pharisees' confident self-assessment — We see — is the very thing that seals their blindness. The only cure for this blindness is the humility that admits it, and that admission is itself a work of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Using the extended metaphor of shepherd, sheep, sheepfold, and hired hand, Jesus declares himself the door and the good shepherd. The discourse is addressed to the Pharisees who have just cast out the healed man (9:34), contrasting the true shepherd who lays down his life with the thieves, robbers, and hired hands who exploit or abandon the flock. The chapter's first half closes with another division among the crowd.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd imagery draws on the entire Old Testament tradition: God as shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34), the coming Davidic shepherd-king (Ezek. 34:23-24; Jer. 23:4), and the contrast between true and false shepherds throughout the prophets. Jesus claims all of these simultaneously: he is the door (the only legitimate access to God), the good shepherd (who gives rather than takes), and the one who lays down his life voluntarily (the self-giving that no hired hand would perform). The death is central: the shepherd metaphor cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice: the recognition of Christ by the elect is not achievement but gift. The sheep do not learn to recognize the shepherd's voice; they already know it because they are his sheep. This is Calvinist soteriology rendered in pastoral imagery: election precedes hearing, calling brings the elect home, and not one of the Father's sheep is lost. The Pharisees cannot hear because they are not sheep (v. 26); the church hears because she has been given ears by the Shepherd himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary: The sheepfold image would be immediately intelligible to a Palestinian audience: a stone enclosure where sheep were kept overnight, with a single door guarded by a doorkeeper or by the shepherd himself. Climbing in another way — avoiding the door — marks the thief. This verse indicts all who claim to speak for God while bypassing the appointed way of covenant authority: false prophets, self-appointed teachers, religious entrepreneurs who exploit rather than serve. Legitimate authority follows legitimate entry; the shepherd comes through the door because the door belongs to him by right.

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary: He calls his own sheep by name: not anonymous management of a herd but personal, individual knowledge. The shepherd knows each sheep with the intimacy that names express — this is the pastoral counterpart to the Father's knowing of the elect by name before the foundation of the world. He goes before them: the shepherd does not drive the sheep from behind but leads from the front, walking into the danger first. The sheep follow because they know his voice — a knowledge that is not acquired skill but Spirit-given recognition, the 'hearing' that is the mark of the elect throughout this discourse.

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sheep discern voices — a spiritual discernment that protects from counterfeit shepherds. The stranger's voice does not ring true to ears tuned to the true shepherd. This is the practical function of the doctrine of Scripture: the sheep who know the Shepherd's voice in the written word can recognize when preachers contradict it. They did not understand: the Pharisees, who have just cast out the man who heard and followed Jesus, cannot grasp the parable that explains their own spiritual condition. They are not sheep; they are the strangers from whom the sheep flee.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the door: the second great I AM of the chapter, and a different metaphor from the shepherd — now Jesus is the access point itself. The only legitimate entry into the sheepfold (the community of God's people, eternal life, the Father) is through Jesus. All who came before me as thieves: not the prophets (who all pointed forward to Jesus) but the false messianic pretenders and exploitative religious leaders who used spiritual authority for personal gain. The sheep's spiritual instinct protected them from these — the elect are not ultimately deceived by counterfeits.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary: I came that they may have life and have it abundantly: one of the great statements of the gospel's positive purpose. The contrast with the thief's agenda — steal, kill, destroy — defines what the enemy does to human souls and what the Shepherd came to undo. Abundant life is not prosperity-gospel plenty but the fullness of the life of God, the comprehensive shalom of the covenant that includes forgiveness, relationship, purpose, community, and the hope of resurrection. This is the positive side of the atonement: not merely rescue from death but gift of life, not merely pardon but adoption, not merely forgiveness but inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The good shepherd lays down his life: the defining act that distinguishes the good shepherd from every imitation. The hired hand's failure is rooted in ownership: he does not own the sheep, so their loss is not his loss. The good shepherd owns the sheep — they are his, given to him by the Father (v. 29) — and therefore their safety is his personal concern. He will not flee because he cannot abandon what is his. The cross is not an external imposition on Jesus but the voluntary act of the owner who would rather die than lose one of his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary: I know my own and my own know me: the mutual knowledge that defines the covenant relationship between Christ and his people. The Greek verb ginosko carries the weight of intimate, personal, relational knowledge — the knowledge of a shepherd who knows each sheep by name, and of sheep who have learned to distinguish the true voice from all others. This mutual knowing is patterned on (v. 15) the mutual knowing of the Father and Son: the intimacy within the Trinity becomes the model for the intimacy between Christ and the church. The sheep know the Shepherd because the Shepherd first knew them.

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary: Other sheep not of this fold: the Gentile mission announced in advance by the Shepherd himself. The boundary of Israel was never God's final boundary; from Abraham the promise was always 'in you all the nations will be blessed.' One flock, one shepherd: the eschatological unity of the people of God across every ethnic, linguistic, and national boundary. There will be no Jewish church and Gentile church, no first-class and second-class disciples — one flock under one Shepherd. This is the vision the book of Acts describes and the book of Revelation celebrates.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary: No one takes it from me: the most explicit statement of the voluntary nature of the atonement. The enemies who arrest, try, and crucify Jesus are not the cause of his death; they are the instruments through which his own sovereign self-giving operates. He has authority to lay down and take up his life — a double authority that no human being possesses. The resurrection is not rescue from an unexpected catastrophe; it is the second act of the same sovereign will that freely laid down its life. The Father's love for the Son is expressed in this very willingness: the Son who lays down and takes up his life perfectly fulfills the Father's redemptive will.

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Division again — the invariable result of Jesus' presence. The anti-party reaches for the stock accusation: demon, madness. This is how the fallen mind processes a claim that exceeds its categories: rather than revise the categories, dismiss the claimant as irrational or diabolical. The words of Jesus are either the sanest words ever spoken or the words of a lunatic or a liar — C.S. Lewis's trilemma applies here exactly. The crowd that says "why listen to him?" has made a choice, but it is not a neutral one; it is the choice of those who prefer their current darkness to the disruptive light.

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of someone who is demon-possessed. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The pro-party has an argument that cannot be answered: demonic power does not heal, it destroys. The opening of congenitally blind eyes is the work of the Creator, not the Adversary. Every authentic healing Jesus performs is an argument against the demonic-attribution hypothesis. The miracle of chapter 9 continues to exercise its evidential weight into chapter 10: healed eyes are facts that persist beyond the controversy they generated. The crowd's question — Can a demon do this? — is rhetorical, but it is also the right question. The answer, which the opposition cannot provide, is no.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), the Jews press Jesus for a direct statement: 'Are you the Christ?' Jesus answers by reference to his works and his relationship with the Father, declares 'I and the Father are one,' and survives another stoning attempt. He then withdraws beyond the Jordan where many believe in him.
verseByVerse.theology: The climactic declaration — I and the Father are one — is the theological summit of the Good Shepherd discourse and of John's presentation of Jesus' identity in the public ministry. The unity is not merely unity of purpose (though it includes that) but ontological unity — the unity of shared divine nature that the Jews correctly understand as a claim to deity (v. 33). Jesus defends the claim not by retreating from it but by appealing to the greater logic: if Scripture can call judges 'gods,' how much more can the one the Father consecrated and sent be called the Son of God? The defense is not a reduction of the claim but an escalation of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Beyond the Jordan, many believe on the basis of John's testimony confirmed by Jesus' works. This is the pattern of fruitful ministry: the faithful witness of the forerunner, confirmed by the reality of the one the forerunner announced, produces lasting faith. The chapter ends not in Jerusalem with hostility but in the wilderness with harvest — a reminder that the gospel often bears its richest fruit outside the centers of established religion.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Feast of Dedication — Hanukkah — commemorated the Maccabean rededication of the temple in 164 BC after Antiochus Epiphanes IV had desecrated it by sacrificing a pig on the altar and erecting a statue of Zeus. When the Maccabees recaptured and cleansed the temple, they found only one cruse of ritually pure olive oil — enough to keep the great seven-branched menorah burning for a single day. According to the Talmud (Shabbat 21b), that oil burned miraculously for eight days — exactly the time needed to prepare a fresh supply of consecrated oil. This is why Hanukkah became specifically known as the Festival of Lights and is observed with the kindling of eight candles over eight nights. Solomon's Colonnade, where Jesus is walking, was a covered portico on the east side of the temple mount, sheltered from the winter cold. John's contextual irony is precise: the Light of the world (8:12) is walking through the temple precincts during the Festival of Lights — the festival celebrating oil that burned beyond all natural supply. Jesus is the inexhaustible light the Hanukkah menorah pointed to: his light comes not from a cruse of oil that might run dry but from the eternal life of the Father. He is himself the true temple (2:21), the true rededication of the sacred to God, the light that the darkness has never overcome (1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Tell us plainly: the demand for a straight answer, which sounds reasonable, is actually a demand for a confession they can use as a charge. They want a 'yes' they can bring to the authorities as blasphemy. Jesus' answer — I told you, and you do not believe — is not evasion but exposure: the problem is not insufficient information but the refusal of what has already been given. The works bear witness: the evidential trail is complete. More words will not produce belief where the works have not; the issue is not the adequacy of the evidence but the disposition of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary: You do not believe because you are not among my sheep: the most explicit statement of the election-before-faith sequence in the gospel. They are not lacking faith because they have not yet heard; they cannot hear because they are not sheep. The capacity to recognize the Shepherd's voice is not a universal human faculty but a Spirit-given gift to those who are the Father's gift to the Son. This is not fatalism but the pastoral realism of grace: the Shepherd knows his own; the question for every hearer is whether the voice of Jesus is recognizable — whether the Spirit has been given to open the ears.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: The double security of the believer: held in the Son's hand and in the Father's hand simultaneously. No one can snatch them: the passive is universal — no force, human or demonic, external or internal, can remove the sheep from this double grip. The security is not the sheep's grip on the Shepherd but the Shepherd's grip on the sheep. This is the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints stated with maximum simplicity: they persevere because they are preserved, and they are preserved because the one who holds them is greater than all. No sheep the Father gave to the Son has ever been lost, and none ever will be.

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I and the Father are one: seven words that contain the christological center of the fourth gospel. The unity is not merely ethical (we agree on all things) but ontological (we share the one divine nature). The Jews understand this immediately: they reach for stones. They are not misreading him. They correctly hear a claim to divine equality and respond with the law's penalty for blasphemy (Lev. 24:16). For the Christian reading this passage on the other side of Nicaea and Chalcedon, this verse is the scriptural anchor for the Trinitarian theology that the church has confessed since: one God in three persons, the Father and Son of one substance.

There is a detail in the Greek here that settles two errors at once, and it is worth having, because both are still met today. The word for one is neuter — one thing, not one person. Had Jesus wanted to say that he and the Father are a single person he had the masculine form available and did not use it. So the sentence will not carry the reading of those who say the Father and the Son are merely two names for one individual, a view the early church met in Sabellius and which is taught today by Oneness Pentecostalism: John has just told us the Word was with God, and you cannot be with yourself. And it will not carry the opposite reduction either, the one the Jehovah's Witnesses press, that this is only unity of purpose, two wills agreeing — because the men listening did not hear a claim about agreement, and men do not pick up stones over a shared policy. They tell us themselves what they heard, two verses on: you, being a man, make yourself God.

One thing, not one person: distinct, and undivided. That is precisely what the church later put into the creeds, and it was not an invention of the fourth century. It was already sitting in the grammar of a sentence spoken in a temple colonnade in winter, by a man about to be stoned for saying it.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary: You, being a man, make yourself God: their charge is accurate and their penalty is specified in the law. What they cannot accept is the claim's truth. Jesus inverts the accusation: he is not a man claiming to be God but God who has become man — the direction is opposite. The stoning attempt for blasphemy is the legal mechanism by which the crucifixion will eventually operate: the charge at the trial will be the same (19:7). The authorities are building their case; Jesus is allowing them time to demonstrate the depth of their rejection. Every move toward the cross is simultaneously a move toward the resurrection that vindicates every claim they deny.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument from Psalm 82:6 — where judges are called "gods" because they exercise divine authority in God's name — operates a fortiori: if derivative, functional divine language can be applied to human judges by Scripture, the Scripture's own authority is the foundation (Scripture cannot be broken). Jesus uses the text against those who claim to honor it, demonstrating that their outrage is selective: they accept the language when applied to human judges but reject it when applied to the one the Father actually consecrated. The inerrancy of Scripture is here the fulcrum of the argument.

Few verses in the Bible have been wrenched further from their meaning than this one. "Ye are gods" is quoted by Mormonism to teach that faithful men and women may themselves become gods, and by the prosperity and Word-of-Faith teachers to tell congregations that they are "little gods" with the creative power of deity in their mouths. Anyone who has had that verse quoted at him on a doorstep deserves to know what the psalm actually says.

So read the whole of Psalm 82, which takes about a minute. God stands up in the assembly and puts the "gods" on trial. They judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked (v. 2); they will not defend the weak, the fatherless, the afflicted and destitute (vv. 3-4); they walk about in darkness and the foundations of the earth are shaken by their misrule (v. 5). And then the sentence falls in verse 7: "nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any one of the princes." That is the psalm. It calls them gods and then condemns them to death precisely because they are not. The word is a title of office — men entrusted with God's own authority to judge — and the entire point of the psalm is to strip it off them. To quote it as a promise of divinity is to quote the indictment and mistake it for the reward.

Nor is Jesus lowering himself here to the level of a judge. His argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if Scripture can use that word even of corrupt magistrates, the charge of blasphemy against the one the Father consecrated and sent collapses. And notice that his hearers did not take it as a retreat — they do not put the stones down; they try again to arrest him (v. 39). The claim of verse 30 stands undiminished.

The rest of Scripture allows no other reading: "before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me" (Isa. 43:10); "I am the LORD, and there is no other" (Isa. 45:5). The line between Creator and creature is never crossed by promotion. What we are actually promised is better than the counterfeit and different in kind: not deity by nature but adoption by grace, and a likeness that is real — "we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is" (1 John 3:2). Sons, not gods. The offer of godhood was first made in a garden by someone else, and it has never once been kept.

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Consecrated and sent: the two verbs define the Son's relationship to the Father in the mission of redemption. Consecrated — set apart, as the high priest was set apart, as the temple was set apart — points to eternal election. Sent — commissioned into the world — points to the incarnation. How can the one the Father himself consecrated and sent blaspheme by claiming the status that the consecration and sending confer? The charge of blasphemy assumes that Jesus is claiming unauthorized status; Jesus' defense is that the authorization is the most complete possible: the Father himself. The argument is unanswerable on its own terms.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary: Believe the works: Jesus offers an empirical test — evaluate the works against the claim. If the claim is false, the works should not be possible. The works are themselves arguments for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son: that the Father is in me and I am in the Father. The mutual indwelling (perichoresis in later Trinitarian theology) is the inner-Trinitarian reality that produces the Son's works in the world. You cannot believe me, then believe the works — an act of gracious condescension: use whatever entry point you can find, just come to the truth. Jesus meets each person's capacity for faith wherever it begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary: He escaped from their hands: not by miraculous teleportation but by the sovereign timing of the Father — the hour has not come. Jesus withdraws to the place of John's ministry at the beginning — the Jordan crossing, the threshold space — and remains there. The geography is retreat for renewal, not defeat. The ministry that began in public proclamation in Jerusalem will end in Jerusalem, but between the controversies Jesus withdraws to the places of beginning. Every sustained ministry requires times of withdrawal from the center of conflict to the places where the work first started and faith is simpler.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary: Everything John said about this man was true: the Baptist's ministry, concluded years before, is now being vindicated by the people who heard it and now see its fulfillment. John did no sign — his witness was entirely verbal and confessional — but his words were accurate. Faithful verbal witness, even without miraculous confirmation, produces durable fruit. The people of the Jordan region believed Jesus not on the basis of signs alone but on the confirmed truth of John's testimony. Many believed there — outside Jerusalem, in the wilderness, among the people John had baptized. The harvest that Jerusalem refused, the margins received.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The raising of Lazarus is the climactic sign of the fourth gospel, the seventh and greatest miracle, the one that crystallizes both faith (Mary, Martha, the disciples) and murderous opposition (the Sanhedrin's decision to kill Jesus, v. 53). Jesus allows a two-day delay that ensures Lazarus is undeniably dead before he arrives, then raises him with a word — a sign so overwhelming that it forces a decision: believe or destroy.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is a preview of Jesus' own resurrection and, through his, the resurrection of all who are in him. I am the resurrection and the life (v. 25) is not merely a claim about what Jesus can do but about what he is: the source and substance of resurrection-life, the one in whom the age-to-come has already broken into the present. Those who believe in him will never die — not because they avoid physical death but because they have already passed from death to life (5:24). Lazarus' resurrection is the bodily demonstration of what Jesus gives spiritually to every believer.
verseByVerse.examples: The weeping of Jesus (vv. 33-35) is one of the most theologically dense moments in the gospel: the one who knows he is about to raise Lazarus weeps with those who grieve. His tears are not ignorance of the outcome but solidarity with human grief, genuine compassion that does not remove itself from suffering even when it is about to overcome suffering. This is the incarnation at its most moving: God in the flesh does not observe human sorrow from a distance; he enters it, feels it, and weeps in it — before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary: Lazarus of Bethany: a specific person, known by name, in a specific village with known sisters. The incarnation insists on particularity — grace comes to specific people in specific places with specific stories. John identifies Mary by her anointing of Jesus (12:3), proleptic identification that ties the death of Lazarus to the anointing that anticipates Jesus' own burial. The beloved family is introduced under the shadow of illness: love and suffering are inseparable in the world the gospel addresses, and Jesus' response to both will define his character and his mission.

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." When Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It leads to the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary: He whom you love is ill: the appeal is to relationship, not formula. They do not ask for a specific outcome; they simply report the need to the one who loves. This is the perfect model of prayer: bringing the need to the one who cares, without prescribing the solution. This illness does not lead to death: not a denial that Lazarus will die (he will) but a statement about the final destination — the glory of God, not death. Every suffering that the sovereign Lord oversees has a destination beyond itself. The illness leads not to the last word of death but to the first word of resurrection glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary: So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days: the conjunction 'so' (oun) is the most startling word in the verse. Because Jesus loved them, he stayed. Divine love does not always look like immediate response; sometimes it looks like deliberate delay that serves a deeper purpose. The two-day delay ensures that Lazarus will be four days dead before Jesus arrives (v. 39) — beyond any possibility of natural resuscitation. The delay is the setup for the greatest sign. Love that seems absent is often love preparing the most magnificent display of itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Let us go to Judea: the disciples immediately recall the stoning attempt of 10:31. The journey to Lazarus is simultaneously the journey toward the cross; Bethany is two miles from Jerusalem, and this return trip will set in motion the events that lead to Calvary. The disciples' concern is rational — the last visit to Judea nearly ended in stoning. Jesus' answer will frame the decision in terms of day and night, of the Father's appointed time. He does not deny the danger; he places the danger within the larger framework of sovereign timing that makes the danger, in the end, no threat at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Twelve hours of daylight: the appointed time for work and walking. Jesus operates within the day the Father has given him — while the light lasts, while his hour is not yet come. The one who walks in the day does not stumble; the one who walks in the night does. Jesus is the light of the world; walking in his presence is walking in the light that eliminates stumbling. For the disciples, following Jesus to Judea is not reckless courage but light-directed obedience: the Light is going; following the Light is the safest path, however dangerous it looks by the world's reckoning.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary: Fallen asleep: Jesus uses the language of sleep for death — not euphemism but theological claim. Death for those who are in Christ is sleep, a temporary rest from which they will be awakened. The disciples hear literally and respond literally: good, then he'll recover on his own, no need to risk Judea. They consistently read the physical level of Jesus' speech and miss the spiritual. This is not stupidity but the characteristic failure of those who have not yet been illuminated by the Spirit: the natural mind cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. So Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus told them plainly: when the metaphor fails, he speaks directly. Lazarus has died. The plain speech is harder than the metaphor; death is death, and the disciples must face it without softening. Jesus does not protect his followers from the hard truths but waits until they are necessary and then speaks them clearly. The move from metaphor to plain speech is also a move toward the disciples' deeper understanding — and toward the journey that will demonstrate what plainly-stated death means in the hands of the resurrection and the life.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary: For your sake I am glad: the delay that seemed like absence was actually for the disciples' benefit — to produce a faith deeper than what a bedside healing could generate. Thomas's response — let us go and die with him — is part loyalty and part fatalism: he expects the Jerusalem visit to end in execution. His courage, however tinged with despair, is real. He will go. This is imperfect faith at its best: uncertain of the outcome, fearful of the cost, but following anyway. Jesus does not wait for perfect faith before accepting it; he works with what is offered and refines it along the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four days in the tomb: the rabbinical tradition held that the soul departed the body after three days (when decomposition became visible). Four days removes every possibility of natural resuscitation; Lazarus is undeniably, irrevocably dead. The proximity to Jerusalem — two miles — ensures that the miracle will be public and will reach the authorities immediately. The raising of Lazarus is not performed in private; it happens in the full view of mourning Jerusalem, with witnesses from the city present (v. 31, 45). The sign cannot be hidden; it is designed to force a decision.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, while Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary: The two sisters respond characteristically: Martha goes out to meet Jesus (active, confrontational in the best sense), while Mary remains in the house (contemplative, weighted with grief). Neither response is wrong; both will receive what they need. The crowd of mourners from Jerusalem will become witnesses to the greatest sign — providentially gathered for consolation, they will see resurrection. Human mourning becomes the context for divine glory. God uses our ordinary responses to grief as the occasion for his extraordinary self-disclosure.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Lord, if you had been here: the grief-inflected if is not accusation but confession of faith in his power. Martha believes Jesus could have prevented the death; she does not understand yet that he can undo it. But even now: the qualifying phrase that opens the door to something more. She does not know what she is asking for, but her 'even now' expresses a faith in Jesus' ongoing relationship with God that goes beyond the specific request. This is intercessory faith in its early form: more than human comfort can provide, less than resurrection expectation — but oriented in the right direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary: Your brother will rise again: Jesus' promise is deliberately ambiguous, and Martha hears it in the most conventional sense: the general resurrection at the end of history. Her theology is correct and orthodox — the Pharisaic resurrection hope. But Jesus is about to collapse the eschatological future into the present: not the last day but today, not the general resurrection but a specific resurrection that prefigures and guarantees the general one. Martha's faith is real but limited to the categories she has. Jesus is about to expand those categories beyond anything she can imagine.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the resurrection and the life: not 'I will bring resurrection' or 'I teach about resurrection' but I am — the resurrection is located in his person, not in a future event. The fifth great I AM saying of the gospel is its most comprehensive claim: he is the source and substance of all resurrection-life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live: physical death cannot terminate the life received from Jesus. Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die: spiritual death has no power over those who are in him. Do you believe this? — the question presses every listener to personal decision. Christology is always invitation.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha's confession — Christ, Son of God, the one coming into the world — is the gospel's full christological formula. The Evangelist has been building to exactly this throughout the book (20:31). Like Peter's confession (Matt. 16:16), Martha's confession is elicited by Jesus' own question and goes beyond what she can yet fully comprehend.
